Sports.title: What do England do with Bethell for Australia ODIs?
Sports.content:
England have a top-order dilemma. Albeit, one of the 'good problem to have' variety.

Though still ranked a lowly eighth in the world in the 50-over format, and with the 2027 Cricket World Cup in Africa less than a year away, England's ODI cricket has largely been trending in the right direction this year until their tri-series troubles in Pakistan in October.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player After England's closing ODI tri-series victory over Sri Lanka, Brendon McCullum discussed his side's performances throughout the series

The team appears to be a settled one as they steel themselves for a three-match series against Australia - with five T20s to follow - but for the decision as to who opens the batting come the opening match in Perth on Friday.

Will it continue to be Ben Duckett and Tom Banton? Or will the fit-again Jacob Bethell come straight back into the side?

Do England stick with status quo?

Bethell has long been earmarked as England's future, with a magnificent maiden hundred in an ODI win over South Africa to close the 2025 summer swiftly followed by further tons in the fifth Ashes Test in Sydney and the 2026 T20 World Cup semi-final against India.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at the best bits from Jacob Bethell's first professional century during the final ODI of the 2025 summer between England and South Africa

England moved him up to open for the ODI series against India in the summer, which he then capped with a fine 91 off 93 balls as part of a magnificent 192-run opening stand with Duckett that helped the hosts clinch the series.

England's top two locked in foreseeable. Or perhaps not…

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jacob Bethell scored his first half-century as an ODI opener with an excellent 91 from 93 balls against India at Lord's this summer

A knee injury has sidelined Bethell since, granting Banton an opportunity, which he has seized with both hands.

The 27-year-old has averaged 56.28 in his seven innings since as opener, cracking four fifties and a magnificent 126 off 105 balls against Sri Lanka at The Oval.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch every boundary from Tom Banton as he scored his maiden ODI hundred for England against Sri Lanka at The Oval

He and Duckett are averaging 71 together as a partnership, with the latter signing off the tri-series with back-to-back hundreds, making that three in his last eight ODIs.

As such, there's absolutely no chance of Duckett being dropped. But what about Banton?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look at the best bits from Ben Duckett's hugely impressive 167 against Sri Lanka during the ODI tri-series in Pakistan

It might well be the case that he's afforded another go and Bethell doesn't come straight back in. He didn't play in the warm-up match against Western Australia at the weekend, if that is any indication, with Duckett (59) and Banton (14) once more leading the side out.

Who else could Bethell return for?

While Bethell might not dislodge Banton at the top of the order, that doesn't necessarily mean he won't feature in Australia.

Jos Buttler is sitting out the tour with a hamstring injury, with Jordan Cox - whose talents England appear desperate to find a more regular space in the side for - currently slated to earn that middle-order berth and don the gloves.

Image: Jordan Cox averages 23.57 across his eight ODI caps for England so far, scoring one half-century

However, Cox didn't hugely grasp his opportunity in Pakistan, returning a top score of 43 from four matches - albeit he wasn't required with the bat in one of them.

The selectors could choose to drop Cox, make Banton keep wicket and bring Bethell back in this way, especially seeing as he would provide a helpful left-handed option in among the run of righties from Joe Root down.

Sam Curran, at No 6 or 7, is currently the only exception, so the addition of Bethell would allow for greater flexibility in the batting lineup as well as give opposing captain Mitch Marsh one or two more headaches in terms of managing his field placings.

It would also allow England to kick the Banton/Bethell dilemma down the road until Buttler's return, granting both the opportunity to further stake their claim for a permanent place in the side.

The issue is that Cox's absence would force Banton to keep, which though he's an able understudy, and is certainly an option behind the stumps in the shorter T20 format, it would be a touch unfamiliar and unfair solution across 50 overs - particularly in addition to him opening.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Nasser Hussain and Kumar Sangakkara discuss how the mentorship of Kevin Pietersen on the England coaching staff can help Tom Banton improve

What about Bethell as an extra spinner?

This is the least likely option of all routes back in, but Bethell first earned a spot in the ODI side at No 7 and providing an extra left-arm spin option - so could that be the answer?

England were content to play just two spinners in Pakistan, with Adil Rashid a surprise omission for much of the tri-series as Liam Dawson and Will Jacks were preferred.

Image: Adil Rashid played only one game out of four in the tri-series in Pakistan as Liam Dawson was preferred to the leg-spinner

If that's the approach in the sub-continent, then it's very unlikely they'd tweak things for Australia of all places, nor for next year's World Cup which is being held in South Africa, Zimbabwe and Namibia.

BUT, the form and fitness of Curran is a bit of a concern, as having missed the back-end of the summer with a groin injury that required surgery, he was far from his best in Pakistan where he was underused and expensive when he was.

Image: Sam Curran (right) struggled on his return to the England ODI side during the tri-series in Pakistan

He claimed four wickets at 54.75 in the four matches, bowling only five overs in the first and conceding an England ODI-record 103 from nine overs as Sri Lanka chased down a staggering 430 in Rawalpindi, before being largely anonymous the rest of the series.

Might Curran benefit from a spell out of the side to build back up to his best? If so, Bethell could stand to benefit - albeit the 23-year-old's immense batting talents would be wasted that low down the order.

Though England could surely cope with Jofra Archer, Gus Atkinson and Jamie Overton as the lone pace options in the absence of Curran, it's more likely that the tourists would only go down this route if looking to get Rashid back into the team, in addition to Dawson and Jacks.

Image: Jofra Archer is expected to return for the first ODI against Australia in Perth on Friday after being rested for last month's tri-series

In that scenario, everyone would bump one up the order, leaving Overton to do a job at No 7, and Bethell again warming the bench.

England will no doubt be thrilled to have their golden boy back in their midst, but that does appear to be Bethell's most likely destination in Australia: the bench. At least for now.

Clarke went into both of those fights perceived as the underdog and won both by stoppage.

Billam-Smith, renowned for his toughness, had never been knocked down before. He'd never even been dropped before.

But Clarke put him down twice, heavily, and hammered him to an inside-the-distance defeat.

He's in the kind of form that should make him a candidate for British boxer of the year.

"He definitely should be [on the shortlist] and hopefully next year he could maybe get a world title and be the UK fighter of the year," Dan Azeez, a former European champion, told Sky Sports.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch back to when Chris Billam-Smith and Cheavon Clarke faced each other in their amateur bout more than ten years ago.

"He had two back to back losses and then he's come back, beat Jack Massey in a stoppage, got off the canvas to win, and now he's just beat Chris Billam-Smith.

"He's just come and destroyed him in excellent fashion," Azeez added. "Those are the kind of stories that inspire people."

Britain has strong contenders for boxer of the year, not least Daniel Dubois becoming a two-time heavyweight world champion.

"It has to be Daniel Dubois, if I'm being honest," Azeez said, adding other contenders: "Willie Hutchinson WBC light-heavyweight champion… Ellie Scotney [who went undisputed].

"Chev, he could be," he continued. "He's definitely in the mix, he's done very well this year and my guy Denzel Bentley [who became world champion and beat Shane Mosley Jr]."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Denzel Bentley landed a big right hand to floor Shane Mosley Jr in the second round before boxing to an impressive points victory.

Former world champion George Groves told Sky Sports: "He's had a great year." Though Dubois would be his overall pick too.

"When you talk about Willie Hutchinson winning a world title this year, Daniel Dubois - two Wardley fights. Probably Dubois. To get off the floor in the first fight and look so spectacular in the second fight," he noted.

Clarke though deserves full credit for his performance against a former world champion in Billam-Smith.

"A great win for him," Groves said. "He had a plan, he stuck to it and found that shot that no one's found so far who's fought Chris Billam-Smith. It was a great, great performance from him."

It was an expert finish. "He stayed on him, didn't get reckless," Groves said. "Chris Billam-Smith's got fantastic powers of recovery, can weather a storm, can fight tired, can fight buzzed and still be effective so good for him."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Groves is confident Jai Opetaia will emerge victorious against Deontay Wilder on Tyson Fury's undercard with Anthony Joshua, saying 'it's not going to be pretty' for the former world heavyweight champion.

It probably a merits a fight with someone like Jai Opetaia, widely regarded as the best fighter in the division. But Opetaia has a heavyweight bout against Deontay Wilder in December and won't be available to box for some time.

What should Clarke do next? "Does that feel like a step down if he fights [Ryan] Rozicki or [Brandon] Glanton? It would be a good fight," Groves said.

"Maybe Chris Billam-Smith will campaign for a rematch but maybe that's not the best thing for him right now.

"Chev's got the world at his feet in many ways now."

Sports.title: Brundle's verdict as Mercedes seal title in 'chaotic Interlagos style'
Sports.content:
This year's edition of the Sao Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos served up its usual fascinating challenges and surprises. The race was great, perhaps only missing a late surprise or crescendo.

I must first congratulate the whole Mercedes Benz team, car and power unit combined, for once again winning the Constructors' Championship for a ninth time as a team.

A tally which draws team boss Toto Wolff level with Sir Frank Willams as the most in F1 history, and with a further eight Mercedes drivers' titles on his watch, equalling Sir Ron Dennis' combined total of 17 as team principal. That's outstanding company in the hierarchy of F1. Well done to every person concerned.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes party on the Brazil podium after sealing their ninth Constructors' Championship title

Driver of the weekend for me was Lando Norris, although we didn't have the chance to witness the full extent of Max Verstappen's talents, more of which later. Max was voted the fans' driver of the day for the sixth time in the last seven races.

There has been relatively little wet running in the all-new 2026 cars, Sepang notwithstanding, and none in Interlagos until the 'qualifying hour', which took a total of 146 minutes to conclude, with Lando on pole position.

The rain fell heavily and the cars floated around even on full wet tyres, and so it had to be red flagged for a good while. Luckily there was a window here and there to get the whole process done, even if the last six minutes on a once more saturated track understandably saw no action.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Torrential rain brings out the red flag a minute after the Qualifying session begins in Sao Paulo

George Russell was aggrieved he didn't 'win' qualifying before he took his five-place grid penalty for needing an extra internal combustion engine over and above the annual allowance. George came across Alex Albon's Williams during a small window in the level of water on the track, and together with his pit wall decided to abandon that lap and make some space for a final effort, but it was too wet. If they had continued, there's a chance it would have been provisional pole, and George needs every ounce of good news he can find at the moment.

He was in fine form all weekend, saying he felt like his old self despite the conditions, but a spin in the pit lane after his first stop in the race may well be the image which sums up his year. He'll bounce back, I have no doubt.

'Another Max special'

Through all the trials and tribulations emerged Lando in his upgraded McLaren, the only team to have new parts in Brazil as the season heads towards conclusion. The track had been resurfaced in places too, and it was a mission to find the best grip whilst not dismantling the car against the barriers.

The higher ride height and more supple 2026 cars looked quite controllable in the conditions as it turned out, but the skills on show were impressive to say the least.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater gives his verdict on a wet Sao Paulo GP, where Lando Norris won, Max Verstappen fought from the back and Mercedes took the constructors' title at Interlagos

Rafael Camara had a baptism of fire on his F1 debut for the Haas team, in Esteban Ocon's seat, at his home Grand Prix. He clouted the turn three exit barriers hard in Q1 but survived to make Q2, where he once again made it nose first into the turn 12 barriers on the cruel downhill wet grass. In the race, he would cross the line 20th and in last place, having achieved seven of the overall 22 track limit infringements, but at least he saw the flag, albeit two laps down.

Verstappen was taking a host of power unit penalties and guaranteed to start from the back of the grid and so only participated in the first part of qualifying. Saving some of the precious rain tyres, limited to two sets of full wets and five sets of intermediate tyres for the whole weekend, was paramount given that the race was expected to be wet.

From 21st and the back row, Max would carve through many cars even before the exit of turn three, including Charles Leclerc who started his Ferrari in 14th. We then witnessed another Max special as he finished second at the flag, beaten only by Lando on imperious form.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Karun Chandhok looks at how Max Verstappen went from 21st to second at Interlagos

It must be said that his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar had a fine race too for the final spot on the podium. He was asked to move over for the flying Verstappen at one point and then appeared to hang onto his gearbox with relative ease, although at the finish he was 9.8 seconds behind his team leader, who was similarly 14.6 seconds behind Lando.

With Oscar Piastri finishing down in sixth place after pitting a lap too late for the final set of intermediate tyres once the rain kicked in again on lap 61 of 71, this meant that McLaren and Red Bull earned 33 points each in their battle for third in the Constructors', which is advantage Red Bull heading into the final three races.

Ups and downs for Mercedes, Hamilton

Kimi Antonelli led the opening stages on intermediates after an excellent start, but as soon as he went onto dry tyres on lap 17 his race began to unravel. Struggling for warm-up of the tyres and therefore confidence too, he spun off in the first corner and flat spotted his tyres, which handed the lead to Lando before he then quickly came under pressure from both Red Bulls.

Like George in the sister Mercedes, he was experiencing a weird feeling in the car of something broken and pulling one way, and that remained a mystery to the team even at the airport later that evening. Perhaps it was a mismatch of tyre temperatures and pressures, perhaps the unique track layout and surfacing, including the numerous sections diamond cut to aid drainage and reduce aquaplaning.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli loses the lead by going off track twice to slip to third

Russell had a strong and very long middle stint, such that pitting for intermediate tyres on lap 61 meant he undid some of the lost time from that pit-exit spin to end up fourth and ahead of his newly-crowned world champion team-mate Antonelli in fifth.

In true Interlagos chaotic style, this meant the only time a Mercedes driver was on the podium post-race was for the team's Constructors' Championship celebrations.

Lewis Hamilton, like Verstappen, had a tremendous start from 20th on the grid and moved swiftly forward. However, his starting intermediate tyres seem less happy than most and he was first over the radio to urgently want to pit, and indeed to pit, on lap 14.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton nearly crashes out in the rain before entering the pits on slick tyres

Lewis had read early that it was time for dry tyres, although I'm led to believe he was reluctant to pit for intermediates later on which meant a high-speed spin in heading to the pits on lap 62 in the now heavier rain, during which he was lucky not to tear the rear wing off. This meant he was consigned to ninth place at the finish, a lap down.

Ahead of him in eighth was Ferrari team-mate Charles Leclerc, who had a strangely anonymous race lacking grip until the final phase on intermediate tyres, which allowed him to pass Niko Hulkenberg and Liam Lawson.

However, during his tussle with Lawson, he nudged the Racing Bulls' rear wheel at turn 12 which attracted a five-second penalty, which in turn elevated Lawson back up to seventh.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc and Liam Lawson touch on lap 70 as they battle for seventh

Lawson put in yet another strong performance for Racing Bulls, running as high as second in the early stages, to further complicate their decision on driver line up for next season. He's been on fire since returning to the team having substituted for the injured Hadjar in the senior Red Bull team.

That concluded a breathless six F1 races in seven weekends, with a slight breather now before a Las Vegas, Qatar, and Abu Dhabi triple-header to finish the season.

Sports.title: Man Utd Q&A: Carrick, Poch, INEOS and more answered
Sports.content:
Kaveh Solhekol has answered your latest questions on Manchester United, with Michael Carrick's future up in the air, the club in the relegation zone and more issues behind the scenes.

Answering your questions live on Sky Sports News, the chief correspondent discussed a range of topics on the situation at Old Trafford.

Read on for his answers in the latest Q&A...

Will Man Utd ever be sold?

Mikey asks: Will the board sell the club? Changing the manager will make no difference. How can United actually improve?

I don't think it's up to the board to sell the club. The Glazer family could decide to sell their stake in Manchester United, but somebody would have to offer them billions and billions of pounds or dollars for them to be tempted to sell.

Who knows? If they get an offer, they may think, we've had enough of all the grief that's associated with owning Manchester United. Even though we've made a lot of money from it, now is the time to make even more money.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports correspondent Kaveh Solhekol speaks on the scheduled meeting between Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Jason Wilcox and Omar Berrada in Monaco on Wednesday regarding the potential sacking of Michael Carrick

I think if they were going to put Manchester United up for sale, they would do what they did last time around, four or five years ago, which is to instruct a merchant bank or an investment bank to sell the club. I think last time around, it was a Raine Group who were based in New York.

There's been no indication that anyone has been instructed to sell the Glazers' shareholding in Manchester United. If you wanted to buy Manchester United or some of the shares, you could also go to Jim Ratcliffe, make him an offer for his 30 per cent share.

There's also the interesting situation where I think if you bought the Glazer family's shares, then there are things called drag-along rights, which would mean that Jim Ratcliffe and INEOS would also have to sell their shares as well.

That complicates the picture as well. Look, if you're asking me today, are Manchester United for sale? No, they're not. No one has said that they are for sale, but who knows what is going on behind the scenes?

There could be billionaires out there who are thinking about making a bid to buy Manchester United, but we have no information that that is the case, and there's been no official word that that's the case.

Is a Middle Eastern takeover a possibility?

Adam asks: Is there any talk of a potential takeover by a UAE or Middle East consortium?

The rival bidder was from Qatar. It was Sheikh Jassim. One of the things he was going to do was to pay off Manchester United's debts so there would be no historic Glazer family debt, and he had big plans for the club, but the Qataris were unwilling to overpay.

Their feeling was that the Glazer family were asking for just too much money and the numbers did not make sense for them. I don't know. I think there was talk of like five, six billion pounds, and the Qataris were thinking, hey, we bought PSG for around 100 million pounds.

Abu Dhabi, members of the royal family there, bought Manchester City for around 150, 160 million pounds. So why should we be paying five, six billion pounds for a club that we don't think is in a particularly good state?

Now, are there people from that part of the world looking at buying Manchester United at the moment? I don't think so because there's the Middle East conflict going on at the moment. There's a lot of instability in that region that has affected finances.

The price of oil has been going up and down. You can't get oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. So I think people in that region have more on their plate at the moment than launching a bid to buy Manchester United.

Are Man Utd still a draw as a big club?

Mark asks: Do we have to just accept that Manchester United are not the big club they once were and do not have the pull that they used to have?

Absolutely. Manchester United used to be the richest club in the world. Number one club in the world.

Richer than Real Madrid, Barcelona. Always number one. And that was 10, 15 years ago.

Things have changed. Now they're about the eighth or ninth richest club in the world. They've been overtaken by Real Madrid, Barcelona, Bayern Munich.

In England, they've been overtaken by Arsenal, Liverpool, Manchester City as well. So no, I agree with that question. They do get a lot more media attention than they deserve considering where they are and what they've become.

But if you speak to anybody in the media, they will say that if you want to make money in the media, talk about Manchester United because there is so much interest in them. I think when it comes to English clubs, Manchester United, Liverpool, and Arsenal are the big three.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports provides an update on Michael Carrick's future at Manchester United with a departure from the club looking most likely

Why did they keep Carrick on?

Tom S asks: Why did they keep Carrick on after the end of the season? I could see this happening from a mile off. Solskjaer 2.0.

That's a good point. I think the reason they decided to go with Michael Carrick was that he did well as the interim. He got United into the Champions League.

They finished third. And also, he was the least risky option, I suppose. Looking back, you can argue it was a mistake because there were lots of other managers available.

Normally, managers are not really available and out of work, but you could have had your pick. You could have taken Andoni Iraola. You could have taken Xabi Alonso.

You could have taken Thomas Frank. You could have taken Oliver Glasner. Assuming they all wanted to come. Marco Silva. There were lots of managers. Antonio Conte was available.

Roberto De Zerbi, before Spurs got him towards the end of last season. He was available after he was sacked as well. So there were a lot of managers out there, but United decided to go with Carrick.

Should Man Utd stick with Carrick?

Stu asks: Surely at some point Manchester United have to stick with the manager and the board should give Carrick time and the support he needs. Does Kaveh agree?

100%. I would like to see Carrick keep his job.

I think the way he has been treated, especially over the past few days and weeks, leaves a really, really bad taste in the mouth. You're talking about somebody who's won 11 major trophies with Manchester United. He's won five league titles with Manchester United and basically, he's been hung out to dry.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol breaks down what fee Manchester United could potentially need to pay to appoint Mauricio Pochettino as the club's new manager

Isn't Poch just another stop-gap?

Trev asks: What is the thinking behind selecting Mauricio Pochettino as the next Manchester United manager in your view? This would be his sixth club in 12 years. His career to date suggests he is a stop-gap manager and not the answer to United's problems.

I'd agree with a lot of that.

I don't think Mauricio Pochettino jumps out at me as the man, as though he's the new Alex Ferguson. I think he's got unfinished business in England. I think Manchester United are a club close to his heart.

I think he's got a lot of respect for Alex Ferguson. There were stories that back in 2013 he went for lunch or dinner with Ferguson and that led to reports that he was being groomed to take over.

So I think one day he would like to manage Manchester United, but having seen what the job has done to so many other managers and knowing Pochettino to be such a nice guy, I'm not sure I would wish the Manchester United job on him in the present circumstances.

Why not go for Ancelotti?

Kieron F asks: If the club are considering paying up Pochettino's US contract, why not go all the way and go for Carlo Ancelotti from Brazil? World-class and proven in so many ways.

I can't see that happening. I was at the World Cup in the summer, covered a few Brazil games, went to Brazil training sessions, saw Carlo Ancelotti.

He's managing Brazil. Why would he want to swap that for managing Manchester United when they're 18th in the Premier League?

Are Berrada and Wilcox's futures in doubt?

Dave asks: Have any indications been given as to whether Berrada and Wilcox's futures will be discussed as part of this review with Ratcliffe?

Well, it's interesting because what we are hearing is that the chief executive and the director of football are going to go and see Jim Ratcliffe and present to him the findings of their review. And they're likely to recommend that Michael Carrick should be replaced.

Ratcliffe is very, very successful. He's a very rich man. He's built a massive business empire.

And I don't think at that meeting he will just sit there in silence. I think he will have questions as well. And I think some of his questions will be looking at those two people and thinking, are you part of the solution or are you part of the problem? Because you are supposed to be in charge of hiring managers, buying players, yet here we are again.

And now it's worse than ever because we're in the relegation zone. And for the third season in a row, people are saying to me that we need to sack a manager, pay him off, we need to appoint a new manager, pay compensation to get him as well. I've got to speak to the Glazers as well.

What are they going to make of this? Maybe they've got a different point of view as well. So I don't think it's going to be a very simple meeting. It's not just going to be a case of, these are our findings, this is what we think you should do.

Ratcliffe saying, yeah, I hear that, yeah, I'm going to do that, thank you very much. It would be awkward for them. I think it would be quite awkward.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Paul Merson discusses Manchester United's transfer activity under INEOS and why it has led to poor results

Ratcliffe doesn't live in a bubble. He will be, even though he hasn't been to United games recently, he'll be watching all United games. I know for a fact that he reads some of the media.

So he will be aware of everything that is going on. And I'm pretty sure that there would have been meetings at INEOS to discuss what needs to be done.

So I don't think the recommendation that he's going to get tomorrow is going to be the be-all and end-all of everything.

I think he's across everything and I think the Glazer family are across everything as well. And they'll be aware of the results and the performances and also be aware of the fact that they're getting a lot of heat from United fans again.

Should Utd change recruitment strategy?

Andy asks: Do you think Manchester United should adapt and approach recruitment like Brentford or Brighton?

That's what everyone would like to do. What has been really strange about Manchester United's recruitment strategy, is something that really has never been done in football before, which is to spend one summer buying forwards, then the next summer buying midfielders, then next summer buying defenders.

If you speak to anybody in football, they say what you need to do is build the spine of a team. Have a really good goalkeeper, centre-back, midfield, and a really, really good forward. They say United should have signed players like Declan Rice, like Harry Kane.

You know, they need somebody like Virgil van Dijk. They need character, personality, like they used to have in the old days. They don't have that anymore.

So I think recruitment has been a big, big problem at United, and it's been a problem as well because they've had to cut their cloth accordingly. Because I think Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos have come in and they've looked at some of the contracts the players have had, the wages they've been earning, and recruitment has been so, so bad, and so much money has been squandered that they have said, look, enough is enough. We have to be much, much more careful with the money we spend.

You need to spend money like it's your own money. I think that is one of the sort of mantras at INEOS, and that is one of the mantras that has got Jim Ratcliffe to where he's got to in the business world.

Sports.title: F1 planning to finish season in Middle East as Imola deadline passes
Sports.content:
Formula 1 chiefs are proceeding with plans to hold the final two rounds of 2026 in the Middle East after a deadline to move one of the season-ending races to Italy passed.

F1 had to cancel races scheduled in April in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia due to conflict in the Middle East, which has continued throughout the year to cast doubt over the final two rounds in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

A contingency plan had been arranged for Imola to host a season-ending race in the first week of December, but those in charge at the Italian circuit were informed on Tuesday that it will not be needed, which confirms F1's intention to go ahead with the final two rounds as planned.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2025 Qatar Grand Prix

The Qatar Grand Prix is scheduled for November 27-29, with the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix set to follow from December 4-6. The races complete a triple-header that starts with the Las Vegas Grand Prix from November 20-22.

F1 president Stefano Domenicali has maintained throughout the season that the final races would be held at their scheduled venues unless the situation in the Middle East deteriorated.

Formula 1 2026 remaining races Las Vegas November 20-22 Qatar November 27-29 Abu Dhabi December 4-6

The Italian has also insisted the safety of everyone involved in F1 remains his priority, and it is understood the sport's bosses wouldn't hesitate to cancel the races should the situation change over the coming weeks.

Image: Imola had been on standby to host the final race of the 2026 season

The sport's teams and drivers have repeatedly expressed trust in F1's judgement on the situation, and there has been no suggestion that any of the 11 squads are against completing the season as planned.

The season is set to fall just one short of it's original 24-race schedule, with the Bahrain Grand Prix having been rescheduled and hosted by Malaysia in October.

The Lusail International Circuit, which hosts the Qatar Grand Prix, staged a round of the MotoGP season from November 6-8.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes party on the podium after sealing their ninth Constructors' Championship title

There had been security concerns ahead of the event, which led to Japanese constructor Yamaha opting not to attend, but it passed without incident.

Kimi Antonelli sealed the F1 drivers' title in Mexico City before his Mercedes team closed out the constructors' title a week later in Brazil.

Ben Sulayem: We are ready for Qatar and Abu Dhabi

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem posted on social media on Tuesday insisting that the sport's governing body is "fully prepared" for the final two rounds of the season.

"We are ready for Qatar and Abu Dhabi," Ben Sulayem wrote on Instagram.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino interested in leaving USMNT job for Manchester United
Sports.content:
US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is interested in a move to Manchester United, multiple sources told the Guardian, with those same sources characterizing the interest as mutual.

United are expected to sack their head coach, Michael Carrick, after a disastrous start to their season which leaves them at risk of relegation from the Premier League, their worst opening to a campaign in four decades.

Securing Pochettino’s services is far from simple or inexpensive. The Argentinian’s contract contains a release clause in the neighborhood of $10m (£7.5m), multiple sources familiar with the deal told the Guardian this week, a figure that grows should United choose to retain Pochettino’s staff, including his longtime assistant and confidant Jesús Pérez, who has worked with Pochettino for 16 years. The Athletic first reported the details of Pochettino’s buyout.

Pochettino was brought on by the US in 2024 and guided the USMNT to a last-16 finish at the 2026 World Cup, by most accounts a disappointment. US Soccer brought him back through 2030, with both sides expressing a mutual belief and commitment towards not only brightening the fortunes of the US men but also overhauling the federation’s approach towards youth development.

“Every time we sign a contract, it’s to go to the last day of the contract,” Pochettino told reporters after his contract renewal. “If we sign a four-year contract, we need to think to arrive there. And we signed the contract because we really believe that we are going to be four years there. Because if not, it’s bad. If we don’t believe in that process, if we don’t believe in that journey, why sign [for] four years? Only to be sure that we are going to receive a salary at the end of the month? That is not nice. It’s not the way that we think. We really signed that contract because we really believe that we can arrive to the end.”

Pochettino, who has been linked with a host of high-profile club openings since his arrival in the United States, tempered those remarks by adding another: “In life, nothing is sure. Less in football.”

The USMNT are days from a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches against Haiti in Cincinnati and Miami, their first competitive fixtures of the 2030 qualifying cycle. Pochettino is scheduled to address reporters on Friday afternoon.

Why would Pochettino be interested?

Pochettino has repeatedly expressed his interest in returning to the Premier League during his time with the US. As recently as September, he spoke to Sky Sports about the idea of winning the league and “building a project with the possibility of winning”. In late 2025 he said much the same, telling the BBC he believed the league was the best in the world and adding “of course I am missing it. I am so happy in America but am thinking but also thinking one day to come back.”

Beyond his stated interest, Pochettino is also widely known as a coach who enjoys the day-to-day responsibilities of coaching and he’s widely regarded as an excellent man-manager who thrives in the daily rhythm of life at a club. He maintains a home in London and speaks glowingly of the UK and the football culture that permeates it. In short, there are no shortage of reasons for him to leave the US.

What would US Soccer do if he leaves?

Most federations have contingency plans developed for the departure of a head coach and the US federation is no exception, especially given the repeated interest in Pochettino over the years. Prior to bringing the Argentine on board, US Soccer reached out to or spoke to several other high-profile candidates, most notably former Liverpool and current Germany boss Jürgen Klopp.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In the nearer term, several domestic candidates could fit the bill – current U-23 head coach Steve Cherundolo being one. Nashville SC head coach (and former US interim head coach) BJ Callaghan could be another candidate close to home, having guided the MLS club to a league-record points total this season.

In some respects, there is no better time for Pochettino to depart; doing so now would allow an incoming coach the majority of a four-year cycle to work with and the federation itself would earn millions just months after Pochettino could’ve departed for free.

Is Pochettino likely to leave without his coaching staff?

That feels highly unlikely. Pochettino enjoys an unusually close relationship with his assistants, in particular his second-in-command, Jesús Pérez. Pérez has served alongside Pochettino at every stop in his coaching career, from La Liga side Espanyol in 2010 to stops at Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur, PSG and Chelsea in the 15 years that followed. It’s rare to see Pochettino anywhere in a professional capacity without Pérez at his side.

Pochettino has similarly close bonds with his other assistants – Miki D’Agostino, goalkeeper coach Toni Jiménez and several others. They, too, have been with the Argentine since the start.

Sports.title: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number
Sports.content:
The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure.

1

Lev Yashin

One is the loneliest number, but it also allows you to stand out – especially in football, where you play by different rules and wear different attire. Nobody stood out quite like Yashin, the almost mythical USSR and Dinamo Moscow goalkeeper of the 1950s and 1960s. He often wore a flat cap in goal, and his trademark kit led to the nicknames “Black Spider” or “Black Panther” (strictly speaking, it should have been the less catchy Very Very Dark Blue Spider). Yashin remains the only goalkeeper to have won the Ballon d’Or; with a respectful nod to Dino Zoff, Peter Schmeichel and others, he was a simple choice.

View image in fullscreen Lev Yashin dives to make a save during the Soviet Union’s World Cup semi-final against West Germany at Goodison Park in July 1966. Photograph: Central Press/Getty Images

2

Cafu

It would be a crime against dynamism and flair if we didn’t give one of the traditional full-back numbers to a Brazilian. Some of their great right-backs didn’t actually wear No 2 – Djalma Santos and Carlos Alberto, World Cup-winners of 1958 and 1970, sported No 4 – but that still leaves us with the richest pickings. It’s hard to look beyond Cafu, a bullet train on the right for Brazil, Roma, Milan and others. He won two World Cups and is the only man to play in three consecutive finals. Chuck in more than 700 club games, and that’s a mind-boggling amount of runs up that right flank.

View image in fullscreen Cafu captained Brazil to World Cup glory in 2002 and also won the trophy with the national team in 1994. Photograph: Gunnar Berning/Bongarts/Getty Images

3

Paolo Maldini

Few could dispute this choice. Maldini is No 3. Milan retired his number – it can only be used again if one of his sons plays for the club – and it’s almost a surprise Fifa didn’t do the same. As a left-back or left-sided centre-back, Maldini came as close as anyone to perfecting defending; on the ultra-rare occasions he was given a chasing, by Chris Waddle or Karel Poborsky, it was a JFK moment. It’s an oddity that he didn’t wear No 3 at Italia 90 or USA 94. But for most of his career, to see Maldini with any other number would have been like seeing James Bond in a shell suit.

View image in fullscreen Paolo Maldini drives past Zlatan Ibrahimovic during a Milan derby in March 2007. Photograph: Etsuo Hara/Getty Images

4

Javier Zanetti

For longevity and sheer class – on and off the field – Zanetti pips Pep Guardiola, Sergio Ramos and the aforementioned Brazilian right-backs to this number. A Swiss Army knife of a footballer, Zanetti was one of the first players to show that the positions of right-back and centre-midfield spoke the same language. He won 16 trophies in 19 years at Inter, 15 of them as a quietly inspirational captain. José Mourinho said “it was an honour to coach him”, while Maldini called him “my most respected enemy”. As was the case with Maldini, Zanetti’s number was retired by a Milanese giant.

View image in fullscreen Javier Zanetti well and truly leans into his role as Inter captain during a Milan derby in October 2003. Photograph: Etsuo Hara/Getty Images

5

Franz Beckenbauer

With apologies to Zinedine Zidane, Fabio Cannavaro and Obdulio Varela, the terrifying and granite-willed captain of Uruguay’s 1950 World Cup winners, this was never in doubt. Beckenbauer, libero and captain of the all-conquering West Germany and Bayern Munich sides of the 1970s, was born to stroll around a football field, No 5 on his back, an imaginary Andrex-soft sax jazz soundtrack playing in the background. His biographer, Uli Hesse, wrote that the number “became synonymous with his unique interpretation of the libero role”. Nobody did it better; nobody ever will, which is essentially why, quite rightly, Bayern retired their No 5 shirt in December 2024.

View image in fullscreen Franz Beckenbauer in majestic action for West Germany against the USSR in June 1972. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

6

Franco Baresi

Iconography trumps tactics on this one. In modern football, a No 6 is a deep-lying midfielder, but in the 20th century it was indelibly associated with a specific genre of centre-back: captains, leaders, legends. The list is headed by Bobby Moore, Tony Adams and the don; Baresi, a manager on the field for Arrigo Sacchi and Fabio Capello during Milan’s golden age, his shirt retired by the club in 1997. Baresi died this year; if you have any doubts that he is the definitive No 6, just look at the pictures from his funeral in August of this year.

View image in fullscreen Franco Baresi, left, prepares to lead Milan into battle against Gianluca Vialli’s Juventus in November 1992. Photograph: Etsuo Hara/Getty Images

7

Cristiano Ronaldo

This probably should have been given to Garrincha, who wore No 7 when he single-footedly won the 1962 World Cup for Brazil, but you can’t argue with a trademark. Never mind the trifling matter of almost 1,000 career goals, CR7 is a brand that includes fragrances, underwear, footwear, lifestyle hotels, a fitness app … even bottled water. It all started in 2003, when Sir Alex Ferguson encouraged the teenager from Portugal to embrace one of the most iconic shirts in football – Manchester United No 7s include George Best, Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and David Beckham. On a global scale, Ronaldo, now retired from international duty, is the most famous of the lot.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo celebrates in trademark style after scoring for Portugal against Hungary in September. Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPA/Shutterstock

8

Marcel Desailly

Desailly embraced the No 8 shirt when he was repurposed as a central midfielder at Milan then wore it when he played centre-half for the France team that won France 98 and Euro 2000. Desailly won the lot as a No 8, with the enduring memory of him in that number coming from the 1994 Champions League final, as the then 25-year-old rampaged through Barcelona to score the final goal. Xavi, for Spain, Andrés Iniesta, for Barcelona, and Socrates were strong shouts, all more traditional No 8s, but Desailly got the nod.

View image in fullscreen Marcel Desailly celebrates France’s World Cup triumph of 1998. Photograph: Colorsport/Shutterstock

9

Ronaldo

A choice that was painfully obvious, romantic and a bit dispiriting. Let’s start with the good stuff: Ronaldo 1.0 was the greatest young player we’ve ever seen, blessed like nobody before or since with the holy trinity of power, speed and skill. The dispiriting bit is that his Nike Mercurial R9 boots, unveiled in the buildup to France 98, catalysed an age of naked commercialism that football has never escaped. (Paradoxically, Ronaldo was wearing No 10 for Inter at the time, though that would soon change.) Let’s just remember the good stuff – R9, the first PlayStation footballer, and the platonic ideal of a distinctly Brazilian brilliance.

View image in fullscreen Ronaldo celebrates scoring for Brazil at the 2002 World Cup, one of eight goals that O Fenômeno secured at the tournament. Photograph: Ullstein Bild/Getty Images

10

Diego Maradona

“No matter what happens and no matter who is in charge, the No 10 shirt will always be mine.” We’re not going to argue with Maradona, even if Lionel Messi, Pelé or Ferenc Puskas were the most compelling alternatives. To Maradona, the No 10 was a way of life, part of a uniquely Argentinian identity – that of the pibe, the creative genius from a poor background blessed with celestial skill and the vicious defiance of an alley cat. He even had the No 10 tattooed on his back. Close your eyes and you can probably see the font.

View image in fullscreen Diego Maradona during a practice session in Mexico City during the 1986 World Cup, when the Argentinian confirmed his status as the best player on the planet. Photograph: Jorge Duran/AFP/Getty Images

11

Ryan Giggs

“I remember the first time I saw him,” said Sir Alex Ferguson. “He was 13 and just floated over the ground like a cocker spaniel chasing a piece of silver paper in the wind.” Giggs wore a lot of different numbers at the start of his career – 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 – but from the moment the Premier League introduced squad numbers in 1993, he was Manchester United’s No 11, even when he changed position in his dotage. There were other 24-carat contenders, including the Brazilian collective of Garrincha, Rivellino, Eder, Romario, Rivaldo and Ronaldinho, but none can match Giggs’s longevity or medal collection.

View image in fullscreen Ryan Giggs scores that goal in that FA Cup semi-final replay between Manchester United and Arsenal at Villa Park in April 1999. Photograph: Shaun Botterill/ALLSPORT

12

Marco van Basten

After an injury-ruined season with Milan, Van Basten started Euro 88 on the bench, both literally and numerically. He came in for the second game against England, scored a hat-trick and never looked back. A Hitchcockian late winner against the hosts, West Germany, was followed by an entirely preposterous volley in the final against USSR. From then on he was the Netherlands’ No 9. But the legend of No 12 endured, particularly when Thierry Henry was playing for France: he chose No 12 because of Van Basten. Were it not for the Dutchman, another Frenchman, the great Alain Giresse, would have been our choice.

View image in fullscreen Marco van Basten lets fly for the Netherlands against USSR in the final of the 1988 European Championship, scoring one of the greatest goals of all time. Photograph: Ullstein Bild/Getty Images

13

Gerd Müller

The German sense of humour has always been underrated: they, more than any other country, have embraced the No 13 shirt. It’s been worn at major tournaments by Rudi Völler, Karl-Heinz Riedle, Michael Ballack, Thomas Müller – and Gerd Müller. He picked it for the 1970 and 1974 World Cups, and a triumphant Euro 72, as a nod to his childhood hero, Max Morlock, who scored in the 1954 World Cup final win over Hungary. Muller played 13 World Cup games and almost finished with 13 goals. The alternative ending was better: his 14th, in the 1974 final against the Netherlands, won the World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Gerd Müller scores for West Germany against the Netherlands in the final of the 1974 World Cup. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

14

Johan Cruyff

Cruyff’s first encounter with No 14 came by chance. Ajax’s Gerrie Muhren couldn’t find his usual No 7 shirt, so Cruyff gave him the No 9 and pulled the first spare shirt out of the bag. Ajax won, Cruyff kept wearing No 14 and embraced every connection: for example, he’d married his wife, Danny, on 2 December 1968 and pointed out that 2+12 and 6+8 both equal 14. The Cruyff Foundation later set up Schoolyard14, the key principle of which is the 14 Rules of Johan Cruyff. If he were a young footballer in 2026, Cruyff would be the first to have a symbol instead of a number.

View image in fullscreen Tributes are paid to Johan Cruyff during the 14th minute of the Netherlands’ friendly with France at the ArenA Stadium in Amsterdam in March 2016. Photograph: Peter Dejong/AP

15

Falcão

This was the toughest of the teens, with nobody demanding selection. We plumped for a man who, as far as we can tell, spent only five games in the No 15 shirt. Falcão, an imperious box-to-box playmaker, missed all Brazil’s World Cup qualifiers for Spain 82 – Roma didn’t have to release him, so they didn’t – and as a result was not among Nos 1-11. But he played all five games at the tournament in the No 15 shirt and won the Silver Ball, which makes him officially the best player in the greatest attacking team many of us have ever seen.

View image in fullscreen Falcão in full flow against Argentina at the 1982 World Cup for one of the greatest Brazil sides of all time, if not the greatest. Photograph: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images

16

Rodri

Sham! Yes, it’s somewhat awkward having a certain era of Manchester City players on this list given “events” a few weeks ago, but, equally, it’s impossible to ignore them entirely given their achievements on the pitch, and that’s very much the case when it comes to Rodri, a man who completed football by the age of 30. He’s won the World Cup, the Euros, the Ballon d’Or, the Golden Ball, the Treble … the lot. When he moved to Barcelona in the summer, Rodri asked Fermin López if he could take the No 16 shirt that has served him so well. We assume it was a short conversation.

View image in fullscreen Rodri poses during this summer’s World Cup, when he captained Spain to glory and was recognised as the tournament’s best player. Photograph: Johnnie Izquierdo/FIFA/Getty Images

17

Kevin De Bruyne

It’s all because of Wilfried Bony, you know. Bony was wearing No 14, the number Kevin De Bruyne wore at Wolfsburg, when De Bruyne moved to Manchester City in 2015. He picked No 17 instead. It’s apt there’s a “7” in there somewhere, such was De Bruyne’s devastating impact in the inside-right channel during his decade at the Etihad. His creative genius made him an irresistible choice, despite the appeal of Emmanuel Petit, Frank Rijkaard, Vitinha and even a young Cristiano Ronaldo. For a fair chunk of his time in England, De Bruyne was the best player in the best league in the world.

View image in fullscreen Kevin De Bruyne celebrates scoring for Manchester City against Liverpol in April 2022. City beat Jürgen Klopp’s team to the Premier League title the following month. Photograph: Carl Recine/Action Images/Reuters

18

Ivan Zamorano

If you’re going to launch the toys, you might as well do it in style. When Ronaldo took the No 9 shirt at Inter in the summer of 1998 – the Brazilian had joined the club 12 months earlier and initially wore No 10 – the incumbent had an idea. Ivan Zamorano had worn No 9 for Chile, Sevilla, Real Madrid and Inter and took enormous pride in the symbolism of the shirt. So he switched to No 18 and had a plus sign stitched into the shirt: 1+8. Long before Lionel Messi, this was a different kind of false nine.

View image in fullscreen Ivan Zamorano sporting his truly unique squad number for Inter against Vitesse Arnhem in November 2000. Photograph: kolvenbach/Alamy

19

Paul Gascoigne

The Golden Ball winner at Italia 90 wore No 19. But enough about Toto Schillaci. Gascoigne’s unfettered, painfully innocent brilliance drove Bobby Robson’s team to the semi-finals of a tournament they were expected to stink out, and ultimately changed the game in his country. In 2009, England and West Germany met in a charity-match repeat of the 1990 semi-final. England wore Nos 1-11 – except Gascoigne, who had No 19 on his back. Robson, who died five days later, attended the match in a wheelchair. On the way home, he had one pressing question for his son: “How did Gascoigne play?”

View image in fullscreen Paul Gascoigne is all smiles before England’s World Cup semi-final with West Germany at the 1990 World Cup. His mood would be markedly different after the game in Turin. Photograph: David Cannon/Getty Images

20

Diogo Jota

Paolo Rossi, Clarence Seedorf and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are among those who have worn No 20 with great distinction but no one is, and probably ever will be, as synonymous with it as Jota. It was referenced in the song Liverpool fans sung about him with great lustre when he was alive and with great poignancy after he died, with the club’s retirement of the number and building of a ‘Forever 20’ memorial outside Anfield further tying the late Portuguese striker to the digits. Gone far too soon, Jota will never be forgotten.

View image in fullscreen Liverpool fans pass by a mural dedicated to Diogo Jota before Liverpool’s Premier League game against Wolves – Jota’s former club – in December. Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty Images

21

Andrea Pirlo

The Italian was always a mature vintage, a smooth midfielder who could spot a pass from any angle. He could have played many of his games with a glass of wine in his hand and when he had his own vineyard, 21 Brut Rose was produced by Pratum Coller in honour of the great man’s squad number. No 21 adorned Pirlo’s back at Inter, Milan, Juventus and New York City, as he collected six Serie A titles and a couple of Champions League winner’s medals, not to mention a World Cup with Italy in 2006.

View image in fullscreen Andrea Pirlo glides past Scott Parker during Italy’s victory over England in the quarter-finals of Euro 2012. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/Reuters

22

Kaká

The 2007-08 Ballon d’Or was an inevitability for the magical Brazilian, who spent the year running riot with his third-choice of two little ducks. The attacking midfielder wanted No 8 or No 10 when he arrived in Milan but Gennaro Gattuso and Rui Costa were already in possession of those respective when he joined from São Paulo and the youngster was not going to mess with two legends. His time at Real Madrid, after a €67m move, was far less successful and Kaká returned to Milan after four years, taking back No 22 in the process.

View image in fullscreen Kaká falls to his knees in celebration following Milan’s victory over Liverpool in the 2007 Champions League final. Revenge was sweet for the Brazilian. Photograph: Etsuo Hara/Getty Images

23

David Beckham

With Raúl wearing No 7, Beckham needed a plan upon joining Real Madrid in July 2003. He turned to Michael Jordan for inspiration, asking for his iconic digits as he became a galáctico. When Beckham moved to LA Galaxy four years later, he stuck with No 23. “The connection with Jordan and how important the No 23 was, I just felt it was the right thing to do,” Beckham said. Sol Campbell was another strong contender for No 23 given he wore it at Tottenham and Arsenal, as was Marc-Vivien Foé, whose No 23 shirt was retired by Manchester City after his shock death in June 2003.

View image in fullscreen David Beckham on his debut for Real Madrid, which came at the Bernabéu in a Spanish Super Cup second leg with Real Mallorca in August 2003. Photograph: Shaun Botterill/Getty Images

24

Lorenzo Insigne

“I really hope to stay in the heart of this city so that one day, Napoli also retire the No 24,” Insigne said. The Naples-born forward spent 16 years with his boyhood club, which is certainly a good way to ingratiate himself with the fans, some of whom wanted him to take Maradona’s iconic No 10. “Maradona’s 10? I’m very superstitious, plus I wear 24 because it’s my wife’s birthday and it’s brought me luck,” Insigne said.

View image in fullscreen Lorenzo Insigne celebrates scoring for Napoli against Roma in November 2020. Photograph: Ciro Fusco/EPA

25

Gianfranco Zola

It says something about a player’s association with a number that his blessing is required before it can be passed on to someone else. And so it was in August 2023 that Zola gave Moisés Caicedo the go ahead to be Chelsea’s No 25, with no else deemed worthy of taking that status from the Italian for two whole decades. A bit much? Not really given the brilliance of Zola’s performances across seven seasons at the club. There was the skill, the goals, and that sense of joy that made him popular far beyond the boundaries of west London. Quite simply, everybody loved to watch Franco play.

View image in fullscreen Gianfranco Zola in full flow during Chelsea’s victory over Manchester United in the 2000 Charity Shield, one of the last notable games played at the old Wembley Stadium. Photograph: Dan Chung/Reuters

26

John Terry

Many academy graduates are desperate to rid themselves of their first squad number once they have settled into the first team but the Chelsea centre-back stuck with what he was given for 18 years. One of the reasons Terry did so was because he saw supporters getting it printed on their own shirts and did not want them to buy another. What a nice captain, leader, legend, and indeed why fix something that isn’t broke? When a mural of Terry and Antonio Conte was painted on to Stamford Bridge, the “26” was far more prominent than his face, which really does say something.

View image in fullscreen John Terry after Chelsea’s victory over Bayern Munich in the 2012 Champions League final. Famously – infamously – Terry changed into a full Chelsea kit for the celebrations having been suspended for the game. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

27

Fabio Quagliarella

It was at Sampdoria where the No 27 became imprinted on Quagliarella’s back, and in tribute to his former teammate Niccolo Galli, who died in a road accident aged 17. “I have no doubt that had he lived, he would have been captain of Arsenal and of Italy,” Arsène Wenger said of Galli, who he managed in north London before his passing in February 2001. Quagliarella continued to honour Galli throughout his career, taking in moves to Udinese, Napoli and Juventus, every time ensuring he got the number he wanted. At Juve he spent two seasons with No 18, but the forward’s cherished number was with him for two Serie A titles.

View image in fullscreen Fabio Quagliarella celebrates scoring for Sampdoria against Udinese Calcio in October 2021. Photograph: Getty Images

28

Kolo Touré

History shows that No 28 is often discarded by those seeking fame and fortune – Cristiano Ronaldo had it at Sporting as a kid, Steven Gerrard likewise at Liverpool – but Touré wore it for four seasons at Arsenal, a period that saw him become an Invincible. That perhaps explains why, after a three-season dalliance with No 5, he reverted to what he knew upon joining Manchester City in July 2009, going on to win another Premier League title with this most random of numbers on his back. Quite clearly it meant a lot to him, and justifiably so.

View image in fullscreen Kolo Touré challenges Ryan Giggs during a clash between Arsenal and Manchester United in March 2004. Touré ended the season as an Invincible. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

29

Kai Havertz

“I have had it now for many years,” Havertz said of the number he’s worn at Bayer Leverkusen, Chelsea and Arsenal. “When I became a professional, I took it because it has some history with my brother – we used to take it always when we played video games together. Since then I just took it, and for me it’s the perfect number. I love to wear it in a red shirt again.” It’s as good a reason as any, to be honest, and given Havertz’s success in No 29, why he gets the nod over some other contenders, including Monaco-era Kylian Mbappé.

View image in fullscreen A 21-year-old Kai Havertz takes control of possession while playing for Bayer Leverkusen against Cologne in June 2020. Photograph: Sascha Steinbach/EPA

30

Jesper Grønkjær

Sometimes it only takes a goal to etch a player into a club’s history, and when that goal is genuinely seismic, the number he wore at the time also takes on a grand status. And so it is that Grønkjær is our No 30 given that’s what the Danish winger had on when he scored Chelsea’s winner against Liverpool on the final day of the 2002-03 season. Chelsea subsequently secured Champions League football over Gérard Houllier’s side, which convinced Roman Abramovich to buy the club that summer and change Chelsea’s fortunes, as well as the landscape of modern football, for ever.

View image in fullscreen Jesper Grønkjær celebrates scoring for Chelsea against Liverpool on the final day of the 2002-03 season. No one knew then just how significant a strike it would prove to be. Photograph: Ben Radford/Getty Images

31

Bastian Schweinsteiger

Upon signing for Manchester United in July 2015, Schweinsteiger was given the No 23 shirt. He quickly changed to No 31 and, really, that was no surprise given that was the number he wore throughout his golden 13-year spell at Bayern Munich, coming through the ranks to win eight Bundesliga titles and the Champions League. The midfielder kept it during his two years at United and also wore it during his two years at Chicago Fire. Quite simply Schweinsteiger is No 31 (albeit he mainly wore No 7 for Germany) and no one else comes close to challenging him on that.

View image in fullscreen Bastian Schweinsteiger is joined in celebration by Arjen Robben after scoring for Bayern Munich against Arsenal in March 2014. Photograph: Alexander Hassenstein/Bongarts/Getty Images

32

Carlos Tevez

This feels like a number that should have generated a lot of candidates but ultimately there weren’t many, and certainly no one as notable as Tevez. From the shock, awe and controversy of his three years at West Ham, to the rampaging success of his two-year spell at Manchester United, to the wild, wonderful and also controversial nature of his four years at Manchester City, Tevez well and truly made No 32 his own, going on to also wear it at Shanghai Shenhua and upon his return to Boca Juniors. With apologies to Joël Matip, but it wasn’t even close in the end.

View image in fullscreen Carlos Tevez celebrates scoring for West Ham during the 2006-07 season, the Argentinian playing a decisive role in the club avoiding relegation from the Premier League. Photograph: Jamie McDonald/Getty Images

33

Petr Cech

This was an immediate lock-in given Cech’s reasons for taking this number upon joining Arsenal from Chelsea in 2015. He was 33 at the time, had played 333 games in the Premier League and – wait for it – 33 is number of vertebrae in the human spine. “Hope to be a part of the spine of the team,” Cech posted on social media on 11 July 2015. Seriously, what a guy. Speaking of Arsenal, Riccardo Calafiori was also in contention given he wore No 33 at Basel and Bologna before nabbing it upon his arrival at the Emirates two years ago.

View image in fullscreen Petr Cech dives to save a Troy Deeney penalty during Watford’s visit to the Emirates Stadium in March 2018. Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty Images

34

Granit Xhaka

The choice for this number came down to Nigel de Jong or Xhaka. The former wore it throughout his five seasons at Manchester City, four at Milan, one at LA Galaxy and one at Galatasaray. Strong but not strong enough given Xhaka wore it during his three seasons at Basel, four at Borussia Monchengladbach, five of his seven at Arsenal, two at Leverkusen and throughout his time so far at Sunderland. And here’s the clincher: the Switzerland captain adopted No 34 in the first place because that was the number of the bus he took to training when in the youth ranks at Basel. It just had to be him.

View image in fullscreen Granit Xhaka in action for Basel, his boyhood club, against Bayern Munich during the 2011-12 season. Photograph: sampics/Corbis/Getty Images

35

Igor Akinfeev

A couple of Argentinians were in the running for this number, namely Pablo Aimar, who wore No 35 at different times for Valencia and River Plate, and Diego Placente, who wore it throughout his five seasons at Bayer Leverkusen, a period in which he played an important role in them finishing runners-up in the Bundesliga and Champions League. But ultimately this was no contest given Akinfeev’s remarkable association with No 35, the Russian goalkeeper taking it on upon graduating from CSKA Moscow’s youth ranks to the first-team squad in 2003 and, 23 years later, still retaining it. That, folks, is dedication to your squad number.

View image in fullscreen Igor Akinfeev during a Russian Premier League match between CSKA Moscow and city rivals Spartak in May 2023. Photograph: Ivan Vodop’janov/SIPA/Alamy

36

Matteo Darmian

Martín Zubimendi was a strong candidate for this number given the reason he adopted it upon joining Arsenal in July 2025 was because he also wore it when making his debut for Real Sociedad, his boyhood club, six years earlier. But, in the end, longevity overruled sentiment in favour of Darmian, who wore No 36 across a 10-year spell for Milan, Padova, Palermo, Torino, Manchester United, Parma and Inter. There doesn’t appear to be any specific reason why the Italian full-back was so wedded to such a random number, but he was, and for a long time.

View image in fullscreen Matteo Darmian raises the Serie A trophy with Inter at San Siro in May 2024. Photograph: Mattia Ozbot/Inter/Getty Images

37

Micky van de Ven

Van de Ven has only worn No 37 for the past four seasons, ever since joining Tottenham from Wolfsburg in August 2023. He didn’t wear it while at the German club or at Volendam, where the Dutch centre-back began his career. But his reason for doing so is why he’s the clear choice. “A friend of mine passed away when we were young and it was always his favourite number,” Van de Ven revealed in a February 2024 interview. “So when I had the opportunity to choose No 37 when I signed for Tottenham … to be honest, it’s for him.”

View image in fullscreen Micky van de Ven celebrates scoring for Tottenham, for whom he has always worn the No 37 shirt. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

38

Dylan Tombides

Born in Australia and raised in Macau, Tombides joined West Ham’s academy in 2008 as a promising teenage striker. He had talent and dedication and made his first-team debut in a League Cup tie against Wigan in September 2012. That game came a year after Tombides had been diagnosed with testicular cancer. He died from the disease in April 2014, aged only 20. Shortly after, West Ham retired his No 38 shirt. It was only the second time the club had done such a thing, the first being with Bobby Moore’s No 6 shirt, a sign of just how well thought of young Tombides was in east London.

View image in fullscreen Tributes are paid to Dylan Tombides at the London Stadium at a West Ham game in April, 12 years after his death. Photograph: Tony O Brien/Reuters

39

Bruno Guimarães

Guimarães chose No 39 upon making his debut for Athletico Paranaense in 2017 and has worn it ever since, at Lyon, Newcastle and now Arsenal, because it was the dispatch number of the taxi his father drove in Rio de Janeiro. Quite clearly it means a lot to the Brazil midfielder, as he made clear in an article published by The Players’ Tribune in February 2023. “For me 39 is special. No, it’s more than that. It’s magical. It gave me everything in life”. Sorry Marcus Rashford in his first season at Manchester United, but you’re not topping that.

View image in fullscreen Bruno Guimarães takes in the acclaim of the St James’ Park faithful after scoring for Newcastle against Manchester United last April. Photograph: Adam Vaughan/EPA

40

Besian Idrizaj

Idrizaj joined Swansea from German club Eilenburg in August 2009 as a promising 21-year-old striker. He went on to make three first-team appearances that season with plenty more seemingly on the horizon. But on 15 May 2010, Idrizaj died of a suspected heart attack while at home in his native Austria. It was a sad shock that led to Swansea retiring the former Liverpool player’s No 40 shirt. That showed how much everyone at the club thought of him, which was seen again when Swansea’s players wore T-shirts bearing Idrizaj’s name after winning the 2011 Championship playoff final.

View image in fullscreen Swansea City players pay tribute to Besian Idrizaj following victory over Reading in the 2011 Championship playoff final. Photograph: Matthew Ashton/Corbis/Getty Images

41

Declan Rice

Rice’s reason for wearing No 41 throughout his time in West Ham’s first team and ever since joining Arsenal in July 2023 is pretty straightforward. “It was a number I was given in the [West Ham] academy by the kitman, Jamo. It’s stayed with me since,” he said. “Regardless of what happens in my career, I might stay with 41. ‘Rice 41’ has a nice ring to it”. That’s debatable, but what’s for sure is that Rice has become distinctly associated with the number as he’s gone about establishing himself as one of the best midfielders in the world.

View image in fullscreen Declan Rice celebrates after scoring the second of his sensational free-kicks in Arsenal’s 3-0 victory over Real Madrid in April 2025. Photograph: Stuart MacFarlane/AFC/Getty Images

42

Yaya Touré

Touré chose No 42 upon joining Manchester City in July 2010 because it was the reverse of the No 24 he had worn at Barcelona. A simple if somewhat odd motivation that very much did not backfire as the Ivorian went about making the number his own during an eight-year spell at City that saw him win three Premier League titles, two FA Cups, two League Cups and become one of the most impactful, impressive midfielders on the planet. Touré retained No 42 upon joining Olympiakos in September 2018 before going back to 24 at his final club – Qingdao Huanghai in China.

View image in fullscreen Yaya Touré scores for Manchester City against Manchester United in the 2011 FA Cup final. It was the only goal of the game. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

43

Mateusz Klich

“It was my first number in professional football, it’s a lucky number I guess”. Klich’s reason for wearing No 43 is, like with many others, based on what was given to him at the start of his career, which in Klich’s case occurred at Cracovia in his native Poland. He subsequently wore it for two seasons at PEC Zwolle, one at FC Twente, six at Leeds, two at DC United, one at Atlanta United and now back at Cracovia. Klich never wore No 43 at Wolfsburg, Kaiserslautern or Utrecht, so it clearly doesn’t mean that much to him, but he’s done enough to make it on this list.

View image in fullscreen Mateusz Klich lines up to take a corner for DC United in a Major League Soccer match against Columbus Crew in April 2024. Photograph: Kirk Irwin/Getty Images

44

Ivan Perisic

Has a man ever loved No 4 as much as Perisic? It feels unlikely given he has worn various versions of it – namely “4”, “14” and “44” – throughout his career. He’s not No 4 on this list because that is Javier Zanetti, which is also the reason why Perisic couldn’t have No 4 upon joining Inter in August 2015 – the number had been retired by the club in honour of the Argentina great the previous year. Perisic subsequently took No 44, which the Croatian also wore at Club Brugge and Borussia Dortmund. That’ll do as far as this list is concerned, especially given his only real rival is Massimo Oddo.

View image in fullscreen Ivan Perisic tussles for possession with Yossi Benayoun during Borussia Dortmund’s Champions League encounter with Arsenal in September 2011. Photograph: Alex Morton/Action Images/Reuters

45

Mario Balotelli

Why [always] him? Well, it could’ve been Roméo Lavia or one or two others, but ultimately it had to be the man who wore No 45 with great fuss and furore at Inter, Manchester City and Liverpool before also doing so at Milan, Brescia, Monza, Adana Demirspor, FC Sion and Genoa. No 45 has become the number for one of the careers of the modern era and the association is only strengthened by its sweet origin story. As Balotelli explained: “When I first played with Inter, the numbers for young players were No 36 to No 50. I took No 45 because four plus five is nine – and I scored. It brings me luck.”

View image in fullscreen Mario Balotelli in seemingly contemplative mood while playing for Milan against Empoli in January 2016. Photograph: Fabio Muzzi/EPA

46

Salvatore Sirigu

The Italian goalkeeper represented 12 different clubs in a 19-year career and only wore No 46 at one of them. But he gets the nod because of the nice, circular nature of the association. Sirigu wanted No 6 before making his Serie A debut for Palermo in 2009 but was told he couldn’t because it wasn’t appropriate for a keeper by the manager, and someone who knows a thing or two about shot-stopping, Walter Zenga. So he chose No 46 because it was the one worn by the legendary Italian motorcyclist Valentino Rossi. Sirigu left Palermo in 2011 before returning 13 years later. The number he chose upon doing so? 46.

View image in fullscreen Salvatore Sirigu is congratulated by teammate Federico Balzaretti during Palermo’s Serie A encounter with Juventus in September 2010. Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty Images

47

Phil Foden

This was a shoo-in for a couple of reasons: Foden has worn the number throughout his time as a first-team player at Manchester City, which is verging on a decade and seen him win everything going, and because of the origin story. Foden’s grandfather Ronnie, a big City fan, passed away when he was only 47. “I was young when we lost him,” said Foden in a 2024 interview. “My dad said he loved playing football with me and that it would be amazing if I took the shirt number. I have loved it ever since.” Foden’s tribute to Ronnie extends to having “47” tattooed behind his right ear.

View image in fullscreen Phil Foden not only wears No 47 – he has the digits tattooed on the side of his neck, all in tribute to late grandfather, Ronnie. Photograph: George Wood/Getty Images

48

Curtis Jones

There’s no point sugarcoating it – this is a stretch. Jones only wore No 48 for two years at Liverpool, from 2018-2020, and there appears no interesting reason for him doing so. But the midfielder gets the nod because the competition is razor-thin bordering on nonexistent. It certainly helps Jones’s cause that he wore No 48 when scoring the winner in Liverpool’s FA Cup third-round victory over Everton at Anfield in January 2020. It was a superb, long-range curling finish that made Jones, at 18 years and 340 days, Liverpool’s youngest goalscorer in a Merseyside derby since Robbie Fowler in March 1994.

View image in fullscreen Curtis Jones scores for Liverpool in their FA Cup third-round victory over Everton in January 2020. It remains, almost certainly, the standout goal of his career. Photograph: Carl Recine/Action Images/Reuters

49

Myles Lewis-Skelly

“Forty-nine, forty-nine, Lewis-Skelly” sing Arsenal supporters in praise of their academy graduate as well as in recognition of why he has kept hold of such a random number even after establishing himself in Mikel Arteta’s first-team squad. Lewis-Skelly was given the choice of changing to a more established number ahead of last season but stuck with No 49 because of its association with Arsenal’s Invincibles-era unbeaten run of games, and an Arsenal song ever since (‘Forty-nine, forty-nine undefeated’). Sound reasoning and enough to earn the 20-year-old a place on this list ahead of Ronaldinho, who wore No 49 at Atlético Mineiro and Querétaro.

View image in fullscreen Myles Lewis-Skelly was not born when Arsenal’s Invincibles had their record 49-game unbeaten league run from May 2003 to October 2004. Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty Images

50

Lazar Markovic

Another shoo-in given the unsurprisingly sparse options for this number and the fact Markovic has worn it for the bulk of his long, nomadic career. He first adopted it when he broke through at Partizan Belgrade in 2011 and continued to do so at Benfica and Liverpool, as well as at Fenerbahce, Hull and Anderlecht – who he joined on loan during his time at Anfield – before taking it again upon his permanent return to Partizan in 2019. The Serbian winger has since gone on to wear it at Gaziantep FK, Trabzonspor, FC Baniyas and Apollon Limassol. Markovic is No 8 at current club, FK Cukaricki, but clearly, at heart, he’s Mr No 50.

View image in fullscreen Lazar Markovic bursts through two Feyenoord players while playing for Partizan Belgrade in March 2022. The winger returned to the club where he began his career in 2019. Photograph: Olaf Kraak /ANP/Getty Images

Now we want to hear from you.

Sports.title: Fujino’s double sparks WCL comeback win for Manchester City against Inter
