Sports.title: F1 scraps back-up plan to race at Imola if Middle East GPs are cancelled – reports | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has committed to holding the final two rounds of the 2026 world championship in the Middle East or not at all.

The series had made contingency arrangements to relocate the final round it Imola in Italy if it decided the risks posed by the war in Iran meant it should not proceed with its races in the Middle East. Multiple reports now claim F1 has told Imola it will not be required to hold a race.

The world championship will resume at Las Vegas in the USA next week. Following that it is due to race at the Losail International Circuit in Qatar and Yas Marina in the United Arab Emirates on the following weekends.

The series cancelled its grands prix in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia earlier this year due to the war between Iran and the USA. It later held an event using the ‘Bahrain Grand Prix’ title at Malaysia’s Sepang International Circuit.

The political situation in the Middle East remains uncertain. US president Donald Trump this week suggested he would not escalate its military campaign in the region, but has made similar comments since beginning his war in February, only to subsequently launch further strikes. The US retains a significant military presences in the region and moved more troops there last month.

However Moto GP, which like F1 is owned by Liberty Media, raced in Losail on Sunday. It postponed its Qatar round in April due to the war.

Four bikes were missing from the field as Yamaha did not participate. Most of the series’ riders expressed concerns over visiting the country and asked the championship to provide extra guarantees for their security.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff defended Moto GP’s decision to race in Qatar. He criticised riders who expressed concerns about racing there, saying they “know nothing” about the situation.

Many television broadcasters also opted not to send their staff to the region.

The 2027 F1 season is due to begin in the Middle East with races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia next March. F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali told investors last week “the disruption we experienced in the Middle East this year does not change our long-term regional strategy and ongoing partnership with our promoters.”

“This year, we currently remain scheduled to complete our calendar season and at this stage, continue to plan to finish the season in Qatar and Abu Dhabi,” he added. “We will continue to monitor the situation. As always, the safety and security of everyone in the sport will remain our first and foremost priority.”

Many other series have cancelled events in the region due to the war in the Middle East. The World Endurance Championship called off its planned rounds in Qatar and Bahrain, replacing them with races in Italy and Spain. The 2027 Dakar Rally, previously held in Saudi Arabia, will take place in Africa. The 2026-27 Asian Le Mans series, which previously raced at Dubai Autodrome and Yas Marina, will take place in Europe under the name ‘Winter Le Mans Series’.

Sports.title: Hadjar kept asking Red Bull if they would reverse his position swap with Verstappen | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Isack Hadjar was quick to comply when Red Bull ordered him to let his team mate pass him in the Brazilian Grand Prix.

But he made sure Red Bull did not forget how readily he let Max Verstappen through – especially as Hadjar appeared to lose more time over the following laps as his team mate did not pull away from him.

Excerpts from Hadjar’s radio communications in the Brazilian Grand Prix

Hadjar was dismayed to see how easily George Russell pulled away from him when the Mercedes driver overtook. He told his race engineer Richard Wood it was as if they were in a different category.

Lap: 8/71 HAD: 1’27.039 Hadjar Yeah, zero grip now. The tyres really took a hit. Wood Copy, so front is in the window, rears are plus 10 to target. Lap: 9/71 HAD: 1’27.134 Hadjar Alright, we are stuck. We are stuck. Lap: 11/71 HAD: 1’28.110 Wood Russell passes Hadjar

The only thing we have for turn 12 is push toggle. Hadjar Ah, we are in a different championship. Crazy. Wood Copy, update track conditions when you can. Some people are talking about slicks soon. Sports.title: No F1 engine manufacturers to get extra upgrades after FIA’s third ADUO evaluation | Formula 1
Sports.content:
The FIA will not to offer any engine manufacturers the chance to perform extra power unit upgrades following its latest Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) evaluation.

Under new rules introduced as part of Formula 1’s 2026 power unit regulations the sport’s governing body controls how often manufacturers can upgrade their internal combustion engines.

The evaluations take place periodically throughout the season. The FIA has completed its third such evaluation and, as was the case during the second, determined no further engine homologation opportunities should be offered.

The third evaluation period concluded after the United States Grand Prix last month. The second followed the Hungarian Grand Prix.

The first evaluation period, which ran from the start of the season to the Canadian Grand Prix, remains the only time any additional upgrade opportunities were awarded. On that occasion Red Bull-Ford were found to have the top-performing power unit.

Audi, Ferrari and Honda’s units were found to be more than 4% less powerful. They were permitted two extra homologation opportunities this year and two more next year. Mercedes were found to be within 2% and 4% of the leading power unit and therefore received one extra upgrade this year and next.

Separately, in May the FIA changed the ADUO rules to allow any manufacturer which was 10% off the leading design to spend more money. The revision was expected to assist Honda following their poor start to the season.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Some have likened F1’s ADUO to the World Endurance Championship’s heavily-criticised Balance of Performance regulations. The FIA’s single-seater director Nikolas Tombazis defended the regulations but indicated they may be revised in coming seasons.

“Based on the quality of the data and the robustness of the assessment process, we are confident in our findings and the conclusions reached,” he said.

“The first year of implementation has also reinforced our belief that the ADUO concept is the right one for Formula 1. However, it is important that the system continues to evolve to ensure it remains efficient, relevant and fit for purpose.

“To that end, we have been working closely with the power unit manufacturers and teams to explore refinements to the methodology that will support the continued effectiveness of ADUO in future seasons.”

Lewis Hamilton could have avoided his high-speed spin when the rain returned in the latter stages of the Brazilian Grand Prix.

His Ferrari team summoned him into the pits before he began the lap. Liam Lawson immediately in front of him did pit but Hamilton stayed out. But the conditions had deteriorated and he spun on his next lap.

Hamilton made a strong start to the race from 20th and briefly ran as high as ninth. But Max Verstappen overtook him and Ferrari then told him to let Oliver Bearman past.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Wants Ryan Garcia After Paro
Sports.content:
Devin Haney is talking about Ryan Garcia and undisputed crowns at 147, but public wish lists rarely match promotional reality. Haney insists Garcia is his primary target after Liam Paro, presenting a four-belt unification as the ultimate prize. If Garcia falls short against Teofimo Lopez in their proposed clash, Haney claims he will gladly face Lopez instead.

Haney has to deal with Paro on December 19 at the Chase Center in San Francisco before any of those grand scenarios can materialize. Paro is not a prop. He is a tough, natural junior welterweight titleholder stepping up in weight, possessing the physical strength to test Haney inside. Haney enjoyed a distinct frame advantage at lightweight, but welterweight erases those physical cushions. Overlooking a durable southpaw to game-plan a dream tournament is a familiar trap in boxing.

“The Ryan Garcia fight is the fight that I want the most,” Haney said to the media. “It starts with Liam Paro, but, yeah, for sure. Once I win this fight, you guys know who I got my eyes on.”

Haney wants to believe that collecting straps automatically grants him control over Garcia. That is a tactical miscalculation. Belts do not dictate commercial power in modern boxing, pay-per-view draws do. Garcia demonstrated in their first meeting that he can generate massive gates and pay-per-view numbers on his own terms. Even if Garcia beats Lopez to capture the WBC and WBA belts, he does not need Haney to command enormous paydays. Haney needs Garcia to attempt to erase the most damaging night of his career.

Devin and Bill Haney have spent years operating under the purist boxing currency: belts equate to leverage. In their minds, capturing the WBO and IBF straps against Liam Paro gives them undisputed collateral, and in the traditional sanctioning body system, two champions meeting for all four belts automatically calls for an even split.

In the modern commercial landscape, belts do not sell pay-per-views. Garcia proved in April 2024 that his platform dwarfs the hardware. He brings millions of casual eyeballs, viral reach, and ticket sales that Haney simply cannot generate as an A-side. Ryan knows who drove the commercial engine of their first fight, and he knows who held the psychological upper hand by the final bell. Demanding parity from a fighter who views himself as the sole economic driver of the promotion is an immediate non-starter.

Without third-party intervention, Ryan has zero incentive to capitulate. He holds the win that damaged Haney’s commercial aura, meaning Haney is the one chasing closure, redemption, and a career-defining check. Ryan can fight Rolly Romero, Conor Benn, Gervonta Davis, or even pursue exhibition routes and generate massive purses without ever having to accommodate the Haney camp’s contractual demands.

The single wildcard that alters the math is His Excellency Turki Alalshikh. Riyadh Season has repeatedly shown a willingness to distort traditional pay-per-view economics by simply overpaying both sides to eliminate negotiating hurdles. If Saudi backing arrives with an astronomical flat guarantee that makes Ryan indifferent to the split, the fight happens.

If the bout has to survive on standard domestic pay-per-view metrics, Haney’s 50-50 stance is a poison pill. Unless Haney swallows his pride and accepts the reality of being the B-side on the financial sheet, the rematch remains trapped behind a wall of commercial delusion.

Haney addressed the possibility of facing either man, attempting to maintain an air of indifference while clearly favoring the grudge match.

“If Ryan is victorious, still got to beat Teo … or even if Teo is victorious, it doesn’t matter. I would take either-or for undisputed,” Haney said. “But obviously I want Ryan Garcia to win so that I could right that wrong.”

Garcia wandering into exhibition talks with Floyd Mayweather illustrates the fundamental problem with Haney’s strategy. Garcia moves wherever the maximum money and spectacle lie. Haney, meanwhile, is betting his trajectory on the sanctioning bodies and conventional promotional pathways.

When asked about the Mayweather rumors, Haney took a reserved stance. He pointed out that Mayweather’s name routinely circulates around potential bouts that never reach the ring, treating the talk as typical posturing until contracts get signed.

The promotional terrain presents an even larger hurdle than fighter preferences. Haney points to his DAZN deal as the vehicle that will deliver these mega-fights, but DAZN does not control the entire board.

“Other people were offering me crazy money,” Haney said. “Of course, DAZN gave me a great deal, but most importantly, if you don’t have the opponents, how can I become a great in the sport?”

Cross-platform negotiations between competing networks and rival promoters routinely swallow undisputed fights whole. Landing belts at 147 might look clean on paper, but turning a regional fight in San Francisco into a massive multi-network blockbuster against Garcia requires solving promotional gridlock that sanctioning body hardware cannot fix on its own.

Sports.title: William Zepeda vs. Jadier Herrera Announcement Expected Soon From Golden Boy
Sports.content:
Jadier Herrera is set to challenge WBC lightweight champion William Zepeda after the WBC passed him over when the full title was vacant. The fight will settle who holds the WBC’s only belt at 135 pounds.

Golden Boy is expected to announce the bout soon, according to Darshan Desai. From a pure business perspective, taking on Jadier Herrera is a terrible risk-reward calculation for Zepeda. Herrera brings almost zero casual name recognition, practically no box office draw, and zero commercial upside. What he does bring is slick Cuban pedigree, southpaw counter-punching skills, and enough technical ability to make Zepeda look ordinary.

If Zepeda dominates him, casual fans will shrug and dismiss Herrera as an obscure mandatory. If Zepeda struggles or gets outboxed, his entire commercial standing evaporates overnight. Meanwhile, the alternative landscape offers massive paydays and legitimate star-making opportunities. A unification clash against WBO champion Abdullah Mason is by far the biggest pure boxing event at 135 pounds right now.

Mason carries immense promotional backing and serious buzz. Unifying the belts against him would instantly establish the winner as the true king of the lightweight division. An in-house Golden Boy matchup with Floyd Schofield delivers pure domestic pay-per-view numbers and massive promotional traction. Schofield talks, sells tickets, and brings a built-in fanbase that turns any clash into an event.

A blockbuster showdown against Gervonta Davis remains the ultimate lottery ticket in the weight class, offering career-defining money and mainstream reach. Compared to those blockbusters, defending the WBC belt against Herrera is pure sanctioning body tax. It does nothing for Zepeda’s bank account, nothing for his profile, and risks everything he built by winning the title from Roach.

The only reason Zepeda is entertaining it is that the WBC forced his hand with a mandatory order to clean up its interim title mess. Outside of keeping the green belt, the matchup is all downside.

Herrera has held the interim title since January, when he stopped Ricardo Núñez. That same month, Shakur Stevenson moved up to light welterweight and beat Teofimo Lopez. The WBC subsequently stripped Stevenson of its lightweight title, citing unpaid sanctioning fees.

The WBC could have elevated Herrera or put him in a fight for the vacant championship. Instead, it approved a deal the promoters had already put together for Zepeda to fight Lamont Roach Jr. The winner was expected to face Herrera, and Zepeda took the belt by unanimous decision on August 1.

Zepeda had a case for the opportunity. He had held the interim belt himself before losing to Stevenson, and both he and Roach were highly ranked. Their promoters also had a fight ready to go. The WBC could fill the vacancy by sanctioning a bout that had already been agreed, leaving Herrera to wait for the winner.

The wait cost Herrera a chance to be one of the two fighters chosen for the vacant title. When the belt opened up, the WBC could have made Zepeda or Roach fight Herrera to win it. Its decision gave Zepeda a chance to become champion before he had to face Herrera. The interim belt secured Herrera the next fight. A deal between two promoters secured the first one.

Sports.title: Ramon Cardenas Tests Junto Nakatani After Inoue Loss
Sports.content:
Ramon Cardenas provides an immediate measuring stick for Junto Nakatani following his first career defeat. The veteran counterpuncher possesses the exact timing required to test Nakatani’s willingness to commit after taking a solid hit.

Promoter Sampson Lewkowicz confirmed at the WBC convention that Cardenas reached a deal with Nakatani’s promoter, Akihiko Honda, via reporting from Darshan Desai of EverythingBoxing.

Cardenas proved his danger by dropping Naoya Inoue with a sharp counter left hook in the second round of their May 2025 meeting before Inoue halted him in the eighth. Facing a southpaw like Nakatani presents a distinct target profile.

The orthodox overhand right carries lethal potential, particularly because Nakatani tends to finish straight lefts in an upright stance and retreat along a direct line. That straight exit negates his reach advantage, leaving a clear path for Cardenas to press forward while Nakatani carries his guard low.

The technical tell will surface in subsequent exchanges. Nakatani must establish his right jab to unlock sustained punch combinations. That constant offensive pressure forces Cardenas into a shell, taking away his counter opportunities.

Firing isolated straight lefts gives Cardenas a predictable timing read on Nakatani’s backward retreat. Protracted lulls between combinations only grant Cardenas extra seconds to plant his feet and set traps.

Discipline inside the pocket will prove decisive. Absorbing a heavy punch requires Nakatani to tie up immediately. Pivoting out to open canvas gives him room to re-establish distance without trading out of pride. Firing back instantly without set feet hands Cardenas a clean opening to string punches together.

A wide points victory will not reveal the entire picture. The critical details lie in Nakatani’s punch selection the minute after Cardenas lands flush, alongside his defensive movement once combinations conclude. Those exact sequences will expose whether lingering hesitation from the Inoue loss remains.

Sports.title: Reynoso Lists Five Options for Canelo Alvarez in 2027
Sports.content:
Trainer Eddy Reynoso expects Canelo Alvarez to enter the ring two or three times in 2027, eyeing five distinct paths according to The Ring. The lineup features a super middleweight unification, a mandatory defense against Lester Martínez, a light heavyweight clash with Willy Hutchinson, and return bouts against Terence Crawford or Dmitry Bivol.

The Ring notes that no sequence is locked in. Four specific rivals are on the table, while the unification route hinges on which 168-pound titleholder agrees to terms. That gives Canelo two clear avenues for his WBC super middleweight belt: take on Martínez for the mandatory slot, or meet a rival champion to collect more gold.

That list of five narrows down fast once reality enters the room.

WBA champion Jaime Munguía makes zero promotional or competitive sense. Canelo already dropped and thoroughly handled him in 2024, and sharing gym space only solidifies that neither man is looking across the ring at the other. With Munguía struggling to look convincing against fringe opposition like Nikita Zon, nobody is opening their wallet to see that replay.

Osleys Iglesias, the IBF belt-holder at 168, is pure poison for an aging fighter. He is big, heavy-handed, fundamentally disciplined from the Cuban school, and operates out of a sharp southpaw stance. He gives away none of the physical advantages older counterpunchers rely on to slow down the pace. Putting Canelo in with a prime, hard-hitting super middleweight who can control range with a stiff southpaw stick is precisely the kind of voluntary hazard Reynoso routinely steers clear of.

WBC light heavyweight champion Willy Hutchinson represents another completely unnecessary headache up at 175. He brings awkward angles, relentless volume, legitimate reach, and the kind of high-octane engine that drains Canelo’s low-output, single-shot style. Canelo struggled with movement and pace at light heavyweight against Dmitry Bivol in the past, and Hutchinson has the motor to exploit those exact same stamina traps without offering the massive global brand name that justifies taking the beating.

Speaking of Bivol, that ship sailed the moment the cards were read in 2022. Canelo spent years tossing out casual remarks about rematches under impossible conditions, yet never actually pushed to get back in the ring with him. Bivol completely neutralized Canelo’s offense with a disciplined high guard, clean distance control, and piercing combinations. Revisiting that fight would simply be paying to re-watch a masterclass in how to dismantle Canelo’s flat-footed rhythm.

That leaves the two names that actually make sense for the business plan:

Crawford is the cash cow and the safest big-money avenue on the board. Even coming off a defeat, Canelo knows Crawford cannot hurt him with single-shot super middleweight power. Crawford will be 39, coming off a long, comfortable layoff on the heels of his biggest career win, and has shown zero appetite to sit in the pocket and trade heavy leather.

If Turki Alashikh puts up the bankroll, Canelo gets maximum financial reward with zero danger of taking a devastating beatdown. Turki is not blind to entertainment value. He wants explosive, fan-friendly wars. What Crawford and Canelo produced in September was essentially an expensive sparring session dressed up as history. Crawford boxed on his toes, kept his distance, tapped his way through exchanges, and collected the decision.

Even if Netflix reported huge raw viewer counts for the first encounter simply because subscribers could watch at no additional fee, streaming services track engagement drop-offs and social sentiment. Casual viewers complained about the lack of action, and nobody came away demanding a repeat. Shifting a second fight to standard pay-per-view could result in disastrous buy rates, while Netflix or any other platform would have a hard time justifying paying massive purses for another twelve rounds of cautious circling.

Lester Martínez is the exact type of mandatory Reynoso smiles at. He is straightforward, comes forward in predictable lines, lacks elite defensive nuance, and sits right in the pocket where Canelo can time his signature counter hooks without chasing anybody around the ring. It lets Canelo fulfill an obligation, keep a belt polished, and put on an explosive showcase for the cameras without taking real systemic punishment.

The five-man list is great for keeping headlines spinning, but Crawford for the check and Martínez for the routine defense are the only two realistic lanes on that drawing board.

Sports.title: Jaron Ennis and Kelly Fight for Three Belts February 27
Sports.content:
Jaron Ennis and Josh Kelly meet for three junior middleweight belts on February 27 at State Farm Arena in Atlanta, according to The Ring. The winner leaves the ring holding three world titles, but the route to an undisputed championship leads straight to Sebastian Fundora and Premier Boxing Champions. If Matchroom Boxing tries to lowball him, Fundora has no reason to budge from PBC, leaving the Atlanta winner stuck with three belts and no way to claim the fourth.

Eddie Hearn handled the simple part first. Because Matchroom promotes both Ennis and Kelly, unifying the WBA, WBO, and IBF titles did not require cutting deals with rival promoters or sorting out network broadcast rights. The real struggle starts with pricing the WBC belt away from Al Haymon.

Fundora handled his business in October by stopping Ermal Hadribeaj, dropping his mandatory obligations, and clearing his calendar. With no sanctioning bodies threatening to strip him, Fundora can demand his price on guarantees, pay-per-view percentages, and broadcast rights while risking nothing.

Matchroom keeps talking about a summer date for the undisputed clash, but that schedule is completely unrealistic. Fighting in June or July gives the Atlanta winner barely four months to recover and prepare. That leaves almost no margin to heal bad cuts, rest damaged hands, and jump right into another grueling training camp.

Kelly got sliced to ribbons against Caoimhin Agyarko, while Boots absorbs plenty of clean, heavy shots whenever he trades. If the victor limps out of Atlanta beat up, Fundora has no incentive to accommodate them. He can take a comfortable defense on PBC television, leaving Matchroom to sit on its hands until the end of the year.

The financial picture transforms entirely depending on whose hand gets raised in Atlanta. If Ennis wins, Eddie Hearn gets the all-American clash he covets, a natural pay-per-view headliner for Las Vegas or the Wells Fargo Center in Philadelphia. If Kelly pulls off the upset, those plans evaporate. Hearn would have to drag the entire event across the Atlantic. Staging an undisputed fight in Newcastle or London guarantees a packed stadium gate, but it creates a massive broadcast problem. It forces the bout into an afternoon slot in the United States, driving down what an American network or streaming platform will pay. Hearn has to build two completely separate business models.

Kelly is a live underdog who can cause real headaches inside the ring. He fights with his hands dangling near his hips, daring opponents to lunge in so he can nail them with lightning-quick counters.

If Boots gets reckless and stalks him in straight lines behind basic one-twos, Kelly has the reflexes to clip him coming in. Ennis needs to turn southpaw and negate that timing, targeting blind spots before the Brit can plant his boots and let his hands go.

Whoever survives Atlanta walks straight into a tactical trap with Fundora. Standard boxing wisdom says you crowd a 6-foot-6 skyscraper to smother his reach, but doing that means marching into a blender. Fundora prefers a dirty, phone-booth war. He digs vicious uppercuts right off his belt line, ripping straight through a tight guard before opponents can spot them coming. Hadribeaj managed to push inside and land heavy left hands, but Fundora just leaned into the fire, tore him apart at close range, and closed the show with a single second left on the clock.

Atlanta crowns a three-belt champion for Eddie Hearn, but Sebastian Fundora controls the real prize. The WBC champion can put his feet up, check out what shape the winner leaves the arena in, and demand a small fortune before he ever considers risking his title.

Sports.title: Conor Benn’s 40 Million Problem: Zuffa’s Make-Or-Break Crossroad
Sports.content:
Chris Mannix estimates Conor Benn will clear upward of $40 million across the Regis Prograis win, his knockout loss to Ryan Garcia, and a third bout. If that figure holds, Zuffa’s next move is simple: decide whether Benn is a long-term commercial asset worth rebuilding, or a depreciating commodity to cash out before the floor gives way.

Cheap preliminary bouts can shave operational overhead, but cost-cutting does not rescue a main event that draws too few buyers to carry elite purses. Denzel Bentley is a clean, in-house booking on paper, yet he brings virtually no promotional leverage outside hardcore circles. If Benn stumbles against a rugged domestic contender, his headliner status evaporates on a Tuesday-level attraction.

“Conor Benn in the last three fights, I would estimate he has made. Well, the last two and then there’s one coming up. He’s going to make north of $40 million. Very few fighters make that in their career,” said Mannix.

A third meeting with Chris Eubank Jr. remains a dependable box-office draw across the UK, but it offers zero forward momentum. Without a world title or fresh bad blood, a trilogy simply taxes the same domestic consumer base a third time. It functions as a lucrative exit strategy rather than a platform to expand Benn’s brand.

Shakur Stevenson provides stateside name recognition, yet the financial and stylistic variables work against Zuffa. Stevenson is a naturally smaller fighter moving up in weight. A Benn win does little to erase the Garcia beatdown, while a calculated twelve-round schooling by Stevenson leaves Zuffa covering two astronomical purses for a clinic that actively turns off casual ticket buyers. That dilemma also complicates distribution, as an American-led Stevenson bout targets a prime U.S. broadcast window, whereas an Eubank card requires a UK primetime slot to secure the gate.

If Zuffa intends to actually rehabilitate Benn, it needs a recognizable, established welterweight willing to stand in the pocket. The play is an opponent who commands respect on the marquee, yet offers the stylistic openings Benn requires to deliver a highlight-reel finish that makes his next event an easy sell.

Sports.title: David Benavidez Gives PBC a Condition for Staying
Sports.content:
David Benavidez is prepared to re-sign with Premier Boxing Champions following his December 5 bout against Michal Cieslak, provided his contract permits regular cross-platform appearances.

In an interview with Chris Mannix, Benavidez revealed he launched his own promotional banner, outlining an aggressive roadmap targeting Jai Opetaia in May followed by Oleksandr Usyk in September. The true worth of any future contractual commitment rests entirely on delivering those marquee bouts without bureaucratic delay.

“As long as we’re able to move freely and fight whoever, whatever network we want to do, then we can stay here,” Benavidez stated. “I want these fights to happen immediately.”

Benavidez gives PBC credit for letting him shop around on other networks. He needs that kind of leeway if he wants major unifications, simply because the money has to come from rival platforms or deep-pocketed outside backers.

Starting his own promotional company lets him push for co-promotional billing, a say on fight dates, and a piece of the TV rights. Still, none of that matters unless the opposing camps and money men sign off. Making a fight with Opetaia is one thing; putting together the numbers for a monster event with Usyk is a totally different ballgame.

Despite turning 29, Benavidez carries the mileage of a thirteen-year professional tenure. Eliminating the harsh cut to 175 pounds undoubtedly preserves his conditioning. Yet his relentless, close-range combinations naturally expose him to heavy return fire from full-sized cruiserweights. A punishing clash with Opetaia in May could result in facial cuts, orthopedic damage, or an abbreviated summer training camp ahead of a proposed September date with Usyk.

With Benavidez, the facial wear is catching up to the odometer. He turned pro at sixteen, but the real mileage is the gym work. His whole identity in camp has always been grueling, high-volume sparring where he plays the hammer, walking guys down and eating clean shots just to deliver five of his own. You can get away with that in your early twenties when the recovery is instant, but that kind of daily collision accumulates on a guy’s face and joints.

The weight shifts do not help either. Spending a decade draining a massive frame down to 168 pounds, ballooning between camps, then cutting to 175, and now suddenly filling out toward 200 changes facial structure dramatically. Once a fighter stops that severe water depletion cycle and carries heavier, solid mass into his late twenties, the baby fat is completely gone, and the facial tissue hardens up fast.

The real giveaway will be the first time he faces genuine adversity at cruiserweight. When guys age overnight on the outside, you watch the legs and the punch reaction. If the feet look heavy early or the reflexes to slip counters are a fraction of a second slower against a puncher like Cieslak or Opetaia, that weathered look in camp ceases to be cosmetic and becomes a fighting reality.

Sports.title: Gene Tunney’s Only Loss Explains His Greatness
Sports.content:
Gene Tunney’s best case for greatness is what he did after Harry Greb handed him his only professional defeat. Greb took Tunney’s American light heavyweight title in 1922 by setting a pace Tunney could barely withstand. Three years and four rematches later, Tunney was landing body shots that forced Greb to hold.

The first fight at Madison Square Garden showed how far Tunney had to go. Greb threw from awkward angles and took control in the late rounds as Tunney tired. Bloodied and exhausted, Tunney stayed upright through the 15th. Two days later, he went to the athletic commission’s office to seek a rematch.

Tunney regained the title by decision in February 1923, though many ringside reporters thought Greb had done enough to win. Tunney won their third meeting that December. Their fourth fight, in September 1924, ended without an official decision. The Cleveland Plain Dealer favored Greb, while The New York Times reported that most ringside writers saw an even fight. More than two years after the first bout, Greb was still giving Tunney trouble.

By their fifth meeting in March 1925, Tunney weighed 181 pounds to Greb’s 168. He used those extra pounds to do damage at close range. The Associated Press reported that Tunney concentrated his attack on the body and cut short Greb’s attempts to rally. Greb, who had poured on punches late in the first fight, spent much of the fifth holding. The weight advantage belongs in the story because Tunney had found a way to make Greb feel it where he had once been most dangerous.

Tunney stopped Tommy Gibbons later that year and took the world heavyweight title from Jack Dempsey by decision in September 1926. Dempsey dropped him in the seventh round of their rematch a year later, then delayed the referee’s count by failing to go promptly to a neutral corner. Tunney rose and made it through the round. In the eighth, he dropped Dempsey on his way to another decision. Tunney stopped Tom Heeney in July 1928 and retired as champion.

The Long Count still invites people to imagine what Dempsey might have done with those extra seconds. The Greb series shows what Tunney did with four more chances against a man who had already beaten him. The first rematch gave him his title back, but the disputed decision left plenty to argue about. By the fifth fight, the clearest evidence was in the way Greb fought. The man who had set the pace over 15 rounds in 1922 was holding to buy himself a few seconds at a time.

Ghana News.title: Meghan’s father back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
Ghana News.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in Tampa, Florida, on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. The court also ordered him to wear a location-monitoring device.

The BBC has contacted his representatives.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

Ghana News.title: Government’s spending cuts are cooling economy and squeezing demand – Bokpin
Ghana News.content:
Professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin

Economics professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin says government’s heavy reliance on spending cuts is cooling the economy and squeezing demand, even as key economic indicators improve.

Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said the approach was helping restore stability. But its benefits would take time to reach ordinary Ghanaians.

“So if you rely extensively on expenditure cuts, you restore macroeconomic stability. You cool the economy.”

“You are shrinking aggregate demand as a way of also bringing inflation down, rather than expanding the economy's severe or restricted supply capacity.”

His assessment comes ahead of the 2027 Budget, scheduled for presentation to Parliament on Thursday, November 12.

The government plans to use its New Economy agenda to shift from stabilisation to investment, jobs, and higher incomes.

The Minority has questioned how the programme will be financed. It has also demanded an account of existing flagship programmes, citing weak sales and concerns about the gap between falling inflation and household living costs.

Prof Bokpin said the 2026 Budget remained heavily dependent on spending restraint, continuing the approach adopted in 2025.

He warned that Ghana’s infrastructure needs made extensive spending cuts particularly difficult to celebrate. He argued that government spending was needed to address constraints on growth.

“If you choose that approach, you will get the result, but the impact will not be felt by Ghanaians.”

He illustrated the disconnect with travellers' experience of long journeys on poor roads.

“If somebody is spending nine to 12 hours to travel from here to Kumasi, inflation of 5.2% means nothing to that person.”

For him, that explains why improving national figures may offer little immediate comfort.

“It's simply because the approach we have adopted in restoring macroeconomic stability is going to take a while to reflect in the lives of Ghanaians.”

Still, Prof Bokpin credited the government with progress. He cited falling inflation and interest rates, reserve accumulation and the cedi’s relative resilience despite renewed pressure.

He said restoring stability had been the administration’s stated priority for its first two years. The approach also reflected the IMF programme's stabilisation objectives.

“I would say they've done quite well in restoring macroeconomic stability,” he said.

Ghana News.title: Managerial ‘inconsistency’ hurting Ghana – Hughton
Ghana News.content:
Kim Bjorkegren (right) is in interim charge of Ghana after Carlos Queiroz left the Black Stars by mutual consent

As Ghana prepare for two make-or-break 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with women's coach Kim Bjorkegren in temporary charge, former boss Chris Hughton has called for greater consistency in the Black Stars dugout.

The West Africans face Somalia in back-to-back fixtures over the next week, having lost their first two games in Group C against Ivory Coast and The Gambia last month.

Those defeats resulted in the departure of Carlos Queiroz, whose brief period in the hot seat was characterised by uncertainty.

The Portuguese's exit means Swede Bjorkegren, who has been in charge of the Black Queens since January 2025, has now been asked to lead the men's team against Somalia.

"When you have inconsistency in the amount of time when a manager is staying, it's never good," Hughton told BBC Sport Africa.

"You want that consistency in the players [and] the players want that consistency in what they see in the manager."

Queiroz, who had two spells as Sir Alex Ferguson's assistant at Manchester United, was initially appointed in April and led Ghana to the last 32 of the Fifa World Cup, holding England to a goalless draw in the group stage, before announcing his own departure shortly after the team were eliminated 1-0 by Colombia in the last 32.

However, the 73-year-old was reappointed in early September, with the Ghana Football Association (GFA) praising his "extensive international experience" gained during time in charge of South Africa, Egypt, Portugal, Iran, Colombia, Qatar and Oman.

But Queiroz's return lasted less than a month following a 2-0 defeat by the Ivorians in Bouake and a 4-2 humbling against the Gambians in front of home fans in Accra.

"What I saw in the World Cup is that they represented the country very well, particularly the England game," said Hughton.

"And although it was very much a defensive outfit, there were opportunities to score."

Hughton, however, admits that regular sackings can create an "attitude" within a squad, with players knowing that "if he (the coach) doesn't do well then he won't be there".

Ghana's managerial merry-go-round

Ghana suffered group-stage exits at the 2021 and 2023 AFCONs under Milovan Rajevac (left) and Chris Hughton (right) before failing to qualify for the 2025 edition under Otto Addo (right)

Hughton's Ghana reign was also short lived.

Appointed as technical director by the GFA in February 2022, he moved into the head coach role in February 2023 but lasted less than 12 months before being sacked in January 2024 after his team failed to get out of their group at the 2023 Afcon in Ivory Coast.

The former Ireland full-back, who won two FA Cups and a Uefa Cup with Tottenham Hotspur and coached Newcastle, Norwich and Brighton in the Premier League, is one of five men who have taken on the Ghana job in the past six years.

Charles Akonnor, Milovan Rajevac, Otto Addo and Queiroz are the others, with the chopping and changing further illustrated by the fact that Addo had two spells in charge during that time.

Kwesi Appiah, the current Sudan boss, lasted 33 months during his second stint with the Black Stars between April 2017 and January 2020 - the longest anyone has managed since legendary Afcon-winning coach Fred Osam-Duodu in the late 1970s and early 80s.

With Ghana in real danger of missing out on a second successive Afcon finals, Hughton believes the situation has been exacerbated by under-investment and what he describes as "fearsome" competition across the continent.

"Many years ago Ghana were at a level that was, if not the best team in Africa, certainly right up there," said the 67-year-old.

"You've seen the emergence of so many other good African nations that have made the competition levels that much higher.

"Some of these countries have so many other problems, but I do think that there needs to be an injection of government money into the structure and into the system."

Hughton feels more needs to be done to encourage the development of the game in the West African nation.

"In Ghana, the local game that used to produce so many good players, the support level is not there," he said.

"They're playing on pitches that are not of a great level and the supporters are not coming.

"The supporters in Ghana love the Black Stars most, first and foremost, and of course the Premier League is massive there, but there isn't that support for the local game that there used to be.

"I think the government needs to do more as regards putting money into the infrastructure."

World Cup success, Afcon failure

oventry City midfielder Caleb Yirenkyi scored the only goal as Ghana beat Panama at the World Cup in June

While Ghana have failed to make it past the second round of Afcon since 2017, the country's World Cup record is far more impressive.

They have qualified for five of the past six finals since their debut in Germany in 2006, reaching the knockout stage on three occasions including a quarter-final appearance at the 2010 tournament in South Africa.

Having cruised through qualification for this year's World Cup in Canada, Mexico and the United States, losing only one of 10 games as they topped their group under Addo, Queiroz could reasonably claim he was hamstrung by multiple withdrawals ahead of his first Afcon qualifiers.

Six players named in the original squad, including Antoine Semenyo, Mohammed Kudus, Jordan Ayew and Baba Rahman, dropped out, followed subsequently by some of those called up as replacements.

Hughton hopes it is a situation which is not repeated - and which was not caused by the uncertainty around Queiroz's position.

"Whether that was a reason or not, I don't know. And I probably don't think so," he stated.

"You always want your best players and it's always a concern to the level of the group when you have so many players pull out.

"There isn't too much you can do about that [and] you have to work around that."

With the team's chances of reaching next year's AFCON in East Africa in serious peril, a lot rests on the shoulders of interim coach Bjorkegren.

As Ghana's long wait for a first continental title since 1982 continues, finding some long-term stability in the Black Stars' coaching set-up would be a good first step.

*Chris Hughton was speaking to BBC Sport Africa at the Best of Africa Awards

Ghana News.title: Lecturer’s bid to challenge FIFA president Infantino
Ghana News.content:
University lecturer Peter Auf der Heyde is launching an ambitious bid to challenge Gianni Infantino for the FIFA presidency.

The former journalist and football club owner is seeking nomination to challenge the incumbent Infantino, and wants to be paid just $1 (75p) per year if he wins the role.

South African Auf der Heyde lectures in journalism at Southampton Solent University and previously served as sports editor at Germany's Deutsche Presse-Agentur (dpa).

He was president of the Grahamstown Soccer Association in South Africa and both owned and managed second-division side UDW FC in the early 1990s.

"I feel very strongly that there needs to be a challenge in any election," Auf der Heyde told BBC Radio Solent.

"There should not be an uncontested election, and in this case Infantino needs to be challenged. It's important for accountability and transparency."

For Auf der Heyde to challenge Infantino in the March 2027 election, he will need to be nominated by five football associations.

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is also considering standing against the current president, who faced calls to stand down following a controversial plan to sell off stakes in the governing body's competitions to private investors.

Infantino insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, and laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning his position.

He is seeking a fourth and final term but faces competition from Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association, and former Tottenham Hotspur and Switzerland defender Ramon Vega.

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino is 18 November.

"I'm not asking for countries to vote for me, I'm asking for them to nominate me," added Auf der Heyde.

"Once you have a nomination and become an official candidate, you can then ask questions [to other candidates] that you can't ask otherwise.

"Infantino earned around $6m (£4.49m) last year, which I think is ridiculous. I would suggest that $450,000 (£337,259) is a very adequate salary, and in my case I would ask to be paid $1 per year, and after four years, if I have maintained my promises, then I can get the remaining money."

'Emerging nations World Cup' part of manifesto

Auf der Heyde revealed that so far he has written to all 211 of Fifa's member associations, with replies already from the Jamaican and English Football Associations.

He broke down his manifesto for the role into three sections, with a key part of that being a new global competition for smaller footballing nations.

Only 48 nations qualify for the men's World Cup finals every four years with 163 missing out.

"I'd like to see an emerging nations World Cup," said Auf der Heyde, who covered 13 consecutive Africa Cup of Nations as a journalist.

"This would be for countries like Eswatini, Andorra and San Marino, who will quite frankly never qualify for the World Cup.

"They should be allowed in my view to play for a global competition where only these kind of countries have a chance to play.

"It would be wonderful if winning teams from that competition could then qualify further for the World Cup."

Ghana News.title: Kompany back at Bayern training after collapse
Ghana News.content:
Head coach Vincent Kompany has returned to Bayern Munich's training ground after collapsing at the end of last month.

The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train.

Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Bayern said in a statement: "Vincent Kompany is on the road to recovery and has been back at the training ground since the start of the week."

However, the Bundesliga leaders did not hold a training session, with most players away on international duty.

English coach Aaron Danks has taken charge during Kompany's absence, leading Bayern to four wins and a draw.

They face Cologne next on 20 November, after the two-week international break ends.

Ghana News.title: Wenger considers standing against Infantino
Ghana News.content:
Arsene Wenger (left) joined Fifa as chief of global football development in 2019

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is considering standing against Gianni Infantino as a candidate in FIFA's presidential election.

For weeks, senior figures in European football have been hoping the Frenchman would run for the job, and he is now giving it serious thought.

Wenger is 77, leading to questions over whether he could provide long-term leadership for the sport.

But some of his supporters have told BBC Sport that they would be happy for him to win the election, then stand down before serving a full four-year term.

Infantino's position was plunged into crisis by a backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

But he retains support in South America, Africa and Asia, and recently insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

However, that support could be tested if Wenger stands.

FIFA's head of global development would have the backing of UEFA, which has spearheaded opposition to Infantino, and he has credibility throughout the footballing world.

Sources close to Wenger say he is yet to decide whether to stand, and they still believe Infantino is favourite to win a fourth and final term in next year's election.

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November.

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.

Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.

This month Fifa said "key documents" relating to Infantino's plan to sell stakes in the World Cup would be made available to members of its council, but they will have to travel to its Zurich base, and access will be under "strict protocols".

Last month UEFA gave football's world governing body until 2 November to release details about the controversial FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and to answer questions relating to its decision-making.

That followed a council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the abandoned sell-off plot but failed to explain how the proposal was devised, asking that questions be submitted in writing.

Amid the fallout over FFE, Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said at the time.

"The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent FIFA that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."

Wenger has caused controversy at times in his FIFA role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups and a "daylight" offside law.

But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.

Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received on the continent.

Ghana News.title: Ghana’s next oil bet: Can the Voltaian Basin end the country’s dependence on offshore fields?
Ghana News.content:
The Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) says a rig could be on site by the end of the year. The big question is what happens to Ghana’s oil industry if the three main fields decline, and whether a basin drilled only once in 50 years can help.

Ghana’s oil story has so far been written almost entirely at sea. Jubilee, TEN and Sankofa, the three fields that carry the country’s oil output, are all offshore. Now the national oil company wants to try something different: drilling on land.

At the 2026 Petroleum Commission Local Content Conference, GNPC’s Chief Executive, Kwame Ntow Amoah, said the first piece of well equipment, the conductor casing, has already arrived at the drilling site. The company hopes to finalise its contracts and get a rig there by the end of the year. His reason was blunt: “It is simply too risky to depend on Jubilee, TEN, and Sankofa alone.”

The place GNPC is looking at is the Voltaian Basin. Think of it as a huge underground bowl of rock that may hold oil and gas. It covers about 103,600 square kilometres, roughly 40 percent of Ghana’s land area.

The idea is not new. Geologists began mapping the basin between 1957 and 1969. Soviet teams later drilled at Buipe and found oil and gas shows. In the 1970s, Shell collected seismic data, which works like an underground ultrasound, and drilled a well called Premuase-1 in 1974. After that, the basin went quiet for about 30 years, with only studies and promotions. GNPC began a structured exploration programme in 2005.

GNPC’s 2025 annual report shows how much has been done since then. A gravity survey of the whole basin is complete. Over 6,000 line-km of 2D seismic data has been collected, along with 1,539 soil and rock samples. About US$160 million has been committed, and three exploration licences have been awarded. The report also points to four old boreholes with bitumen shows and two confirmed natural oil seepages, which GNPC says are signs of “an active and working petroleum system”.

But these are hints, not proof. Nobody knows yet whether there is enough oil to produce profitably, and only a well can answer that. The planned well will be the first drilled in the basin in over five decades, and the CEO admits it could come back empty. “Exploration carries uncertainty, but the knowledge and capabilities we build will endure whatever the drilling outcome is,” he said.

That is why the project matters even before any discovery. It is a test of GNPC itself. Richard Ellimah, former PIAC chair and natural resource governance analyst, says that if it succeeds, it would be “the first oil well whose development will be led by our own national oil company”, apart from the decommissioned Saltpond Field. He believes it would show “the readiness of GNPC to take over the upstream petroleum industry”.

It could also change who earns the money. Mr Ellimah argues that in a successful Voltaian operation, Ghana would be the major shareholder for the first time in a significant oil project, so the returns to the national purse would be significant. GNPC’s own engineers would run the field, with no need to depend on foreign expertise.

But, the US$160 million committed so far is only the start, because drilling is expensive. Mr Ellimah says GNPC can raise funds on international markets and is exploring strategic partnerships, though partners usually expect a share of the rewards.

Timing is also unclear. The annual report targets the well for the fourth quarter of 2026, but the CEO’s latest remarks only promise that a rig will be mobilised by the end of the year. Drilling itself could slip into 2027.

Beyond the drilling itself, the project invites a bigger conversation about the future of GNPC. Mr Ellimah suggests listing it on the Ghana Stock Exchange in the long term, so ordinary Ghanaians can own a share. He also suggests it to diversify beyond petroleum and mining, as national oil companies in Indonesia, Saudi Arabia and Brazil have done in areas such as real estate, airlines, shipping and refining. He says this matters because the global energy transition could hurt oil and gas investment over time. Finally, he wants the state to reduce its political influence so GNPC can operate as a purely commercial entity.

Some of this is already moving. Mr Amoah says GNPC is working with the Energy Minister on new subsidiaries for oil and gas trading and shared services, with a possible path to listing on the Ghana Stock Exchange.

The Voltaian Basin is not a sure thing. If the well finds oil, Ghana could gain a second source of petroleum, onshore and under national control. The real test is whether GNPC can run a major project on its own, on time and on budget.

Ghana News.title: Spending cuts delaying benefits of economic stability – Bokpin
Ghana News.content:
Economics professor Godfred Alufar Bokpin says Ghana’s reliance on spending cuts to stabilise the economy is delaying the benefits Ghanaians expect from improving economic indicators.

Speaking on JoyNews’ PM Express on Tuesday, he said the government had made progress. But its approach was squeezing demand while leaving infrastructure constraints unresolved.

“If you choose that approach, you will get the result, but the impact will not be felt by Ghanaians.”

Prof Bokpin said the 2026 Budget remained heavily focused on fiscal consolidation, with expenditure cuts central to the effort. This followed a similar approach in 2025.

He warned that a country with major infrastructure gaps needed spending to unlock growth.

“So, for a country that is saddled with a huge infrastructure deficit, imposing restrictions on the growth drivers of the economy, such a country cannot celebrate extensive austerity expenditure cuts.”

His comments come ahead of the 2027 Budget, scheduled for presentation on Thursday, November 12. The government says its proposed New Economy programme will shift attention to investment, production and jobs.

The Minority in Parliament has questioned how government will finance the proposed $10 billion programme. It is demanding a detailed funding plan and accountability for earlier commitments under the 24-Hour Economy initiative.

For Prof Bokpin, the challenge is how stabilisation translates into daily relief.

“You cool the economy. You are shrinking aggregate demand as a way of also bringing inflation down, rather than expanding the economy's severe or restricted supply capacity.”

He used difficult journeys between Accra and Kumasi to illustrate the gap between economic figures and lived experience.

“If somebody is spending nine to 12 hours to travel from here to Kumasi, inflation of 5.2% means nothing to that person.”

He said the policy approach explained why improvements would take time to reach households.

“It's simply because the approach we have adopted in restoring macroeconomic stability is going to take a while to reflect in the lives of Ghanaians.”

Despite his concerns, Prof Bokpin credited government with progress on inflation, interest rates and currency stability.

He said restoring macroeconomic stability was the administration’s stated objective for its first two years. The approach also aligned with the IMF’s stabilisation programme.

“I would say they've done quite well in restoring macroeconomic stability.”

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
