World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: French far-right author Zemmour launches second presidential bid
World.content:
Zemmour wants to kick out ‘foreign unemployed people’ after last month’s violent protests.

French far-right Eric Zemmour, known for his anti-Islam and anti-immigrant stance, says he’ll be standing in next year’s presidential election.

“I can confirm to you that I will indeed be ⁠a candidate in the presidential election”, Zemmour told TF1 TV, adding that he was running to “keep a France that is French”.

Zemmour, a 68-year-old Jewish author and veteran television commentator, finished fourth in the 2022 presidential election.

This time, he says he wants to expel foreign offenders who are in prison, as well as “foreign unemployed people who have been out of work for more than six months”, even if they are legal residents.

He says he wants “two million fewer immigrants” in France, who are seen by many among the far right as key instigators of violence during last month’s student-led cost of living protests.

Last month’s violence has led to the soaring popularity of frontrunner Marine Le Pen, with whom Zemmour will be competing against in April 2027.

Le Pen, who is the leader of the far-right National Rally party, is widely projected to win the election to replace Emmanuel Macron, who will end his term as president of France.

Meanwhile, far-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon of the France Unbowed party, who has been accused of encouraging the unrest, unveiled his programme on Saturday to some 17,000 supporters.

World.title: Russia expels Moldovan diplomat in tit-for-tat move
World.content:
Relations between Moscow and Chisinau have worsened since the 2022 Ukraine war.

Russia has expelled a Moldovan diplomat in retaliation for Chisinau’s expulsion of a Russian embassy employee over the crash of a drone in Moldova.

Russia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said on Tuesday that it had summoned Moldova’s ambassador, Lilian Darii, and informed him that a member of the Moldovan embassy’s staff had been declared unacceptable “on the basis of the principle of reciprocity”.

“A strong protest was lodged with the ambassador after the Moldovan authorities on October 23 declared an employee of the Russian embassy in Chisinau persona non grata,” the ministry said in a statement.

It said Moldova’s decision was made “under the formal pretext of the alleged discovery on the territory of the republic of debris of an unmanned aerial vehicle carrying explosives”, calling it “another unfriendly step”.

The ministry said the “true goal” of the move was “to further undermine the centuries-long history of Russian-Moldovan relations”.

‘Crashed near homes’

Last month, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said a “Russian attack drone” had violated the country’s airspace and “crashed near homes and an energy facility”.

Moldova then declared a staff member of the Russian embassy “persona non grata”.

Drones have penetrated Moldovan territory on multiple occasions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Since then, Russia’s relations with former Soviet states, such as Moldova, have hit an all-time low, compounded by the push by some of those states to join the European Union.



On Sunday, Moldova officially launched a new power line connecting the country to neighbouring Romania and the European grid to reduce its dependence on Russian energy.

The 400-kilovolt extra-high-voltage line, which runs from the city of Vulcanesti to Chisinau, allows Moldova to cut reliance on the Cuciurgan thermal power plant in Transnistria.

Other European-aligned states in the Black Sea region say they are experiencing renewed attacks allegedly carried out by Moscow, such as a drone strike that sank a cargo ship off Romania’s Black Sea coast in October.

World.title: US House Republicans reject effort to impeach Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth
World.content:
Defence Secretary has been accused of spearheading war on Iran without required congressional approval.

Republicans in the United States House of Representatives have nixed an effort to advance the impeachment of Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, following a midterm election in which voters vented frustrations over the Iran war Hegseth has helped spearhead.

The lower house of the US Congress voted in favour of a motion to refer the impeachment charges to the Republican-led House Judiciary Committee in a procedural vote on Tuesday, effectively killing an effort to remove Hegseth from his position led by Republican Representative Thomas Massie.

That push also won support from Democratic representatives, setting up a test of whether Republican lawmakers would break with the Trump administration and distance themselves from the unpopular war after a rebuke at the polls.

The final vote on Tuesday was 211 in favour and 204 against, with Massie the lone Republican to vote against it. The result means that Republicans will be able to slow-walk the process and can avoid a direct vote on the eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, which cover issues such as the Iran war.

“The Democrats’ attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!” Trump said in a social media post following the vote. “Every single Republican, except Thomas Massie, a major LOSER, voted in favour of Pete.”

Regardless of the outcome of Tuesday’s vote, an impeachment conviction in the US Senate, where it would require a two-thirds vote and Republicans have a 53-seat majority, was seen as unlikely.

‘Farce’

Massie’s resolution included eight separate articles of impeachment, accusing the combative Pentagon chief of launching an illegal war against Iran without congressional approval and overseeing a campaign of strikes targeting alleged drug trafficking vessels that legal scholars say are extrajudicial killings.



Hegseth has denounced the resolution as “sabotage” and a “farce”, while US President Donald Trump and prominent members of his administration expressed their continued support for him.

Speculation about Hegseth’s position within the administration has circulated as polls suggest that voters partly blame the war for surging prices of goods such as gasoline and groceries, and has grown stronger after Republicans faced punishing losses in the midterm elections.

“Is he being truthful in the way the war is going?” outgoing Republican Senator Joni Ernst said of Hegseth on Tuesday.

World.title: UNIFIL patrol comes under fire in southern Lebanon
World.content:
UNIFIL said on Tuesday that ‘about a dozen rounds’ were fired at one of its patrols, without identifying the assailants.

Share UNIFIL patrol comes under fire in southern Lebanon on social media

A United Nations peacekeeping force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) patrol has come under fire in southern Lebanon, the force said.

UNIFIL said on Tuesday that “about a dozen rounds” were fired at one of its patrols near Wadi Jilu, in Lebanon’s Tyre district, without specifying the entity behind the shooting.

The patrol returned fire, after which the shooting stopped. UNIFIL reported no casualties and called for an investigation.

“We reiterate the obligation under international law for all actors to ensure the safety and security of UN personnel and property at all times. Deliberate attacks on peacekeepers are violations of Security Council resolution 1701 and international humanitarian law,” UNIFIL said.

Security limbo

UNIFIL is a peacekeeping mission established by the UN Security Council in March 1978, days after Israel invaded Lebanon.

The force has acted as a buffer between Israel and Lebanon ever since, but its presence has been unable to prevent several rounds of conflict, including the latest between Israel and Hezbollah.

Israel continues to occupy swaths of southern Lebanon, despite a so-called ceasefire and a US-brokered framework agreement through which the Israeli military would withdraw from those areas and the Lebanese army would move in to disarm Hezbollah.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday that the G7 foreign ministers agreed on “the need to avoid a security void” in Lebanon after the UNIFIL mandate expires at the end of 2026.

The foreign ministers backed “the need to move quickly toward a new security architecture”, Barrot said after the group met in Paris.



However, the French foreign minister acknowledged that there had been no breakthrough regarding replacing UNIFIL, which comprises some 7,500 personnel from nearly 50 countries.

The UN Security Council last year voted, under US pressure, to end UNIFIL’s mandate on December 31, 2026. Lebanese officials have called for the mandate to be extended.

World.title: US poll shows death penalty lost majority support for first time since 1971
World.content:
Support for capital punishment has been declining in the US for years over concerns such as fairness and racial bias.

A new Gallup poll has found that support for the death penalty in the United States has fallen below 50 percent, marking the first time that the controversial practice has lost majority support since 1971.

The poll released on Tuesday found that 49 percent of people said they are in favour of capital punishment for those convicted of murder, the lowest level since 1966, while 45 percent say they are opposed.

“While statistically similar to last year’s 52 percent, the latest update marks the first time support has been below the majority level since 1971, when it was also at 49 percent,” Gallup said in a statement.

Support for the death penalty has been declining for decades amid concerns about issues of fairness, racial bias, high costs, botched executions and the possibility of innocent people being put to death. Decades of scholarship have also cast doubt on the argument that capital punishment deters crime.

Age, party divide

The latest Gallup poll found stark divides by age and partisan affiliation. While 54 percent of people aged 50 and older support the death penalty, that figure drops to just 39 percent for those younger the age of 30.

About 73 percent of Republicans are in favour, compared with 50 percent for independents and 28 percent for Democrats.

But all of those groups have seen support decline over the last three decades, dropping by 11 points for Republicans, 29 points for independents, and 47 points for Democrats since 1994, during the heyday of tough-on-crime politics in the US.



In that period, a punitive approach to criminal justice embraced by both parties transformed the US into one of the most prolific jailers on the planet and saw an increase in the number of crimes that qualified for execution.

A debate about the legacy of the policies championed during that era, including the death penalty, has been pushed forward by protests for racial justice in recent years.

While 27 US states still have the death penalty, 23 have done away with the practice and four have paused it through executive action, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit research group.

Rise in federal executions

Many states that still have capital punishment on the books have gone years without carrying out an execution, and lengthy appeals processes have meant that many prisoners spend years or even decades on death row.

President Donald Trump has been an exception to the move away from capital punishment, overseeing a massive increase in federal executions during his first term in office and promising to continue using it during his second.

The prevalence of botched executions, such as that of Christa Pike via failed lethal injection in the state of Tennessee last month, has also raised questions about whether the practice violates the constitutional prohibition on cruel and unusual punishment.

World.title: IBM’s biggest division ends most US foreign worker sponsorships
World.content:
United States technology giant IBM has said it will stop sponsoring US foreign worker visas and green cards for most roles in its largest division.

A company spokesperson told Reuters on Tuesday that its consultancy unit had opted to end sponsorship for most roles.

The company said its participation in US high-skilled visa programmes had been declining for years, adding that the decision came “as skill availability and client needs have evolved”.

IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 of IBM’s 264,300-strong global workforce.

IBM has become less reliant on so-called H-1B visas for highly skilled foreign workers in recent years. Only 1,611 H-1B petitions were approved for the company in fiscal year 2026, according to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services.

The announcement comes as the Trump administration has increased pressure on major companies to cut down on their highly skilled foreign workforce in the US. US President Donald Trump has claimed the programme is often subject to fraud and takes work away from skilled Americans and gives it to immigrants.

Last year, the administration announced it would require a one-time $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions.

The administration said in October it was suspending a number of tech companies from a programme that allows H-1B workers to apply for green cards, saying it was cracking down on fraud and ensuring American workers were not being laid off and replaced by foreigners.

The suspended companies included Adobe and top H-1B employers Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services and Microsoft.



The suspensions were announced within hours of Trump honouring Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.

India-born Nadella was one of six business leaders honoured by Trump. Five were foreign-born US citizens, including Tesla boss Elon Musk, who was born in South Africa, and Google co-founder Sergey Brin, who immigrated from Russia with his family as a child.

World.title: 2026 Midterms: Blue wave or anti-establishment backlash?
World.content:
Emma Vigeland and Olivia Troye join Josh Rushing to discuss the fallout of the 2026 midterm elections.

The midterms are over, and Democrats have scored a decisive victory, exceeding even their most optimistic expectations. But does this result signal a country turning blue – or a country simply fed up with the status quo? And how much of this was a rejection of a system, rather than an endorsement of the Democratic Party?

Josh Rushing is joined by Emma Vigeland, cohost of The Majority Report, and Olivia Troye, who served as a national security adviser to former Vice President Mike Pence, to unpack the results and what they reveal about the state of American politics.

Contributors:

Emma Vigeland – Cohost, The Majority Report

Olivia Troye – Former national security adviser to Mike Pence

World.title: White House announces funds for law enforcement programme in several cities
World.content:
Trump administration awarded more than $60m each to St Louis, Missouri, and Jackson, Mississippi, in crime push.

The administration of United States President Donald Trump has said that it will award the cities of St Louis, Missouri, and Jackson, Mississippi, more than $60m each to expand law enforcement resources as part of a bid to combat violent crime.

The White House stated in a social media post on Tuesday that the so-called “Model Cities Initiative” would help the municipalities increase their capacity for prosecutions and policing activities.

“The Model Cities Initiative reflects the Trump Administration’s commitment to reducing crime across the country and ensuring the safety of every American,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release describing the programme last month.

The initiative has said that it will distribute nearly $300m for such efforts among the cities of St Louis and Jackson, along with Jacksonville, Florida, and Baton Rouge, Louisiana.

The Trump administration has promoted a largely punitive approach to combatting crime in cities across the country, including controversial steps such as the deployment of the National Guard to large, Democrat-led cities that have drawn accusations of executive overreach, civil liberties violations and political intimidation.

While Trump and his supporters have credited their policies with a drop in violent crime, that trend predates his return to office and has taken place in cities with a wide variety of approaches towards criminal justice across the country.

Homicides in St Louis, for example, have been falling for several years after a brief surge during the COVID-19 pandemic, and hit their lowest levels in more than a decade during the first half of 2026.



While Democratic officials have denounced Trump’s crackdowns, some Republican-led states have embraced them.

The government deployed members of several federal agencies to the city of Memphis, Tennessee, governed by Democrats at the local level but located in a Republican-led state.

The Trump administration has touted that effort as an inspiration for the Model Cities Initiative along with other cases, such as Washington, DC.

The government has hailed the Memphis deployment as a success, but some residents and civil liberties groups have accused the task force of widespread civil rights violations and excessive force.

A video released earlier this month as part of an investigation into a shooting by a member of the Tennessee National Guard, deployed in Memphis as part of Trump’s task force, showed the soldiers aiming their guns at a man as he lay dying on the street after being shot in the back.

World.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
World.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

The BBC has contacted his representatives.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

Markle has called the allegations "sick lies".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

World.title: Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions
World.content:
Malaysia's disgraced former Prime Minister Najib Razak has arrived home to begin serving the rest of a jail sentence for corruption under house arrest.

There was a big media presence at his Kuala Lumpur residence to see the 73-year-old return from prison in an SUV late on Tuesday night, escorted by a heavily armed police convoy.

Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund.

The 1MDB scandal brought down his government and made headlines around the world when it came to light a decade ago, embroiling prominent figures from Malaysia to Goldman Sachs and Hollywood.

Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (Â£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors.

Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large.

World.title: Israel's new parliament sworn in as leaders compete to form government
World.content:
Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together.

Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension.

Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats.

Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other.

"[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties.

He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran".

Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments.

"I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute."

The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months.

One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.

The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition.

World.title: Violence erupts in Bangladesh as ousted PM's supporters stage protest
World.content:
Traffic was disrupted in some parts of the country as protesters tried to set up roadblocks using burning tyres.

Several passenger vehicles were also set on fire in various parts of Bangladesh in the run up to the protest.

A 60-year-old driver of a passenger bus was killed by smoke inhalation after people set fire to the vehicle in the city of Faridpur early on Tuesday.

Elsewhere, about 200 protesters briefly blocked traffic on the 6.2km (4 mile)-long Padma bridge across the Ganges, that connects the capital Dhaka with the south-western region.

Bangladeshi local media said dozens of crude bombs exploded in the past few days in Dhaka and elsewhere.

"Any attempt to worsen the law-and-order situation or create instability through any conspiracy within the country from across the border (India) will not be allowed to succeed," Bangladesh Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said.

"Our supporters were not responsible for the violent incidents. They were carried out by unknown miscreants. We believe in peaceful protests," a senior leader of the BCL, who is now in exile in a foreign country, said.

Hasina fled to neighbouring India two years ago following a massive uprising, bringing an end to her 15-year reign.

Opposition parties accused Hasina of jailing political rivals, supressing dissent and overseeing widespread human rights abuses. She always denied the charges.

World.title: Spain's king and queen attend memorial service for rail crash victims
World.content:
Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia were among those who have attended a memorial service in tribute to the 69 victims of last month's deadly train crash.

The accident occurred when one train, travelling at high speed, ploughed into the back of another that was stationary on the Madrid-Seville line, near the small town of Urda, about 40 miles from Toledo.

It was the worst rail tragedy in Spain since 2013. Twenty-eight people remain in hospital.

"The tragic accident in Urda has left our families, our towns and our society with a pain that is difficult to accept," Archbishop Cerro Chaves told those present.

Representatives of those killed carried lit candles to the front of the cathedral and placed them next to the main altar. The first reading of the service was by Ana BenÃ­tez, sister of David BenÃ­tez, a 38-year-old father-of-two who died.

The king and queen were met with applause by bystanders as they entered the cathedral and at the end of the service, after Catholic Mass, they spoke to relatives of the victims.

Senior politicians also attended the service, including the leader of the opposition People's Party, Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano GarcÃ­a-Page, and Transport and Economy Minister Carlos Cuerpo.

Cuerpo took on the transport portfolio following the resignation last week of Ãscar Puente from the post.

World.title: Anti-homosexuality laws in Trinidad and Tobago overturned
World.content:
A UK court has overturned laws criminalising same-sex intimacy in Trinidad and Tobago.

London's Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC), the Caribbean island's final court of appeal, ruled the laws were not in keeping with the "fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life."

The judgement is the result of an 11-year legal battle brought by dual-citizen Jason Jones, 62, who said he hoped it would "accelerate the fight for full equality."

Jones had successfully challenged the laws in 2018 in Trinidad's High Court, however the ruling was overturned on appeal by the Trinidadian government.

It is the first time the JCPC has ever decided on a case to decriminalise same-sex intimacy, and campaigners hope it will spark similar successful legal challenges elsewhere in the Commonwealth.

Prior to this historic decision, Trinidad and Tobago was one of some 34 Commonwealth countries continuing to criminalise homosexuality based on colonial-era British laws.

Under these laws, consensual same-sex intimacy is punishable by imprisonment, and in some cases carries the death penalty.

The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago had argued that the law was protected from legal challenges by the "savings law clauses" - which carried over existing British laws into newly independent states.

Representatives for Jones argued that the laws violated an individual's right to privacy and argued the government's changes to the laws in 1986 - which saw stricter punishments introduced - meant the savings clause protections no longer applied.

The judicial committee unanimously found in favour of Jones.

Handing down the judgement, Lord Sales told the court the laws "cannot be regarded as reasonably justifiable in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual".

Jones, human rights campaigner and appellant in the appeal, said: "These laws never reflected who we are as a people and a nation - diverse, multiracial, and secular.

"They told LGBTQ+ people that we were criminals in our own country. That message ends today."

Lawyer Anand Ramlogan SC, representing Jones, said the judgement was a "landmark victory for gay rights, equal dignity and respect for private and family life in Trinidad and Tobago."

World.title: Board of Peace says Israel's aid response after Gaza floods 'insufficent'
World.content:
In rare criticism of Israel, the Board of Peace said it had been urging the Israeli government to authorise the entry of essential goods for temporary shelter and water and sanitation infrastructure.

The Board added that delays in approving the entry of supplies "exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge" and delayed the start of decommissioning weapons and transferring Hamas authority to a transitional government.

It also said Hamas's failure to disarm and transfer power had compounded the difficulties facing Gaza's civilians.

The UN's humanitarian agency OCHA said more than 150,000 tents were outside Gaza ready to go in, but aid efforts were constrained "by Israeli restrictions on the entry of supplies and equipment and funding shortfalls".

UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov said on Monday that stocks of essential shelter and winter items inside Gaza had been exhausted.

"Israeli authorities must immediately lift all restrictions on entry of the supplies," he said, adding "we have run out of time".

Israel's foreign ministry spokeswoman Michal Maayan on Monday said Israel had in recent months put in place a winter plan in coordination with the Board of Peace and international charities.

That plan has brought in more than 91,000 tents and 8,200-plus trucks with tarpaulins, blankets, winter clothing, and other equipment, according to Cogat, the Israeli military body responsible for aid.

Cogat said it would not allow in equipment that could be used for military purposes.

Maayon accused Hamas of hoarding aid, saying: "Hamas is responsible for the delays in making more progress in the Strip, and winter-related hardships are a consequence of Hamas's action and policy."

In response to the Board of Peace, Hamas said in a statement published on Palestinian media that its comment "presents a distorted account of the causes of the disaster". The group denied it was responsible for ceasefire delays, pointing to a statement in August , externalfrom Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators that accused Israel of violations.

Hamas said Israeli restrictions prevent the entry of materials necessary for shelter and recovery - and added the Board as the ceasefire implementor should look at its own "serious shortcoming".

Under the deal to end the two-year-long war in October 2025, Hamas agreed to give up governance and its weapons in exchange for a phased Israeli troop withdrawal from the 60% of Gaza it still occupied. Israel, however, has insisted Hamas must fully disarm before withdrawal.

The dispute has left the next stages of the peace plan stalled, with both sides blaming each other.

The war in Gaza began after the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 when around 1,200 people were killed and 251 others taken hostage.

The Israeli military campaign in response has killed 74,645 people, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures the UN considers reliable. More than 1,600 people have been killed since the ceasefire in October last year.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza since then.

World.title: First day of Ukraine peace talks constructive, Zelensky says
World.content:
The first of two days of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.

While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions, President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved "constructive and quite substantive".

Speaking from Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said the meeting had been "very productive".

Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.

Zelensky also said that humanitarian issues such as prisoner of war exchanges had been discussed.

At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".

Kushner had said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.

Asked later at a news conference in Copenhagen about the approach of US officials to negotiations, Zelensky said: "I see changes. I'm very happy with what I hear."

Kushner and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.

Until now European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.

The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".

However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.

Some proposals favoured by EU officials - such as calling an unconditional ceasefire as a prerequisite for peace negotiations - are routinely rejected by Moscow. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that a truce would just allow Kyiv to regroup. "We will not agree to it," he said.

Moscow and Kyiv's positions are still far apart on ending the conflict.

A key area of disagreement involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".

However, he acknowledged the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it comes under attack again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from Eastern Europe â which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

World.title: NHRC records 384,196 human rights violation complaints in October, cases up 13.4%
World.content:
The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) on Tuesday said it recorded 384,196 reports of human rights violations in October across Nigeria, up by 13.4 per cent from the previous month.

The number of cases stood at 338,810 in September.

In October, complaints on the violation of the freedom from discrimination were the highest at 217, 243.

Giving the report at the NHRC’s headquarters in Abuja on Tuesday, the Executive Secretary, Tony Ojukwu, said 180,000 of the 217,243 discrimination cases were from the camps of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs).

He said, “Every complaint is a person, a family, or a community whose rights and dignity need protection.

“Our responsibility is not simply to document these complaints, but to ensure that the information gathered informs appropriate intervention as well as effective remedy.”

He stressed the importance of ensuring that “displacement does not deprive individuals and families of their dignity, security, and access to basic rights.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Across many states, many Nigerians live under poor conditions of the camps of Internally Displaced Persons (IDP) after fleeing their homes over terrorists’ attacks, banditry and other threats of violence.

The complaints by IDPs reflect a systemic rights issue, social marginalisation, institutional neglect, and discriminatory barriers affecting displaced communities in Nigeria.

Complaints due to insecurity

Other issues of concern highlighted in Tuesday’s dashboard include insecurity, reports of killings, armed attacks, and abductions.

The commission’s Human Rights Observatory documented incidents involving attacks on farming communities, travellers, women, traditional leaders, and security personnel, particularly concerning their reports of mass killings and abductions in parts of Taraba, Borno, Zamfara, Niger, and Plateau State, among other locations.

Mr Ojukwu stressed that the reported incidents are not merely security concerns but also concern issues with “direct humanitarian implications.”

He said, “They affect the right to life, liberty, and dignity, and security of the person. They disrupt livelihoods, restrict freedom of movement, and expose children and mothers.

“The commission reiterates that the protection of lives and property is an environmental responsibility of the state.”

Mr Ojukwu also encouraged political actors to exercise restraint and conduct themselves within the ambit of electoral laws and human rights.

As the 2027 elections draw near, “we should not lose focus on the fact that elections, voting process and outcomes reflect the interplay of various human rights.”

Dashboard details

Senior Human Rights Adviser to the NHRC, Hilary Ogbonna, noted that the human rights complaints recorded by the commission in 2026 have crossed the 2.5 million mark.

The commission recorded 116,739 complaints from the North Central, 65,309 from the South West, 63,120 from the North West, 50,902 from the South South, 49,618 from the North East, and 38,508 from the South East.

The FCT, Lagos, Benue, Kaduna, Borno, Plateau, Kano, Rivers, Imo and Niger were among the top ten states with the highest violation complaints. This is the first time Lagos and Rivers are among the top ten states in 2026.

Mr Ogbonna attributed this to the tension with the upcoming elections, particularly in Rivers State.

The 10 states accounted for 52 per cent of the entire complaints recorded in October.

Women’s right violations

The commission recorded 632 complaints of women denied access to children, 591 abandonment, 339 trafficking and 376 forced marriages.

Mr Ogbonna noted an upsurge in men abandoning their wives.

“Month after month, we try to ask ourselves, even in the commission, what could be the reason for this. It’s not our mandate to go and look for white men abandoning their marriages, but when it becomes a human rights issue, it gives us cause for worry,” he said.

Six rapes, 18 sexual violence incidents, and 1,873 domestic violence incidents were recorded in the month under focus. According to Mr Ogbonna, they each represent a woman who has been given a permanent scar.

Child rights violations

Similarly, child abandonment in October rose by over 250 per cent to 2,479, with Mr Ogbonna describing the trend as a human rights breach.

Also, 2,093 children were forced into marriage, 2,141 cases of sexual abuse, 2,581 were denied their rights to education, and 1,681 were trafficked.

Cases resolved

Among the entire figures recorded in October, the NHRC resolved 1,455 cases.

The commission also visited 108 places of detention, five military formations and summoned the police 45 times.

World.title: Court orders forfeiture of two Mercedes-Benz cars, phones linked to convicted fraudster
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Lagos has ordered the final forfeiture of two luxury Mercedes-Benz vehicles, four electronic devices and other properties linked to a convicted internet fraudster, Ifeanyi Arinze.

Judge Yellim Bogoro made the order on Monday after considering an application by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC).

“The vehicles include a white Mercedes-Benz GLE 53 AMG and a grey Mercedes-Benz GLC 300 AMG, while the electronic devices comprise an orange iPhone 17 Pro Max, a silver Samsung Fold 7, a blue iPhone 13 and a silver iPad,” according to a statement issued on Tuesday by the EFCC Head of Media and Publicity, Dele Oyewale.

According to the statement, the court had earlier granted an interim forfeiture order on 17 July. It directed the EFCC to publish the order in a national newspaper.

The publication was intended to give any interested person or organisation an opportunity to explain why the properties should not be permanently forfeited.

When the commission’s lawyer, C. C. Okezie, moved the application for final forfeiture on Monday, she told the court that the EFCC had complied with the directive.

She ordered the commission to publish the interim forfeiture order in The Guardian newspaper on 16 September 2026.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ms Okezie also informed the court that no interested person or organisation had come forward to challenge the forfeiture.

After considering the application and affidavit evidence, Judge Bogoro granted the application and ordered the final forfeiture of the properties to the Federal Government.

Proceeds of fraudulent activities

The commission alleged in the statement that the properties “were reasonably suspected to have been acquired with proceeds of unlawful activities.”

EFCC to file the application through its lawyer, Ms Okezie.

In a supporting affidavit accompanying EFCC’s forfeiture application, an EFCC operative, Buluebiere Karamo, stated that the commission received intelligence alleging that Mr Arinze led a syndicate of fraudsters operating in Lagos.

The EFCC alleged that he used the identity “Tonya” on iMessage to contact several victims in the United States. He allegedly instructed them to create foreign financial accounts, including Zelle, Apple Pay, PayPal, Cash App and Venmo.

The victims were then allegedly directed to transfer funds received through those accounts to a Chinese national identified as “Chinko Applepay”.

The Chinese national allegedly credited Mr Arinze’s Kuda Bank account with the naira equivalent of the funds. He then transferred the money to other members of the syndicate and retained 10 per cent as commission, according to the EFCC.

The commission maintained that an analysis of his Kuda Bank account allegedly revealed total inflows of N2,149,495,381.42 between August 2022 and February 2026.

“Further investigation revealed that Arinze operated 49 Gmail accounts, alongside several Facebook and Instagram accounts, which were allegedly used for his fraudulent activities.” the EFCC wrote.

it said arrested Mr Arinze on 20 April 2024 during a sting operation on Remi Olowude Street, Lekki, Lagos. Several other individuals were also arrested.

He was subsequently charged before the Federal High Court on two counts of computer-related fraud.

The EFCC said he pleaded guilty and was convicted on 5 June 2024 by Judge Aneke. The judge ordered him to be of good behaviour and desist from further involvement in cyber-related offences.

However, the commission alleged that he breached the terms of the judgement by continuing to engage in money laundering and computer-related fraud after his conviction and payment of the option of a fine.

The EFCC said it later received fresh intelligence indicating that Mr Arinze had continued his alleged fraudulent activities. This prompted another investigation.

During the investigation, the commission said it traced the properties listed in the forfeiture application to proceeds of fraudulent activities committed after his earlier conviction.

Asset forfeiture

Nigeria’s Proceeds of Crime (Recovery and Management) Act 2022 provides for the recovery and forfeiture of assets reasonably suspected to have come from unlawful activities. The law allows courts to order forfeiture through civil proceedings, separately from criminal prosecutions. This means that an asset can be forfeited even without a criminal conviction against its owner.

The Act provides for a two-stage process. A court first issues an order to preserve the property while interested persons are notified and given an opportunity to challenge the forfeiture.

The court may then grant a final forfeiture order if the evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the property is linked to unlawful activity.

World.title: Stop following Tinubu to rallies, Uzor Kalu tells APC leaders
World.content:
Abia North Senator Orji Uzor Kalu has advised All Progressives Congress (APC) leaders to prioritise grassroots mobilisation ahead of the 2027 general elections instead of accompanying President Bola Tinubu to campaign rallies across the country.

Mr Kalu, a former governor of Abia State, said party leaders should remain in their respective political constituencies to engage voters, strengthen party structures and build support at the ward and local government levels.

The senator, who coordinates parliamentary mobilisation for the South-east, made the recommendation in a statement titled, “The APC Presidential Campaign Council and the Need for a Leaner Campaign Train,” Vanguard newspaper reported on Monday.

He argued that the president should be accompanied by a smaller campaign entourage, while other influential party members concentrate on mobilising support in their political strongholds.

APC adopts grassroots mobilisation strategy

Mr Kalu’s position comes days after the APC Presidential Campaign Council directed ministers, political appointees and members of its campaign council to attend only rallies organised in their respective home states.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that the council issued the directive in a circular dated 3 November and signed by its Director-General, Abdulaziz Yari.

The directive was addressed to directors and heads of directorates within the campaign council and was intended to improve coordination and strengthen grassroots mobilisation ahead of the elections.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The council also adopted a pyramid-style mobilisation strategy that emphasises building political support from polling units through wards and local government areas to the state level.

Under the arrangement, party officials are expected to mobilise voters within their respective jurisdictions rather than concentrate their activities around the president during campaign events.

Kalu cites political mobilisation in Abia

Citing his political activities in Abia, Mr Kalu said effective mobilisation must begin at the ward level, where party leaders have direct access to voters.

He recalled leading more than 4,000 APC members from Igbere Wards A and B in Bende Local Government Area during the party’s presidential primary in May.

According to him, the experience showed the importance of building political structures and consolidating grassroots support.

Mr Kalu maintained that the party’s chances in the 2027 elections would depend largely on its ability to sustain direct engagement with voters across communities.

He stressed that a campaign’s effectiveness should not be measured by the number of political leaders accompanying the president to rallies, but by the strength of the party’s structures and its connection with voters at the grassroots.

Mr Kalu’s comments reinforce the campaign council’s recent directive restricting political appointees and campaign officials to rallies in their home states as the APC begins preparations for the 2027 general elections.

World.title: NNPC, Oando join global push to end gas flaring as Nigeria’s emissions rise
World.content:
The Nigerian National Petroleum Company (NNPC) Limited and Oando are among oil and gas companies committed to ending routine gas flaring by 2030 under a global decarbonisation initiative, even as Nigeria continues to record rising gas-flaring volumes.

The companies are signatories to the Oil and Gas Decarbonisation Charter (OGDC), which on Tuesday released its 2026 Status Report at the ongoing United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye.

The report, released three years after the initiative was launched at COP28 in Dubai, shows that 41 signatory companies now have action plans to eliminate routine gas flaring, representing a 78 per cent increase from the 2024 baseline.

The initiative is particularly noteworthy for Nigeria, one of the world’s largest gas-flaring countries, where regulatory weaknesses and inadequate infrastructure have continued to undermine efforts to reduce emissions from oil and gas operations.

According to the World Bank’s Global Gas Flaring Tracker, Nigeria flared 6.6 billion cubic metres of gas in 2025, compared with 6.1 billion cubic metres in 2024 and 5.1 billion cubic metres in 2023.

The figures indicate that gas flaring in Nigeria has increased for three consecutive years, despite the country’s commitments to eliminate routine flaring by 2030.

The OGDC brings together 57 oil and gas companies operating in more than 100 countries and representing one-third of global oil and gas production.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Its signatories have committed to achieving net-zero operational emissions by or before 2050, near-zero upstream methane emissions and zero routine flaring by 2030.

Beyond NNPC and Oando, other companies with Nigerian operations identified among the charter’s signatories include ExxonMobil, which has its subsidiaries in Nigeria as Esso Exploration and Production Nigeria Limited and Esso Exploration and Production Nigeria (Deepwater) Limited; Shell, through its subsidiary Shell Nigeria Exploration and Production Company (SNEPCo), and TotalEnergies.

Shell also holds a 25.6 per cent interest in Nigeria LNG Limited.

More companies develop emission-reduction plans

The 2026 report indicates increasing participation by companies in emissions monitoring, planning and investment, although progress remains mostly measured through corporate disclosures and commitments.

Of the 56 companies that were members during the reporting period, 52 submitted emissions data, covering 97 per cent of the charter’s operated production.

Four companies reported their operational emissions for the first time, while another national oil company established its emissions baseline and shared data with the initiative for the first time.

The number of companies that have set interim 2030 targets to reduce Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions also rose to 46, up from 42 in the previous reporting year.

Of these, 42 have developed action plans to achieve their emissions-reduction ambitions, representing a 40 per cent increase from the 2024 baseline.

Scope 1 emissions are those generated directly by a company’s operations, including emissions from burning fuel and gas flaring, while Scope 2 emissions arise indirectly from purchased electricity, heating and cooling.

The report also found that 39 companies had developed methane action plans, representing a 63 per cent increase from the 2024 baseline.

Methane is the principal component of natural gas and a potent greenhouse gas. It escapes into the atmosphere through leaks, venting and incomplete combustion during gas flaring.

Billions of dollars committed to decarbonisation

The report also highlighted growing financial commitments to reducing operational emissions.

Thirty-five signatory companies, accounting for 84 per cent of the initiative’s operated production, have allocated capital towards achieving their interim emissions-reduction targets.

Half of these companies said their allocated budgets now cover their entire decarbonisation roadmaps.

In addition, 34 companies reported $28 billion in lower-carbon investments and acquisitions in 2025.

The report also identified improvements in emissions verification, with 39 companies, representing 92 per cent of the initiative’s operated production, having individual third-party verification procedures for their emissions data.

Twenty-one companies now use direct measurement technologies for most of their reported methane emissions, while another 18 use the technologies for some of their reported emissions.

The report said 30 companies also provided the OGDC secretariat with information not currently publicly disclosed, allowing the initiative to assess progress and identify areas needing further support.

Nigeria’s persistent gas-flaring problem

The commitments come against the backdrop of Nigeria’s persistent difficulties in enforcing regulations intended to curb gas flaring and methane emissions.

A PREMIUM TIMES report published on 24 September, titled Inside Nigeria’s methane problem, found that Nigeria’s gas-flaring volumes increased from 5.1 billion cubic metres in 2023 to 6.6 billion cubic metres in 2025.

The investigation attributed the persistent problem to weak regulatory enforcement, inadequate infrastructure and the transfer of environmental liabilities following the divestment of assets by international oil companies to indigenous operators.

It also found that only 15 of the 62 companies covered by the Nigeria Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative‘s (NEITI) first upstream greenhouse gas audit submitted emissions data, while 47 companies did not.

NEITI warned that the poor disclosure rate posed a significant risk to Nigeria’s ability to meet its climate commitments.

A separate PREMIUM TIMES investigation published on 1 September found that oil companies continued to violate gas-flaring regulations without facing corresponding sanctions.

Another investigation published on 12 October examined TotalEnergies’ declaration that it had ended routine gas flaring in Nigeria. PREMIUM TIMES’ analysis of satellite data and observations around the company’s assets identified persistent flare activity despite the company’s claims.

The investigation also showed that TotalEnergies failed to report its methane emissions in Nigeria.

Nigeria’s Petroleum Industry Act and subsequent regulations have established obligations for oil and gas operators to reduce flaring, monitor methane emissions and implement measures to eliminate routine flaring.

However, flaring persists, raising questions about the effectiveness of regulatory enforcement and how well companies are translating climate commitments into measurable reductions.

Bjørn Otto Sverdrup, head of the OGDC secretariat and chair of the Executive Committee of the Oil and Gas Climate Initiative, said the report showed increasing participation in emissions reporting, the development of action plans and the allocation of capital towards decarbonisation.

“Our focus now is to build on that momentum towards delivery,” he said.

He said improved data, practical support, collaboration and technology were helping companies identify emissions sources, prioritise interventions and accelerate decarbonisation.

“With four years to go until 2030, the priority is to get more complete data, scale proven solutions and turn plans into more projects,” he added.

The OGDC said more than 4,000 professionals from signatory companies had participated in its technical workshops and training programmes since the initiative began.

World.title: Zamfara among top 10 best performing states in fiscal viability – BudgIT
World.content:
Zamfara State was ranked among the top 10 states in the Fiscal Viability Index, a new report released by BudgIT has revealed.

The new report titled, “State of States 2026: States ‘ Performance on Pillar B/ Fiscal Viability,” was released on Monday.

This comes days after a renowned economist and former Governor of Nigeria’s Central Bank, Emir Muhammadu Sanusi, said he was impressed with the transformational feats recorded by Governor Dauda Lawal in the last three years in Zamfara State.

The BudgIT report assesses the fiscal performance of 35 Nigerian states in 2025, the organisation said.

“We call this ranking “Fiscal Viability”, but the real name is: Can your state survive without federal handouts?” the organisation said while releasing the report said.

“States that rank higher on the Fiscal Viability pillar demonstrate a comparatively stronger capacity to manage their expenditure obligations within the limits of their available revenue,” BudgIT said in the new report.

The report explained that “True fiscal sustainability means a state can fund its public salaries, overheads and debt obligations from its own pockets, while managing the demands on its total revenue.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

BudgIT is a civic organisation that uses creative technology to simplify public information, stimulate a community of active citizens, and enable their right to demand accountability, institutional reforms, efficient service delivery, and an equitable society.

The new report said Zamfara came in 10th on the Fiscal Viability Index, scoring 74.97 per cent, with Enugu (98.38%) and Bayelsa (88.83%) states clinching the first and second positions.

The report said Zamfara remained the second-least-indebted state in the federation, with a debt per capita of N19,464.

Zamfara is one of the only three states from the northern part of the country that made it to the top 10 positions of the Fiscal Viability Index.

The two other states are Gombe (78.07%) and Niger (76.03%), ranking 7th and 9th positions respectively.

The report also examined how states generated revenue, managed public expenditure, sustained their finances and prioritised spending across critical sectors.

The organisation said the 2026 assessment adopted a revised methodology built around four pillars: revenue performance (40 per cent), fiscal viability (30 per cent), debt sustainability (15 per cent) and spending on selected critical sectors (15 per cent).

It also examined states’ dependence on Federation Account allocations, expenditure patterns, capital investments, debt obligations and fiscal pressures across the federation.

“This edition introduces a revised methodology that gives greater attention to the developmental impact of public spending, with an assessment of expenditure in agriculture, health, education, and water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH),” the report said.

Through its assessment of revenue performance, fiscal viability, debt sustainability and spending in critical sectors, the report provides insights into state governments’ fiscal decisions and how public resources are managed to support development.

In 2025, BudgIT revealed in its 2025 States of the States Report that Zamfara’s fiscal performance recorded a boost from 36th position in 2023 to 17th position in 2025 under Governor Lawal.

The report said Zamfara’s fiscal performance took a 13-step up in its fiscal performance ranking to 17th. It ranked 26th in 2024, the report said.

The state was ranked 36th in 2023 when Governor Lawal took over.

World.title: Court strikes out EFCC’s N6bn money laundering charge against Mompha
World.content:
The Lagos State Special Offences Court in Ikeja has struck out the N6 billion money laundering charge brought by the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) against social media personality Ismaila Mustapha, popularly known as Mompha, and his company, Ismalob Global Investment Limited.

Trial judge Mojisola Dada struck out the charge on Tuesday, ruling that the EFCC’s decision to prosecute the defendants while a related case was pending before the Federal High Court amounted to an abuse of court process.

The judge faulted the commission for pursuing the two cases simultaneously, describing the action as forum shopping.

She also questioned the inclusion of the eighth count in the charge, which she described as an afterthought intended to distinguish the Ikeja case from the one before the Federal High Court.

On the allegation that Mr Mompha failed to disclose some of his assets, Ms Dada said there was no intention to conceal the items recovered from him.

She noted that he had disclosed them in an extrajudicial statement on 22 October 2019, two days after submitting an asset declaration form.

The EFCC arraigned Mr Mompha and his company on 12 January 2022 on an eight-count bordering on conspiracy to launder proceeds of unlawful activities, retention of proceeds of crime, failure to disclose assets and possession of documents containing false pretences.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The commission alleged that Mr Mompha, Ahmadu Mohammed, who is said to be at large, and the company conspired in 2016 to conduct financial transactions worth N5,998,884,653.18 to promote unlawful activities, including obtaining money by false pretences.

The defendants pleaded not guilty.

During the trial, the prosecution, led by Suleiman Suleiman, called six witnesses and tendered documentary exhibits.

Mr Mompha stopped attending court after being granted bail and was represented by his lawyers, Kolawole Salami and Ademola Adefolaju.

The defence called no witnesses but urged the court to discharge the defendants, arguing that the prosecution was an abuse of court process.

In November 2025, Ms Dada dismissed a no-case submission filed by Mr Mompha and his company, ruling that the EFCC had established a prima facie case requiring them to enter their defence.

The defendants subsequently challenged the ruling at the Court of Appeal.

The prosecution and defence adopted their final written addresses on 30 June, after which the judge reserved judgement.

The EFCC had also filed a separate money laundering case against Mr Mompha and his company before the Federal High Court in Lagos. In that case, the commission accused them of using company accounts to retain about N32.9 billion suspected to be proceeds of unlawful activities.

The charge was initially filed in 2019 and later amended.

The existence of the related proceedings before the Federal High Court was central to Ms Dada’s decision to strike out the case before her court.

Mr Mompha has faced several EFCC prosecutions since 2019 over allegations of laundering billions of naira for cybercrime syndicates and using companies to disguise illicit funds.

He has consistently denied the allegations.

World.title: 2027: Donald Duke signals readiness to step down for consensus opposition candidate
World.content:
Former Governor Donald Duke has signalled his willingness to relinquish his 2027 presidential ambition in favour of a consensus opposition candidate if opposition parties reach a collective agreement.

Mr Duke, the presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP), said he would respect a democratic decision by opposition parties to support a stronger candidate against President Bola Tinubu, insisting that an opposition coalition should extend beyond selecting a presidential candidate.

Speaking on Tuesday in Abuja at the unveiling of his running mate, Sule Mohammed, and the party’s manifesto, Mr Duke said a coalition that merely brings politicians together to share political positions without agreeing on a common national vision would fail to address Nigeria’s challenges.

According to a report by The Punch, he was responding to a question on whether he would step down for a stronger candidate if the PRP and other opposition parties agreed to support one person against Mr Tinubu.

He said the coalition must first establish the direction in which it wants to take the country before deciding who should lead it.

“A coalition is not just about picking a presidential candidate. That’s the mistake we’re all making. It’s about us coming together to agree on where we would like to take our nation to,” he said.

Although he acknowledged the prominence of the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress, Atiku Abubakar and that of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, Peter Obi, he said he did not want to prejudge the outcome of the negotiations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“But at the end of the day, I’ll be sportsmanlike about it. If the group, and so far there are quite a number of us, comes up with an agreement that this is the best person to lead the coalition, you can’t say you’re a democrat and not be subject to the rules of democracy,” he said.

Mr Duke added that he would expect other presidential aspirants to demonstrate the same willingness to respect a collective decision if he emerged as the preferred candidate.
