World.title: How Liberia ignored a World Bank warning while its neighbors built their way past port gridlock
World.content:
Nine years ago, a World Bank study warned that West Africa’s container traffic would nearly triple by 2025 and that existing ports could not cope. Côte d’Ivoire, Sierra Leone, Benin and Senegal responded by building new terminals and quays. Liberia added no new terminal. Today, ships wait offshore for weeks, cargo is diverted to neighboring ports, and Liberian traders say their capital has been trapped in containers for up to seven months.

MONROVIA – From the beaches of Liberia’s capital, the crisis is plain to see. Cargo ships sit at anchor on the horizon, waiting for a berth at the Freeport of Monrovia, the country’s main gateway for food, fuel, building materials and consumer goods.

By Rodney D. Sieh



On Tuesday, about 1,500 Liberian businesswomen and importers marched to the Capitol Building to demand action. Goods ordered from China, they told lawmakers, are taking as long as seven months to arrive. With the Christmas trading season weeks away, the money they borrowed and invested is sitting in steel boxes somewhere between Asia and Monrovia.

The crisis did not arrive without warning.

A warning on the record

In June 2017, the World Bank published a regional study, Container Terminals Concessions: Making the Most of Ports in West Africa. It projected that by 2025, container traffic across the region would reach almost three times its 2011 level. Its conclusion was blunt. Better port performance alone would not absorb growth on that scale. Countries would need to expand terminals at existing ports and develop new ones.

The study covered the whole region, not Liberia alone. But Liberia, where the Freeport handles more than 90 percent of the country’s imports, had as much at stake as anyone.

What the neighbors built

Across the region, governments and private operators poured money into new capacity:

• Côte d’Ivoire opened a second container terminal at Abidjan in late 2022, at a cost of about US$953 million. It can handle more than 1.5 million TEUs (twenty-foot containers) a year and berth ships drawing 16 metres.

• Sierra Leone completed a US$120 million, 270-metre quay extension in Freetown in 2018. The port can now take ships carrying up to 6,000 containers.

• Benin finished the first phase of its Cotonou port expansion in January 2026.

• Senegal is building a US$1.2 billion deep-water port at Ndayane, due in 2028, because its main port at Dakar is running near its physical limits.

Some of these projects were already planned before the Bank’s report. All of them reflect the same reading of the region’s future: traffic was coming, and ports had to grow to meet it.

What Liberia did

Liberia’s major port reform came earlier, in 2010. That year, the government handed the Freeport’s container operations to APM Terminals, part of Denmark’s Maersk group, under a 25-year concession. The company rebuilt a quay that dated to the 1940s and was close to collapse. It also paved a container yard and installed new gates. By 2015, its stated goal was to double the port’s annual capacity to 200,000 TEUs by 2017.

That work restored a war-damaged port. It did not prepare the port for the next decade of growth. In the nine years since the World Bank’s warning, Liberia has added no new container terminal.

Talks with Morocco’s port operator Marsa Maroc show how slowly things have moved. The two sides signed a memorandum of understanding in late 2024. A contract to manage two jetties followed in February 2026. The bigger prize is a proposed US$230 million concession for a new three-berth multipurpose terminal, and it remains under review.

Dredging may be the most telling failure. Under the 2010 arrangement, the Liberian government, not the operator, was responsible for dredging the port. Lawmakers now say repeated dredging delays are one reason larger vessels cannot berth. The National Port Authority (NPA) says a dredging contract is imminent but has given no completion date.

The cost of waiting

The NPA has publicly acknowledged that the Freeport cannot keep pace with the size and number of ships now calling. Yard space is full.

Shipping lines are passing the costs on. Since November 1, French carrier CMA CGM has added a congestion surcharge of €250 per dry container and €600 per refrigerated container on Monrovia-bound cargo from Northern Europe. Those charges will reach Liberian consumers through market prices.

Some Liberia-bound vessels spend more than 30 days at sea. Their cargo is routed through ports in Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana while it waits for space in Monrovia. In effect, Liberia’s neighbors are receiving its goods before Liberians do.

APM Terminals this week announced emergency measures to clear the backlog. It also said Maersk will make Monrovia the first port of call on one of its West Africa services from January 2027. The House of Representatives has summoned the port authority, the terminal operator and shipping agents to explain the delays.

A fair accounting

New berths alone will not end the crisis. Part of the delay comes from congestion at regional transshipment hubs, where Liberia-bound containers change ships. Tema in Ghana and Freetown in Sierra Leone face CMA CGM surcharges too. Clearance through customs, cargo tracking and inspection adds its own days.

But there is a difference. Liberia’s neighbors are managing growing pains on top of new capacity. Liberia has the growing pains without the capacity.

What decisive action looks like

• Dredge: sign and publish the long-promised dredging contract, with a firm completion date.

• Decide on Marsa Maroc: send the proposed terminal concession to the Legislature in full, for open and timely review.

• Tie the APM review to investment: finish the review of APM’s concession, and link any extension to binding commitments on new yard space and berths.

• Ease the bottlenecks: open inland container depots, and set enforceable clearance timelines for every agency in the chain.

Since 2017, Liberia has held elections, summits and hearings. Officials who had the diagnosis nine years ago are now asking market women what went wrong. The answer has not changed since the World Bank wrote it down. Expand the port, as Liberia’s neighbors have.

World.title: Liberia: Weah Accuses Boakai Government of Political Persecution
World.content:
At the CDC’s National Martyrs’ Day commemoration in Kinjor, former President George Manneh Weah accused the Unity Party-led government of weaponizing the justice system against political opponents, demanded the release of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor and CDC youths detained in the Capitol arson case, and defended former officials convicted in the Saudi-donated rice scandal. In a message delivered by MOVEE Political Leader and former Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah, Weah also challenged the government to account for the 2024 Kinjor killings and warned that electoral victory does not place any administration above constitutional limits.

KINJOR, Grand Cape Mount County — Former President George Manneh Weah has used the Coalition for Democratic Change’s (CDC) National Martyrs’ Day commemoration to launch a sweeping political attack on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s administration, accusing the ruling Unity Party of selective justice, political persecution and abuse of state power.

By Willie N. Tokpah



In a strongly worded message delivered Saturday, November 7, by former Foreign Affairs Minister Ambassador Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah Sr., Weah demanded the release of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, defended former officials of his administration convicted in the Saudi-donated rice scandal, and called for the release of young CDC supporters detained in connection with the Capitol Building arson case.

He also challenged the government to account for the February 29, 2024 killings in Kinjor, where protesters and security personnel clashed during demonstrations in the Bea Mountain mining area.

The address, delivered under the theme, “They Carried the Struggle, We Carry Their Legacy,” went beyond commemorating fallen CDC supporters. It was a pointed challenge to the Boakai administration over its handling of justice, human rights and political opposition, with Weah reminding the governing party that an electoral mandate does not confer unlimited authority.

“A tyrant with a certificate of return is still a tyrant,” Weah declared, recalling remarks he said he made before the Nigerian Bar Association in Port Harcourt.

The ceremony brought together CDC National Chairman Atty. Janga Augustus Kowo, members of the party’s National Executive Committee, the CDC Legislative Caucus, opposition political leaders and representatives, keynote speaker Paulita Cece Wie, bereaved families and supporters from across Liberia.

Kemayah, who serves as Weah’s Senior Adviser and Chief Special Envoy, is also the Political Leader of the Movement for Economic Empowerment (MOVEE).

His delivery of the message placed him at the intersection of the CDC’s political mobilization and the wider opposition community.

Kinjor killings put Boakai government on the spot

Speaking from Kinjor, the community where residents were killed during the February 29, 2024 confrontation involving protesters and security personnel deployed in the Bea Mountain mining area, Weah called for accountability over the deaths.

He accused the Liberia National Police of using live ammunition against protesters and characterized the incident as an act of “unprovoked brutality.”

“The killings in Kinjor demand accountability,” he declared.

Addressing bereaved families, Weah said their loved ones were citizens entitled to protection and deserving of a government response that respected their dignity.

“Your loved ones were citizens of this Republic. Their lives did deserve protection. Their grievances did deserve attention. Your community deserves a Government’s response that respects human dignity,” he said.

In a symbolic gesture, Weah called for a separate moment of silence for the Kinjor victims, placing their deaths alongside those of CDC supporters remembered during the annual commemoration.

He argued that poverty and lack of political influence should never determine the level of protection citizens receive from the state.

“No community’s poverty makes its people less deserving of protection. No lack of political influence of any citizen reduces the value of that citizen’s life,” he said.

His remarks renewed attention on the government’s response to the Kinjor killings, particularly the accountability measures pursued against security personnel and the support provided to affected families.

Weah demands release of Jewel Howard-Taylor

Weah also threw his political weight behind former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, whose ongoing criminal proceedings have become a major point of political contention.

Describing her continued detention as political persecution, the former president demanded her release.

“Her continued detention is political persecution. I condemn it unequivocally and demand her release,” Weah said.

Howard-Taylor, who served as vice president during his administration, faces criminal allegations arising from an investigation into an alleged transnational narcotics network. She has denied the allegations.

Her arrest and subsequent court proceedings have generated controversy within opposition circles, with supporters questioning the circumstances surrounding the case.

However, the allegations remain subject to judicial determination, and Weah’s characterization of the proceedings as political persecution represents his political position rather than an established finding about the case.

Defends Kemayah, Sirleaf and other convicted officials

In another significant portion of his address, Weah defended former officials of his administration convicted in the Saudi-donated rice scandal, including Kemayah, who delivered the message on his behalf.

Others he identified included former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, former Deputy Foreign Minister for Administration Thelma E. Duncan-Sawyer, former Deputy Internal Affairs Minister Momolu S. Johnson and former General Services Agency Deputy Director-General for Operations Edris Bility.

Weah described the verdict against Kemayah as unjust and accused the Boakai administration of pursuing what he called a political witch hunt against members of his former government.

He nevertheless distinguished his opposition to what he considers politically motivated prosecutions from his support for genuine anti-corruption efforts.

“I support any genuine evidence-based fight against corruption, and detest any political persecution and political witch hunt against any Member of my Family and Former Government Officials and/or any individual, for that matter,” he declared.

The Saudi rice case involves 29,412 bags of rice donated by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for disaster victims and vulnerable communities in Liberia. Prosecutors alleged that thousands of the donated bags were diverted from their intended beneficiaries.

Following a lengthy trial at Criminal Court C, a jury returned mixed verdicts on October 9, 2026, convicting several defendants while acquitting others.

The outcome has generated legal and political debate, with defense lawyers challenging aspects of the proceedings and pursuing available legal remedies.

Weah’s public defense of the convicted officials underscores his continued political ties to members of his former administration. His position, however, does not determine the legal merits of their convictions, which remain subject to the judicial process.

Capitol arson case also draws Weah’s attention

The former president also called for the release of young CDC supporters detained in connection with the Capitol Building arson case.

The case followed the fire at the Capitol Building and involves former House Speaker Cllr. J. Fonati Koffa and several other defendants.

Although Weah did not address the individual allegations or evidence against those charged, he placed their detention within his broader criticism of what he described as the government’s use of the justice system to intimidate political opponents.

“The Boakai-Koung-Unity Party Led Government must stop using the machinery of justice to intimidate political opponents,” he said.

His remarks signal the CDC’s intention to keep the cases involving its members and associates at the center of the national political debate, even as the judicial proceedings continue.

Warns Unity Party against abusing electoral mandate

Weah’s broader argument centered on the distinction between electoral legitimacy and the constitutional responsibilities of government.

He maintained that winning an election does not place a government above the law or give it the authority to suppress dissent.

According to him, democratic governance requires the protection of citizens’ lives and civil liberties, impartial administration of justice, respect for judicial independence, legislative oversight and the right of citizens to criticize those in power.

“Our place in opposition does not diminish our citizenship,” he declared.

He also revisited the 2023 presidential election, saying he accepted the outcome because national stability and the decision of the electorate were more important than his personal desire to remain in office.

But he directed a pointed message toward the ruling Unity Party ahead of the next presidential election.

“We expect the Unity Party Government to submit peacefully to the decision of the Liberian people in 2029,” he said.

The statement places the question of peaceful political transition firmly within the opposition’s emerging political messaging as the country moves toward another electoral cycle.

Kemayah’s dual political role adds opposition dimension

The decision to have Kemayah deliver the address added another dimension to the gathering.

A former chief diplomat in the Weah administration, Kemayah now serves as Weah’s Senior Adviser and Chief Special Envoy while leading MOVEE, an opposition political party.

His presence was significant because the message he delivered defended former members of Weah’s government, criticized the current administration and called for greater protection of opposition rights.

The participation of other opposition political leaders and representatives also gave the gathering a broader political character, although the event did not announce any formal coalition arrangement.

The repeated calls for political solidarity, accountability and respect for constitutional freedoms nevertheless highlighted issues around possible cooperation among opposition parties while they maintain their separate political identities.

From martyrs’ remembrance to political legacy

Despite the political attacks, the commemoration remained centered on the CDC’s efforts to preserve the memory of supporters who died during the party’s political struggle.

Weah recalled the contributions of ordinary Liberians who helped build the movement, including market women selling bitterballs and peppers, young campaigners, commercial motorcyclists, laborers and families who sacrificed their limited resources because they believed in the party’s vision.

He specifically remembered Papie Solo, whom the CDC recognizes as its first martyr and whom Weah said he knew personally from Sasstown, the village of his childhood.

Others remembered included Morris Kromah, associated with the November 7, 2011 Bloody Monday events; Tamba Momo; Joshua Solomon; Janjay Baikpeh; Christmas Wen Sailey; Nelson Korquoi; Ranny S. Gbatu; James Gray; Munah Pelham Youngblood; and Ma-Watta Kumba Soliyah-Larmie.

He also paid tribute to the late Gabriel Baccus Matthews, whom he described as the father of Liberia’s multiparty democracy and credited with providing revolutionary guidance that contributed to the birth and development of the CDC movement.

In an emotional segment, Weah called out the names of martyrs from all 15 counties and the Liberian diaspora, with each call followed by a solemn declaration that the fallen comrades had not answered and that their memories would be honored.

The symbolic roll call underscored the party’s effort to present its history as a national political struggle rather than one confined to a particular county or community.

Weah also pledged that the contributions of the departed supporters would remain part of the CDC’s institutional memory and that their children deserved to know the sacrifices their parents made for the party.

2029 elections loom over Weah’s message

The concluding portion of the address left little doubt that Weah wanted supporters to look beyond the commemoration and toward the 2029 elections.

He urged CDC members to remain confident in the people’s right to choose their leaders and determined to ensure that every vote is respected.

He praised CDC National Chairman Atty. Janga Augustus Kowo, the National Martyrs’ Day Committee, keynote speaker Paulita Cece Wie, county delegations, diaspora chapters, opposition representatives and residents of Kinjor and Grand Cape Mount County.

The address closed with the party’s rallying declaration:

“They Carried the Struggle, We Carry Their Legacy, The Party Remains Supreme.”

For Weah, the Kinjor gathering provided an opportunity to defend his political legacy, stand behind embattled former officials, challenge the government’s record on justice and human rights, and remind the Unity Party that its electoral mandate is not permanent.

For the Boakai administration, the accusations raise questions that extend beyond partisan exchanges, including accountability for the Kinjor killings, the handling of criminal cases involving opposition figures and public confidence in the impartiality of the justice system.

And for the opposition, Kemayah’s dual role as Weah’s special envoy and MOVEE Political Leader offered a visible reminder of the political relationships shaping engagement beyond the CDC.

Although the 2029 elections remain years away, Weah’s message from Kinjor makes clear that the struggle over political accountability, opposition rights and the country’s democratic direction is already taking shape.

World.title: UN Sea Level Rise Declaration Could Strengthen Case for Coastal Protection Money But Major Loss of Land is Now Inevitable
World.content:
Advancing Atlantic Ocean damaged private properties along Sinkor’s shoreline. Photo credit: R. Joyclyn Wea

Summary

A new UN declaration could strengthen Liberia’s appeal for coastal protection funding as 230,000 people set to lose homes and livelihoods by 2100.

Coastal erosion is destroying homes, threatening ports and fishing livelihoods across Liberia while monitoring and early warning systems remain limited.

Officials say defending the coast could cost at least US$1 billion.

By Nemenlah Cyrus Harmon, climate and environment reporter with New Narratives

A new United Nations declaration could help Liberia press for international support to protect a coastline where erosion is destroying homes and threatening ports and fishing livelihoods, international officials and climate experts say.



The UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration on Sea Level Rise in September calling for stronger international cooperation, better coastal monitoring and early warning systems, and long-term planning to protect vulnerable communities.

For Liberia the threat is growing by the day.

“It is true that God is not making new land,” said Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo, executive director of the Environmental Protection Agency, referring to a remark made by Liberia’s president in February. “So when the sea level rise is taking the land from the coast, it’s reducing the land of the country, literally. Not figuratively — literally it’s taking land.”

Global warming is raising sea levels in two ways: warmer seawater expands, and meltwater from land ice flows into the ocean, with the ice coming chiefly from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets and glaciers around the world.

Warming is caused by burning fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas which release greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide and methane, which have warmed Earth’s atmosphere beyond what natural causes can explain, with deforestation and agriculture adding to the problem. The biggest emitters of greenhouse gases are China, the United States, India and the European Union. All of Africa is responsible for just 4 percent.

Liberia’s coastal communities are already losing land and homes. About 0.8 km² of land has been lost to coastal erosion in recent decades. In West Point, Monrovia, more than 6,500 people have been displaced and about 800 houses destroyed since 2013 because of sea-level rise and coastal erosion, according World Bank and Liberian government assessments .

The Bank’s has found that with a one-metre rise in sea level, more than 230,000 people will lose their homes and livelihoods. Major cities including Monrovia, New Kru Town, Buchanan, River Cess and Robertsport will face significant damage.

For Liberia, the stakes extend from crowded coastal settlements in Monrovia to ports in the southeast. Yarkpawolo estimates that defending the country’s threatened coast would cost “not less than a billion dollars.”

At the moment Liberia lacks a sophisticated system to monitor coastal risks in real time putting lives and livelihoods in danger when high swells happen without warning.

The UN declaration could strengthen its appeal to donors, said Isaac Nyaneyon Kannah Teah, a Liberian climate expert. It is not legally binding and guarantees no new funding yet but it’s another importation step to encourage the world’s heaviest emitters of the gases causing climate change.

“It’s an open door for financing of our coastal land,” Teah said.

The country has already secured nearly US$40 million for combined coastal defense projects including the US$10 million coastal defense project is underway in Sinoe County to protect Greenville. And the $25m project designed to place boulders along the shoreline at West Point to protect the settlement for 40 years. All of them have faced yearslong delays because of a lack of Liberian experts with technical knowledge for the projects and Weah government failure to provide agreed co-financing. Projects have slowly resumed progress under the Boakai administration.

“We’ve already been receiving a lot of financing of our coastal land, but this will also add more opportunities as well,” said Teah.

Land is already disappearing

In Greenville, Sinoe County, Yarkpawolo has seen how quickly sea is encroaching. In May last year, he stood beneath three coconut trees on Mississippi Street with a United Nations Development Program official to break ground for the US$8.9 million Sinoe Coastal Resilience Project, funded by the Global Environment Facility, to put rocks along the shoreline to protect communities there. When he returned in September, the trees were gone. The ocean had swallowed them in a matter of months.

Land near 17th Street, Sinkor where Yarkpawolo trained as a track athlete in the early 2000s is now several meters out to sea, he said. Waves are also undermining fences in a nearby neighborhood.

“Sea erosion is very, very, very serious,” Yarkpawolo said.

Teah said World Bank data put the average loss along Liberia’s roughly 580-kilometer coastline at one to one-and-a-half meters a year, with some areas losing land faster.

Illegal sand mining adds to the erosion, Teah said.

A US$10 million coastal defense project, meant to protect citizens of Sinoe County from sea erosion. Photo credit: EPA Facebook page

Farther southeast, Yarkpawolo warned that the Port of Harper in Maryland County could be lost within ten years without intervention. Greenville’s port is also threatened, he said, but faces a less severe risk.

The damage extends beyond homes and ports. Erosion is destroying sites where fishing communities land boats and process their catch. Mangrove loss is damaging fish breeding grounds, while saltwater intrusion is affecting soil and drinking water in low-lying farming areas.

In Greenville, parts of streets, including Mississippi Street, have been submerged, damaging roads, sanitation systems and homes.

“It’s going to affect our homes, it’s going to affect infrastructure, it’s going to affect a lot of things,” Teah said. “It’s an economic, food security, infrastructure, and public health and development issue.”

Coastal projects face a much larger funding need

Yarkpawolo said the EPA has mapped vulnerable areas along the coast and developed County Climate Action Plans covering 2026 to 2035. Liberia has submitted a US$17 million funding proposal to the international Loss and Damage Fund, another global fund made available to vulnerable countries, to protect the coastline behind JFK Memorial Hospital and the stretch toward Bernard Beach community, Yarkpawolo said.

Yarkpawolo’s estimate of at least US$1 billion reflects the broader cost of combining natural protection with engineered defenses along the country’s threatened coast. But Liberia’s financing challenge is part of a wider gap between the money developing countries need to adapt to climate change and the support they receive.

At the UN meeting, General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman said developing countries’ annual adaptation needs could reach between US$310 billion and US$365 billion by 2035. But international public adaptation finance reaching those countries totaled just $26 billion in 2023.

A portion of Mesurado wetland in Paynesville, hosting mangroves.

Better monitoring is another urgent need

The September UN declaration also calls for better data, risk assessments and early warning systems. For Liberia, those priorities address gaps that Yarkpawolo and Teah said limit the country’s ability to understand and prepare for coastal threats.

The EPA is working with international partners, including the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization, to develop a data center capable of tracking storms and tsunamis. A national coastline observation system to record tides, shoreline changes and storm data over time.

Yarkpawolo said public awareness is also urgent. Sand mining, building on wetlands and close to the shore can increase communities’ exposure to coastal hazards. He warned that Liebrians can’t wait for international help to save them. We need to work together to protect what land we can.

World.title: Through High-Standard Opening-Up Zero-Tariff Treatment Takes China–Africa Economic and Trade Cooperation to a New Level
World.content:
On November 5, the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) opened in Shanghai. This year’s Expo brought together 162 countries, regions and international organizations, with 4,142 overseas exhibitors, including 4 from Liberia. Its total exhibition area exceeded 440,000 square meters for the first time. Notably, the free exhibition space provided for least developed countries increased by 17%. Through institutional arrangements such as zero-tariff treatment and streamlined customs clearance, the Expo helps developing countries foster domestic industries and strengthen their capacity for self-sustaining development. The CIIE serves as a mirror, reflecting the defining spirit of openness based on mutual benefit and win-win cooperation.

By H.E. Yin Chengwu, contributing writer

Opening-up is an essential pathway to development and a defining feature of Chinese modernization. At a time when the global economic recovery faces challenges, unilateralism and protectionism are on the rise, and uncertainty surrounding global development continues to increase. China remains firmly committed to advancing high-standard opening-up and creating more opportunities for the world through its own development. China’s implementation of a zero-tariff policy for all African countries with which it maintains diplomatic relations is a concrete measure to expand opening-up and share the benefits of development. By reducing trade costs and broadening market access, this policy creates favorable conditions for African countries to leverage their resource advantages and expand exports to China.



Liberia was among the first countries to benefit from China’s zero-tariff policy, and China has become the fastest-growing market for Liberian exports. According to China Customs’ statistics, Liberia’s exports to China reached US$131 million in 2025, representing a year-on-year increase of 23.9 percent. Since the beginning of this year, economic and trade cooperation between the two sides has shown an accelerating momentum. In the first nine months of 2026, Liberia’s exports to China exceeded US$629 million, an increase of more than eight-fold year on year. Of this total, iron ore exports reached US$594 million, while rubber exports amounted to US$32 million. These figures demonstrate the deepening of China-Liberia economic and trade cooperation and the vast opportunities that the Chinese market offers to Liberian products.

Liberia’s development potential extends well beyond minerals and rubber. The country has favorable conditions for developing specialty agricultural products, including coffee, cocoa, cashew nuts, cassava, palm products and chili peppers. The Liberian Government is actively promoting commercial chili pepper cultivation and exports. The Liberian Ministry of Agriculture has distributed more than 600,000 chili pepper seeds to farmers, while Chinese companies have expressed interest in purchasing Liberian chili peppers for the Chinese market. With further improvements in production organization, quality management, inspection and quarantine, and market access, more high-quality Liberian agricultural products will be able to enter the Chinese market.

Zero-tariff treatment offers not only opportunities to expand exports but also new prospects for investment and industrial development. Policy benefits do not automatically translate into industrial competitiveness. Liberia needs to continue improving product quality, expanding large-scale production, and strengthening logistics, warehousing and processing capacity, while ensuring compliance with China’s market access requirements and relevant standards. At the same time, Chinese enterprises can leverage their strengths in capital, technology, markets and industrial supply chains to participate in Liberia’s agricultural production, agro-processing, mineral development, logistics and warehousing sectors, helping enhance local productive capacity and the value added of Liberian products.

The agricultural investment by China’s Mainland Group in Liberia is a positive example. The Group announced in August 2025 a plan to invest approximately US$100 million in Liberia over the next five years, focusing on rice, cassava, cocoa, coffee, sugar production, warehousing and logistics, with the aim of developing an integrated model encompassing agricultural cultivation, processing and trade. The company has already invested approximately US$10 million. Its cassava starch deep-processing project is under construction, alongside efforts to establish raw material production bases. Such investments will help expand agricultural production, create jobs, increase farmers’ incomes and improve access for Liberian agricultural products to China and other international markets.

In recent years, China-Liberia economic and trade cooperation has continued to deepen. In 2024, the two countries signed the Framework Agreement on Economic Partnership for Common Development, providing an institutional foundation for further expanding bilateral economic and trade cooperation. China stands ready to work with Liberia to better align the zero-tariff policy with Liberia’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID), taking into account the country’s resource endowments and development priorities, and to further explore cooperation in mining, agriculture, agro-processing, infrastructure and logistics. China welcomes more capable and interested Chinese enterprises to invest and do business in Liberia, and encourages both sides to extend their cooperation beyond traditional trade to industrial investment, processing and manufacturing, and greater coordination across value chains.

Liberian Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung was invited to attend the above-mentioned CIIE and held talks with Ding Xuexian, Chinese Vice Premier of the State Council, injecting fresh impetus into efforts to deepen China-Liberia economic and trade cooperation. China will continue to advance high-standard opening-up and leverage the strengths of its vast market to create more development opportunities for African countries, including Liberia. China stands ready to work with Liberia to seize the opportunities presented by the CIIE and the zero-tariff policy, promote coordinated development in trade, investment and industry, and transform resource potential into tangible development outcomes. Together, we will deliver greater benefits to the peoples of both countries and achieve more substantive results in the China-Liberia Strategic Partnership.

H.E. Yin Chengwu is Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to the Republic of Liberia.

World.title: Editorial: Liberia’s Budget Shows Twisted Priorities
World.content:
More for lawmakers’ fuel than for the nation’s medicines. More for retired politicians than for the poor. Liberia’s biggest-ever budget has its priorities upside down.

LIBERIA HAS NEVER had this much money to spend. The draft national budget for 2027 comes to US$1.54 billion, 18 percent more than this year. In September, revenue collection passed US$1 billion in a single year for the first time. The Finance Ministry’s slogan for the budget is “A Growing Budget for Bigger Impact.”

THE QUESTION IS who gets the impact. Read the budget’s 845 pages line by line, as we have, and the answer is uncomfortable. The extra money goes mainly to the people who write the budget, approve it, guard it and lend to it. The Liberians the budget says it serves, the farmer in Lofa, the mother in a Rivercess clinic, the poorest household in West Point, are left with what remains.



Fuel for the Capitol, crumbs for the farm

START WITH THE Legislature, which will soon review and pass this budget. It is set to receive US$58.2 million. That is more than three times what the entire agriculture sector gets, in a country where farming produces more than a quarter of the economy and feeds most rural families.

THE DETAIL IS worse. Lawmakers’ vehicle fuel is budgeted at US$5.47 million. The Ministry of Health’s budget for drugs and medical consumables, for the whole country, is US$4.23 million. The Legislature’s allowance for “entertainment and representation” is US$2.66 million. The Ministry of Agriculture gets just under US$1 million for seeds, tools and other farm inputs.

WHEN A GOVERNMENT plans to spend more fuelling lawmakers’ cars than buying medicine for its hospitals, the problem is not a lack of money. It is a choice.

Rewarding those who overspend

THE LEGISLATURE IS not being rewarded for discipline. By 30 September, with a quarter of the 2026 fiscal year still to run, it had already spent US$64.3 million against an approved US$57.2 million. Its “constituency visits” line was budgeted at US$1.12 million; it spent more than US$6.2 million. Committee hearings were budgeted at US$1.4 million and cost US$6.5 million.

THE 2027 BUDGET responds by more than tripling the constituency-visit allowance. The National Security Agency, which also overspent its 2026 budget by more than 20 percent, gets an increase too. Meanwhile, the Ministry of Health had not spent a cent of its 2026 capital budget by September, and the Ministry of Agriculture had spent nothing of the US$5.5 million approved for farm projects. Money flows freely to the Capitol and the security services, and barely to the clinic and the farm.

Promises broken on paper

LIBERIA, LIKE OTHER African Union members, has pledged to spend 10 percent of its budget on agriculture. This budget gives it 1.2 percent. Under the 2001 Abuja Declaration, African governments promised 15 percent for health; this budget gives 8.8. Education, at 10.6 percent, is below the 15 to 20 percent recommended internationally.

PRESIDENT JOSEPH BOAKAI’S ARREST Agenda puts Agriculture first in its name, yet agriculture comes last in this budget. If that mismatch is unintended, the Finance Ministry should fix it. If it is intended, the government should say so.

The poor and the powerful

THE BUDGET’S FLAGSHIP Social Protection Safety Net, meant for Liberia’s poorest households, receives US$1.05 million. The same budget sets aside US$2.23 million in benefits for former elected officials. Debt service, much of it owed to Liberian commercial banks and the Central Bank, takes US$275.5 million, twice the entire health budget. Debts must be paid. But the budget makes room for retired politicians before it makes room for the poor.

GEOGRAPHY REPEATS THE pattern. Of the spending the budget assigns to a specific county, Montserrado, home to the capital Monrovia, takes US$52 million. Rivercess gets US$837,710. The Monrovia City Corporation’s budget rises 74 percent, partly for a US$4 million “smart sanitation and city beautification” programme, while much of the countryside waits for basic services.

Questions that demand answers

SOME LINES RAISE questions beyond priorities. They go to transparency, and the Finance Ministry owes the public clear answers before the Legislature votes.

• WHY DOES THE Ministry of Local Government’s budget include new “transfers” of US$7.1 million to three mining companies: Cavalla Resource Liberia Inc., China Union Mining Company and Hummingbird Resource Liberia Inc.? Is the government paying these companies, or passing on money they owe to communities? The budget does not say.

• WHAT IS THE US$14 million “Transfer to Vendor Share”?

• WHY DOES SPENDING on “intelligence services” across government rise from US$21 million to nearly US$29 million, with no explanation of what it buys?

• WHY IS NIMBA University’s US$2 million subsidy booked under Grand Bassa University, leaving Nimba University’s own allocation at US$386,200?

• WHY DOES FOREIGN air travel at the Ministry of Local Government jump 44-fold, from US$17,690 to US$780,357, and domestic travel at the Ministry of State for Presidential Affairs rise more than fifteenfold?

THE DOCUMENT IS also full of basic errors. Its cover reads “Fiscal Year 20276.” It gives two different figures for how much the budget has grown and two for how many soldiers will be recruited. Seventeen of the 20 state-owned enterprises missed the deadline to submit their budgets. A budget this careless with its own numbers cannot ask citizens to trust it with their money.

What must happen now

THERE IS GOOD news in this budget, and it deserves credit. Revenue is rising. The economy is growing. Teachers will finally be paid according to their qualifications, with the same minimum salaries in every government school. Police officers will see raises tied to their rank. These are real gains.

BUT A BUDGET is a statement of values, and this one says that comfort for those in power comes before the welfare of ordinary people. The Legislature, which benefits most from this budget, now has the job of scrutinising it. We urge lawmakers to show they can put the country ahead of their own allowances. Cut the fuel, the entertainment and the inflated travel. Move that money to medicines, farm inputs and the safety net. Demand answers on the mining transfers and the unexplained lines before a single vote is cast.

LIBERIANS HAVE HEARD enough slogans. They will judge this budget not by how much it grows, but by whether any of it reaches them.

World.title: Liberia: Ganta Delegates  Agreed and Signed  Resolution Setting Out Recommendations for a Broad National Review of Liberia’s  1986 Constitution
World.content:
GANTA, Nimba County — Delegates, who attended Liberia’s three-day National Constitutional Reform Symposium in Ganta City, Nimba County, have agreed and signed a resolution setting out their recommendations for a broad national review of the country’s 1986 Constitution.

By Franklin Doloquee

The proposed resolution will provide a basis for wider consultations on whether Liberia should amend specific constitutional provisions or pursue a more comprehensive rewriting of the 40-year-old document.



The agreement to prepare the resolution does not in itself constitute a final national decision to replace the Constitution.

Once finalized, the document is expected to be presented for consideration by the Executive Branch, the Judiciary, the House of Representatives, the Senate, civil-society organizations, traditional chiefs and elders, the media, youth organizations, women’s groups, People living with disability, organizations representing persons with disabilities, political parties representations, Superintendents Council representations, counties nine men council members and other stakeholders.

Delegates emphasized that the future of the Constitution should not be determined solely by political leaders, legal experts or participants at a single gathering.

Instead, they called for an inclusive, transparent, and nationally owned process that gives Liberians across all 15 counties a meaningful opportunity to contribute.

Building National Agreement

The symposium was convened by the Governance Commission and the Law Reform Commission, with support from the United Nations Development Programme, ( UNDP) under the theme: “Advancing Constitutional Reform through National Ownership, Inclusion and Democratic Governance.”

Participants included representatives of government ministries and agencies, lawmakers, lawyers, civil-society organizations, professional bodies, traditional authorities, women, young people and persons with disabilities.

Their agreement to develop a resolution marks a step toward consolidating the discussions into a common document.

The resolution is intended to bring together areas of agreement, identify questions requiring further examination and outline a possible direction for nationwide engagement.

At the center of the proposed national review is a fundamental question: can targeted amendments adequately address Liberia’s present governance challenges, or is a more comprehensive constitutional overhaul necessary?

That question remains open for wider public discussion and legal examination.

The delegates’ recommendations are, therefore, intended to inform a national decision, rather than substitute for one.

A Constitution at 40

As Liberia marks four decades under its 1986 Constitution, participants said the country must assess whether its constitutional framework adequately reflects contemporary political, social, economic and governance realities.

The discussions focused on preserving democratic principles while examining provisions that participants believe may require clarification, stronger safeguards, or reform.

Delegates linked the review to public concerns about accountability, citizen participation, local governance, institutional independence and the equitable management of national resources.

The Ganta gathering also forms part of a broader reform conversation. Earlier national discussions organized by the Governance Commission and Law Reform Commission examined the choice between targeted constitutional revision and a more comprehensive overhaul.

Priorities for Reform

During thematic discussions, delegates identified several areas for possible constitutional and legal review: Citizenship and property rights, Natural-resource governance and equitable benefit-sharing, Decentralization, local government and citizen participation.

The tenure, accountability and performance of elected officials. Traditional authority, customary rights, and their relationship with state institutions. Checks and balances among the Executive, Legislature, and Judiciary.

Fundamental rights, inclusion and public accountability. These issues extend beyond the wording of the Constitution.

They concern how public authority is exercised, how communities participate in decisions, how institutions are held accountable and how citizens benefit from the country’s resources.

Participants said the review should ultimately contribute to stronger democratic institutions, improved public-service delivery, social cohesion, and greater confidence in government.

Delegates stressed that consultation must reach beyond national institutions and urban centers.

Their call for participation across all 15 counties places communities, local leaders, and groups whose voices are often underrepresented at the center of the proposed process.

The inclusion of women, young people, persons with disabilities, traditional authorities and civil-society organizations is intended to broaden the range of experiences informing the review.

For that participation to be meaningful, the consultation process would need accessible information, understandable explanations of proposed changes, and opportunities for citizens to raise concerns before decisions are finalized.

The media would also have an important public-information role. At the Ganta symposium, the Press Union of Liberia called for an inclusive reform process and stronger constitutional protection for freedom of expression, press freedom and other fundamental rights.

Calls for Stronger Institutions

Governance Commission Acting Chairman Professor Alaric K. Tokpa has urged that constitutional reform remain nationally owned, inclusive, and focused on practical improvements in governance.

His emphasis on public participation reflects the broader argument that reform should strengthen the relationship between citizens and state institutions, rather than become an exercise confined to political and legal circles.

Civil Service Agency Director-General Dr. Josiah F. Joekai, who delivered the symposium’s keynote address, called for reforms addressing excessive political influence, institutional weaknesses, and inadequate accountability.

He identified stronger checks and balances, decentralization, protection of fundamental rights, inclusive participation, and responsible management of public resources as priorities, while advocating nationwide consultations and technical review of proposed amendments.

From Resolution to Reform

The proposed Ganta resolution is expected to guide further consultations, stakeholder engagement and technical legal review. It would provide a platform for national institutions and the public to consider both the substance of reform and the appropriate process for pursuing it.

However, a symposium resolution cannot itself amend the Constitution. Article 91 requires a proposed amendment to receive the support of two-thirds of the membership of each legislative chamber and subsequent approval by two-thirds of registered voters voting in a referendum held no sooner than one year after legislative action.

Citizens may also initiate the process through a petition signed by at least 10,000 citizens, but the proposal must still secure the required legislative concurrence and referendum approval.

Article 92 further requires proposed amendments to be published, explained to the public, and presented separately when more than one amendment is submitted for a referendum.

Any proposal for a comprehensive rewriting would therefore require careful legal examination; the delegates’ agreement to draft a resolution should not be presented as authorization to replace the Constitution. For the Ganta participants, the immediate task is to turn their discussions into a document that Liberians can examine, debate, and help shape.

Their stated objective is a constitutional framework that responses to present-day needs while protecting democratic values, national unity, the rule of law and the long-term interests of the Liberian people.

World.title: Daka, Banda & Lungu out of Burundi clash
World.content:
Chipolopolo will have to chase six crucial points against Burundi without their talisman.

Patson Daka, Lameck Banda and Gamphani Lungu have all been ruled out injured for the back-to-back Group I AFCON qualifiers – a triple blow that tests the depth of interim coach George ‘Chicken’ Lwandamina’s squad.

But inside the Chipolopolo camp, the message is clear: no excuses.

Team Doctor George Magwende confirmed the trio will miss both legs because their recovery goes beyond seven days.

Daka suffered a right ankle injury in Hamburg SV’s 3-1 win over Monchengladbach on 6 November.

“Ultrasound revealed he had a mild strain that will require about 7-10 days to recover,” Dr Magwende said.

Banda is out for at least two weeks with a left hamstring injury, while Lungu faces 14 to 21 days out with a right ankle sprain.

They join Kingstone Mutandwa, Ackim Mumba and Jackson Phiri on the injury list.

Lwandamina has moved swiftly, calling up Israel-based Edward Chilufya, Green Eagles’ Derrick Bulaya and Prince Mumba of Al Garaf in Iraq.

It is a chance for the replacements – and for in-form local stars like Zesco United striker Kennedy Musonda – to prove Zambia is more than one man.

The stakes could not be higher. Zambia host Burundi on Friday, 13 November at Levy Mwanawasa Stadium at 15h00, before the return in Bujumbura on 17 November.

Algeria lead Group I on four points. Zambia are second on three, level with Togo. Burundi are bottom on one.

Six points from six would put Chipolopolo in command on the road to AFCON PAMOJA 2027 in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania.

Lwandamina, in charge on an interim basis, knows momentum is everything. Without Daka, he will need others to step up – starting on Friday in Ndola.

World.title: Government releases 3 million kwacha meant for the compensation of settlers in Nakonde
World.content:
Government has signed compensation agreements with 34 settlers from Mwenzo area in Nakonde district who were living along a stretch set aside for the construction of an access road leading to the International Airport project site in Nakonde District, Muchinga Province.

The compensation follows the release of 3 million kwacha meant for the compensation of settlers under phase two.

Muchinga Province Assistant Secretary, Evans Hichilema, who interacted with the settlers, has implored them to find alternative resettlement once compensated, to pave way for construction of access road.

He disclosed that the government has since given the affected settlers a 90-day ultimatum to relocate from the area to facilitate construction of the access road.

Mr Hichilema made the remarks today during a compensation agreement signing ceremony held at the District Administration Office in Nakonde District.

He said construction of the Airport will commence soon and is expected to come with a lot of advantages for the local people, such as jobs.

He also emphasized the need for the contractor to consider the locals in the employment once work begins.

“As construction of the Airport starts, there should be consideration of the local people for employment, “he said

Meanwhile, Nakonde District Commissioner, Marvelous Sikapizye, anticipates enhanced development once the International Airport is completed.

Mr Sikapizye said Nakonde has seen massive development, and attributed these to the sound policies of the UPND government under President Hakainde Hichilema.

Meanwhile, the settlers talked to by the media are happy with the compensation under Phase One and have called on the government to speed up payments for settlers under Phase Two.

Zundani Silavwe has appreciated the government for the timely compensation of settlers under Phase One.

“We are just appealing to the government to speed up the payment process for settlers earmarked for compensation under Phase Two,”he saidAnd another settler, Annie Nanyangwe, said the settlers were given a good package and has since advised fellow beneficiaries to use the money wisely.

Recently, the government compensated 93 Mwenzo settlers under Phase One, who have since started relocating to pave the way for construction of the International Airport in Nakonde District.

World.title: Kabompo Youths welcome plans to construct a Skills Centre
World.content:
Youths in Kabompo District of Northwestern Province have welcomed the government’s plan to construct a University in Northwestern and a skills training centre in Kabompo District under the 2027 National budget.

Speaking in an interview with the media in Kabompo, Diana Makiko a Kabompo based youth said the construction of a skills training centre in the district will help bridge the gap of accessing tertiary education within the province.

Ms Makiko said she was delighted to hear the construction of the Northwestern University and a skills training centre in Kabompo kabompo during the budget representation on Friday 6th November ,2026.

She said construction of a skills training centre in the district is a welcome move to youths in kabompo as they have been longing for such an institution in the district.

“One of the most exciting news I got was when the Minister of Finance Dr Situmbeko Musokotwane mentioned in his speech during the 2027 proposed budget presentation on Friday last week that government will construct a skills training centre in Kabompo District under the 2027 national budget,” she said.

Ms Makiko said the skills training centre once constructed is going to bridge the gap of accessing tertiary education in the district.

“This is a dream come true for us youths in Kabompo because for one to access tertiary education one has to go to Solwezi or other Provinces just to acquire a skill or other programmes while covering long distance which is costly on our part, so we welcome the development in our District,” she said.

Another youth Raphael Kajila added that the construction of a university in the province is a welcome move that will benefit a lot of youths in the province to access tertiary education within the province.

He said the construction of the two infrastructures in the province will also create jobs for the locals during the construction of the two projects.

“We are grateful to the government that it has plans for us to have a university in Northwestern Province and skills training centres within our reach next year, we believe the construction of the two projects in the province will also benefit youths through job creation because most of the people who will be working at these sites are locals.” He said.

He further urged youths in the Province to take advantage of government sponsorships under the constituency development fund and get a skill that will better their livelihoods.

Mr Kajila appealed to the government to expedite the construction of the university project and the skills training centre.

“Our only appeal to the government is that let the construction of the two projects commence next year, it should not just be on paper. We really need this development like yesterday,” he said.

In Northwestern Province the construction of the skills training centres will be undertaken in Kabompo and Mushindamo Districts.

World.title: Government committed to expanding social and economic opportunities for Persons with disabilities
World.content:
Mixed Member Proportional Representation Member of Parliament (MMPR) for Persons with Disabilities, Lazarus Hakalebula, has reaffirmed government’s commitment to expanding social and economic opportunities for Persons Living with Disabilities.

Mr Hakalebula says the government is advancing inclusive governance and development planning to improve the wellbeing of Persons with Disabilities.

He was speaking during an engagement meeting with Persons with Disabilities and social welfare stakeholders in Chilanga District.

“As Persons with Disabilities, let us show ourselves through our talents and skills and find alternative ways of earning a living, without waiting for charity and handouts,” advised Mr Hakalebula.

Meanwhile, Mixed Member Proportional Representation Member of Parliament for Persons with Disabilities, Misheck Mweemba, stated that the government will continue to uplift the lives of Persons with Disabilities through enhanced social protection programmes.

Mr Mweemba noted that President Hakainde Hichilema assented Bill 7 into law to create an opportunity for inclusion and empowerment of Persons with Disabilities through representation in Parliament.

“Persons with Disabilities will now have a voice at the table. We must change the narrative and recognise Persons with Disabilities as entrepreneurs and leaders, because their talents and skills are key to the Grow Zambia Agenda,” he noted.

Chilanga District Zambia Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ZAPD) Chairperson, Shadreck Kankwala, thanked Government for electing five Members of Parliament to represent Persons with Disabilities under the Mixed Member Proportional Representation system, describing it as a milestone achievement in social protection.

Mr Kankwala, however, cited challenges still facing Persons with Disabilities, including limited employment opportunities, difficulties in accessing health services, and inaccessible public buildings without ramps and lifts.

He called on the Government to advance social protection programmes by including more persons with disabilities under the social cash transfer and Constituency Development Fund Programmes.

“We should not be viewed as recipients of aid, but utilise our talents and skills to help ourselves without waiting for aid,” said Mr Kankwala.

Zambian Disability Network Director of Programmes, Felix Mutale, urged the MMPR Members of Parliament to undertake countrywide engagements with Persons with disabilities.

He noted that there are many persons with disabilities across the country with various needs, therefore the five MMPR Members of Parliament representing them must find time to interact with them in order to hear their needs.

And Chilanga South Member of Parliament, Ngenda Situmbeko, encouraged Persons with disabilities to harness their talents to drive the Grow Zambia Agenda.

“Each and every individual has a role to play in the grow Zambia Agenda Including Persons with disabilities who have alot of potential, skill and talent which when utilised well can go a long way in growing the economy,” noted Mr Situmbeko.

World.title: Increased road accidents in Eastern worry authorities
World.content:
The Road Transport and Safety Agency (RTSA) has in October 2026 recorded 45 Road Traffic Accidents (RTAs) across five districts in Eastern province.

The RTAs were recorded in Katete, Sinda, Petauke, Nyimba and Luangwa districts, of which 21 resulted in fatalities and the majority of them involving motorbikes.

‎

‎Speaking during the District Epidemic Preparedness and One Health Technical Working Group meeting, Petauke District RTSA Road Traffic Inspector, Frank Mbulo said the statistics highlighted the growing road safety concerns associated with motorbike use in the region.

‎

‎”In a month we get over 40 accidents. In this case, nearly one in every two accidents ended up being fatal, while two in three involved a motorbike,” he said.

‎

Meanwhile, Petauke District Commissioner (DC), Wachepa Phiri, expressed concern over the number of motorbike accidents recorded in the district.

‎

‎Mr Phiri said the accidents were particularly worrying because most of the affected riders were young people aged between 18 and 30 years, whose livelihoods depended on the motorbike business.

‎

‎”We are losing a generation. Most of the riders are between the ages of 18 and 30 years old. Young people who have found jobs in riding these motorbikes and looking at the statistics, we are losing a lot of people in the productive ages,” he said.

‎

‎And Petauke District Council Director of Health Services, Helen Nyangu called for improved compliance with road traffic regulations and capacity building for motorbike riders to promote road safety.

‎

‎Dr Nyangu said motorbike accident victims often sustain severe injuries, including head injuries, fractured limbs and excessive bleeding, with some cases resulting in death or permanent impairment.

‎

‎She said the increasing number of motorbike accident victims was also placing an additional burden on health facilities through the consumption of medical supplies and other resources.

‎

‎”The few of you may have an idea of what these accidents do. Those involved in a motorbike RTA normally come in bad condition. Some end up dying while others sustain injuries that impair their quality of life,” she said.

‎

‎Dr Nyangu said the situation was not only distressing for victims and their families but also placed pressure on hospitals.

‎

‎”Motorbike RTAs look horrific on the patient and very unfortunate on the family but it also affects the hospital because it literally means that we are utilizing a lot of our commodities that we were supposed to be using in other spaces,” she said.

World.title: Mpika residents urged to work with civic leaders
World.content:
A civic leader in Mpika District has urged residents to work closely with the local authority to promote development and address the various challenges affecting their communities.

Mpika Council Chairperson Chola Chilumba said meaningful and sustainable development can only be achieved through unity, cooperation and a shared commitment between community members and their civic leaders.

Speaking to media after visiting St Anthony Catholic Church in Mpika, Mr Chilumba said progress in any community depends on people and their leaders pulling in the same direction.

He encouraged residents to remain prayerful and to commit themselves and their civic leaders to God.

He stressed the importance of seeking divine guidance in daily life and in leadership responsibilities.

Mr Chilumba also announced the drilling of a small piped solar-powered borehole water reticulation system at Chipundu Primary School.

“The project is among five shared borehole projects being implemented in different parts of Mpika District,” he said.

He explained that the water system would be connected to a network of small pipes and taps adding that it will extend water access to residents within a radius of approximately two kilometers from the borehole.

Mr Chilumba is happy that the project would help address the water challenges facing the community and allow residents to have access to safe, clean and reliable water closer to their homes.

He expressed satisfaction that drilling of the boreholes was going well and that the works had reached an advanced stage.

Mr Chilumba assured residents that he would personally monitor progress to ensure timely completion, so that the community could begin benefiting from the facility as soon as possible.

He reiterated that the success of such projects depended on residents and the council working hand in hand.

Meanwhile, Chipundu resident Joyce Bwalya welcomed the project but asked for more boreholes to be drilled in the area, especially in Muneshi.

She said some streams in Muneshi had been polluted by illegal gold miners who were using hazardous chemicals to process gold.

Ms Bwalya said the drilling of boreholes was very welcome but the government must also continue penalising and removing any gold miner found polluting the water streams in the area.

And John Sinkala, also a Chipundu resident, appealed to civic leaders and others involved in selecting projects under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to prioritise the drilling of boreholes in this year’s allocation.

“Water is a critical basic need that must be readily available every time and easy to access,” Mr Sinkala said.

World.title: Government distributes Pasture seeds
World.content:
Government has distributed two varieties of pasture seeds, namely Brachiaria and Panicum maximum, to 19 livestock farmers in Lavushimanda District in Muchinga Province to promote pasture production and enhance livestock productivity.

Speaking during a training session on pasture establishment and management held at the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock offices, Lavushimanda District Livestock Production and Extension Officer Godfrey Singoyi said the two varieties are drought-tolerant and can last for up to 20 years.

Mr Singoyi urged farmers to take keen interest in establishing and properly managing their pasture fields to ensure sustainable production.

He explained that the pasture varieties provide nutritious feed for livestock, including cattle, sheep, goats, chickens and pigs, throughout the year, particularly in the face of climate change.

Mr Singoyi said the pasture varieties are capable of withstanding changing climatic conditions, making them a reliable source of animal feed.

“We have emphasized that they need to take keen interest in looking after the fields for this pasture,” he said.

He added that pasture production will also serve as a source of income for farmers, as those with surplus feed will be able to sell it to other livestock farmers.

Mr Singoyi noted that the initiative has presented an opportunity for farmers to produce enough pasture for their animals and generate additional income by selling the excess, especially as some parts of the country continue to experience poor rainfall due to El Niño conditions.

Meanwhile, livestock farmer from Spoon Village, Evans Mbulo, has thanked government for providing the pasture seeds, saying the initiative will help him establish pasture fields to benefit his animals.

Mr Mbulo said farmers have been experiencing challenges during the dry season because natural grass dries up, leaving livestock with inadequate feed.

“What the government has done, we are thankful for helping us with these seeds. We will make sure to put them to good use so that our animals can benefit from the government programme,” he said.

He further encouraged fellow farmers to make proper use of the initiative and appreciate the benefits of establishing and maintaining pasture fields.

World.title: Explosives kill two, injure two during dam excavation
World.content:
Two people have died while two others have sustained serious injuries following an explosion involving construction explosives at Kawambwa Sugar Company in Kawambwa District.

The incident occurred on Friday, November 6, 2026, around 18:00 hours during excavation works for an irrigation dam being constructed by D&W Drilling and Blasting Company.

Luapula Province Police Commanding Officer Lucky Munkondya confirmed the incident in a statement.

Ms Munkondya said after two explosions, cables connected to the third explosive were damaged, prompting the supervisor to leave the pit to collect replacement cables.

She said while the supervisor was returning, lightning reportedly struck, triggering another explosion that killed Mwanashendi Lewanika, 36, and Chris Mukelebai, 49, on the spot.

Ms Munkondya said two other workers, Collins Kizimoto, 41, and Kabwe Kasenge, 32, sustained serious injuries and are currently admitted to Kawambwa District Hospital in critical condition.

She added that the bodies of the deceased have been deposited at Kawambwa District Hospital Mortuary, awaiting postmortem examinations.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 10, 2026
World.content:
Nine Zimbabweans Arrested Over Alleged Russia-Ukraine War Recruitment

Nine Zimbabwean nationals have been arrested in South Africa on suspicion of attempting to travel abroad to fight in the Russia-Ukraine war. The suspects, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in Johannesburg. Five were detained at OR Tambo International Airport and four at a hotel in Bruma. They face charges under South Africa's Regulation of Foreign Military Assistance Act, which prohibits unauthorised mercenary activities. Authorities have not disclosed whether the group intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine, or which organisations allegedly facilitated their recruitment. The arrests come amid growing concern over the recruitment of African nationals into the conflict. Zimbabwe previously reported that several of its citizens had been killed after being recruited to fight for Russia. South Africa has also helped repatriate citizens allegedly tricked into joining the war.

Kenya Seizes $27 Million Methamphetamine Haul in Major Drug Bust

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Kenyan authorities have seized 454 kilograms of methamphetamine worth an estimated 27 million dollars in an operation targeting international drug trafficking networks. Three suspects, two Tanzanians and a Ugandan, were arrested in the coastal region following a joint intelligence-led operation involving Kenyan and Tanzanian anti-narcotics officers. Investigations suggest the network operates across several African countries, including Kenya, Tanzania, South Africa and Mozambique, as well as Afghanistan and the United Arab Emirates. Authorities believe some of the drugs seized in Tanzania may have entered through Kenya's port of Mombasa. The latest seizure is among the largest in Kenya's history and comes amid growing concerns about East Africa's role as both a transit route and destination for illegal drugs. Police said that investigations are continuing, with further arrests possible.

U.S. Deports Rwandan Genocide Suspect Jean Léonard Teganya

The United States has deported Rwandan genocide suspect Jean Léonard Teganya, who was handed over to authorities in Kigali and arrested. The 55-year-old is accused of participating in the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi, including alleged killings at a hospital and student dormitory in Butare. Teganya was previously convicted in the US in 2019 of immigration fraud and perjury after concealing his alleged involvement in the genocide. Rwanda's National Public Prosecution Authority said that he is the eighth genocide fugitive to be deported to the country from the US since 2007. His American trial focused on immigration offences. However, prosecutors presented evidence linking him to the Interahamwe militia and alleged involvement in the killings. Rwandan authorities say his deportation forms part of ongoing international efforts to ensure accountability for genocide crimes.

21 Killed in Bus and Truck Collision in Tanzania

At least 21 people, including two young boys, have been killed and five others injured in a road crash in Tanzania's Iringa Region. The collision involved a passenger minibus and a cargo truck at Kiponzero Junction along the Iringa-Njombe Highway. Police said that preliminary investigations suggest the minibus driver entered the main highway from a feeder road without ensuring it was safe, resulting in the crash. President Samia Suluhu Hassan has sent condolences to the bereaved families, while the injured are receiving medical treatment. The fatalities comprised 10 men, nine women and two boys aged between three and five. Two of the injured have been transferred to Iringa Regional Referral Hospital for further treatment, while the others remain at a local dispensary.

Ethiopian Families Fleeing to Kenya Face Food, Water and Shelter Shortages

Around 50,000 people have fled violent clashes in Ethiopia and crossed into Kenya's northern Moyale region since late October, prompting calls for urgent humanitarian assistance. The displaced are facing severe shortages of food, clean water, shelter and healthcare, according to an assessment by Kenyan authorities and humanitarian partners. An assessment found that 80 percent of households said their most urgent need was food and 44% did not have adequate access to drinking water. More than half of the displaced are children, adding pressure to already stretched host communities. Most of the arrivals have fled Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regions, with nine in ten households reporting that their entire villages had been displaced. Humanitarian agencies warn that urgent funding is needed to support both the displaced families and the communities hosting them.

Close 

Malawi Unveils Strategy to Tackle Transnational Organised Crime

Malawi is developing a new national strategy to combat organised crime, including human trafficking, cybercrime and cross-border criminal networks. Homeland Security Minister Peter Mukhito says the government will strengthen cooperation between law enforcement agencies and international partners to tackle increasingly sophisticated criminal operations. The proposed strategy includes establishing a National Task Force and developing a clear implementation plan. Police Chief Richard Luhanga says authorities are also investing in specialised training to equip officers to tackle emerging threats, particularly cybercrime. Malawi is among only six countries to develop a dedicated national strategy against transnational organised crime. The government says the framework will provide a coordinated, long-term response to criminal networks that threaten national security, economic stability and public safety.

World.title: South Africa: Matlala Blames Medication for R500K Bribery Claims - South African News Briefs - November 10, 2026
World.content:
press review

Matlala Claims Medication Affected R500K Bribery Statement

Alleged crime kingpin Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala has told the Madlanga Commission that he was heavily medicated and not mentally well when he made statements alleging he paid former police deputy commissioner Shadrack Sibiya R500,000, reports EWN. Matlala has denied making the payments, claiming he gave Sibiya only R50,000 during the SAPS Excellence Awards in KwaZulu-Natal. The statements were part of a failed plea agreement in a R360 million tender fraud case involving his company, Medicare24. Matlala is set to return to the witness stand.

Senzo Meyiwa Trial Continues



Defence witness Thabiso Buthelezi is set to continue testifying in the Senzo Meyiwa murder trial at the Pretoria High Court, reports SABC News. Buthelezi has told the court that his late uncle, Simphiwe Buthelezi, was seriously ill and mentally incapacitated when police allegedly obtained a statement from him in June 2020. He claimed his uncle could barely speak, feed himself, or hold a conversation and therefore was not in a condition to make or sign a statement. The defence is challenging the circumstances surrounding the alleged statement.

UK Triple-Murder Suspect Seeks to Withdraw Guilty Plea

UK fugitive Ndodana Tshuma is set to appear in the Johannesburg Magistrates Court as his extradition to Britain remains delayed, reports EWN. Tshuma, who is wanted over the alleged murders of his wife and two daughters at their London home in July, is seeking to withdraw his guilty plea to charges of possessing an unlicensed firearm and contravening immigration laws. He previously told his lawyer he could not remember signing the plea and sentence agreement, despite weeks of negotiations. The proceedings are expected to determine whether the court will allow him to retract his plea, further affecting the extradition process.
