World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: 66 Soldiers Sentenced to Death for Cowardice
World.content:
Dozens of defendants were put on trial over accusations that they abandoned their posts and refused to follow direct orders.

Some 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in DR Congo on charged of cowardice, mutiny, and failure to obey orders. The sentence was handed down by the Goma Garrison Military Court.

At least 71 members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) were arrested in several separate incidents related to the fierce fighting between the military and rebel groups near the country's borders with Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi.

They were arrested on allegations of abandoning their posts or running away from clashes with FRN rebels. Prosecutors had sought capital punishment for 70 of the defendants, while asking for a 10-year jail term for an intelligence officer. The court, however, acquitted four defendants,

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Major Dieudonné Kasereka, head of communications for FARDC in the affected region, said that the charges were necessary to reinforce discipline in the country's embattled North Kivu and South Kivu regions.

What is the FRN?

The Front for the Refoundation of the Nation is an umbrella group of rebels that also includes the March 23 Movement (M23) and Alliance River Congo (AFC).

The group's origins can be traced back to the Rwandan genocide in 1994 and the ensuing ethnic conflict, as it emerged from the Congolese Tutsi militias of the time.

It is led by former DR Congo President Joseph Kabila. When current President Felix Tshisekedi came into power in 2019, Kabila found himself increasingly ostracized politically and went into self-imposed exile in an area occupied my what was then M23. Further complicating the conflict is the involvement of the FDLR rebel group, an ethnic Rwandan Hutu militia also active in South Kivu.

Although Rwanda's strongman president Paul Kagame denied involvement in the conflict, both DR Congo and many in the international community held that evidence of Rwandan involvement was clear. Indeed, Rwanda was involved in the 2025 US-brokered peace deal — which was seen as mostly serving US economic interests and doing little to resolve the long-running conflict.

Earlier this year, the United Nations condemned FRN and Rwandan soldiers for "murder, torture and other ill-treatment, corporal punishment, forced unlawful recruitment and abusive labor, and use of child soldiers."

Edited by Kieran Burke

World.title: Africa: Africa Seeks Terms For Backing COP31's Global Electrification Push
World.content:
The COP31 presidency wants electricity to make up 35% of global energy use by 2035, but African countries question how it will be financed and whether it can support industrial growth.

A proposal to accelerate global electrification has emerged as one of the major energy initiatives at COP31, placing Africa's electricity needs and the cost of expanding power infrastructure firmly in the climate debate.

The Turkish presidency is seeking support for a target that would increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, from around 23% today.

The initiative, known as the 35 by 35 pledge, is intended to encourage governments to expand electricity use across transport, industry, buildings and other sectors.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

COP31 President Murat Kurum has described the target as an attempt to establish a clear international goal for electrification, linking the initiative to energy security, economic growth and the need to reduce dependence on imported fuels.

"We need the 35-by-35 target because until now electrification has not been underpinned by a clear global goal," Kurum said.

Chris Bowen, Australia's climate minister and COP31 President of Negotiations, has placed particular emphasis on the investment needed to make the target achievable.

"Ambition matters, but it must be backed by investment, infrastructure and implementation," Bowen said.

For African countries, the proposal comes at a time when expanding electricity access has become central to economic planning. Governments are investing in generation, transmission networks and regional power markets to support manufacturing, mineral processing, agriculture and rapidly growing urban populations.

Yet the scale of the investment required remains considerable. Roughly 600 million people in sub-Saharan Africa were living without electricity in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency. Many more households and businesses contend with unreliable supply, expensive backup generators and power systems unable to meet rising demand.

The proposed target has therefore opened a discussion about the financing arrangements, energy choices and national priorities that would determine how African countries participate in a global electrification drive.

Kapwani Kavenuke, lawyer and an energy campaigner at Power Shift Africa, said the initiative needed to reflect the circumstances of African countries, where access to electricity remains a major development challenge.

"Electrification is a good way to go because we are trying to transition away from fossil fuels," Kavenuke told bird story agency on the sidelines of COP31.

She said the continent's priorities should include expanding access to renewable electricity in communities still outside existing power networks, alongside efforts to improve electricity efficiency.

African negotiators are expected to examine how the initiative accommodates different levels of development and the substantial investment required to expand electricity supply across the continent.

Their position could influence whether the target is incorporated into the final COP31 outcome, and under what terms.

The financing question

The scale of Africa's electricity deficit provides a measure of what is at stake.

The IEA estimates that annual financial commitments for new electricity connections in sub-Saharan Africa remain below $2.5 billion, with concessional finance needing to increase roughly sixfold to support universal access goals.

The African Development Bank and World Bank have already placed electricity access at the centre of their development programmes through Mission 300, an initiative intended to connect 300 million Africans to electricity by 2030.

The programme is expected to mobilise public and private investment, expand national grids, support decentralised renewable energy systems and encourage regulatory reforms that make electricity projects commercially viable.

Its progress will offer an important test of whether international financing can translate into connections at the pace required.

The financing discussion gained fresh momentum on Tuesday with the launch of the Electrify Now Finance Coalition, bringing together governments, development banks and private financial institutions to support electrification in emerging and developing economies.

The World Bank and African Development Bank will become the coalition's inaugural co-chairs in 2027, placing two institutions already involved in Africa's electricity expansion efforts at the centre of the new initiative.

The COP31 presidency is also working with the International Renewable Energy Agency on a programme to help developing countries identify distribution grid investment needs, prepare projects and access finance.

For African governments, financing also extends to the terms on which money is available. High borrowing costs, currency risks and the financial condition of national utilities can make otherwise viable power projects difficult to finance.

Transmission networks require large amounts of capital upfront and often generate returns over several decades. Distribution companies must also recover enough revenue to maintain equipment and invest in new connections, while keeping electricity affordable for consumers.

These challenges are particularly acute in countries where public debt already consumes a significant share of government revenue.

Kavenuke said Power Shift Africa was pressing for grants to play a larger role in financing electrification, particularly for communities with limited access to existing electricity networks.

"What we are pushing for is instead of having loans in order to finance electrification, it needs to come in terms of grants," she said.

She also called for greater involvement of civil society organisations in directing financing towards community-level projects, drawing on her experience working with communities in Uganda and Zanzibar.

The financing demands have also gained support from a coalition of civil society organisations pressing the COP31 presidency to strengthen the proposed electrification framework.

In an open letter updated ahead of the summit, more than 120 organisations called for significantly increased public climate finance, with grants and concessional funding directed towards developing economies.

The signatories also want financing to reach smaller enterprises, community energy providers and local organisations, arguing that the expansion of electricity networks must be accompanied by measures to improve affordability and access.

The proposed COP31 pledge could provide a framework for increasing international investment in electrification. Its value for African economies will depend in part on how financing is mobilised, the instruments available and the extent to which support reaches countries facing the greatest electricity deficits.

Electrification and industrial growth

Africa's electricity needs extend well beyond household connections.

Reliable power is increasingly important to the continent's efforts to process more of its agricultural produce, manufacture consumer goods and capture greater value from its mineral resources.

Countries including Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo are seeking to expand mineral processing and related industries, while South Africa, Morocco and Egypt are pursuing investments in manufacturing, renewable energy and cleaner industrial production.

These ambitions depend on electricity systems capable of supplying large industrial customers at competitive prices.

The challenge is particularly important for Africa's position in global supply chains. As international markets introduce stricter environmental requirements, the cost and carbon intensity of electricity could increasingly influence where manufacturers choose to invest.

For countries seeking to develop battery materials, green steel, fertiliser production and other energy-intensive industries, electricity policy has become closely linked to trade and industrial strategy.

Damilola Ogunbiyi, chief executive of Sustainable Energy for All and the UN Secretary-General's Special Representative for Sustainable Energy for All, has identified industrial development as one of the major opportunities associated with the proposed target.

"Electrification presents an opportunity to industrialize, create jobs, improve livelihoods and strengthen energy independence," Ogunbiyi said.

Sustainable Energy for All has worked with the COP31 presidency on a new report, The Electrification Opportunity, examining the challenges and opportunities facing emerging markets and developing economies.

Kavenuke expressed a similar view, arguing that renewable-powered electrification could create economic opportunities for communities and support the development of African industries.

"It's not just about household lighting. It's not just about having e-mobility or e-cars. It's about economic transformation and what opportunities then does it bring?" she said.

The 35 by 35 initiative could provide additional momentum for investment in these sectors, particularly if international financing supports generation capacity, transmission infrastructure and regional electricity trade.

It also raises questions about how the benefits of electrification will be distributed. Large industrial projects may attract financing more readily than rural distribution networks or smaller enterprises, even as both contribute to economic development.

The terms of international support could therefore shape which parts of African economies gain access to new electricity supplies and at what cost.

The debate over energy sources

The COP31 initiative is also attracting scrutiny over the sources of electricity that would support the proposed expansion.

In an analysis published ahead of the summit, the Heinrich Böll Foundation argued that the pledge leaves considerable room for governments to increase electricity consumption using fossil fuel generation.

The foundation pointed to language referring to diverse and sustainable energy sources, arguing that the proposal needs stronger provisions linking electrification to renewable energy and the transition away from fossil fuels.

The concern has also surfaced in the wider international debate. Portugal has advocated cleaner electrification, while climate-vulnerable Pacific countries are seeking clearer progress on reducing fossil fuel dependence, according to Reuters.

The COP31 pledge already recognises renewable energy, energy efficiency, nationally determined policies and the need for affordable finance. It also calls for investment in grids, storage and decentralised generation, including through grants and concessional instruments for developing economies.

Power Shift Africa is among the organisations calling for a stronger emphasis on renewable energy within the proposed electrification framework.

"Our position is it must push forward for renewables," Kavenuke said.

She argued that renewable energy investment could help countries expand electricity access while developing local industries and creating employment.

The distinction between expanding electricity consumption and increasing renewable generation matters for African countries, where national energy systems differ considerably.

South Africa continues to depend heavily on coal, while countries including Kenya and Ethiopia generate substantial shares of their electricity from renewable sources. Natural gas also features in the electricity development plans of several African economies.

These differences will influence how governments approach an international electrification target and the financial and technological support they seek.

Africa also has significant renewable energy resources, including solar, wind, hydropower and geothermal potential. Developing these resources at scale requires investment in transmission, storage, regional interconnections and electricity markets capable of attracting long-term capital.

Close 

The COP31 presidency is seeking to address some of these infrastructure challenges through an international programme on distribution grids, supported by IRENA, and a tracking mechanism led by the IEA to monitor electrification progress.

IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol said electric technologies were increasingly competitive and could improve energy security for countries dependent on imported fuels. The agency will support the COP31 initiative by monitoring global and regional electrification trends.

"Electric technologies are often cost-competitive and can improve energy security for fuel importers," Birol said.

Utilities participating in the Utilities for Net Zero Alliance have also increased their annual investment commitment for grids, renewable energy and storage from $148 billion to $156 billion.

A global target, different national realities

The proposed 35% target measures electricity's share of final energy consumption globally. It does not prescribe an identical target for every country.

This is an important consideration for African economies, where electricity consumption remains low, and access gaps are substantial.

An increase in the global share could be driven largely by electric vehicles, industrial equipment and heating systems in economies that already have extensive electricity networks.

For many African countries, the immediate priorities include building those networks, connecting households, expanding generation capacity and providing sufficient electricity for economic activity.

Kavenuke said the proposed timetable needed to be considered alongside the practical challenges facing communities that have yet to gain electricity access.

Drawing on her work in Uganda and Zanzibar, she said some communities still rely heavily on charcoal and other traditional fuels for cooking and have limited access to electricity infrastructure.

"So when you go present this idea to people in those grassroots communities about we want to do this by 2035, which by the way is just around the corner, they are saying how?" she posed.

The pace of electrification will therefore depend on national circumstances, available technology, investment conditions and the structure of domestic energy demand.

The pledge acknowledges these differences through its emphasis on nationally determined policies and development priorities.

African negotiators will have an opportunity to establish how those provisions should be reflected in any wider COP31 outcome and whether additional language is needed on finance, access and implementation.

The COP31 presidency has presented electrification as a central part of its effort to accelerate implementation of existing climate goals.

Its progress in Antalya will provide an early indication of how governments intend to translate those goals into investment and national energy policies.

For Africa, the discussion comes as governments and development lenders seek to accelerate electricity connections through Mission 300 and attract investment in generation, transmission and industrial power supply.

World.title: Gambia: Electoral Commission Says 12 Presidential Aspirants Submit Papers As Six Withdraw
World.content:
Twelve of 18 presidential aspirants submitted nomination papers by Monday, November 9, while six withdrew from the process, the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) says.

IEC chairperson Joseph Colley said the nomination period began on November 3 and will close on November 14.

The six who withdrew after collecting nomination papers were the All Inclusive Party, Gambia Action Party, National Unity Party, Musa Jallow, Ismaila Joof and Alkali Cham.

Four of the 12 submissions had not been processed because the required D1 million deposit had not been paid. They were the Democratic Party, Salifu Jallow, Yusupha Dumbuya and Joseph Henry Joof. The latter three are standing as independent candidates.



The IEC said it had also not processed the submission by the Gambia Labour Party, which is sponsoring Bamusa Dukureh. The Commission said Dukureh had publicly acknowledged holding dual citizenship, and his senior secondary school certificate had been sent to the relevant authorities for verification.

The IEC provided updates on seven other aspirants whose papers had been processed or reviewed. Some still need to provide signatures or documents, and the Commission has not yet announced the final list of candidates.

Modou Lamin Sima of the Alliance of Progressive Citizens must submit 1,040 more registered-voter signatures to reach the national requirement of 5,000.

Independent aspirant Isatou Touray needs 12 more signatures from the Kerewan Administrative Area to meet the regional threshold of 200.

Ansu Sanneh of the National Builders Party must provide 144 additional signatures from Banjul, 23 from Basse and 379 nationally. The Commission is also carrying out further checks on his citizenship.

Kebba Bojang of the National Democratic Party needs five more signatures from Banjul, 21 from Kanifing and 1,914 nationally. The IEC is also verifying his senior secondary school certificate.

Independent aspirant Bakary K. Badjie needs 125 more signatures from Banjul, 36 from Kanifing, 110 from Kerewan, 127 from Mansakonko, 44 from Janjanbureh and 91 from Basse. He needs another 2,310 signatures nationally.

Ebrima Tabora Manneh of the People's Alliance Party must provide 57 more signatures from Kanifing, eight from Mansakonko and three from Janjanbureh. He also needs 1,507 additional signatures nationally.

The IEC said Talib Ahmed Bensouda of the Unite Party did not need to submit further documents or signatures.

The Commission said the nomination process remained open and more aspirants could submit papers before the November 14 deadline. It said it would continue updating the public on submissions and corrections, and announce the approved candidates later.

World.title: Nigeria: Nigerian Airline Removes Passenger After Threat to 'Burn Down' Aircraft
World.content:
"The anger I am feeling can burn down this plane," a passenger allegedly told cabin crew before Air Peace returned its aircraft to the airport ramp and removed him.

A Nigerian airline has removed a passenger from one of its aircraft after he allegedly threatened that his anger could "burn down" the plane during a confrontation with the cabin crew before take-off.

The incident occurred aboard an Air Peace flight P47866, scheduled to fly to Asaba, Delta State, after the passenger, identified as Celestine Ezeudu, allegedly refused repeated instructions from the cabin crew to stop taking pictures and put away his device.

The Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection at the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), Michael Achimugu, disclosed the incident in a post on X on Monday.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

According to Mr Achimugu, the situation escalated when another crew member approached Mr Ezeudu, leading to a wrangle during which he allegedly made the threat.

"The passenger ignored the instructions and when a second member of the crew approached, an altercation broke out, and the passenger made a statement: 'The anger I am feeling can burn down this plane,"' Mr Achimugu said.

He said the crew immediately alerted the captain, who initiated a ramp return at 15:57, allowing the passenger to be removed from the aircraft.

Mr Ezeudu reportedly complied with instructions to disembark without further resistance, while his travelling companion also left the aircraft voluntarily.

Mr Achimugu said the passenger later explained that his anger stemmed from missing an earlier flight, but he had not anticipated that his conduct would lead to the aircraft returning to the ramp.

The incident comes amid recurring confrontations between passengers and aviation personnel in Nigeria, some of which have triggered flight disruptions, arrests and sanctions.

In August 2025, Ibom Air reported a confrontation involving passenger Comfort Emmanson on its Uyo-Lagos flight.

The airline said the incident began before a take-off in Uyo when Ms Emmanson refused to switch off her mobile phone after being instructed to do so in line with aviation safety procedures.

Although the situation was initially resolved and the flight departed, the airline said Ms Emmanson later confronted the cabin crew member who had given the instruction after the aircraft arrived in Lagos.

Ibom Air alleged that she assaulted the crew member, another cabin crew member and security personnel, and attempted to remove a fire extinguisher from the aircraft.

She was subsequently restrained, removed from the aircraft and handed over to the police for investigation. The incident generated widespread public debate after videos of the confrontation circulated online.

Close 

Another aviation disruption occurred in August 2025 involving Fuji musician Wasiu Ayinde, popularly known as KWAM 1, at the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport, Abuja.

The incident followed a disagreement over a flask containing liquid he was attempting to take aboard a ValueJet aircraft bound for Lagos.

The Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria said Mr Ayinde allegedly obstructed the aircraft from taxiing after boarding had been completed, prompting airport security personnel to intervene.

The NCAA subsequently initiated action over the incident, while the aviation minister announced sanctions that were later reviewed following the musician's apology.

It has repeatedly warned against unruly behaviour on aircraft, including verbal abuse, physical assault, refusal to comply with crew instructions and conduct that threatens aviation safety.

Passengers who have complaints about airline services are expected to use appropriate channels rather than confront crew members or interfere with flight operations.

World.title: Somalia: U.S. Airstrikes Target Islamic State Positions in Somalia's Puntland Region
World.content:
Bosaso — A series of airstrikes targeted suspected Islamic State positions in Somalia's northeastern Puntland region overnight, with the strikes hitting areas in Qandala district, security sources said.

The bombardments mainly struck the areas of Dabablayaal and Hal Baalade, east of Dhaadaar, near key positions held by Puntland's regional security forces around the Togga Jaceel Sare area, according to local security information.

The strikes were reportedly carried out by US forces supporting operations against Islamic State fighters in the Cal Miskaad mountains, where Puntland forces have been conducting a prolonged campaign against the group. There was no immediate official confirmation from US Africa Command or Puntland authorities.



Security information gathered over the past four weeks indicated that Islamic State operatives, particularly members involved in operational activities and planting landmines, had been gathering in Hal Baalade and Dabablayaal, according to local sources.

The fighters were also reportedly active near the Wangable well and the settlements of Goob and Gardaadin, all within Qandala district. Some of the militants had previously operated east of the Togga Jaceel area, where Islamic State maintained bases and strategic positions.

The latest reported strikes come amid continued efforts by Puntland forces, backed by US air support, to weaken the group's presence in the rugged Cal Miskaad mountain range. The area has served as a major stronghold for Islamic State's Somalia branch.

The group last carried out direct attacks in the Dasaan area on September 27, using explosive-laden drones, according to security information. The incident highlighted its continued ability to deploy improvised aerial weapons despite sustained military pressure.

On September 5, a landmine explosion that was reportedly unsuccessful occurred between Sheebaab and Dhaadaar, killing one Islamic State member, according to the same sources.

Islamic State maintains a smaller presence in Somalia than Al-Shabaab but has established networks in the mountainous areas of Puntland, where it has faced repeated military operations by regional forces and US support.

The number of casualties and the extent of damage from the latest airstrikes were not immediately known.

World.title: Kenya: Millions Spent, No Flights - Ruto Makes Fresh Promise On Kisii Airport
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has renewed his promise to transform Suneka Airstrip into a fully operational airport, years after millions of shillings were spent on the facility without delivering the commercial flights residents have been waiting for.

Ruto said his government would partner with Kisii Governor Simba Arati to expand the runway and upgrade the facility to accommodate bigger aircraft.

The President made the announcement on Tuesday while addressing residents during the third day of his Gusii region tour in Bonchari Constituency, where the airstrip is located.

"I want to tell the people of Bonchari as well, and Simba, that we are going to build that new airport," Ruto said.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

He acknowledged that the facility had experienced numerous challenges but said he had reached an agreement with Arati to address them and ensure the project is completed.

"That airport had many challenges, but I have agreed with this Simba that we are going to build that new airport," he said.

Ruto said the two leaders would work on extending the runway to allow bigger aircraft to land in Kisii, reducing residents' dependence on airports in neighboring counties.

"He will plan with me how we will extend that runway so that the big aircraft can land here for the people of Kisii," he added.

The latest promise comes after years of uncertainty, stalled construction and changing government plans that have left Suneka Airstrip struggling to achieve its ambition of becoming a commercial aviation hub.

Millions spent but airport remains unfinished

Suneka Airstrip first received major rehabilitation in 2015, when a Sh52 million project was launched to improve its facilities.

The first phase included a passenger lounge designed to accommodate 200 people, toilets, a car park, an administration block, a perimeter fence and runway markings.

The Kisii County Government announced the works in February 2015, saying the improvements would boost tourism and business in the region.

However, the bigger ambition of accommodating commercial passenger and cargo aircraft required further investment and runway expansion.

In 2020, the national government allocated an additional Sh300 million towards expanding the facility to accommodate larger aircraft.

The Kenya Airports Authority subsequently undertook Phase II runway rehabilitation works under a contract initially valued at Sh134 million before being revised to approximately Sh129.2 million.

But the project stalled after the contractor abandoned the site.

According to the authority's 2021/2022 audited accounts, construction had reached only 58 per cent before the contractor demobilized equipment in April 2022.

Ruto previously announced plans to close the airstrip

Close 

In August 2023, Ruto announced plans to decommission Suneka Airstrip, citing insufficient land for the Kenya Airports Authority to undertake the required expansion.

The announcement dealt a major blow to residents and local leaders who had pushed for years to have the facility upgraded.

However, the government later changed direction.

In August 2025, Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba announced that the government was moving to recommission the airstrip following consultations between Ruto and Gusii leaders.

Ogamba said the President had directed leaders to review the facility's status and facilitate the resumption of construction.

The revival efforts received another boost in July 2026 when Interior Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo announced that a new contractor had taken over the stalled project.

Omollo said the previous contractor had encountered challenges and that the necessary documentation had been completed to allow construction to resume.

World.title: American Airlines plane nearly hit by Air France jet after takeoff at LAX
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Two passenger jets operated by Air France and American Airlines came dangerously close in the air after departing from Los Angeles International Airport recently.

The incident happened at about 12:20 a.m. on Nov. 7 after the Air France aircraft made a turn it had not been cleared to make, according to a statement the Federal Aviation Administration provided to Fox News Digital.

"The crew of Air France Flight 28 made an unauthorized turn after departing Los Angeles International Airport and went into the path of another aircraft that departed from a parallel runway," the FAA said.

JET PLUNGES 27,000 FEET IN 10 MINUTES AS OXYGEN MASKS SUDDENLY DROP ABOARD FLIGHT

Air traffic control audio captured the tense exchange as controllers worked to redirect the flights.

"Air France 028 heavy, fly heading of 270 immediately," a controller can be heard telling the Air France crew.

Moments later, the controller issued a traffic alert to American Airlines Flight 1660, warning its pilots that another aircraft was directly ahead and less than a mile away.

"Traffic alert, traffic 12 o'clock, less than a mile, maintain 2,000," the controller said.

"OK, we'll go back to 2,000," an American Airlines pilot responded.

Fox News Digital reached out to the two airlines for comment.

"Give me a minute," a pilot responded.

"Air France departed from the north side of Los Angeles Airport on a parallel runway from where an American Airlines aircraft took off," Steven Arroyo, an aviation expert and retired airline captain based in Florida, observed to Fox News Digital (he was not connected to the incident).

"All of a sudden, unannounced, the Air France aircraft made … an unauthorized left-hand turn toward the American Airlines aircraft," he said.

"They came within 400 feet of each other and less than one mile. That is dangerously close," Arroyo noted.

Once the immediate conflict was addressed, the controller questioned the Air France crew about why the aircraft had turned.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES

"Air France 028 heavy, you were instructed to climb via SID, not turn to a heading," the controller said.

A SID, or Standard Instrument Departure, is a published departure procedure that can be assigned to an aircraft as part of its flight clearance, according to the FAA's air traffic control procedures.

"The FAA will certainly want to take a closer look at this."

The controller then asked the Air France crew which departure procedure it had been instructed to follow.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Give me a minute," a pilot responded.

"No problem," the controller said.

The crew later confirmed it had been assigned the SUMMR TWO departure, a published departure procedure from LAX. It was instructed to resume the route, according to the audio.

The FAA said air traffic control immediately issued corrective instructions after the Air France aircraft entered the American Airlines jet's path.

"This was a very dangerous situation and thank goodness, air traffic control was extremely proactive and turned the Air France aircraft heading west before it converged with the American Airlines flight," Arroyo said.

"The FAA will certainly want to take a closer look at this, especially since it's happened several times already here in the past years," he noted.

World.title: Dear WNBA media, please stop telling fans to stick to basketball when the drama is what sells
World.content:
During a recent episode of OutKick’s "Don’t @ Me with Dan Dakich," Dakich asked me, "What will be the biggest storyline in the WNBA this season, and will it have anything to do with basketball?"

The second part was easy. No.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

ANGEL REESE’S WNBA FINALS SHOWED HOW CRITICISM OF HER PLAY BECOMES AN ACCUSATION OF RACISM

And believe me, I care. I just spent over two weeks flying between San Francisco and Atlanta to cover the WNBA Finals. Who won was almost beside the point for me. I was there to ask why both teams were leaving the court before the national anthem and to hear what the players, coaches and the league had to say about it.

In July, ESPN’s Chiney Ogwumike went on "First Take" and called for a reset in how the media covers Caitlin Clark and the WNBA. "In my opinion, we should be giving airtime to the beautiful basketball being played in the 30th year of the WNBA," she said.

As for that beautiful basketball, are you sure that's where you want our attention?

OK, let’s talk about the basketball

Gabby Williams and Angel Reese entered Game 7 as co-favorites to win WNBA Finals MVP. Through six games, the two had combined to shoot 34.4% from the field. For context, the lowest field goal percentage ever recorded by an NBA Finals MVP was Kobe Bryant's 40.5% in 2010.

At halftime of Game 7, Atlanta led 30–24. That’s 54 points on 31.8% shooting between the two teams. Reese and Williams combined for seven points on 3-for-8 shooting, with five from Reese and two from Williams.

WHY ISN’T ANGEL REESE HELD TO THE CAITLIN CLARK STANDARD WHEN FANS ATTACK HER TEAMMATES?

Then Williams scored 28 points in the second half as Golden State beat Atlanta 68–63 to win its first WNBA championship. She hit the go-ahead three with under three minutes left, finished with 30 points and four blocks, and deserved the trophy. She also shot 32.6% for the series, the lowest field goal percentage by a WNBA Finals MVP.

Reese shot 40.5% from the field in the Finals, including 41.8% in the paint. She missed 28 of her 53 layups. She averaged nearly 13 rebounds, which is one reason you keep her on the floor. You’d still like your 6-foot-4 forward to make a few more shots around the basket.

Is that the basketball that you want us to talk more about, WNBA media?

Drama sells in the WNBA

After Game 3, Reese taunted Golden State with the "too small" gesture, then smiled and waved as the Valkyries walked off the court. She’d just put up 21 points and 12 rebounds, Atlanta was up 2–1, and Reese claimed that she was getting inside the Valkyries’ heads.

She proceeded to shoot 4-for-20 over the next two games and started complaining about the officiating. By Game 6, the player who’d called Golden State too small was one loss from going home.

We’d seen this with Reese before. In the closing moments of the 2023 national championship game, Angel Reese followed Caitlin Clark around the court, taunting her with the "you can’t see me" gesture and pointing to her ring finger. A year later, 12.3 million people watched Clark's Iowa Hawkeyes eliminate Reese's LSU Tigers in the Elite Eight.

This August, Clark’s Fever and Reese’s Dream drew 2.6 million viewers, ESPN’s biggest WNBA audience ever. Clark is the biggest draw in women’s basketball. Put Reese on the other side and you’ve got a rivalry people have been arguing about since they were in college.

The WNBA reported 3.3 million viewers for Game 7. That’s a great number for the league (although it deserves the context that I provided in a recent column). If you tuned in to root against Angel Reese, you still got to watch Gabby Williams take over a championship game.

If you want more people to watch, quit telling them what they’re supposed to care about.

World.title: Nick Foles believes Bears are team to beat in loaded NFC North: 'Something's brewing in Chicago'
World.content:
The NFL trade deadline has passed, contenders have bolstered their rosters, and now the mad dash to the playoffs truly begins as we head into Week 10.

Looking around the league, the NFC North has cemented itself as the best division in football. If the regular season ended today, all four teams would be in the playoffs, though there can only be one division winner.

Super Bowl-winning quarterback Nick Foles knows all about the battles that occur in the NFC North year after year, and OutKick asked him who he believes will come out on top in the division during a recent interview.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

He didn’t say so specifically, but one of his former teams during his playing days is standing out right now. They also happen to be atop the division at 7-2.

"There’s something brewing in Chicago, even [Monday] night with, what was it, four interceptions or something? Caleb [Williams’] still slinging it. They’re playing and making plays. [Head coach] Ben Johnson is steady, calm, cool and collected. I think the big thing, too, is if anything happens in the game, watch how he handles the referees. He really doesn’t even mess with them — he’s on to the next one. He’s just locked in, and as players, you look at your head coach and how he responds.

"So, I look at that and say, ‘Man, this team is going to stay locked in. Calm, cool and collected.’"

The Bears are riding high on a four-game win streak, but have barely set themselves apart in the division because the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings are 6-2, followed by a very good Green Bay Packers squad at 6-3.

But Foles sees something in the Bears this season that is different than when he was even there.

"Chicago’s always struggled with an explosive type of offense. They’ve always been a defensive, run-first-type of team. It’s different, man," he said. "Defense is locked in. Dennis Allen is holding it down. Offense is just how many points are they going to score? They can go off at any time, even if you throw four interceptions. They’re still so dangerous."

Foles, though, doesn’t want to discredit the rest of the teams in the division, especially the Vikings with an amazing defensive unit that makes them very scary down the stretch. They also just traded for quarterback Kirk Cousins a day after OutKick interviewed Foles.

"Minnesota Vikings defense, Brian Flores with what he’s doing there — it’s outstanding. Their offense will be their downfall — not doing anything really," Foles said. World.title: House GOP leaders block Massie's Hegseth impeachment push
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is safe from an impeachment vote in the House of Representatives after GOP leaders successfully stopped a looming vote led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

A vote to refer Massie's resolution to the House Judiciary Committee for consideration — which effectively killed it in its tracks — passed on Tuesday evening by a 211-204 margin, averting a potential impeachment vote on Wednesday.

The GOP had been worried about having a significant number of absences on their side after their brutal midterm election performance last week, but it appears Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., wrangled one more victory on his way out the leadership door.

HEGSETH IMPEACHMENT VOTE LOOMS AS HOUSE REPUBLICANS PRIVATELY WARN IT COULD PASS

Massie's resolution is a wide-ranging piece of legislation accusing Hegseth of misusing his office via eight impeachment articles, spanning issues including the Iran war, U.S. strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean and his retaliation against Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., over a video calling on troops to disobey "unlawful orders."

Hegseth railed against the effort and criticized Massie personally during a news conference Tuesday morning.

HEGSETH LABELS IMPEACHMENT PUSH A POLICY DISPUTE, BUT DO LAWMAKERS' ALLEGATIONS RISE TO HIGH CRIMES?

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said.

The outgoing Kentucky Republican was able to force Tuesday night's vote over the objections of House GOP leaders by filing a privileged resolution, a mechanism aimed at bypassing the will of the chamber's majority. A privileged resolution must be considered within two legislative days of being filed.

REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: HOW MIDTERMS MAY CHANGE THE HOUSE IMPEACHMENT EQUATION FOR HEGSETH

All Democrats present backed moving forward with the impeachment on Tuesday evening, as expected. All Republicans but Massie voted to kill the resolution.

But some were worried earlier in the day about weak attendance potentially clearing the path for an actual impeachment vote.

"I'm going to vote no," Rep. Jake Ellzey, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital. "I don't know if any Republicans other than Massie will be in support of his articles of impeachment, but I don't even know how many Republicans will be here by the time of the vote. The real question is how short are we. Numerically, if they're all here and we're not, what happens then?"

Ellzey called the impeachment effort "a ridiculous waste of time."

Even House Republicans who are critical of Hegseth were hesitant to support Massie's resolution.

"I think it's an effort to scapegoat Pete Hegseth for Congress shirking their own duty and, frankly, the president taking action that, in my view, is unconstitutional. but it's also not unprecedented," Rep. Warren Davidson, R-Ohio, who is opposed to the Trump administration's involvement in Iran, said.

"What would be unprecedented is to hold the secretary of defense accountable for a decision the president makes. Or, frankly, it would have been unprecedented for the secretary of defense to kind of break ranks on something that is clearly not unprecedented in terms of what has become the standard operating procedure for administrations going back to the Korean War."

Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a vocal critic of Hegseth's, told reporters Tuesday, "I'm personally not a fan of the secretary. I don't think he was the right guy in the job. But, also, when you read Massie's impeachment, I don't agree with it."

World.title: Former Seattle Mariners player Dave Edler critically injured in Yakima crash that killed his wife
World.content:
A 26-year-old Washington man faces felony charges after a deadly head-on crash Sunday afternoon killed the wife of former Seattle Mariners player and Yakima mayor Dave Edler, leaving the former big leaguer critically injured.

According to the Yakima Police Department, the collision occurred around 4:30 p.m. in the 7600 block of Coolidge Road near South 76th Avenue.

Investigators stated that an oncoming vehicle traveling westbound at high speed crossed the center line into the eastbound lane, slamming into the Edlers' car. Emergency responders had to cut both victims from the crushed wreckage. Susie Edler, 67, and Dave Edler, 70, were rushed to MultiCare Yakima Memorial Hospital with catastrophic injuries.

Susie Edler died shortly after arriving. Dave Edler was stabilized and airlifted to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle, where he remains in critical condition.

Authorities identified the driver of the other vehicle as 26-year-old Trevor Allen Stockton of Yakima.

Law enforcement stated that alcohol impairment is suspected to have been a direct factor in the wreck.

MORE PROOF THAT ANY TEAM TRADING FOR DANIEL JONES AT THE NFL TRADE DEADLINE IS CHASING FOOL'S GOLD

Excuse us while we yawn.

The Colts added a fourth- and fifth-round pick for Downs in their trade with the Kansas City Chiefs. The Colts also added a sixth-round pick in 2027 from the San Francisco 49ers for Allen.

The Colts have been a grand disappointment this season.

Bob played longer than his father, spending 19 seasons in the big leagues. He played for the Philadelphia Phillies for 10 seasons, the California Angels for seven seasons and the final two seasons with the Kansas City Royals.

World.title: Republican-led House rejects Hegseth impeachment effort
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Republican-led House on Tuesday narrowly rejected a push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over how he has carried out the war in Iran and other military hostilities in Yemen, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

The vote was 211-204 to send the impeachment resolution to committee, effectively killing the effort. Even vocal GOP critics of Hegseth said they didn’t think that the secretary’s action rose to the level of “high crimes and misdemeanors.”

The impeachment resolution was authored by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a fierce critic of Hegseth and President Donald Trump; both helped oust Massie in his GOP primary race earlier this year. Because Massie had filed the motion as “privileged,” Republican leaders were forced to call a vote within two legislative days.

Hegseth “has violated the norms of war, and it’s to the disadvantage and the dishonor of our country, and to the danger of our soldiers in future conflicts,” said Massie, the lone Republican who voted with Democrats to keep the impeachment resolution alive on Tuesday.

“Somebody’s got to put their foot down and say, are we going to follow the laws that are on the books? Are we going to follow the Constitution?” he continued. “And the best way to do that is to have an impeachment against Pete Hegseth.”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is on track to be elected speaker in January, has said Democrats will “run Pete Hegseth out of town” when they take over Congress next year.

But Hegseth is safe for now, and Trump said he is standing by his defense secretary, who has clashed with not only Democrats but a handful of Republicans in the Senate and the House.

The vote came at the end of a dramatic day in Washington that Hegseth kicked off with a morning news conference at the Pentagon, where he slammed the impeachment as a “political spectacle.”

“It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt and everybody knows it,” Hegseth said.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his record during a news conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday. Chip Somodevilla / Getty

He argued that all of the military actions cited by Massie were “lawful” and called the impeachment a direct affront to the men and women carrying out those missions. Hegseth also equated Tuesday’s impeachment vote to the two Democratic-led votes to impeach Trump during his first term — first over a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the second over the Jan. 6 attack at the Capitol.

“If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week,” Hegseth said.

Shortly after Hegseth’s appearance, Trump posted his support for the defense secretary on Truth Social, saying he “gets an ‘A’ PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!”

Trump posted again after Hegseth survived the vote Tuesday evening, saying the vote was an “EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot.”

“The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!” he added.

Hegseth, a former Fox News co-host, has been a polarizing figure in Washington, surviving a bruising Senate confirmation battle in 2025.

However, one GOP critic, outgoing Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., said he has had plenty of disagreements with Hegseth but didn’t like how the impeachment resolution was led by Massie.

“I don’t really align with the impeachment itself,” Bacon, an Air Force veteran, told reporters before the vote. “But I surely, if you would have put in [a line] about firing 80 generals, if we talk about firing 80 generals and not spending appropriated money, I’d feel a little differently about it.”

Another Republican leaving Congress this year, Rep. Darrell Issa of California, suggested Massie was pushing impeachment because he was upset about his primary defeat. And he added that even if it did pass the House, there are not 67 senators who would vote to convict him in a Senate trial.

“It’s going to die in the Senate; it’s just that simple. It doesn’t really matter what happens in the House. The secretary has committed no high crimes or misdemeanors,” Issa said. “The Senate often has to protect against the rashness of the House.”

Massie’s resolution included eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth.

The first article charges Hegseth “with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat,” according to Massie.

Three others that are related to Iran fault Hegseth with continuing the war after both the House and Senate directed the removal of U.S. forces; continuing hostilities after the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period had expired; and ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties.

Another article charges Hegseth with directing “extrajudicial killings” of suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean Sea and Eastern Pacific Ocean, secondary strikes on survivors, and overseeing orders to U.S. personnel not to rescue shipwrecked persons.

The others say Hegseth illegally seized and deposed Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro “to assert U.S. control over Venezuela’s oil reserves”; used the Defense Department to retaliate against and demote Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., for telling service members they should not follow unlawful orders; and carried out an unlawful war in Yemen.

Hegseth on Tuesday morning defended his record and said every operation was a lawful one. “We destroyed terror regimes’ capabilities. We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it’s the job well done,” he said.

World.title: What are childhood vaccination rates in your community and schools?
World.content:
This is part of The Vaccine Divide, an updated data investigation into America potentially losing its measles-free status as the deadly virus roars back and childhood vaccine defenses continue to crack and crumble.

As vaccination rates among children go down, the risk of getting sick from a vaccine-preventable illness such as measles goes up.

Use these maps to see the childhood vaccination rates for your community.

World.title: Behind the data: How NBC News tracked the decline in childhood vaccinations
World.content:
Editor’s note: This 2026 NBC News data investigation is an update of The Vaccine Divide, which was originally published in September 2025. The methodology for both projects is similar. The new data was collected from June to October 2026.

For “The Vaccine Divide,” NBC News gathered massive amounts of data from state governments and archives of public records. With the help of infectious disease researchers at Stanford University, NBC News filed scores of requests for documents, including materials obtained under the Freedom of Information Act, and wrestled different types of data into a standardized format to map and compare rates across thousands of counties.

Methodology

How NBC News collected the data

NBC News built a database of childhood vaccination and exemption information using data provided by state governments, primarily health agencies. The data combines public information available for some states and data provided directly to NBC News.

The data covers kindergartner vaccinations for each academic year.

After collection, the data was collated, and exemption rates were calculated in order to be analyzed. The analysis focuses on four facets of the data:

Medical exemptions: Exemptions granted when students have medical conditions that could make vaccination harmful. Nonmedical exemptions: Exemptions for students who opt out of required vaccinations because of personal beliefs or religious convictions. MMR (measles-mumps-rubella) vaccinations: For states where data is subdivided by number of doses, MMR vaccination is counted by the second dose. Some states track measles, mumps and rubella immunization separately; in those states, measles was used to represent MMR rates. Up-to-date vaccinations: Students are considered “up to date” with their vaccinations if they have received the full vaccination series required for enrollment in their schools.

How the data was processed

With a hodgepodge of formats, jurisdictions and collection practices across states, the task required extensive work to ensure that possible inconsistencies in the data were managed.

Certain states, such as Ohio and New York, required further calculations to aggregate the state-supplied data.

Other states required hand input of hundreds of rows of tabular data.

All data was checked for accuracy.

Analyzing the data

This analysis of childhood MMR vaccination rates focused on states that provided MMR figures for the 2025-26 school year. Accompanying the analysis were several variant analyses, which confirmed that the results were robust. The variant analyses all yielded similar results, mostly within 1 percentage point. We also examined the scale of MMR vaccination rate decline across counties, with almost 4 in 10 counties declining by over 5 percentage points since 2019 and about 1 in 8 declining by that amount since 2024. Fewer than 2% of counties declined by 0.1 percentage points or less since 2019.

Variations in the data

Many states collect and report their data differently. Some use health districts instead of counties. Some states provided over a decade of data; others provided only two years’ worth. Some states redacted certain data because of privacy concerns.

World.title: GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar wins re-election in Florida after clashing with Trump
World.content:
GOP Rep. María Elvira Salazar has won re-election in her Miami-based congressional district, NBC News projects, after clashing with President Donald Trump over his immigration agenda.

A recount that was completed Tuesday, one week after Election Day, showed that Salazar was narrowly ahead of her Democratic challenger, Eliott Rodriguez, by roughly 1,000 votes. In 2024, Salazar won re-election by nearly 20 percentage points.

Salazar drew national attention in September when she released an ad criticizing Trump’s aggressive deportation policy. She said that many Hispanics felt “betrayed” by the crackdown and that the administration’s tactics had “gone too far,” with many deportations targeting individuals without criminal records.

Trump carried Salazar’s district, which is heavily Hispanic, by 15 points in the 2024 presidential election. He responded to the ad by amplifying social media posts that labeled Salazar a “backstabber” and called for her to be replaced as the district’s GOP candidate.

Rodriguez, a former local news anchor, attempted to capitalize on the rift. He said Salazar had become “so politically toxic that now even Daddy Trump appears to be distancing himself from his problem child.”

But Trump never officially rescinded his initial endorsement of Salazar.

Democrat Eliott Rodriguez. Marta Lavandier / AP

The close election spurred a legal battle after Rodriguez sued Miami-Dade’s election supervisor, Alina García, last week, alleging that she was biased in favor of Salazar and should recuse herself from the recount. Rodriguez claimed that García’s son-in-law was representing Salazar in the recount, which he said raised concerns of impartiality. Rodriguez also cited an interview García gave to The Miami Herald in which García said “Maria Elvira is the winner, with or without a recount.”

A federal judge dismissed the lawsuit Monday, saying the allegations Rodriguez laid out were not adequate grounds to remove García from carrying out her duties, while adding that García’s remarks had been “perhaps unwise.”

With one of the largest concentrations of immigrants in the U.S., Miami has been on the front lines of Trump’s deportation campaign, with more than 130,000 pending removal cases — the most of any county in the nation. Salazar’s district has been heavily affected, as it spans multiple working-class, largely Hispanic enclaves, though it also encompasses some of the wealthiest ZIP codes in the nation.

Notably, the district is also home to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who previously represented Florida as a U.S. senator.

In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate to carry Miami-Dade County in 36 years. Florida’s 27th District is now set to be home to Trump’s presidential library.

Salazar was first elected to the seat in 2020, when she defeated former Health Secretary and former University of Miami President Donna Shalala in a major upset. The victory foreshadowed the Miami area’s rightward shift in the years that followed.

World.title: Senior U.S. Army soldier arrested in U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence
World.content:
LONDON — A senior U.S. Army soldier was arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of assisting Russian intelligence, British police said Tuesday.

The 41-year-old man was arrested “as part of an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing” near the ⁠city of Gloucester, ​in the west ⁠of England, London’s Metropolitan Police said in a statement, adding that he remained in custody at a police station in London.

He was ​arrested ⁠on suspicion of ‌offenses under sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act, ‌the statement said. They relate to obtaining ‌or disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service.

“The country to which the allegations relate is Russia,” the statement added.

Three people familiar with the matter told NBC News that the soldier was based at NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters at Imjin Barracks on the outskirts of Gloucester.

A senior NATO military official also confirmed the location of the soldier’s assignment.

“We can confirm that the American service member arrested by British police was assigned to NATO’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC),” the official said in a statement.

FBI Director Kash Patel was quoted in the statement as saying that the arrest was “important” and that it “involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.”

The FBI, he added, “has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners.”

Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, was quoted in the police statement as saying, “The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.”said.

“This case demonstrates the strength of our partnerships and the resolve of the counterintelligence community,” he added. “I am grateful to the U.K. and the FBI for their professionalism and teamwork throughout this investigation.”

Calling the allegations “very serious,” Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Britain’s senior national coordinator for counterterrorism policing, said the “investigation is very much ongoing.”

The investigation is not linked to any other ongoing counterterrorism operations, the statement said.

The arrest comes at a time of heightened tensions around the threat from hostile states, with British security services saying Russia and Iran have both used proxies to commit crimes on U.K. soil.

Officials in the U.K. have said proxies linked to Iran have been behind a string of arson fires and other attacks in Britain and other countries, many of them targeting the Jewish community and intended to sow fear.

The U.S. has moved military aircraft from an air base in the U.K. amid threats from Iran.

A U.S. official confirmed to NBC News that several military aircraft had left RAF Mildenhall as the security posture there had increased.

At least eight air refueling tankers and three Osprey tilt-rotor military transports left the base in Suffolk, eastern England, on Monday, flight tracking data showed.

World.title: House blocks Massie's effort to impeach Hegseth
World.content:
Washington — The House on Tuesday blocked an effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, largely over the war with Iran.

The House voted 211 to 204 to refer the resolution to the Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it. Massie was the lone Republican to vote with all Democrats against it. Though Republicans have been frustrated with Hegseth's handling of the war that has stretched into its ninth month, many did not think his conduct rose to the level of impeachment.

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, said Monday he would not bring up another resolution to impeach Hegseth. He is retiring in early January after losing his primary earlier this year. Democrats could still force the issue, especially when they retake control of both chambers in January.

The impeachment resolution accused Hegseth of abusing his office by launching the Iran war without congressional approval, ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties, directing extrajudicial killings for the Pentagon's boat strikes in the Caribbean, directing the kidnapping of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations.

In a news conference Tuesday morning, Hegseth denounced the impeachment effort, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle."

"None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," Hegseth argued. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."

Only two Cabinet secretaries in U.S. history have been impeached. Secretary of War William Belknap was impeached over a corruption scandal in 1876, and Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached over his handling of the southern border in 2024. Belknap was acquitted by the Senate, while Mayorkas had his charges dismissed.
