World.title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
World.content:
Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.

But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.

Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:

Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.

Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.

Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.

North Carolina

Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of a week after the election, nine Democrats had won — including Davis — while one Republican won reelection and CBS News estimated four districts with GOP incumbents were toss-ups, making the state a dummymander.

Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives — the 6th District.

As of Monday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 5th and 6th Districts will go to runoffs. If Democrats ultimately win either of those districts, the redistricting effort will not have netted the GOP any extra seats.

Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority-Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled.

Tennessee

Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Monday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.

Florida

Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. In the midterms, both parties won the same number of seats as before, with Democrats winning in all four districts that Republicans had targeted, meaning the redistricting effort did not net the GOP any seats.

Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.

Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.

Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held on to their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.

South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Democrats have picked up one other seat, and another race is considered a toss-up.

California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. A week after the election, Democrats won in 46 districts, while CBS News estimates another two are likely Democratic. Republicans have won three districts, and one is a toss-up.

Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.

Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.

Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.

Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.

Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.

Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.

The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

World.title: These House and Senate midterm races don't have winners yet
World.content:
Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats — in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.

The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in two Senate races and more than two dozen House races. They include GOP-held districts with razor-thin margins, a few Democratic seats that could flip to Republicans and several races in California and other Western states that still need to count ballots.

Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:

Senate Battlegrounds

Democrats are set to enter next year with at least 54 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44. Two Senate races still haven't been called — one has long been viewed as a battleground, and the other came out of nowhere.

Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results aren't expected until 15 days after Election Day. Both the Sullivan and Peltola campaigns have argued they have the upper hand.

Mississippi Senate: The race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom was not widely expected to be competitive, but it remains close. State officials say thousands of mail ballots are outstanding and can legally arrive within five days of the election, and there are an unknown number of "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be checked. Colom and Hyde-Smith have both predicted that they'll emerge victorious.

Democrats on Defense

The dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of Tuesday night, but a few Republican House candidates are still trying to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.

Maine's 2nd District: This red, pro-Trump district is one of Republicans' top opportunities to flip a House seat, after moderate Democratic Rep. Jared Golden's decision not to run for reelection set the stage for a contest between former GOP Gov. Paul LePage and Democrat Matt Dunlap. Even though Dunlap conceded, officials in Maine say the race will proceed to a ranked-choice tabulation because LePage was just shy of the 50% mark. The tabulation will start Nov. 9.

Louisiana's 6th District: This formerly blue-leaning, majority-Black district was redrawn after the Supreme Court voided the state's maps, finding that mapmakers relied too heavily on race and narrowing the Voting Rights Act. It's now significantly redder, but since no candidate won a majority under the state's "jungle" primary system, it will go to a runoff between Democrat Chauna Banks and Republican Blake Miguez.

GOP-Held Battlegrounds

Several races held by Republicans still don't have projections — including in districts that Democrats are hoping to flip.

Colorado's 4th District: Firebrand Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert is running against Democrat Eileen Laubacher. Boebert switched to the district two years ago, after narrowly winning reelection in a more competitive district in 2022.

Minnesota's 1st District: Republican Rep. Brad Finstad is locked in a tight battle against Democrat Jake Johnson, after Finstad won by 17.2 points in 2024. Under state law, candidates who are behind by less than 0.25 points can request a recount.

Tennessee's 4th District: GOP Rep. Scott DesJarlais is defending his seat against Democrat Victoria Broderick. It's a red district, though it was made somewhat less red in redistricting.

North Carolina's 3rd District: GOP Rep. Greg Murphy is running against Democrat Raymond Smith. The district was made slightly bluer during redistricting last year, but it still favors Republicans.

North Carolina's 5th District: GOP Rep. Virginia Foxx is facing Democrat Chuck Hubbard. First elected over 20 years ago, Foxx is the longest-serving member of the Tar Heel State's congressional delegation, which was shaken up in the midterms, with Democrats flipping several House seats and a Senate seat.

North Carolina's 7th District: Republican Rep. David Rouzer is running against Democrat Kimberly Hardy.

North Carolina's 10th District: Republican Rep. Pat Harrigan faces Democrat Ashley Bell.

South Carolina's 2nd District: Longtime Republican Rep. Joe Wilson is running against Democrat Zyon Khalifa.

Please hold...

Results could take a while in some House districts, either because ballots still need to be counted or because of runoffs. In some California districts, both candidates belong to the same party, so they don't have any implications for the makeup of Congress.

Alaska's At-Large District: Republican Rep. Nick Begich is running against Bill Hill, an independent endorsed by Democrats, and a few other candidates. Remember: Alaska has ranked-choice elections, so further tabulation may be needed.

California's 4th District: In the Napa Valley area, longtime Rep. Mike Thompson is running against businessman and fellow Democrat Eric Jones.

California's 7th District: This seat was changed significantly by redistricting. Democratic Rep. Doris Matsui is running against another Democrat, Mai Vang.

California's 23rd District: Republican Rep. Jay Obernolte is running against Democrat Tessa Hodge.

Louisiana's 5th District: Democrat Patricia Moore and Republican Gabe Firment are headed to a December runoff in this deeply conservative district. It's currently held by GOP Rep. Julia Letlow, who was elected to the Senate this week.

World.title: House votes to kill Hegseth impeachment measure
World.content: House votes to kill Hegseth impeachment measure The House on Tuesday voted to block a resolution targeting Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for impeachment. CBS News' Taurean Small and Nancy Cordes report. More

World.title: Why did Hegseth face an impeachment push? Inside the 8 articles
World.content:
Washington — Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky led a now-blocked push to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, accusing the Pentagon chief of a broad range of high crimes and misdemeanors stemming from his conduct in office.

The charges were laid out in a 34-page impeachment resolution spanning eight articles that Massie introduced in the lower chamber on Monday. The House voted late Tuesday to refer the resolution to a committee, effectively killing it, after no Republicans joined Massie and House Democrats.

The impeachment resolution focused on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term: the war with Iran, boat strikes in the Caribbean, an attack on an Iranian school and the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth called the resolution "political spectacle" in a press conference Tuesday morning.

Here's a look at what the impeachment resolution says:

Article I: Starting the Iran war without authorization

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. AP Photo/Nathan Howard

The first impeachment article accuses Hegseth of following illegal orders to begin the Iran war.

"Secretary Hegseth directed and caused United States Armed Forces to be introduced into hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," even though Congress had not declared war or authorized an attack, Article I says.

The resolution says Hegseth acted in violation of the War Powers Resolution of 1973, which allows the president to use force without congressional authorization in narrow circumstances.

"Secretary Hegseth nevertheless knowingly executed and implemented the order to commence such hostilities, employing the powers, personnel, weapons, and resources of the Department of Defense to initiate military action against another sovereign nation," the article says.

Article II: Ignoring Congress to continue the war

The second article accuses Hegseth of ignoring a resolution approved by both chambers of Congress that directed the administration to end the Iran war.

The House and Senate both approved a measure in June that ordered the administration to "remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities against the Islamic Republic of Iran," the mechanism for Congress to force the executive branch to end fighting under the War Powers Resolution. Massie's impeachment article notes that this was "the first successful passage of such a legislative vehicle by both chambers of Congress" in history.

"In response, and without lawful cause or excuse, Secretary Hegseth continued to direct United States Armed Forces into hostilities with the Islamic Republic of Iran on June 26, 2026, and continues to do so," the impeachment article says.

At the time, the administration argued that "hostilities" with Iran had already ended, rendering the war powers measure inapplicable.

Article III: Ignoring the War Powers Resolution's deadline

The War Powers Resolution says the executive branch must end the use of force within 60 days if Congress has not approved the operation, with another 30-day window to safely remove troops.

Mr. Trump notified Congress of the hostilities on March 2, so the 60-day window closed on May 1. In a letter that day, the administration told Congress that "hostilities" had "terminated." Hegseth told senators: "We are in a ceasefire right now, which in our understanding means the 60-day clock pauses or stops in a ceasefire."

But the impeachment resolution says Hegseth kept directing hostilities after that deadline and beyond June 1, "the date on which even the maximum possible additional 30-day withdrawal period would have expired."

The article also says Hegseth directed U.S. forces to keep fighting "in a manner calculated not to terminate the unauthorized use of such forces and bring about their prompt removal, but rather to continue prosecuting the war to pursue additional military objectives not authorized by Congress."

Article IV: Ignoring laws meant to minimize civilian casualties

The fourth article accuses Hegseth of dismantling systems and processes at the Pentagon that Congress established to minimize civilian casualties, saying that his actions led to the deadly strike on an Iranian school in the first wave of attacks against the country in February. The Tomahawk missile strike killed roughly 170 civilians, most of them children, Iranian media has reported. The U.S. has not directly accepted responsibility for the attack.

The resolution says Hegseth oversaw "the systemic deterioration and removal of Department of Defense infrastructure that Congress had mandated by law to limit collateral damage to civilians and non-military objects during military operations." The article cites Hegseth's cuts to staff dedicated to mitigating civilian casualties, his firing of the military's top lawyers and his public comments about the "stupid rules of engagement."

Hegseth's actions laid the groundwork for the strike on the school, Massie alleges.

"By directing the Department of Defense in a manner that foreseeably dismantled the safeguards necessary to distinguish civilian objects from military objectives, Secretary Hegseth thereby effected the murder of civilians," the article says.

"The strike on the elementary school was not an isolated targeting failure divorced from the conduct of the Secretary of Defense, nor can Secretary Hegseth's conduct be dismissed as a single targeting error or isolated failure in the fog of war," the resolution says.

Article V: Carrying out "extrajudicial killings" through boat strikes

Video of a U.S. strike on an alleged drug-smuggling boat in the Caribbean on Sept. 19, 2026. U.S. Southern Command

The fifth article centers on the Pentagon's campaign against alleged drug-smuggling boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific Ocean. The resolution says the strikes have killed at least 243 people since September 2025.

Massie accuses Hegseth of using the military to target suspects of crimes.

"By subjecting persons merely suspected of criminal conduct to lethal military force without judicial process, without congressional authorization, and without establishing a lawful basis for treating such persons or vessels as military targets, Secretary Hegseth arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner and asserted a unilateral power to determine who may live and who may die," the article says.

The article also cites the first strike of the campaign, on Sept. 2, 2025, when the military hit the same boat a second time.

"The strike destroyed and capsized the vessel. Approximately 45 minutes later, while two survivors clung to the wreckage, a secondary strike was ordered, killing both survivors," the resolution says. "In doing so, Secretary Hegseth has endangered members of our Armed Forces in future military engagements by encouraging adversaries to subject American service members to the same treatment."

Article VI: Retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly

Sen. Mark Kelly speaks after departing federal court on Feb. 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Heather Diehl / Getty Images

The sixth article accuses Hegseth of "retaliating against a Member of Congress for constitutionally protected speech," specifically Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona.

In November 2025, Kelly, a retired Navy captain, appeared in a video with other lawmakers to deliver a message to members of the military and intelligence community: "Our laws are clear. You can refuse illegal orders."

Hegseth issued a letter of censure and threatened to reduce Kelly's rank, which would have cut his retirement benefits. A federal judge blocked the move.

Massie's resolution says Hegseth "weaponized the Department of Defense to chill a core function of the Legislative Branch" and "place the First Amendment rights of millions of United States veterans at risk of irreparable harm."

Article VII: The capture of Venezuela's Maduro

Nicolás Maduro arrives in handcuffs at a Manhattan helipad in New York on Jan. 5, 2026. XNY/Star Max/GC Images

Article VII deals with the military operation to capture Maduro and his wife in Caracas in January 2026. It calls the raid "an act of war against a sovereign country executed under the guise of narcotics law enforcement, though in actuality intended to assert U.S. control over Venezuela's oil reserves."

The resolution says the operation involved more than 200 special operations personnel and more than 150 aircraft and drones, and killed at least 83 people. It argues Hegseth acted without a declaration of war or authorization from Congress, in violation of the War Powers Resolution.

The article cites Mr. Trump's remarks after the raid that "we're going to run the country" and that U.S. oil companies would "go in… and start making money."

Hegseth "gambled the lives of Army, Navy, Air Force, and Marine Corps personnel in order to facilitate the illegal taking of national oil," the article says.

Article VIII: Strikes on Yemen

The eighth and final article focuses on more than 1,100 U.S. strikes against Houthi targets in Yemen between March and May 2025.

The article again accuses Hegseth of using military force without congressional authorization and says the strikes led to civilian casualties.

"In less than eight weeks, there were nearly as many civilian deaths in Yemen as United States military actions had caused in that country during the preceding twenty-three years," the article says.

The article cites leaked messages from Hegseth and other top officials in a group chat on Signal that The Atlantic published last year. It argues that the conversation shows the administration knew the Houthis did not pose an imminent threat that would have required an immediate U.S. response.

World.title: Hegseth decries impeachment effort with vote expected tonight
World.content:
Update: The House on Tuesday night blocked the effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Read earlier developments below.

Washington — Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday defiantly denounced the impeachment effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle" ahead of an expected vote in the House on the measure later in the day.

"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said.

The defense secretary called Massie's impeachment effort an attempt to harm President Trump because of his own "personal animus" for the president and dislike of the Trump administration's policies.

"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said.

The House is expected to take up the impeachment resolution Tuesday evening, Massie said, but will likely first hold a procedural vote to table the measure.

In his remarks at the Defense Department, Hegseth claimed that the impeachment effort targeting him is only the first step and will next lead to actions against service members who participated in strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the eastern Pacific Ocean and Caribbean Sea.

"None of these are high crimes or misdemeanors," he said. "They're partisan policy disagreements from people who want to politicize our military."

Hegseth likened the attempt to impeach him to Mr. Trump's two impeachments. While the House voted twice to impeach the president during his first term, he was acquitted both times by the Senate.

"If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I'll take that company every day of the week," he said. Hegseth said the House never moved to impeach his predecessor, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, who served during the Biden administration.

Hegseth listed the actions the Defense Department has taken so far during Mr. Trump's second term, including launching military operations against Iran, and hailed the president for demonstrating leadership by going to war with Tehran.

The defense secretary said he has a "ton of support" on Capitol Hill and said Republicans "don't want to vote for something that isn't real," echoing his claim that the articles of impeachment are "flimsy."

Shortly after Hegseth finished his remarks, Mr. Trump praised his Pentagon chief and denounced Massie.

"Pete Hegseth gets an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS for his defense against a disgruntled, angry, defeated, former Congressman, Thomas Massie, a TOTAL LOSER!" the president wrote on Truth Social.

The briefing comes one day after Massie introduced updated articles of impeachment against Hegseth. The resolution accuses Hegseth of abusing his office by launching the Iran war without congressional approval, ignoring laws designed to minimize civilian casualties and retaliating against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly, among other allegations. Under House rules, the chamber has two legislative days to schedule a vote.

Massie, a Kentucky Republican, has criticized Hegseth for months. But his renewed impeachment push follows Republicans' sweeping defeats in the midterms, which members of both parties blamed on the Iran war and soaring energy prices. The war's status is unclear: Mr. Trump said Monday he plans to maintain the "status quo" and doesn't believe escalating the war will be necessary.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, who represents New York, said Monday afternoon he's a "hard yes" on the impeachment resolution, telling reporters Hegseth "abused his power" and is the "architect of the reckless and costly failed war of choice in Iran."

It remains to be seen whether Republicans other than Massie will vote in favor of the articles of impeachment. Massie said Monday afternoon he did not have a commitment from any other Republicans that they would support it.

Until Democrats take control of the House in January, any impeachment effort would need support from at least three Republicans — if all Democrats vote in favor and depending on any absences. Removing Hegseth from office by convicting him in the Senate is a much heavier lift, requiring more than a dozen Republicans to join the effort.

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told CBS News "impeaching a Cabinet secretary right now … in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look."

The GOP leader told reporters Tuesday that he expects the House will defeat the impeachment push.

"You don't impeach a Cabinet secretary lightly," Johnson said. "They had no due process. There's nothing that went into this. This is just purely for people to get attention, and it's shameful."

Other Republicans have not definitively ruled it out. Rep. French Hill of Arkansas said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" over the weekend, "I want to hear the debate on it to see if it merits impeachment versus some other disciplinary action or action by the president if he's not getting the job done in leading the Department of War."

Republican Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a moderate who is retiring in January, said Monday he's "wrestling" with the issue, telling reporters, "I don't think he's been a good secretary, but do you impeach a guy for that?"

Asked by reporters about the impeachment bid, Hegseth said Monday, "We're not worried about that."

In a social media video last week, Hegseth criticized Massie, who is leaving Congress in January after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said in the video.

Mr. Trump told reporters Monday he will stand by Hegseth if he's impeached, defending his Pentagon chief and calling Massie a "stone-cold loser."

"What has Hegseth done?" he said. "Pete Hegseth won two wars. 'Oh, let's impeach him.'"

Massie said Monday: "I would like to see him go through the eight articles of impeachment. Just make the argument from a podium. You can use notes. Get the lawyers to help you. Tell us why you are not guilty of each of these eight articles of impeachment."

World.title: House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
World.content:
House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

The House has voted 211 to 204 to refer the articles of impeachment filed against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to committee, effectively killing the impeachment effort spearheaded by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky.

Tuesday's vote short circuits any potential floor vote on the articles of impeachment, and virtually guarantees the measure will not be taken up before the current session of Congress expires.

World.title: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
World.content:
Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones

toggle caption i Halle Zander

On a rare overcast day in late summer, red-and-white fire trucks pepper a grassy strip of land in the mountains of western Colorado.

A persistent buzzing rises and falls as several uniformed staff from the Aspen Fire Protection District huddle around an iPad, watching one of their volunteer firefighters control a massive drone.

This first-of-its-kind machine looks like a giant bug. Black and white with propellers attached to four large arms, it's about 10 by 12 feet wide — roughly the size of a small U-Haul trailer.

While firefighters have used drones to monitor wildfires for decades, this new product could use AI to help extinguish fires.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Halle Zander

Eye of the swarm

Developed by the California-based company Seneca, the drones are designed to work in a swarm. Similar to a small fire engine, five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters in Aspen reported they were easy to operate.

"We were just joking that my 12-year-old could fly these things," said Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire.

When Aspen Fire officially launches its new drone program, as early as next year, it'll be the first fire department in the world to operate the drones independently. So far, they've only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.

toggle caption i Halle Zander

Fisher wants to send these drones to hard-to-reach fires, like remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen, famously home to billions of dollars in real estate, is surrounded by dense forests — like an expensive tinderbox with few evacuation routes for residents and visitors.

"If we could get it quick, keep them small and attack them while they're smoldering instead of waiting for the wind to pick them up, I feel like that's the most ideal use case," Fisher said.

According to Seneca's founder Stuart Landesberg, the drones can bypass steep or otherwise treacherous terrain quickly and have a range of 5 to ten miles — double that if they're empty.

Sponsor Message

Hovering over a fire, they use an AI-supported "sensor suite," that can calculate distance and wind speed, then release water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity to tamp down flames.

"You can think about it almost like a flying Waymo," he said.

But will they make a difference?

Landesberg said the drones won't replace air tankers on big fires, but they can carry tools, monitor ongoing fires and help extinguish lingering hot spots. Compared to helicopters, they could also make aerial firefighting more affordable.

"We can be the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost," he said.

Aspen Fire says it'll pay about $2.5 million over the next five years with private donors footing the bill.

Before other fire departments around the country invest in this experimental technology, many are keeping an eye on Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.

Joe Stutler is a firefighter with nearly 60 years experience, including decades as an incident commander on wildfires. He's not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, and said he's a "big proponent of technology."

He's excited that the drones could help fight fires overnight when manned aircraft are often grounded, and he hopes they'll reduce risk for firefighters on the ground and in the air.

"You look at how many wildland firefighters that have died this year — some aviation accidents," Stutler said. "We say, 'Gosh, we really want a retardant or water drop here.' … We transfer risk to those people that are flying those helicopters and those air tankers."

But Stutler remains skeptical. Seneca has tested the drones on prescribed burns, not real wildfires yet.

"I haven't seen any results," he said. "It's one thing to make a claim. It's something else to back it up with data."

If he had access, Stutler said he'd definitely try the new drones, but no matter how effective they prove to be, he still has to put firefighters on the ground.

Sponsor Message

"I've seen very few times that a 3,000-gallon water drop or a 5,000-gallon retardant drop actually put anything out," he said.

The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, and once training is complete, Fisher said the department could start flying the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County.

They can't fly the drones over populated areas, and someone has to have eyes on them at all times. Firefighters can't blindly send a drone over a ridgeline without someone perched on top of a mountain or on the other side to watch them and communicate with the pilots.

But if the drones are useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires around the state.

World.title: U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running
World.content:
U.S. boycotts U.N. human rights review for second year running

toggle caption i Lian Yi/Xinhua via Getty Images

GENEVA, Switzerland — The United States has left an empty chair at a key United Nations human rights review for the second year running, becoming the only U.N. member state ever to do so.

The review, known as the universal periodic review, is meant to be just that: universal. Each state is reviewed every four to five years by fellow member states. The aim is to ensure that every country, however powerful, undergoes a peer review of its human rights record.

As well as diplomats from countries under review, civil society groups are allowed to submit evidence too. Several made the trip to Geneva, led by the American Civil Liberties Union.

Sponsor Message

Jamil Dakwar, the ACLU's human rights director, told journalists that the current U.S. administration was continuing to violate human rights "unabashed," citing the treatment of immigrants, student protesters and the LGBTQ community as examples.

Dakwar said the U.N. must hold the U.S. accountable, warning that the Trump administration wanted to "dismantle human rights." In a written response, the State Department pointed out that Washington had already formally withdrawn from the U.N. Human Rights Council, accusing it of "pushing anti-American rhetoric."

In fact, leaving the council, which has 47 elected members, does not mean the U.S. can easily get out of the review process, which is obligatory for all 193 U.N. member states. Human rights groups see Washington's stance as part of a pattern of disengagement and even active opposition to multilateral organizations, pointing to U.S. sanctions on the International Criminal Court and the decision to leave the World Health Organization.

So what happens now? The U.N. has few sanctions against a country that does not cooperate with the review process. Israel skipped one review back in 2013 in protest at what it said was anti-Israel bias, but returned nine months later after the U.N. rescheduled. Until today's no-show by the U.S., no country has ever failed to turn up twice.

Sponsor Message

Rights groups would like the U.N. to hold the review anyway, and take evidence about alleged violations in the U.S. Member states had already drawn up a list of questions for Washington's diplomats, including questions about the use of the death penalty and restrictions on abortion.

But U.N. insiders fear that holding the review when there is no one to answer those questions could set a risky precedent. Even authoritarian regimes such as North Korea take part in the review process. If the U.N. allows a review to go ahead without U.S. participation, it could encourage other member states to stay away, too, leaving rights groups to present their evidence, as one put it, "in a vacuum."

For now, the U.N. has decided to postpone tricky deliberations about how to react until early next year. In the meantime, a process regarded as a last resort for the victims of human rights violations is not available to U.S. citizens. It is, one rights activist said in Geneva, "a crisis of accountability."

World.title: Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says
World.content:
Americans across the economic spectrum feel a 'panic' about finances, author says

toggle caption i LM Otero/AP

How much money would it take for you to feel financially secure? Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist Mona Chalabi spent five years following 10 Americans, from those living paycheck to paycheck to those earning hundreds of thousands of dollars a year, in an effort to answer that question. Her new book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are, explores why financial security can feel so elusive.

"It's called 10 Lives because I specifically didn't just want to focus on the 1%," Chalabi says. "Instead I wanted to talk about how the 99% of us aren't all in it together, and the kind of power differentials between us."

Sponsor Message

Chalabi says almost everyone she profiled in the book was deeply worried about their financial future, even those who earn plenty of money.

"Across the board, everyone just seemed to be expressing this feeling of panic that I think is really, really particular to U.S. capitalism, which is an incredibly precarious and cruel system where you are one crisis away from experiencing a real economic shock," she says.

Chalabi also noticed that many of the people she profiled considered themselves middle class, regardless of what their actual income was. She says that disconnect between actual wealth and a sense of class has consequences — not just for how we see ourselves, but also in how we judge everybody else.

"To be poor in this country is to encounter an enormous, enormous array of obstacles, including assumptions about your intelligence [and] your educational level," she says. "And so it's actually quite rational sometimes for people to try to present themselves as middle class, maybe even to try and signal wealth with the clothes that they buy or the cars that they drive. I don't think it's simply aspirational. I also think it is them trying to avoid the discrimination that they might face if their real income level were disclosed."

Sponsor Message

Interview highlights

Penguin Random House

On the importance of parents when it comes to financial security

If you really want to understand somebody's economic security, you need to understand who they can turn to when times get hard, and obviously a household is an imperfect measure of that. People sometimes even live with spouses that they can't necessarily lean on. ... But one of the things that came out time and time and time again from the book is how much money your parents have is so profound in shaping your economic security. …

Class is about more than the number that is printed on your pay slip or the number that's in your bank balance. Our class identities are very often tied to our households that we were in growing up. They're tied to the professions that our parents had. ... Most people who are born in poverty in this country do not make it out.

On younger generations choosing partners for economic compatibility

Who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.





There was this TikTok trend that I saw a while ago with people talking about how they were looking for a partner who was 6'5", blue eyes and working in finance, which has never been any partner of mine. I grew up with a particular model of feminism that was about being able to support yourself, not relying on a man. But I also think that for my generation, there was this ... understanding of romance that it's somehow supposed to be post-materialist, that you're not really supposed to talk about wanting a partner from a particular set of economic circumstances. …

[There] was a study that was published by the National Bureau for Economic Research. And they compared 1960 to 2005 and what they found was that it's not necessarily that people are seeking out partners in the same income bracket, but people very often seek out partners with a similar educational background, and education has a huge impact on income. So they actually found that over that period from 1960 to 2005, the trend has gotten even stronger. So we are much more likely now to date someone with a similar educational backgrounds to ours. And the reason why this is important to scrutinize is because I would say who we date, along with how much money we inherit, are probably two of the biggest factors that affect the level of inequality overall in this country.

Sponsor Message

On being transparent about her own finances, including her large book advance

I felt the people that I was speaking to had a right to understand my economic privilege, my vantage point as I'm asking them these deeply personal questions. And as you know, as journalists, we typically do not pay people for their time for interviewing them. … But that's a very different kind of equation when you are asking people to share these vulnerable parts of their lives, and especially when I am profiting from those stories.

At the start of every interview with everybody that I spoke to, I told them a number of things. I said, one, I will be paying you $40 per hour for your time. If that feels uncomfortable for you, let's talk about it. I said that anything that I asked them as a journalist, they had the right to ask me back. So if I asked them how much money they made, they had the right to ask me that exact same question.

On making judgments about her class from her accent

The accent thing is huge. ... When I'm back in the U.K., people can get a pretty good read, honestly, on my class by my voice. And what's fascinating is that as an immigrant, Americans don't really understand these nuances in the British accent. And so I'm just read as posh here. And I think that has conferred me, actually, these huge class benefits. I think that my accent in the U.S. has been really powerful in counterbalancing some of the obstacles I might have faced because of my race and gender. Because with this voice, it is assumed that I am educated, that I'm cultured. Not sure how true any of these things are, but there's just this assumption that I think is very beneficial in a corporate environment.

Sponsor Message

Anna Bauman and Nico Gonzalez Wisler produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

World.title: Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation remains stubbornly high
World.content:
Gas prices dip below $4 but inflation remains stubbornly high

toggle caption i Ronaldo Schemidt/AFP via Getty Images

Inflation-scarred consumers are finding a bit of relief these days at an unlikely place: the gas pump.

The average price of gasoline dipped below $4 a gallon Tuesday for the first time in three months, according to AAA. The price of regular gas has fallen by 38 cents in the last month to a national average of $3.98.

The overall cost of living, however, remains stubbornly high. Consumer prices in October were up 0.4% from the previous month, according to a report Tuesday from the Labor Department. That's a bigger monthly increase than forecasters had expected.

Rising housing costs accounted for about a third of the monthly increase. Grocery prices were also up sharply during the month.

Sponsor Message

Why gas prices are falling

The drop in gasoline prices in recent weeks is thanks to a combination of falling crude oil prices, refineries' switch to a cheaper blend of winter fuel, and the typical seasonal drop in demand for gas.

"Temperatures are getting colder," says Patrick De Haan, petroleum analyst for GasBuddy. "People who have boats and RVs are probably done for the year. I would say, by Thanksgiving, so long as we don't get any wild cards geopolitically, the national average could be $3.75 a gallon."

Gas prices are still at a record high for this time of year, however — about a dollar a gallon higher than when the U.S. went to war with Iran. Even with the recent drop in prices, this year's drive to grandma's for Thanksgiving could be the most expensive ever.

Diesel prices have also fallen, but more slowly than gas prices. AAA says the average price of diesel fuel is $6.15 a gallon, down about 13 cents from a month ago.

The high cost of diesel fuel is another byproduct of the war — not only the U.S. war with Iran but also Russia's war with Ukraine. Russia is ordinarily a big exporter of diesel fuel, but that supply has largely dried up because of damage to Russia's refineries.

Sponsor Message

"When a country like Russia isn't exporting diesel, that is very impactful for the global market. So diesel prices – they will come down but they will still remain very elevated," De Haan says.

Heating oil prices are also high

Rising diesel prices are also driving up the cost of heating oil in the northeast, because heating oil is a close cousin of diesel.

Mild fall weather has kept heating costs in check so far, but De Haan says a blast of cold air could push heating oil prices even higher.

Higher diesel prices also affect the cost of other goods that have to be moved by truck or train or cargo ship.

"You're starting to see higher freight costs get passed through," says economist Mike Reid of RBC Capital Markets. "We've seen it show up notably in goods that are heavily imported — apparel, recreation goods, IT equipment."

In a speech Tuesday before the inflation release, Federal Reserve Chris Waller suggested that energy shocks could have more lasting effects on inflation that previously though. Waller suggested the central bank may need to raise interest rates more aggressively to curb price hikes than markets had previously expected.

No annual comparison for inflation this time

While Tuesday's inflation report shows how much prices rose in the last month, it does not include the typical reading on how prices have changed over the last year. That's a casualty of last year's government shutdown, which idled hundreds of government price-checkers so prices from October 2025 were never recorded for comparison.

The Cleveland Federal Reserve Bank estimated before Tuesday's release that consumer prices in October were up 3.7% from a year ago. That would outstrip average wage gains of just 3.1% during the year, so the typical worker is losing buying power. That's a big reason for the heavy turnout in last week's mid-term elections. 49.1% of eligible voters took part in the election, the second highest total for any midterm in more than a century.

World.title: 'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent
World.content:
'Like gods reigning over humans': Many defectors see daughter of North Korea's Kim as heir apparent

toggle caption i 朝鮮通信社/KCNA via KNS via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — Until she fled North Korea three years ago, Kim Yumi felt deeply frustrated whenever state TV showed leader Kim Jong Un with his young daughter. The message, she felt, was clear and worrying: North Korea was laying the groundwork for an eventual hereditary transfer of power, this time to Kim's daughter.

Publicly questioning the Kim dynasty's hold on power would mean severe persecution. Already angered by draconian pandemic regulations that ruined her family's fishing business, she defected to South Korea by boat with her family.

"My husband and I didn't want our children to live under a fourth-generation dictatorship. As parents, we thought the best thing we could do for our children was to give them freedom," said Kim Yumi, 32, who now lives in Seoul.

Sponsor Message

North Korea allows no dissent and harshly punishes attempts to flee the country. Established in 1948, the nation is nominally a socialist republic, but in reality it is an authoritarian dynasty, with three generations of the Kim family ruling in succession. There was no known public resistance during its previous two successions — from state founder Kim Il Sung to his son Kim Jong Il in 1994 and then from Kim Jong Il to his son Kim Jong Un in 2011.

This time, North Korea is apparently trying something radical.

Kim Jong Un's repeated public appearances with his daughter over the past four years have led to speculation that she's being groomed as her father's heir.

The question of who will become North Korea's next leader is crucial because that person will face a huge challenge — governing an impoverished, nuclear-armed nation whose 26 million people have little political freedom and live under strict state surveillance while being cut off from much of the outside world.

North Koreans have no say in the selection of their future leader, and analysts and defectors say they will passively accept a third dynastic succession — at least publicly.

To gauge North Koreans' private views, The Associated Press spoke with nearly a dozen defectors who still have contacts in North Korea or witnessed the country's previous power successions, as well as several experts.

Sponsor Message

Most defectors believe the girl is Kim's heir

Not much is known about Kim's daughter except that she's reportedly about 13 and named Kim Ju Ae.

Since late 2022, she has made dozens of public appearances, all of them with her father at big events like weapons tests and military parades. State media has called her Kim's "most beloved" and "respected" child. Her status has been emphasized by images showing an elderly general kneeling before her and her standing in front of her father.

South Korea's spy agency says she is Kim's likely heir. Eight of the 11 defectors interviewed by the AP shared that view; the others disagreed, citing the North's deeply patriarchal culture.

"During her visits to missile launch sites and factories, the way senior North Korean officials treat Kim Ju Ae involves protocols reserved for a successor, not the ones simply for a daughter of Kim Jong Un," said Tae Yongho, a former minister at North Korea's Embassy in London who defected to South Korea in 2016. "They are repeating the same protocol and treatment they provided for Kim Jong Un," when he accompanied his father as his heir.

toggle caption i Lee Jin-man/AP

Kang Mi-Jin, a defector who runs a company analyzing North Korea's economy, said her contacts inside the North told her over smuggled phones that they think Kim Ju Ae is in line to succeed her father.

Jung Gwang-il, a defector who specializes in smuggling outside information to North Korea, said the North Koreans he meets as they visit Chinese border towns also hold the same belief.

Former NBA star Dennis Rodman was the first to reveal her identity, holding her as a baby during a 2013 trip to Pyongyang.

Doubts remain about a woman becoming North Korea's leader

Much of the skepticism about Kim Ju Ae as a potential leader stems from her being female. South Korean officials believe she has a younger sibling whose gender hasn't been confirmed.

Women in North Korea remain deeply underrepresented in senior posts. Only one of 17 department directors for the ruling Workers' Party is a woman. That woman is Kim Jong Un's influential younger sister, Kim Yo Jong, according to South Korea's Unification Ministry.

Sponsor Message

"My contacts in North Korea say it would be nonsensical to revere that little girl as their supreme leader," said Kim Jeong-Ah, a former North Korean army officer who resettled in South Korea in 2009.

Lee Si-young, a defector who heads the Seoul-based Free North Korea Radio station, said that some of her older contacts in North Korea aren't happy with a woman taking power. But she said members of the Kim family "are like gods reigning over humans so gender really doesn't matter."

Kim's push for hereditary power transfer faces little resistance at home

Whether or not the girl succeeds her father, observers agree that Kim Jong Un, 42, is likely to designate one of his children to prolong his family's rule, a move they expect would face little resistance at home. South Korea's spy agency recently assessed that Kim is extremely obese and at high risk of cardiovascular disease but shows no other signs of poor health.

North Koreans will passively "accept a hereditary succession as something that they should go along with," said Ahn Chan-il, a defector and scholar who heads the World Institute for North Korean Studies in Seoul.

During North Korea's first leadership transition, in 1994, the new leader, Kim Jong Il, then 52, had already spent two decades as the official successor working alongside his father to run the country.

The second succession, in 2011, was more uncertain. Kim Jong Un, who was then 27, was seen by outsiders as too young and inexperienced. He quickly consolidated his grip on power, however, by orchestrating high-profile executions and purges, including the 2013 killing of his powerful uncle Jang Song Thaek.

"A hereditary power succession system has been institutionalized in North Korea, just like presidential elections in our system," said Oh Gyeong-seob, an analyst at Seoul's Korea Institute for National Unification. "North Korea's ruling elite accepts it as a matter of course. So do its general citizens."

Sponsor Message

Choi Song-juk, who fled North Korea in 2015, said she had been so brainwashed that she had no complaints about the North's two earlier power successions. She now calls them "nonsense."

Defector Jeon Jae-hyun said North Korea's pervasive surveillance apparatus keeps people from voicing their discontent with the government and helps enforce political loyalty.

Defector Kim Yumi said she had never heard about the girl until Kim Jong Un publicly introduced his daughter at a long-range missile launch site in November 2022.

"Ordinary people know absolutely nothing about private lives of the Kim family," said Kim Yumi, who now runs a YouTube channel on North Korea. "They don't really try to know about it and don't pay attention to it because doing so could put them in danger."

World.title: Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility
World.content:
Indonesia's VP offers resignation as questions mount over his eligibility

toggle caption i Dita Alangkara/AP

JAKARTA, Indonesia — Indonesia's vice president offered to resign during a meeting with President Prabowo Subianto on Tuesday, according to officials, adding to the turmoil at the highest levels of the country's leadership.

Vice President Gibran Rakabuming Raka, the 39-year-old son of former President Joko Widodo, held over two hours of talks with Prabowo, according to State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi.

It was not immediately clear whether Prabowo accepted the resignation, Hadi told reporters at a news conference at the presidential palace. The president advised Raka to "continue pursuing legal avenues to defend the validity of his academic documents," Hadi said.

Sponsor Message

As he left his office later in the day, Raka made a brief statement to reporters without addressing the resignation offer.

"I respect all criticism and feedback from the public regarding the developments that are taking place," Raka said. "I do not want the current situation to become a prolonged political controversy."

The resignation offer comes amid growing pressure on Raka over a court dispute involving his academic credentials. It was apparently not related to an ongoing probe into allegations that top police officials, including the president's chief of staff Gen. Listyo Sigit Prabowo, had been involved in a wiretap targeting the president. Three other police generals have also been implicated in the case.

Listyo previously served as national police chief under Widodo, who has not been implicated in the wiretapping investigation.

The developments come amid a widening political rift between Prabowo and Widodo. The popular former president backed Prabowo's presidential bid after he chose Raka as a running mate.

The controversy over Raka's academic qualifications escalated last month after the Supreme Court ruled that the documents he submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements.

The ruling intensified political pressure on Raka and fueled calls from some lawmakers for his impeachment.

Sponsor Message

Widodo faces unrelated allegations that he used a fake university diploma, which he denies.

World.title: Republicans block impeachment push against Pete Hegseth
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth called the articles of impeachment introduced against him a farce and a stunt at a news conference Tuesday morning. Representative Thomas Massie, a Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment against him on Monday, largely focusing on the war in Iran.

Republicans in the U.S. House of Representatives voted Tuesday evening to sideline a resolution that aimed to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.

The vote halts the effort spearheaded by Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie to remove the Pentagon chief for his conduct in office and his handling of the war in Iran.

The 215 to 209 vote refers the impeachment resolution to a commitee, effectively killing it for the remainder of this session of Congress.

The new Congress, with Democrats in the majority in both House and Senate following their sweeping midterm wins, could resume a new impeachment push against Hegseth.

That couldn't happen until the swearing in takes place on Jan. 3, and it's unclear whether the Democrats will want to make impeachment a top priority.

Massie, who won't be in Congress when the new session begins in January, was the only Republican member of the House to break ranks on the vote.

WATCH | Massie says he's taking a stand, not 'disgruntled': U.S. House Republican moves to force vote on impeaching Pete Hegseth | Duration 2:27 Republican Rep. Thomas Massie moved Monday to force a vote to impeach U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, largely focusing on the war in Iran and his role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela. A vote in the House could come by mid-week, putting pressure on fellow Republicans to decide whether to remove one of the Trump administration's most prominent figures following sweeping midterm election losses.

U.S. President Donald Trump celebrated the vote result in a post on social media, calling it the exoneration of a great American patriot.

"The Democrats' attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has miserably FAILED!" Trump wrote in the post on his Truth Social platform. The Democrats continue to weaponize and abuse the United States of America. They must be stopped!"

The vote came after Hegseth forcefully defended himself in a news conference Tuesday morning.

He said impeachment proceedings would be a "show trial against the president and the secretary of war" and he characterized the articles of impeachment drawn up my Massie as "policy disagreements" that don't meet the impeachment standard of high crimes and misdemeanours.

"The proper remedy for a policy disagreement, it's legislation, it's debate, it's the next presidential election," said Hegseth, holding his first press briefing from the Pentagon since May.

'They will fail again'

The articles of impeachment in Massie's motion lead with the lack of congressional authorization for the war in Iran. The articles also reference Hegseth's role in carrying out military actions in Yemen and Venezuela, and the deadly strikes on boats allegedly transporting drugs in waters near South America.

Massie had introduced a similar measure in September, but the House legislators were sent home before a vote could occur.

"I stand behind every one of these operations," Hegseth said on Tuesday.

He said "thousands of American lives" were saved with every boat strike — even as human rights organizations and international bodies have said they possibly constitute crimes against humanity. Hegseth also said that former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro was "not kidnapped, he was brought to justice by America's best."

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky speaks Monday outside the Capitol about articles of impeachment against Hegseth. (Allison Robbert/The Associated Press)

The articles also refer to attempts to prosecute Congress members Mark Kelly and Elissa Slotkin after they recorded a video advising service members they were not obliged to follow illegal orders.

Massie, who was defeated earlier this year by a Trump-backed Republican opponent in a primary, pushed forward an impeachment resolution over the objections of House Republican leadership, with outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson saying it would be "a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see."

The last House impeachment was of former Homeland Security chief Alejandro Mayorkas in Joe Biden's administration in 2024, for breach of public trust and willful refusal to comply with the law. The Republican-led House cited the surge of migrants at the southern border in just the second ever impeachment of a cabinet secretary, but the Democratic-led Senate then never took up the measure.

Trump was twice impeached in the House, in 2019 and 2021, but acquitted at Senate trials. In the second impeachment, many Republicans argued that Trump's actions leading up to the 2021 Capitol riot were best dealt with in the courts, but Trump completed a remarkable political comeback before criminal indictments he faced were resolved legally.

Hegseth called those Trump impeachments failures and predicted that the current efforts "will fail again."

Razor-thin confirmation

What constitutes "high crimes and misdemeanours" is not spelled out in the Constitution, leaving it to lawmakers to decide.

Democrat Hakeem Jeffries, Johnson's potential successor as the next Speaker, recently said he is a "hard yes" for impeaching Hegseth. Several other Democrats took to social media on Tuesday to say they were in favour.

A vote will put pressure on Republicans, many of whom blamed their midterm election wipeout on the Iran war.

Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who has been critical of Hegseth, told reporters on Tuesday he wasn't a fan of the impeachment articles in their present form. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska has highlighted other concerns not contained in the articles, including Hegseth's firing of dozens of senior military leaders, but he also questioned Massie's motives.

"If we were allowed to amend it, I'd maybe feel a lot of differently," said Bacon.

Republican Rep. Warren Davidson of Ohio said, "blaming Hegseth for a duty Congress shirked and the president made is wrong."

"This isn't about Iran, this about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon," said Vice-President JD Vance.

Vance broke a tie in the Senate to enable Hegseth's confirmation in early 2025. Republicans Susan Collins and Mitch McConnell — each set to leave Congress — voted against his confirmation, as did Republican Lisa Murkowski and all of the Senate Democrats.

Thom Tillis, a Republican also leaving the Senate, has expressed regret for his vote to confirm Hegseth, saying in part in September that the secretary "retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defence."

LISTEN | David Smith, Washington reporter for the Guardian, on Hegseth's influence (March 16): Front Burner 30:05 Pete Hegseth: the Iran war’s chief promoter

Democrats and a handful of Republicans questioned Hegseth's fitness for the job nearly two years ago. Hegseth admitted paying a settlement to a woman who alleged he sexually assaulted her, in order to prevent a costly and drawn-out process.

His confirmation hearings also included allegations of excessive drinking and financial mismanagement at two veterans' organizations he previously led.

During Trump's first term, Hegseth was an on-air Fox News contributor who lobbied the president on behalf of three service members who faced accusations of war crimes in military tribunals, arguing they were being treated unfairly.

Trump ultimately granted clemency to two of the men, and elevated a third in rank.

Hegseth's tenure at the Pentagon has been unconventional, and that was on display on Tuesday. Defence secretaries typically stay away from partisan political statements, but Hegseth laid out criticisms of predecessor Lloyd Austin and disparaged the military recruitment and retention efforts of Biden's administration.

He also told the U.S. troops to "stay the course" while evoking his Christianity, even as he has been sued for imposing his religion on federal workers.

World.title: Tensions between PM, Quebec premier continue to flare in new tiff over U.S. relations
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The relationship between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has gotten off to a rocky start over the past couple of weeks.

The most recent incident happened on Tuesday. Carney was at a news conference in Montreal — highlighting his government's commitment in last week's federal budget to invest in culture — when he was asked about the Quebec government's intention to negotiate directly with American states.

The question came following news that Paul St. Pierre Plamondon had sent letters to 59 newly elected U.S. officials, including Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and re-elected governor Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire .

In the letters, the premier wrote about Quebec's trade relationship with each state, and invited the state representatives to work directly with a Quebec delegate on "new projects and initiatives for the benefit of our respective populations."

That gestured appeared to irk the prime minister. When he was asked about the Quebec premier's efforts, Carney pointed out that "the executive branch, the president, and the American courts," are still the decision-makers for agreements and trade initiatives.

"Secondly," he said, "in a negotiation, it's always a good idea to have a single negotiator."

He then stated that this responsibility lies with the federal government.

'Mr. Carney is not my boss,' says Quebec premier

St-Pierre Plamondon responded to Carney's comments by doubling down.

“Mr. Carney dreams of us not putting on our skates and never setting foot on the ice because he wants the rink all to himself," he said.

"Welcome to Quebec. We have always asserted our place."

He said the letters are something other governments have done before, and that he's doing what he believes is in the best interest of the province.

"And Mr. Carney is not my boss, and he will not prevent Quebec from doing what it has always done, which is to have an international presence that allows us to represent our interests."

St-Pierre Plamondon made his comments to reporters on Tuesday, following a meeting he had at his office with Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-Francois Blanchet (pictured on his right) in Quebec City. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)

St-Pierre Plamondon added that Quebec will continue to assert its place on the world stage over the coming months.

Not the first public spat for Carney and Quebec premier

Earlier this month, the Quebec premier accused the federal government of attempting to muzzle him, when Carney denied him speaking time at the 21st Canada-EU summit that was held in Montreal.

St-Pierre Plamondon opted to withdraw from the summit and sent Quebec's chief diplomat, Pascal Paradis, to represent him during the summit's activities.

Paradis has also been tasked with being the province's chief negotiator, including taking over the trade file with the United States.

Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard said it never would have crossed his mind to boycott the event if he were premier.

"Sulking isn't an option," said the Leader of the Opposition. "I don't think this is the best start to relations between Quebec and Ottawa."

Carney said at the time that it was St-Pierre Plamondon's choice to leave his seat at the table empty.

The prime minister has not yet had an in-person meeting with Quebec's new leader, who was sworn in on Oct. 21.

St-Pierre Plamondon has insisted that their first meeting take place in Quebec City, which the prime minister's schedule has reportedly not been able to accommodate so far.

On Tuesday, however, the prime minister was campaigning in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton ahead of a byelection scheduled there for Dec. 7. The Quebec electoral district is about a two-and-a-half-hour drive from the provincial capital.

Carney and St-Pierre Plamondon are set to meet in meet in Cambodia during the Francophonie Summit later this month.

World.title: 4 grizzly bears responsible for killing mother and daughter in B.C., officials say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with an attack near Bella Coola that left a mother and daughter dead.

Forensic testing confirmed an adult sow and three cubs were involved in the attack that killed Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.

In an update Tuesday, BCCOS Insp. Jeff Tyre said the attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which is considered "very rare."

"We hope the efforts of everyone who responded, as well as these findings, bring some measure of closure," he said.

"Our thoughts remain with everyone affected."

WATCH | Officials give update on Bella Coola grizzly attack: WATCH IN FULL: Officials give update on 4 grizzly bears destroyed following deadly attack | Duration closed caption 8:57



All trapping equipment used in the response has been removed, and the investigation into the attack has concluded, the Conservation Officer Service said in a news release. It said further analysis will examine the response and the circumstances that led to the fatal event.

"They all had to be [killed], because bears that are involved in fatal attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated," explained Tyre.

"This type of behaviour presents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future."

The four bears captured over the weekend were not involved in the 2025 attack on a group of students and teachers in Bella Coola, Tyre said.

The bear responsible for that attack was never found.

Tyre said more than a dozen conservation officers worked to track down the bears involved in this month's attack, often in difficult terrain and weather conditions.

"We remain committed to working with the Nuxalk Nation and the Bella Coola community to help prevent future bear conflicts," he said.

Elected Chief Councillor Samuel Schooner called the event "deeply, deeply unsettling," and said they're still recovering from the attack from last year.

"Our community is rightfully still deeply affected, and will be for generations."

He said they will continue to provide supports for residents for as long as is needed, including night patrols, escorts for children going to school and offering rides to anyone who needs to get around.

The nation is asking community members to continue to take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, ensure spaces are free of any bear attractants and stay away from the Snooka West Trail area.

WATCH | 2 grizzly attacks in same part of B.C.: Grizzly attacks again in same area of B.C. This time 2 are dead | Duration closed caption 7:05

Nuxalk cultural leaders will decide on how the bear remains are used, the nation said in a community update on social media.

"We continue to pray for Jenny and Selah’s family. Your loss is felt with each of us and Nuxalk stands ready to support you during this tragic time," the update read.

"Over the coming months, there will be ongoing discussion about bear coexistence. Nuxalk [leadership] is committed to hearing all perspectives and finding a good path forward."

'Two peas in a pod'

According to family members, Balcarras and Reed were out for a hike on the Snooka West Trail on Oct. 31 but never returned home. They were reported missing the following day.

Jennifer Balcarras and her daughter Selah Reed in this undated photo provided by their family. (Submitted by Matthew Balcarras)

Balcarras's remains were found on Nov. 2, and Reed's were discovered 150 metres away from her mother on Nov. 3.

Balcarras worked as an art therapist in the community, and loved painting, playing guitar and the outdoors. Reed was an education assistant, described as a gentle soul who loved ballet, art and hiking.

The two liked a lot of the same things, according to Josh Balcarras, Jennifer's brother.

"I think they got along really, really well," he said, speaking following their deaths. "They were two peas in a pod. When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her."

World.title: N.S. group apologizes for including woman convicted in a brutal killing on a panel
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Nova Scotia group that supports at-risk women and girls is apologizing after it hosted a panel discussion on violence that featured a woman convicted in the brutal killing of a teenager.

Marissa Shephard was listed as a panel member for the event last week organized by the Elizabeth Fry Society of Mainland Nova Scotia.

The panel was titled "Navigating the Legal System and Community Supports After Violence, Victimization, and Loss." It was the second of three panels supported through the Logan Alexandra Russell Fund, which was created in memory of a Cape Breton woman who was killed in an act of intimate partner violence.

"The fund honours Logan’s beautiful life and loving, empathetic nature, while also striving to protect others from the violence that caused her death by contributing to intimate partner violence prevention efforts," a website for the event reads.

In 2021, Shephard was sentenced to 12 years in jail after she pleaded guilty to manslaughter and arson in the death of 18-year-old Baylee Wylie, who was stabbed 200 times.

Russell's mother posted a message on social media saying the family was not made aware of the decision to include Shephard on the panel, and apologized to Wylie's family.

"I am beyond disappointed and heartbroken that they would use Logan’s legacy in connection with someone like her," Maureen MacTaggart wrote.

Three people sentenced in Wylie's death

Wylie's body was found in Shephard's burned out townhouse in Moncton, N.B., in December 2015.

Shephard was one of three people sentenced in connection with his killing.

Devin Morningstar was found guilty of first-degree murder in 2016, while Tyler Noel pleaded guilty in May 2017 to second-degree murder and arson with disregard for human life, and both received life sentences.

The Nova Scotia chapter of the Elizabeth Fry Society issued a public statement Monday night saying it made a serious mistake while planning the event.

"Our work asks us to consider everyone who may be affected by violence, and above all, to do no further harm. With this event, our actions did not reflect that, and we have harmed those we support," reads the statement.

Baylee Wylie's body was found in a burned-out townhouse in Moncton in December 2015. (Submitted)

The non-profit group said in an email they would not be taking part in media interviews at this time.

"Our staff have received repeated threats of violence, and our priority right now is the safety of our team and the people we support, and respect for families who are grieving," reads the emailed statement sent Tuesday afternoon.

According to court documents, Wylie, Shephard and the two other young men gathered at her home for "some drug-fuelled excitement" that ended tragically with Wylie being tied to a chair, beaten and stabbed repeatedly with a variety of weapons.

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: U.S. comedian Josh Johnson surprised by CBC journalist in viral video
World.content:
