Suspect says he is a 'prisoner of war'

Prosecutors described the defendant held in the US as a Kata'ib Hizballah commander.

Arrested in the spring, the suspect pleaded not guilty in June to charges of plotting at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the US and Israeli war with Iran.

He called himself a "prisoner of war."

British authorities had also linked the alleged Fairford plot to Tehran, which denied involvement. .

All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

UK prosecutors alsoseparately charged two men, both 24, under the National Security Act in October. One is accused of assisting Iran's intelligence service and was granted conditional bail. The other faces a charge of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, relating to an alleged reconnaissance visit to Fairford in August. He was remanded in custody.

World.title: Former Malaysian leader Najib Razak returns home under royal pardon, but faces a separate 15-year prison sentence
World.content:
Najib Razak has left prison under a royal pardon, prompting a minister to resign in protest. Malaysia's former leader still faces a separate 15-year sentence over the corruption scandal that brought him down.

Former Malaysian Prime Minister Najib Razak arrived home Tuesday to serve the remainder of his corruption sentence under house arrest after four years in prison over the 1MDB scandal that saw $4.5 billion siphoned out of the state investment fund.

The transfer followed a royal pardon and a court ruling that ended a legal dispute over his release from prison.

Najib, 73, reached his Kuala Lumpur residence in a convoy escorted by police and prison vehicles, with supporters waiting outside.

"It's a final relief," his lawyer Muhammad Shafee Abdullah told reporters, adding that house arrest was "still an imprisonment because he can't leave the house unless he gets special permission or for a special reason."

Why was Najib allowed to leave prison?

Malaysia's King Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar granted Najib a conditional pardon in September, allowing him to complete his reduced six-year sentence at home once a court-imposed fine was paid.

His political party, the United Malays National Organization (UMNO) which governed Malaysia for six decades following independence, paid the fine on Friday. Najib briefly left prison but was returned hours later after the attorney general sought legal clarification.

The king subsequently warned against defying the pardon, which he said was "clear, explicit and without any ambiguity." The Kuala Lumpur High Court issued a fresh order Tuesday allowing the transfer.

Najib arrived at his Kuala Lumpur residence in a convoy escorted by police and prison vehicles, with supporters waiting outside Image: Vincent Thian/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Transport Minister Anthony Loke resigned in protest against the decision to let Najib serve his sentence under house arrest.

Could Najib return to prison?

Najib's house arrest runs until August 2028 but does not cover a separate 15-year sentence for abuse of power and money laundering. He is appealing that conviction and could return to prison if the appeal fails.

Prime minister from 2009 to 2018, Najib has denied wrongdoing in the looting of state investment fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad, known as 1MDB.

Malaysia's former PM guilty in major corruption scandal To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

According to US investigators, stolen funds paid for luxury properties, a superyacht and artworks — and, ironically, helped finance "The Wolf of Wall Street," a film about financial fraud. The investigators estimated $1 billion of the funds ended up in accounts linked to Najib.

Najib apologized in 2024 for mishandling the affair but said officials and fugitive financier Jho Low had misled him.

World.title: British counterterrorism police arrest US soldier accused of spying on behalf of Russia
World.content:
A member of the US Army has been arrested near Gloucester in England. Police said he was suspected of espionage activity in connection with Russia. Investigators from the US and UK are involved in the probe.

A 41-year-old member of the US Army was arrested near Gloucester on Tuesday in England, the Metropolitan Police said in a statement .

Authorities were searched two locations in the Gloucestershire region, police said, adding: "The country to which the allegations pertain is Russia."

US authorities, the US Military and the FBI were closely involved in the investigation, police said.

The man was in custody at a London police station, authorities said on Tuesday evening as the news emerged.

What did US and UK officials say about the arrest?

Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing called it a "significant arrest" as a result of "close collaboration between UK and US authorities."

"The allegations are serious and our investigation is very much ongoing," Evans said.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the case was of "utmost concern" to the US and its allies.

"While this investigation is continuing, I want to send a clear message — this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," Patel said. He also expressed thanks to UK investigators across various branches and the US Military Counterintelligence Command "for their outstanding work."

Brigadier General Sean Stinchon, the commanding general of US Army Counterintelligence Command also said the case demonstrated the "resolve of the counterintelligence community."

"The alleged conduct of a senior soldier, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent," Stinchon said.

The headquarters of UK signals intelligence agency GCHQ is located not far from the site of Tuesday's arrest Image: Barry Batchelor/PA/picture alliance

Busy area for US and UK military, intelligence communities

The area around Gloucestershire in the west of England, around two hours' drive from London, is home to several sensitive military and intelligence sites as well as outposts for various British and US companies with ties to the defense industry.

RAF Fairford, which was in the news earlier this year amid a security scare at the vast airbase used by both UK and US planes, is not far southeast of Gloucester.

Gloucester's neighboring town, Cheltenham, is one the UK's intelligence hubs outside London. It is home to the headquarters of the country's signals intelligence agency GCHQ.

World.title: UK Privy Council overrules Trinidad and Tobago gay sex law
World.content:
A London court has overturned a Trinidad and Tobago law criminalizing consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. As a result of the colonial legacy, it is the independent country's last court of appeal.

A man from Trinidad and Tobago has won a legal appeal lasting almost a decade in the last court of appeal available to him — the judicial committee of the Privy Council in former colonial power Britain.

Jason Jones, a gay man born in Trinidad and Tobago, had challenged the Caribbean nation's Sexual Offences Act outlawing consensusal sex between adult males, saying that it breached his fundamental rights under the country's constitution.

He initially won his case at Trinidad and Tobago's High Court, but the government and religious organizations managed to partially overturn the ruling once more, prompting Jones to the take the case to the island nation's highest appellate authority — the Privy Council in the UK.

"To discriminate against somebody simply because of who they choose to love is simply ridiculous," Jones told the Associated Press after Tuesday's judgment was rendered.

The Privy Council in London is the final court of appeal for some Commonwealth countries including Trinidad and Tobago, although that issue was already contentious in some circles prior to Tuesday's ruling.

The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council is the final court of appeal for UK overseas territories, Crown dependencies and some Commonwealth countries, including Trinidad and Tobago Image: Photoshot/picture alliance

What did the London court rule?

A panel of five judges unanimously allowed Jones' appeal, dismissing a counter-appeal from the Caribbean country's Attorney General.

It found that two sections of the country's Sexual Offenses Act 1986, criminalizing "buggery" and "serious indecency" respectively among same-sex couples, violated Jones' fundamental rights to private and family life set out in the 1976 constitution.

The court wrote in its ruling that "the rights and interests of Mr Jones which are at stake involve a particularly important facet of his existence and identity since the ability to form an intimate and loving relationship with another person lies at the core of the right to private and family life."

The anti-gay laws that call for up to five years in prison have not been enforced in recent history, but critics say they still send an intimidating message.

Judge Philip Sales said as he announced the ruling that "the current understanding of the fundamental individual right to respect for private and family life is that it protects such a core part of human identity as one's sexual orientation."

Sales added that "laws which seek to criminalize such activities cannot be justified."

Trinidadian authorities argued that because the 1986 laws were passed with a super-majority and constituted criminal penalties that dated back to colonial times, prior to the constitution, they could be considered "existing law" and override the individual constitutional rights in certain circumstances.

But the Privy Council judges found that the so-called "proviso" for this special status — "unless the Act is shown not to be reasonably justifiable in a society that has proper respect for the rights and freedoms of the individual" — had not been met.

One of Jones' lawyers, Anand Ramlogan, is a former attorney general of Trinidad and Tobago and argued against this position earlier in the case.

"Constitutional rights exist precisely because majorities are not always right," Ramlogan said. "They ensure that the dignity and equality of every citizen are not left to the changing tides of public opinion."

Who is the appellant?

Jason Jones is a 61-year-old born in Trinidad and Tobago.

Openly gay since the age of 16, he said he fled the country in 1996 because of homophobic violence and discrimination.

Speaking to the Associated Press on Tuesday after what he termed a "stunning victory," he said he would describe himself as a "very angry gay man," whose anger had helped him persist in his legal appeal for so many years.

"Society has treated me worse than a criminal," he said. "There is a real sense of vindication with this judgment. Finally, the courts are seeing that they need to step up because our politicians are so toothless."

He said he became inspired to speak out after losing friends to HIV/AIDS and after meeting American singer-songwriter Nina Simone when she toured the island nation for three weeks in 1984, when he was 19.

"Nina was the one who said, 'Jason, get off this rock and go see the world,'" he said, calling it a defining and life-changing experience.

New bill in Ghana criminalizes LGBTQ+ activity To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trinidad and Tobago may not enforce its 'buggery' law, but it carries a custodial sentence

Trinidad and Tobago's government, the country's Council of Evangelical Churches and its largest Hindu organization, Sanatan Dharm Maha Sabha, contested the case, which has wound its way through several courts since the appeal was launched in 2017.

In 2018, Trinidad's High Court found the laws unconstitutional. But in 2025, a local appeals court partially reversed the ruling. Trinidad's Court of Appeals subsequently allowed Jones to seek a ruling from the final appeals court in England.

The case was being closely watched by activists across the Caribbean, with similar laws in place in several other countries in the region.

The Bahamas decriminalized homosexuality in 1991.

The UK repealed laws in overseas territories Anguilla, the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands in 2001.

Judges in Barbados, Dominica, St. Lucia and Antigua and Barbuda have also recently struck down similar laws.

But in former British colonies Grenada, Jamaica, Trinidad and Tobago and St. Vincent and the Grenadines it remains a crime.

The UK only decriminalized gay sex in 1967, more than four centuries after the so-called "buggery" laws were first introduced under King Henry VII, and more than a century after the last executions for the crime. People still faced prosecution or the threat of it for consensual adult gay sex until after World War II, with surely the most famous later-years case being that of computing and codebreaking pioneer and war hero Alan Turing.

World.title: Victims of Nazi war in Poland call on Germany for support
World.content:
More than 80 years after the end of World War II, Polish victims of the Nazi regime are still waiting for a "humanitarian gesture" from Germany. The 2027 draft budget hasn't left them much hope for possible reparations.

"We can no longer wait," declared Polish victims' organizations in a dramatic appeal to German civil society, published on November 5 on the website of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation.

"Around 50,000 survivors of Nazi persecution during the German occupation still live in Poland today. They include former concentration camp and prison inmates, people deported to Germany for forced labor and those subjected to other forms of Nazi repression," wrote the signatories of the appeal.

The open letter pointed out that many of the survivors are over 90 years old, struggling with illness and rising costs, and in need of help in their daily lives. "For many, any further delay in deciding to provide assistance means that help will come too late," said the appeal, which was distributed in German, Polish and English.

Unresolved issues of reparations have strained relations between Germany and Poland for decades Image: AP/picture alliance

While Germany has recognized its moral responsibility toward the remaining survivors of Nazi persecution, the signatories pointed out that a corresponding decision on possible reparations by the German federal government has yet to be made.

"Today, we appeal primarily to German civil society to provide humanitarian support to survivors of Nazi persecution living in Poland," they wrote, addressing businesses, foundations, associations and private citizens. "Every donation matters."

Reparations offered to date seen as insufficient

The unresolved issue of war reparations has clouded German-Polish relations for decades.

Following the 1989 democratic transition in Central and Eastern Europe and the reunification of Germany, the federal government provided 500 million deutschmarks to Holocaust victims in Poland. More than 1 million people received support through these funds. Former forced laborers also received payments from the EVZ Foundation, which works to preserve the memory of the victims of National Socialist persecution.

However, given the scale of German crimes during World War II, the reparations provided to date have been considered as insufficient by large parts of Polish society. German occupation policy in Poland was characterized by systematic crimes against the Polish population. An estimated 6 million Polish citizens were killed during the war, including about 3 million Polish Jews.

At 100, Auschwitz survivor recalls life during the Holocaust To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

As part of the "General Plan East," a large portion of the population was to be displaced, enslaved or murdered. As early as 1939, the "Intelligenzaktion" specifically targeted the Polish elites, including teachers, clergy, civil servants and intellectuals. In addition, approximately 2.5 million Poles were deported to the German Reich for forced labor and made to work there under inhumane conditions.

When it came to power in 2015, Poland's right-wing conservative Law and Justice Party (PiS) made the issue of war reparations a central focus of Warsaw's policy toward Berlin. The PiS government estimated Poland's war losses at 6.2 trillion zloty (approx. €1.3 trillion/$1.58 trillion) and officially demanded this sum from Berlin in October 2022.

Tusk rejects €200 million as insufficient

The center-left government led by Donald Tusk has distanced itself from these demands since Tusk's election victory in December 2023. However, the government has also made no secret of the fact that Poland is expecting a "creative solution" from its German partner, according to Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk (front) has made no secret of the fact that he's waiting for a 'creative solution' from Germany Image: Kacper Pempel/REUTERS

Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz had offered €200 million ($224 million) prior to his visit to Poland in the summer of 2024, an offer rejected by Tusk as insufficient. The talks held since then between Berlin and Warsaw have failed to produce a solution.

In a final declaration following the German-Polish government consultations in December 2025, the German government promised to "analyze possibilities for additional support for Polish victims of Nazi aggression and the German occupation of Poland."

"Currently, there is no decision regarding a humanitarian gesture and the draft budget reflects this status," Josef Hinterseher, deputy spokesperson for Germany's Federal Foreign Office, told reporters on September 23.

Germany's Greens still hope for 'humanitarian gesture'

Germany's opposition Greens party has not given up hope of a turnaround in its efforts to secure a "humanitarian gesture."

"Our parliamentary group submitted a request to the budget committee to secure funding for this 'humanitarian gesture.' Unfortunately, the request was rejected," Franziska Brantner, co-chair of the Greens, told DW on Thursday in Warsaw.

Green co-leader Franziska Brantner hasn't given up hope that Germany will still change its stance on Polish reparations Image: Michaela Küfner/DW

"Hope dies last, so we will do everything in our power to ensure that the coalition makes this change after all," she emphasized. Brantner sees the budget committee's "final review session," which will take place this week, as a last chance.

The issue of reparations still plays an important role in Polish society, even more than 80 years after the end of the war. There is hardly a family that did not suffer during the war. In the latest German-Polish Barometer — a representative survey that has been conducted for 25 years — 53% of respondents stated that the suffering of the Polish people is not sufficiently acknowledged in Germany. Only 18% believed that the Germans have done enough.

Poland wants WWII reparations To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

German private donors support the victims' fund

Jakub Deka, chairman of the Foundation for Polish–German Reconciliation, believes the appeal by the victims' associations could now mobilize Germany's civil society. Following an initial appeal in May directed at the German federal government, several hundred Germans responded with donations ranging from €50 to several hundred euros.

To date, a total of more than €35,000 ($39,000) has been deposited into the foundation's account. Several people in need have already received one-time assistance from this fund. "It's a drop in the bucket, but every little bit helps," Deka told DW.

The foundation's chairman quotes Jerzy Tarasiewicz — who led the victims' association in the Polish city of Gdansk for many years — as a cautionary reminder. In January, Tarasiewicz was quoted in an interview with the daily newspaper Gazeta Wyborcza as saying: "They [the Germans] are waiting for us to die."

Tarasiewicz, who was born in 1942 on a German farm where his parents were performing forced labor, died in late September at the age of 84 without being able to witness this "humanitarian gesture."

"It is a painful reminder that the victims cannot wait any longer," said Deka.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Iran denies role in fridge hack, France summons ambassador
World.content:
France has said it rules "nothing" out in response to a cyberattack on supermarket refrigeration units. Iran, however, said it categorically rejected Paris' "baseless and one-sided accusations" of IRGC involvement.

Iran on Tuesday dismissed French accusations that its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was behind a cyberattack on hundreds of supermarkets last month, as Paris summoned Tehran's ambassador to discuss the incident.

"Iran's Foreign Ministry categorically rejects the French government's baseless and one-sided accusations against Iran regarding alleged cyber activities in France," the ministry said, adding that it "strongly condemns this hackneyed policy of leveling accusations against the Islamic Republic."

The alleged attack, which began overnight on October 11-12, raised the temperatures in supermarket refrigerators and freezer units, spoiling produce and even causing fires in isolated instances.

A series of similar incidents have since followed in Europe and beyond, even including a failed attack on cooling units at French blood banks this month, though it is not yet clear if these subsequent events are connected.

France summons ambassador, says it rules 'nothing' out in response

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Tuesday that his government would "rule nothing out and will take all measures — including those we may not disclose publicly — that we deem proportionate and necessary to deter any further attacks."

Barrot was speaking amid a G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris that included discussions with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the conflict with Iran.

Barrot even said that despite a change in tone from the Trump administration since the midterm election defeat in the US, the risk of a renewed escalation with Iran could not be ruled out, "otherwise, we would not have devoted so much time and energy over the past two days to addressing these issues with our American counterpart."

Barrot hosted G7 foreign ministers, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, in Paris this week Image: Brendan Smialowski/REUTERS

France summoned the Iranian ambassador on Tuesday and said it would be seeking European-level sanctions in response.

The EU said it would seek to provide a "swift and united response" pending discussion with member states.

"As the EU, we have consistently called on all states to refrain from malicious behavior in the cyberspace, and we will continue to address such malicious behavior, making use of all the tools that we have, also under the EU cyber diplomacy toolbox, including sanctions," spokesman Anouar El Anouni said.

Barrot said that the goal of any response would be "to deter anyone who might be tempted, in Iran or elsewhere, to do it again."

Iran accuses French of 'projecting' its own failures

Tehran appeared to threaten retaliatory measures of its own if sanctions materialized, saying it would "not hesitate to take necessary and appropriate measures to safeguard its national interests and security in the face of unlawful foreign activities."

It accused France of "merely projecting its own governance failures" with its allegations.

"A government that cannot even manage the temperature of its own refrigerators now seeks to shift the blame onto foreign actors through these preposterous accusations," it said.

Around 700 supermarkets, of a total of roughly 10,000 across France, were affected by the alleged cyberattack Image: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

What did Paris prosecutors say about suspected Iranian involvement?

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said on Monday that she had opened an investigation into leading members of Shahid Kaveh, a cyber unit that is part of Iran's multi-force specialist military, the IRGC, that answers directly to its religious leadership.

She said her office had requested arrest warrants against two Shahid Kaveh officials and was investigating others.

She described the entity as "an offensive cyber unit affiliated with the Electronic and Cyber Center of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps."

French cyber intelligence agencies said the unit conducted "large-scale campaigns targeting industrial equipment for the purpose of sabotage." It said it primarily targeted Israel and the US, but also France and other European countries.

Beccuau said that the attack targeted roughly 700 of France's roughly 10,000 supermarkets. It used web interfaces to "initiate abnormal, indefinite defrost cycles," and also to disable automated alerts from sensors designed to go off when temperatures exceeded certain levels.

Sweden's Civil Defense Minister Carl-Oskar Bohlin warned that more cyberattacks could be expected in the coming months, as AI tools make it easier to detect and exploit vulnerabilities.

He said that it was not yet possible to say if hacks targeted Swedish supermarkets last week were connected, not least because the type of sabotage would have "been easy to copy" after seeing the initial reports in October.

World.title: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
World.content:
Hitler once called Eastern Europe "Germany's India." A new exhibition examines the links between colonialism and Nazism, and the bitter debate over where comparisons illuminate history and where they fall short.

Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men."

But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire, and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared, remains the subject of intense debate. This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust. Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history.

'Murder for the very purpose of murder': The industrialized mass murder carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau had no direct precedent in colonial history. [Pictured: Cans of Zyklon B gas, Auschwitz-Birkenau, German Nazi concentration and extermination camp in Poland] Image: Taiftin/Depositphotos/IMAGO

"I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposed to be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story.

From colonial brutality to Nazi rule

The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers. The juxtaposition highlights the contrast between colonial violence and the industrialized mass murder of the Holocaust. Yet it also points to connections: Whips were used in Nazi concentration camps, while Fascist Italy deployed chemical weapons against civilians and soldiers during its invasion of Ethiopia (then Abyssinia) in 1935-36.

The extreme brutality of Fascist Italy's invasion of Ethiopia, including the use of chemical weapons, caused uproar around the world. [Pictured: The bombing of the Ethiopian village of Dessye by Italian planes] Image: Topfoto/United Archives International/IMAGO

In the 1930s, anti-colonial thinkers from India to the Caribbean argued that colonialism and fascism were two sides of the same coin. "There is nothing new or original about the blustering exploits of Hitler and Mussolini," observed the Trinidadian journalist and Pan-Africanist George Padmore in 1938. "They have all been used before by the British in their efforts to obtain the subjection of less powerfully armed and more industrially backward people."

European colonial rule was marked by the ruthless exploitation of people and resources, often enforced through extreme violence. In "The Origins of Totalitarianism" (1951), German-American philosopher Hannah Arendt argued that colonial territories served as laboratories for racial ideologies and practices of domination that could be applied beyond the legal constraints of Europe. Arendt described how these later "boomeranged" back into Europe and helped shape totalitarian politics in distinct and unprecedented form.

One of the most notorious symbols of King Leopold II's rule was the amputation of hands, inflicted on men, women and children who failed to meet rubber production quotas. [Pictured: A Congolese child with an amputated hand, circa 1900] Image: United Archives/World History Archive/IMAGO

The Congo Free State, King Leopold II of Belgium's private colony from 1885 to 1908, became notorious for its extreme brutality, as colonial authorities used executions, amputations and sexual violence to ensure rubber production quotas were met. Forced labor was central to Nazi rule, with millions of Poles, Ukrainians, Russians and others from the Soviet Union, and Jews, subjected to exploitation and "Vernichtung durch Arbeit" ("extermination through work"). Within a few years, the regime mobilized around 13 to 14 million forced laborers, a scale comparable to the transatlantic slave trade over more than three centuries. The Nazis sought to extract value from their victims at every stage, confiscating their property, exploiting their labor, and even harvesting gold teeth and hair from the dead.

Racism, antisemitism and extermination

While racism underpinned both colonial empires and Nazism, Malinowski says the goals were different. The colonial powers tended to present assimilation as a path to advancement, forcing colonized people to adopt European culture, serve imperial interests, and suggesting that a select, educated few could gain opportunities at elite institutions such as Oxford or Cambridge. "This is definitely not something that the Nazi regime is offering to Poles or to Russians or let alone to Jews," added Malinowski.

"In terms of violence, colonial violence was just as extreme as Nazi violence. But Nazi violence was annihilatory and exterminatory compared to colonial violence in the colonies," says Edward Kissi, a historian at the School of Interdisciplinary Global Studies at the University of South Florida. He points to the example of how, unlike European colonial powers in Africa, the Nazis pursued the elimination of Black-Germans or peoples of African descent in Germany through forced sterilization. "Even in racism, colonial color-based racism and colonial anti-Jewish sentiments were fundamentally different from what the Nazis pursued."

From 1904 to 1908, German colonial rule in present-day Namibia culminated in the genocide of the Herero and Nama, in which tens of thousands died. [Pictured: Concentration camp for Herero and Nama in German South West Africa in 1905] Image: Sam-Cohen-Bibliothek/Scientific Society Swakopmund

On October 2, 1904, German General Lothar von Trotha issued the "Vernichtungsbefehl" ("extermination order") following the Herero uprising in German South West Africa (present-day Namibia). Historians generally attribute the order to a combination of racial ideology, a desire to terrorize the population into submission, and efforts to secure colonial control over land, labor and resources. Between 1904 and 1908, an estimated 60,000 to 80,000 Herero (around 80% of the population) and 10,000 (around half the population) Nama died.

One area where the exhibition draws no direct parallel is the industrialized killing carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka, and Auschwitz-Birkenau. "Where the two things really diverge is the Holocaust and is the systematic mass murder of the European Jews and it's murder for the very purpose of murder," explains Malinowski. The deportation of around 1,800 Jews from the Greek islands of Rhodes and Kos in July 1944 illustrates how Nazi persecution often defied military or economic logic. Even after the war was effectively lost, the community was transported to Auschwitz, where most were murdered immediately upon arrival.

The politics of historical comparison

The issue of the "singularity" of the Holocaust came to the fore during the 1980s "Historikerstreit" ("historians' dispute"). Historian Ernst Nolte argued that Nazism should be understood in the wider context of 20th-century political violence, and as a response to Bolshevik terror in particular. Critics accused him of downplaying German responsibility for Nazi crimes.

Since 2020, a renewed debate dubbed the "Historikerstreit 2.0" has focused on whether the Holocaust should be viewed as a unique reference point in German memory culture or be understood alongside the histories of colonialism, racism and empire. The dispute now is less about the legitimacy of comparison than about its implications.

After being deported to Auschwitz-Birkenau in 1943, French artist David Olère depicted scenes he witnessed. Here, deportees arrive at a crematorium shortly before their murder. [Pictured: David Olère, 'Vers la mort' ('On the Way to Death'), Paris, 1945] Image: Mémorial de la Shoah/Coll. David Olère

The mass murder of tens of thousands of the Herero and Nama during four years of German colonial rule is now regarded as the first genocide of the 20th-century. In 2016, Nama representatives walked out of talks after Germany's chief negotiator said what happened was "incomparable" to the Holocaust. The German government has since recognized the events as genocide "from today's perspective," but it has not yet accepted legal liability or agreed to pay formal reparations.

Rethinking Germany's culture of remembrance

Martinican intellectual Aimé Césaire argued in "Discourse on Colonialism" (1950) that Europe condemned under Nazism forms of violence it had long accepted in its colonies. The exhibition opens amid renewed debates over settler colonialism, the definition of genocide, and the meaning of "never again," sharpened by Nicaragua's case against Germany at the International Court of Justice over German support for Israel during the war in Gaza. These tensions are reflected in visitors' comments in the exhibition's epilogue, even though the exhibition itself does not address Israel or Palestine beyond a reference to Mohammed Amin al-Husseini, appointed Grand Mufti of Jerusalem in 1921.

Germany has unequivocally accepted responsibility for the Holocaust, which is front and center of the country's culture of remembrance. However, Kissi likens Germany's apparent reluctance to reckon with its colonial history to debates in the US over slavery, in Cambodia over the Khmer Rouge, and in Turkey over the Armenian genocide. According to him, Germany's contemporary identity cannot be fully understood without examining its colonial history and the ways the Nazis appropriated and transformed aspects of that legacy. "I think Germans and all other human beings who have experienced violent pasts and difficult pasts should be very careful not to delink or dissociate those facts from their present," Kissi said. "These are historical patterns. It is better to deal with these historical patterns and discomforts than to just fight them and then say this has absolutely nothing to do with German national identity."

"Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence" is on show at the German Historical Museum until April 11, 2027.

World.title: Poland: Krakow shooting suspect 'fascinated' by Norwegian mass murder Anders Breivik, says justice minister
World.content:
The 24-year old suspect was found to have read a significant amount of material about Breivik and other far-right figures. Speculation over his motives have prompted a bitter political feud in Warsaw.

Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek issued an update on Tuesday concerning the case of a mass shooting in Krakow over the weekend.

Accused gunman Michal Oksinski was deeply interested in international far-right movements, Zurek said.

"Authorities have accessed the terrorist's computer. It is clear that he visited websites concerning Anders Breivik," the Norwegian neo-Nazi who killed 77 people in July 2011, the minister added.

Zurek said a search of Oksinski's home turned up a Gadsen flag, a banner dating back to the US Civil War that is now associated with American white nationalists.

Police also gathered evidence that he had recently bought 10 magazines for a semi-automatic rifle and 500 bullets.

"It is clear that this individual was preparing to take action," the justice minister said.

Krakow shooting suspect 'fascinated by far right' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What happened in the attack?

On Friday night, 24-year-old Oksinski is thought to have shot and killed his mother, father, sister and two family cats in the city of Ostrowiec.

The following day at around 3:00 p.m. local time, Oksinski is suspected of opening fire in Krakow's Main Market Square. Six people were killed — four Poles, one Austrian, and one UK national. Another 15 people were wounded.

After the attack in Krakow, authorities discovered the bodies of his family members in Ostrowiec.

Poland then observed two days of national mourning. Oksinski died of wounds sustained during his arrest at a local hospital on Monday.

Initial investigations have uncovered "very solid" evidence pointing to far-right radicalization and psychiatric issues as motives for the attacks, Zurek said.

However, Zurek and the centrist government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk has been accused by members of right-wing populist PiS party of lying about Oksinski's motives.

World.title: Los sindicatos llaman a España a una huelga general por primera vez en 14 años
World.content:
Un centenar de trabajadores con consignas de CC.OO. y UGT han bloqueado este martes por la noche las entradas de Mercabarna, en Barcelona, para dificultar el acceso al turno de noche por la huelga general del 11 de noviembre.

CC OO y UGT piden un seguimiento “masivo” del paro laboral, pero prevén que sea “asimétrico” en función del impacto de la crisis de la vivienda en cada territorio. Esperan una gran movilización por la tarde que sancione la pérdida de poder adquisitivo de los salarios

Salarios, vivienda, precios. Los grandes sindicatos de España, CC OO y UGT, llaman a la clase trabajadora a parar este miércoles con ese lema, en la primera huelga general que convocan en los últimos 14 años. Es un llamamiento “heterodoxo”, como vienen reconociendo las propias centrales, por varios motivos: no contesta a un proyecto legislativo concreto ni a una única Administración pública, parte de un estallido de indignación social por un desahucio y de movilizaciones articuladas por un colectivo que no es un sindicato laboral y se celebra a 18 días de una elecciones generales. Y después de un accidente ferroviario que ha provocado “un cierto cambio en el estado de ánimo de país”, según Unai Sordo.

De ahí que UGT y CC OO, aunque llamen a un respaldo “masivo”, anticipen un seguimiento “asimétrico”, con la previsión de un apoyo menor en los territorios que sufren menos el problema de la vivienda y con dudas respecto a los que sí. Según los datos de un estudio de 40dB. para EL PAÍS y la Cadena SER, el 23% de los encuestados que trabajan dicen que harán la huelga, frente al 36,3% que aseguran que no la secundarán. Hay otro 22,4% que anticipan que no harán huelga, pero que la apoyan, y un 10,3% señala que no sabe qué hará.

Un piquete informativo este martes en Logroño. Raquel Manzanares (EFE)

Los sindicatos defienden la conveniencia de la huelga por el bocado que la vivienda inflige en las nóminas, que crecen menos que los precios por la negativa de CEOE a acordar un pacto nacional de convenios y que el paro general no cae del cielo, que culmina el subidón de la conflictividad en los últimos meses—las jornadas perdidas por huelgas se han triplicado respecto al año pasado—. Llaman al paro en las empresas y también a participar en las movilizaciones de la tarde, sobre las que amenaza una previsión de lluvia en buena parte del país.

En la Puerta del Sol de Madrid, días antes llena de tiendas de campaña en protesta por la crisis de acceso a la vivienda, los secretarios generales de los dos grandes sindicatos han pedido este martes por la noche a la clase trabajadora que participe en la huelga general que ha empezado a las 00.00. “La vivienda es la gran fractura de este país. Jóvenes de España, es vuestro día. Hay que tapar la calle y reivindicar políticas ambiciosas que saquen a este país de la lacra del rentismo”, ha dicho el jefe de CC OO. Ha pedido una “riada de gente” para que las Administraciones públicas “se den por aludidas” y para “sacar a los fondos buitre a gorrazos”.

Comienzan las movilizaciones previas a la huelga general del 11N en Madrid, este martes, con una concentración en las instalaciones de recogida de residuos urbanos de Villaverde (Madrid) para llevar a cabo los primeros piquetes informativos la noche de este martes. Victor Lerena (EFE)

Por su parte, el secretario general de UGT ha denunciado que “no hay salario que aguante el precio de la vivienda”. “Esta huelga interpela a todas las Administraciones. Vamos a dejar claro a quien gobierne después del 29-N que tienen que abrir los oídos”, ha dicho Pepe Álvarez, quien además ha contestado a las palabras de la presidenta de la Comunidad de Madrid. Isabel Díaz Ayuso pidió el martes a Alberto Núñez Feijóo que acabe “con toda la basura sindical”. “Que se vaya a la mierda. Que lo escuche la marquesa de la Puerta del Sol”, ha dicho el ugetista. Tras estos discursos, cientos de sindicalistas ha marchado en dirección a Cibeles al grito de “huelga, huelga, huelga general”.

Alicia del Río, portavoz del Sindicato de Inquilinas, ha dicho este martes a EL PAÍS que el 11-N empieza “un nuevo ciclo de luchas que pueda por fin lograr grandes conquistas en nuestro país que necesitamos, como el derecho a la vivienda y mejorar las condiciones de vida de la clase trabajadora”.

La huelga parte del impulso inicial de la organización de Del Río, el Sindicato de Inquilinas, el grupo que apoyó a Maricarmen durante su desahucio. Fue tal el enfado que la situación de esta mujer madrileña despertó en la ciudadanía que el Gobierno reaccionó aprobando unos decretos con medidas sobre vivienda que, después, no fueron convalidados por la mayoría de derechas del Congreso. Esa decisión del Legislativo el viernes 2 de octubre condujo a unas manifestaciones masivas el sábado 3, lideradas por las Inquilinas y cuyo lema principal fue “hacia la huelga general”.

Manifestante en Madrid el 3 de octubre. Santi Burgos

Entonces los sindicatos mayoritarios expresaban dudas, pero no otros de menor tamaño y que prometían dar respaldo laboral a la convocatoria, como CGT. Es más, las Inquilinas llegaron a afirmar que irían a la huelga sin CC OO y UGT y con sindicatos de menor tamaño si ellos se negaban. El lunes 5 de octubre, horas después de que Pedro Sánchez llamase a las urnas, UGT y CC OO comunicaron su respaldo a la huelga, elevando la convocatoria a otra dimensión. Sin su músculo en las empresas, con 228.000 delegados (más de dos tercios del total), el paro apenas habría tenido impacto. Así sucedió en la última convocatoria de huelga general, la que el año pasado articuló CGT por la masacre en Gaza y que apenas tuvo seguimiento.

El último mes ha sido un torbellino para las centrales, que han puesto a sus cuadros a trabajar para levantar una huelga general en menos de un mes. Fuentes de los grandes sindicatos subrayan que la coincidencia con la campaña ha complicado esa tarea, dadas las acusaciones de electoralismo que les ha imputado la derecha política. “No ha ayudado ni la izquierda diciendo que esta huelga es a la oposición (como afirmó María Jesús Montero) ni la derecha acusándonos de bailarle el agua al Gobierno”, dice un representante de CC OO. Los sindicatos esperan mayor respaldo en los sectores más sindicalizados y en los territorios que más sufren la crisis de la vivienda.

La acusación de electoralismo asociada a la huelga también ha sido apuntalada por CEOE, que anunció que impugnaría el paro porque lo consideraba ilegal. Sin embargo, una vez registrada la convocatoria ante el Ministerio de Trabajo, las patronales no recurrieron a la justicia. La misma aludía a la crisis de acceso a la vivienda, pero también a otros motivos de índole estrictamente laboral, como la pérdida de poder adquisitivo de los salarios.

La estadística oficial de convenios colectivos da cuenta de ese fenómeno: las retribuciones pactadas han avanzado hasta octubre un 3,06%, frente al incremento interanual de la inflación del 4,9%. Esto supone una pérdida de casi dos puntos de poder de compra, un retroceso que supera a la ganancia de poder adquisitivo que sí se dio en los tres años anteriores. Durante los mismos rigió el último pacto nacional de convenios, el acuerdo de patronales y sindicatos que guía la negociación colectiva. Ahora no hay ninguno en vigor, uno de los motivos que CC OO y UGT defienden para convocar la huelga.

Más huelgas

Esa pérdida de poder de compra de las retribuciones, opinan las centrales, es el factor principal que explica el subidón de la conflictividad laboral en lo que llevamos de año. De enero a septiembre 587.000 afiliados a la Seguridad Social han participado en huelgas, más del triple que en el mismo periodo del año pasado (172.000), según los últimos registros oficiales. Esto supuso la pérdida de 1,39 millones de jornadas de trabajo, frente a las 394.000 del pasado ejercicio.

Esta misma semana hay varios paros que coinciden o colindan con el paro general, como el ferroviario que reclama más medidas de seguridad, o el de la industria cárnica para mejorar su convenio, con gran seguimiento de las plantillas. También continúa la huelga indefinida de la educación pública en la Comunidad de Madrid, que recoge el testigo de las que tuvieron lugar en el primer semestre del año.

Según el recuento de CC OO, ya se han adherido al paro unos 4.500 comités de empresa, juntas de personal y secciones sindicales. Son un millar más que el viernes. Entre ellos hay representantes de algunas de las compañías con las mayores plantillas de España, como Mercadona, El Corte Inglés, ONCE, Acciona, FCC, Correos, Eulen, Inditex, Ferrovial, Iberdrola, Santander, BBVA, Telefónica, Carrefour, Ford o Seat.

También respaldan el paro asociaciones de la sociedad civil (como CEAR, la Federación LGTBI+, Greenpeace...), hay un manifiesto suscrito por personalidades de la cultura y, más allá de los sindicatos mencionados, también apoyan la huelga los sindicatos vascos ELA y LAB, los gallegos CIG y CUT, el andaluz SAT, el aragonés SOA, CNT, CO.BAS, Solidaridad Obrera, Alternativa Sindical de Clase, la Unión de Actores y Actrices, la Unión Progresista de Inspectores de Trabajo, el sindicato de guionistas Alma y el sindicato de periodistas FeSP, entre otros.

La mayoría de las centrales corporativas rechazan el paro porque lo consideran electoralista. Son organizaciones fuertes en algunos sectores importantes como la Administración General del Estado, el transporte ferroviario o en el colectivo médico, que por norma general tampoco apoyaron la huelga de 2012. Entre ellas destacan el sindicato de funcionarios CSIF, el de profesores ANPE, el de médicos Amyts, el de ferroviarios Semaf, el de transporte SLT, el de pilotos Sepla, el del comercio Fetico y el del sector financiero FINE, entre otros. Entre los sindicatos que no respaldan el paro sí hay una de clase y que no es corporativa, USO, que sí apoyó la huelga general de 2012.

Manifestaciones

CC OO, UGT, el Sindicato de Inquilinas, CGT, CNT y el resto de centrales convocantes se han coordinado para celebrar manifestaciones unitarias en casi toda España. La de Madrid parte este miércoles a las 18.00 de la estación de Atocha, la de Barcelona arranca a las 17.30 en Jardinets de Gràcia y la de Valencia empieza a las 18.00 en la calle Xàtiva. En la cuarta ciudad más poblada, Zaragoza, los sindicatos mayoritarios y las Inquilinas no han alcanzado un acuerdo y habrá dos marchas distintas. Tampoco serán unitarias las protestas en Granada, Valladolid o Pamplona, con los sindicatos mayoritarios por un lado y los pequeños por otro. Con todo, desde ambos lados y desde el Sindicato de Inquilinas subrayan que en casi todas las ciudades ha habido acuerdo. CC OO y UGT subrayan que para alcanzarlo han accedido a un menor protagonismo del que es habitual para ellos en una huelga general.

A la vez, en Madrid la Coordinadora Juvenil Socialista (CJS) lidera lo que llaman un “bloque de clase” que, aunque parta del mismo lugar, marchará con sus propios lemas y persigue diferenciarse. Este movimiento fue importante en la acampada de Sol y es uno de los que más está confrontando con los sindicatos mayoritarios e incluso con las Inquilinas, lo que ha despertado algunas críticas de las impulsoras de la huelga. En la misma línea, la CJS plantea una manifestación alternativa en Barcelona. “Esta huelga no puede reducirse a una manifestación multitudinaria ni a un día de movilización simbólica o acto electoral, como están intentando los sindicatos de concertación”, dicen fuentes de la CJS, en referencia a CC OO y UGT. Estos sindicatos restan importancia a este movimiento y subrayan el entendimiento general que han alcanzado con las Inquilinas. “Esta huelga general tiene que ser efectiva y lograr paralizar la producción del país”, añade la CJS.

World.title: “Leer te hace más inteligente porque te hace elegir mejor”
World.content:
Paulo Cosín, director editorial de Ediciones Morata, especializada en educación, charla con Mar Buenhombre, estudiante de Bachillerato del IES La Senda de Getafe (Madrid), sobre el lugar que debe ocupar la lectura en los planes educativos

Cuestionado sobre qué hacer para enganchar a alguien a la lectura, Paulo Cosín, director editorial de Ediciones Morata, revela el secreto: “Debemos compartir con esa persona lo que a nosotros nos sucede cuando leemos. Seguro que querrá tener lo mismo que te sucede a ti”. La reflexión de un lector con el hábito tan arraigado como el suyo se complementa con una llamada a la acción, un consejo para cualquiera que desee iniciarse –o recuperar– la pasión por los libros. “Mañana ve a la biblioteca pública, le cuentas tus intereses al bibliotecario y le pides que, por favor, te recomiende un libro. Si no te gusta, lo devuelves y traes otro. Y así vas creando tus gustos literarios”, recomienda a su joven interlocutora, Mar Buenhombre, alumna de 1º de Bachillerato del IES La Senda de Getafe (Madrid), en el nuevo capítulo de Pensemos el mañana, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja y EL PAÍS para responder a los desafíos que presenta la educación del futuro.

“La lectura es la gran herramienta para todas las situaciones de acoso que puedan ocurrir en la escuela”

En la conversación, ambos repasan en qué punto se encuentra la lectura en los planes educativos actuales, en un tiempo en el que las pantallas de los dispositivos móviles colman la atención del mundo. “¿Cuánto tiempo se dedica a la lectura, a las actividades artísticas, en la escuela?”, pregunta Cosín. A lo que la alumna responde: “Pues, según van pasando los cursos, cada vez menos”. Para Cosín, que dirige desde 2005 una editorial especializada en educación que se ha convertido en referencia para profesores y alumnos de toda España, esa verdad supone un grave problema: “La cuestión es si estamos dando a los jóvenes referencias suficientes para ayudarles en su desarrollo. A veces, para comprender las situaciones de sufrimiento ajeno”.

“Según pasan los cursos, creo que cada vez se le da menos importancia a la lectura”

Es ese, a juicio de Cosín, el valor diferencial que convierte a la lectura en una poderosa arma educativa: “Leer te hace más inteligente porque te hace elegir mejor. Es la gran herramienta para todas las situaciones de acoso y de malestar en la convivencia que pueda haber en la escuela”, resume.

Pensemos la educación del futuro ‘Pensemos el mañana’, un proyecto de Fundación Unicaja, busca fomentar el conocimiento, los valores de la educación, un aprendizaje sostenible y responsable y dar respuestas a los grandes desafíos de la educación del futuro. El proyecto pivota sobre seis ejes: 1 Aprendizaje y sentido vital 2 Bienestar y salud mental 3 Futuro y empleabilidad 4 Sostenibilidad y sentido colectivo 5 Tecnología y ética 6 Carácter y ciudadanía ¿Qué está ocurriendo en estos tiempos de cambios profundos y transversales? ¿Cuáles son los grandes retos para afrontar la transformación que viene? ¿Qué educación necesitamos? Diferentes personalidades de todos los ámbitos nos ayudarán a responder a estas y otras preguntas destinadas a impulsar cambios, dinamizar ideas y apoyar propuestas con impacto pedagógico y social. ‘Pensemos el mañana’ es un proyecto inspirador para las futuras generaciones llamadas a conquistar nuevas cotas del saber en un mundo complejo y cambiante.

Paulo Cosín Director editorial de Ediciones Morata En 2005 tomó las riendas de una editorial que hoy es una referencia para la comunidad educativa hispanohablante. Firme defensor de devolver la lectura a un puesto privilegiado en los planes pedagógicos, imparte charlas para refrendar una idea: que leer vuelva a ser fundamental en la escuela Mar Buenhombre Alumna de Bachillerato del IES La Senda (Getafe, Madrid) A sus 17 años se confiesa una apasionada por la lectura que disfruta con el género de la novela policíaca. Para ella, es una forma de evadirse de la excesiva atención que su generación presta a las pantallas. Su pasión por los libros la ha llevado a participar en certámenes y concursos de escritura y lectura

World.title: Un viaje en tren por Georgia a bordo de modernos vagones y reliquias soviéticas
World.content:
Georgia está llevando a cabo una modernización de su sistema ferroviario. En la imagen, un tren en dirección a Bakuriani.

El país puede atravesarse en ferrocarril desde el mar Negro hasta el Cáucaso. Este es un recorrido con inicio en Batumi y final en Tiflis

Recorrer Georgia en tren puede ser un rápido y eficiente trayecto entre el mar Negro y Tiflis o una pintoresca reminiscencia de la época soviética, en vagones destartalados y hasta recónditos pueblos de montaña. Viajar en unos u otros dependerá de la prisa y de la antelación con que uno compre sus billetes, pero, en cualquier caso, podremos visitar de forma segura los puntos más atractivos del país, con vistas que nos mantendrán pegados a la ventana. Puntualmente, para ir a los lugares más apartados, no quedará más remedio que echar mano de una marshrutka, una de esas pequeñas furgonetas que se retuercen por donde no llegan el tren ni los autobuses, a velocidades capaces de infartar al más viajero más tranquilo.

Actualmente, Georgia está llevando a cabo una modernización integral de su sistema ferroviario, que este verano alcanzó el hito de reducir el trayecto entre Batumi y Tiflis a cuatro horas. Los billetes, a partir de 35 lari (unos 12 euros), se agotan rápido en verano, por lo que es conveniente reservarlos con hasta tres semanas de antelación por internet (la web más cómoda es tkt.ge), o tener en cuenta que en las estaciones solo se acepta efectivo. Con dos frecuencias diarias (y hasta cinco en verano), es el único tren de estas características, con paradas solo en Kutaisi, Ureki y Kobuleti. Así que el resto de trayectos nos ofrecerán más margen de improvisación y requerirán mucha más paciencia (y muy poco dinero).

En nuestra ruta desde la ciudad costera de Batumi hasta el pueblecito de Gardabani, en el extremo oriental de la línea, probaremos las dos modalidades, que tan bien reflejan esa Georgia moderna con miras europeas y otra mucho más rural, entregada al paisaje y al contacto humano. La duración del viaje dependerá del tiempo que dediquemos a cada una de las ciudades en las que paramos.

Antes de arrancar, Batumi

La historia georgiana parece escrita en vertical, por colonos otomanos y persas llegados desde el sur o rusos, venidos desde el norte. Aventuras que encontraban en la cordillera del Cáucaso, la más alta de Europa, el límite a sus ambiciones imperiales y el recipiente para un legado que, todavía hoy, hace de Georgia ese crisol del que solo pueden presumir las zonas de frontera.

Sin embargo, a finales del siglo XIX, los descubrimientos de petróleo en Azerbaiyán reformularon el mapa del viajero con el ferrocarril de Transcaucasia, que unía el mar Negro y el Caspio, de Batumi hasta Bakú. Una línea internacional que, por cierto, acaba de reabrir tras seis años cerrada, pero que todavía impide a los ciudadanos de la UE cruzar la frontera azerí (una medida que Azerbaiyán reevaluará a inicios de 2027). Esas mismas vías articulan Georgia en dirección oeste-este.

Una mujer en el andén de la ciudad georgiana de Borjomi. Ryhor Bruyeu ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Por eso, nuestra ruta empieza en el suroeste del país, junto al mar Negro y en la capital de la república de Adjara, Batumi. La segunda ciudad georgiana es una extraña mezcla de historia, naturaleza y consumo desatado. Aquí, el viajero tiene la sensación de asistir a una combinación aleatoria de elementos solo unidos por la exuberancia y el exceso. Por ejemplo, desde la monumental plaza de Europa sale la calle Memed Abashidze, con galerías, cafés y tiendas, pero si uno se deja llevar un poco, hasta la plaza Batumi, es posible que sienta haberse perdido por completo, dada la arquitectura kitsch de estilo veneciano.

Ya cerca del frente marítimo, dará con un Las Vegas caucásico donde nada existe si no es cubierto de neones, y el desconcierto aumenta ante una gigante estatua de Medea, una noria más grande todavía, una torre dedicada al alfabeto georgiano, acristalados hoteles, discotecas y una playa kilométrica. Un paraíso para rusos, turcos, armenios e israelíes que encuentran aquí lo que no les ofrecen sus países: sol, calor, alcohol asequible y casinos 24 horas.

Imagen aérea de Batumi, con la plaza de la Libertad en el centro. Vladimir Zapletin ( GETTY IMAGES )

Batumi-Samtredia

Nuestro primer trayecto en tren, hacia Samtredia (dos horas), transcurre en una lenta y ruidosa sauna metálica, que sirve para recrearnos en dos de las principales virtudes del país: un paisaje que no da tregua y una hospitalidad que siempre se traduce en ritual gastronómico; en este caso, té, jachapuri y galletas que nos ofrece la familia de nuestro compartimento. Desde Samtredia, tenemos dos opciones (ambas, a poco menos de dos horas, pero con frecuencias reducidas).

La primera es dejarnos llevar por la vegetación subtropical hacia la ciudad portuaria de Poti, base para visitar los humedales del parque natural de Kolkheti, cuya biodiversidad es reconocida como patrimonio mundial por la Unesco. De nuevo, las orillas tibias y turquesas del mar Negro, cercadas por una frondosidad selvática.

La segunda opción es otro tipo de naturaleza, más salvaje, como la que se encuentra en el extremo septentrional de la línea, en la pequeña Zugdidi. Ahí comienzan las estribaciones del Cáucaso y una de las mecas europeas para el senderismo: las montañas de Svaneti. Quien quiera caminar por ellas, deberá ir desde Zugdidi hasta Mestia, y hacerlo en marshrutka. Mucho más que la escalada, los trayectos de marshrutka, impenitente adelantadora, serán el verdadero deporte de riesgo en el Cáucaso.

Panorámica de la vía de ferrocarril frente a la costa de Batumi. Ryhor Bruyeu ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Comer en Imericia

Sin embargo, seguimos en nuestro tren abarrotado y lento hacia Kutaisi, cuna de los cólquidas, dos veces capital de Georgia en la Edad Media y actualmente la principal ciudad de la región de Imericia. Referencia arqueológica y del turismo de naturaleza, acaba siéndolo también a nivel gastronómico: el jachapuri imeruli (de Imericia) es el más popular del país y acompaña cada comida. Basta con entrar a cualquier restaurante o tasca y pedir la recomendación del día para comprobar que, aquí, comer es una religión con la que comulgamos. En el restaurante Palaty encontramos la mejor cena posible, con pjali (paté vegetal), berenjena rellena, khinkali (una especie de empanadillas) de cordero y vino saperavi, especialidad de la región.

Una excursión habitual en tren desde Kutaisi es a la zona rural de Sachkhere. El servicio, inactivo entre diciembre y marzo, es uno de los más vetustos, lentos y, a la vez, espectaculares, por cómo se adentra en las montañas hasta dejarnos en la no menos alucinante Chiatura (a casi tres horas), un espectro de la extinta minería de magnesio y conocida por su sistema de teleféricos.

Edificio abandonado en Tskaltubo. Vyacheslav Saltayev ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Algo similar encontraremos en Tskaltubo. Aunque la antigua conexión ferroviaria no opera, merece la pena subirse a otra marshrutka para visitar esta ciudad-balneario, hace décadas famosa por los baños en aguas de radón y ahora como destino de turismo urbex. Es difícil imaginar una definición gráfica más explícita del auge y caída de la Unión Soviética: la propia estación de tren abandonada, las decenas de sanatorios, hoteles y balnearios, construidos en un monumental clasicismo soviético, perecen ahora entre la vegetación como esqueletos de una civilización extinta hace no tanto tiempo, y a la espera de una restauración que no acaba de consumarse. Allí, el baño nº6, el único aún operativo, conserva como un tesoro la sauna personal de Stalin.

Stalin en Gori

La memoria histórica pega un giro aún más brusco cuando el tren nos deja en Gori, en el centro del país, y a unas dos horas y media desde Kutaisi. El propio nombre (montaña, en georgiano) da una pista sobre su orografía, con un aire fresco que ventila los abundantes parques y la colina en la que se asienta la muralla del siglo VII. No obstante, Gori se asocia mucho más con las cruentas —y todavía palpables— batallas de la guerra con Rusia en 2008 y, sobre todo, con la ciudad natal de Iósif Vissariónovich Dzhugashvili; o, para entendernos, Stalin. Su figura es todavía omnipresente, pone nombre a varios lugares de la ciudad y es homenajeada en el Museo Estatal de Stalin.

Un visitante frente a un retrato de Stalin, en el museo dedicado al dictador en su ciudad natal. George Gogua ( picture alliance / Getty Images)

Lejos de un centro documental que informe sobre la vida del dictador, este complejo exalta al que fue el habitante más ilustre de Gori con un estilo rococó de vidrieras, mármol, estatuas y alfombras que le dan el tratamiento de glorioso conquistador. Los guías (la mayor parte de las visitas son en georgiano y ruso) y la colección no escatiman en halagos para quien retratan como justiciero, bardo, revolucionario e indiscutido estadista. Quizá aún le agradezcan que el centro de Gori, pese a su modesto tamaño, posea una arquitectura más propia de una gran ciudad.

Tiflis, fin del trayecto

Apenas nos quedan 70 kilómetros hasta Tiflis, una ciudad que pide hacer un alto de varios días. Joven, multicultural, nocturna, creativa, inesperada, laberíntica, bulliciosa, alegre y reivindicativa, emana la historia y la vitalidad de una capital que trasciende a un país. En ella, se hacen evidentes la diáspora rusa, las tensiones políticas georgianas, la (de nuevo) comunión en torno a la gastronomía y la voluntad de encontrar nuevas vías de expresión. Como fue el tren lo que nos trajo hasta aquí, cabe decir que las estaciones de metro no desmerecen la reputación de otras antiguas capitales soviéticas. Pero, como de lo que se trataba era de cruzar el país, nos volvemos a subir a un viejo vagón para terminar el recorrido en Gardabani, a una hora al este de la Tiflis y ya rozando la frontera con Azerbaiyán.

El puente de la Paz, en el centro de Tiflis. Mirko Kuzmanovic ( Alamy / CORDON PRESS )

Para quien prefiera emociones más fuertes, siempre quedan los viajes en marshrutka hacia Stepantsminda (la base para subir al monte Kazbegi) y la recóndita región vinícola de Kajetia, en la frontera con el Daguestán ruso.

World.title: Senators back plan to cultivate embryos for scientific research
World.content:
The Dutch senate has approved plans to allow specially grown embryos to be used for research into hereditary illnesses and infertility.

The bill, proposed by the liberal parties VVD and D66 during the last cabinet term while D66 was in opposition, achieved a narrow majority of 38 to 35 votes in the upper house.

The Christian parties ChristenUnie and SGP are opposed to cultivating embryos for scientific research because they see it as a violation of the sanctity of life.

The far-right PVV also voted against the plan, which party senator Ilse Bezaan called a “morally reprehensible” measure. “There are good alternatives, we shouldn’t open the door to a sliding scale,” she said.

Until now only embryos that are discarded during IVF treatment could be used for research purposes, but scientists say that using newly fertilised embryos would allow them to study the effect of treatments in the early stages of development.

World.title: Meat sector and government put profits before welfare: report
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The Dutch meat industry and the government are both failing to protect animal welfare, and put profits first as the laws are vague and hard to enforce.

“The system is failing to protect animal welfare: the government and the sector are falling short,” the committee, chaired by former transport inspectorate chief Jan van den Bos, said in its final report.

The agriculture ministry set up the panel in 2024 to review oversight of the meat chain. It found that food safety and animal health are well protected.

Welfare is harmed on a large scale even when companies follow the law, the committee said, because legal standards are vague and current production methods and costs are always the starting point when they are set.

Some 535 million animals are slaughtered in the Netherlands every year, more than 518 million of them chickens. Inspection figures cited in the report show that around 3 million birds arrive at slaughterhouses injured each year.

Two-thirds of 170 pig farms checked in 2023 and 2024 by the food and product safety watchdog NVWA were breaking welfare rules. The watchdog spends just 8% of its capacity on animal welfare.

The committee said the agriculture minister gives the sector too little direction and repeatedly delays decisions.

World.title: “Very dangerous”: Rights group condemns Kristallnacht speech
World.content:
The Kristallnacht remembrance service in Amsterdam’s Portuguese Synagogue has stirred controversy after the keynote speaker condemned the Red Line protests and said labelling the Gaza war a genocide was rooted in anti-Semitism.

In a highly political speech, Chanan Hertzberger, chair of Jewish umbrella organisation CJO, denounced the “genocide lie” in front of a congregation containing senior cabinet members including the prime minister Rob Jetten, who also spoke.

Gerard Jonkman, director of Amsterdam-based Rights Forum, which campaigns on behalf of Palestinian rights, told Dutch News Hertzberger’s speech was “absolutely unacceptable”.

“This is also mixing the issue of anti-Semitism with criticism of Israel,” he said, “which is very, very, very dangerous.”

Hertzberger began his speech by thanking Jetten for not giving in to “the demands of the organisers of yesterday’s anti-Israel demonstration”, which he said amounted “directly or indirectly” to wiping Israel off the map.

“Who is being held responsible, in Arnhem, in Groningen and in Amsterdam for this so-called genocide?” he said. “We, the Jews. In our own own cities. In our streets. In our children’s classrooms. We are being ostracised and pushed to the margins of society.”

Only hours before, Jetten had spoken to RTL Nieuws saying it had been “impossible to miss” the protest and that he decided to stay away (having attended previous ones) because of his new role as PM, which he and his fellow cabinet member have used from the beginning to “increase pressure on Israel”.

“He embarrassed Jetten”

Jonkman said he thought Hertzberger had embarrassed Jetten and that the prime minister should now react to “these ridiculous accusations of hatred towards Israel.”

He said many Jewish people joined Sunday’s demonstration, among them Holocaust survivors and children of Holocaust survivors, and that many people he had spoken to were hurt by the speech.

Linking the protest to anti-Semitism in this way makes Jewish people in the Netherlands appear accountable for the policies of the Israeli government, he said.

Hertzberger said the “lie” that Israel was committing genocide now “marches weekly through our streets”, citing chants at Sunday’s protest, though he added that not all demonstrators were anti-Semites.

Zionism

He claimed that in fact the majority of Jewish people in the Netherlands are Zionists, that Zionism is the recognition of Israel’s right to exist as a “safe, independent Jewish state”, and that those things are now “more important than ever”.

He mentioned the numerous attacks on Jewish schools and synagogues in the Netherlands this year, and said that the images of Gaza left no one unmoved, including himself.

A United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel has committed genocide in Gaza, a finding Israel rejects.

The International Criminal Court in The Hague has issued arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity. Both men have firmly denied the allegations.

The CJO has not yet replied for comment.

Jetten’s premiership has marked a downturn in Dutch-Israeli relations. Since the cabinet enacted a ban on goods from illegal Israeli settlements in occupied Palestinian territories in September, Israel has responded by stripping Dutch diplomats of their status and removing Dutch officials from a US-backed Gaza ceasefire centre.

World.title: Village threatened by port expansion could be saved by new plan
World.content:
A village with 1,100 inhabitants that has been facing shutdown for the last year under plans to expand an industrial port in Noord-Brabant could be saved after the government came up with an alternative, smaller-scale development.

The municipal council in Moerdijk said a year ago that the entire village would have to be demolished to make room for the Powerport development, which needs 400 to 500 hectares of land.

The expansion of the port and industrial site includes high-voltage substations, transformer stations, and pipelines to support the transition to clean energy and supply power to homes and businesses in the coming decades.

But junior climate minister Jo-Annes de Bat said in a letter to parliament on Tuesday that “a new scenario has arisen” that would involve a smaller expansion of around 200 hectares, allowing Moerdijk to remain.

Pim Meijer, spokesman for community group Dorpstafel Moerdijk, gave a cautious welcome to the new plan, but said the uncertainty surrounding the village’s future had taken its toll.

“People have no perspective,” he told Dutch News. “They’re suffering from stress and physical ailments. This year 25 people have already signed up for the scheme that lets them sell their house to the council and that’s a direct result of the uncertainty.”

Quality of life

He said villagers wanted the council, the province and the municipality to set down clear parameters to guarantee the village’s future and quality of life.

“What people don’t want is to see the industrial zone constantly encroaching on the village, which is what’s been going on for years. We want to draw a boundary and say: thus far and no further,” he said.

“If people with children leave that has an impact on our primary schools and our social clubs, and if no houses are built then new people can’t come to live in Moerdijk. But as long as people believe in a future for Moerdijk we will keep fighting for it.”

The government will continue to honour its financial commitments to Moerdijk, including a pledge to fully compensate villagers for their land and property and €25 million in community funding.

De Bat said the amount of space required for the development was less than previously estimated, partly because more efficient batteries were available and the government has downscaled its ambitions to develop hydrogen power.

“Residents of the village of Moerdijk and the surrounding region have rightly been asking for clarity for a long time,” he wrote.

World.title: Toolkit to help teachers spot suspected child abuse goes live
World.content:
Schools have started using a new digital support package to help teachers alert the authorities to cases of suspected domestic abuse and neglect.

The toolkit has been developed to try to increase the number of reports from schools, which is lower in the Netherlands than in neighbouring countries.

It is the product of two years of research that began when a series of cases came to light in which children had been systematically abused and tortured by their families. The children attended school but teachers were either unaware of the problems at home or unwilling to intervene.

Since 2019 teachers have been required to pass on details of children who they suspect of being abused to Veilig Thuis, the agency that specialises in domestic abuse and can compel parents to accept help.

The education minister at the time, Hugo de Jonge, said on average every classroom contained one child who was a victim of abuse or neglect at home.

The number of reports schools has almost doubled in the last seven years to around 4,000, while Veilig Thuis has advised in more than 9,500 other cases.

Need for training

But experts warn that teachers still lack the necessary expertise and are reluctant to contact the authorities because they fear repercussions from parents.

World.title: International student numbers rise as people leave US
World.content:
More international students are coming to study at Dutch universities, partly driven by people choosing to leave the US amid the current political climate, according to broadcaster NOS.

Around 17,600 first-year students this academic year come from abroad, up about 6% on last year, according to provisional figures from the university association UNL and the association of universities of applied sciences (VH), news agency ANP reported.

Universities had agreed to admit no more than 16,766 new international students a year, so that internationalisation would not come at the expense of Dutch students or undermine the Dutch language.

The universities say foreign students are “more often choosing to study in Europe because of developments in the United States”.

NOS linked this to president Donald Trump, who has tightened visa checks, clashed openly with several universities and interfered with academic freedom since returning to the White House.

UNL said the rise in foreign students was good news in itself, because they mainly study technical subjects in a sector short of staff. “We badly need international talent, particularly in priority sectors such as technology,” UNL chair Caspar van den Berg said, according to NOS.

“At the same time, universities have agreed to cap international intake. That is why we are taking targeted extra measures.”

Several universities will cut the number of places on English-taught psychology, economics, business administration and political science courses so that they stay below the agreed maximum next year. National student union ISO said it opposes caps on places and that every student should be free to choose their course.

World.title: Cabinet hopeful of securing majority for capital gains tax plan
World.content:
The cabinet’s plans to introduce a capital gains tax are on course to clear both houses of parliament after three right-wing opposition parties signalled they were prepared to back the measure.

Junior finance minister Eelco Eerenberg said in a debate on Monday that the trio of JA21, BBB and SGP would support the plan, overcoming objections from other opposition parties and criticism by the Council of State.

Coalition parties D66 and CDA also voiced reservations about the reform, with Henk-Jan Oosterhuis of D66 calling it a “rather creative explanation of the budget rules” and Christian Democrat Inge van Dijk admitting that it was “not pretty”.

Luc Stultiens, of the left-wing opposition party Pro, went further, accusing the coalition parties of writing “a blank cheque for €17 billion to the wealthy”, referring to the projected budget shortfall that will be created by the transition.

The three right-wing opposition parties would give the minority coalition a majority in the lower house, but the cabinet would still need to find support from one more party in the Senate.

€10 billion gap

The pensioners’ party 50Plus is seen as the most likely candidate, even though MP Corrie van Brenk said the “signal is red” during Monday’s debate. Oosterhuis pointed out that the latest revision is almost identical to a plan 50Plus tabled previously in the upper house.

Finance minister Eelco Heinen’s reform would replace the current system of taxing investments and savings annually, based on estimated rates of return, with a tax levied when assets are sold.

The finance ministry has estimated that the switch to capital gains tax will leave a €10 billion gap in the short term because investors will no longer pay tax on their assets every year.

The Box 3 levy was struck out in 2021 when the Supreme Court ruled that the use of fictional interest rates was deemed to breach European law.

The government introduced a stopgap measure allowing taxpayers to challenge their tax bill by submitting their actual financial results, but this is costing the treasury an estimated €3.5 billion a year.
