World.title: ‘Evasive,’ conflicting answers test impeach court’s patience
World.content:
“I’M REALLY SORRY, YOUR HONOR” Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan tells the impeachment court on Tuesday she could not remember signing documents or receiving salary from a firm that audited several companies linked to Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio. —Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — Evasive answers, repeated claims of failing to remember important documents, a potential conflict of interest involving a city accountant, and inconsistencies in property records are testing the patience of senator-judges in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, prompting warnings that witnesses who lie under oath could face contempt and perjury charges.

On Day 41 of the trial on Tuesday, senator-judges grilled Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan over her inability to recall signing documents linking her to an accounting firm that later audited companies associated with Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

READ: Tulfo wants VP, whoever prepared her SALN as impeachment trial witnesses

Article continues after this 

They also questioned Island Garden City of Samal assessor John Kenneth Enumerables over conflicting details in property records involving the Vice President.

The exchanges drew expressions of disbelief and frustration from several senator-judges, with Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo even proposing that Bajan be cited for contempt for allegedly evading questions.

Failed recollection

Bajan was the defense’s third witness on Article 2, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth, failing to fully disclose her assets and liabilities in her statements of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALNs), and failing to divest her business interests while in public office.

READ: Highlights: Day 41 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Nov. 10, 2026

Bajan is called to testify that the P64,194.72 paid to Duterte by the Davao City local government in 2023 represented a salary differential, not double compensation. The prosecution’s cross-examination and the senator-judges’ interjections, however, centered on questions over her credibility.

Article continues after this 

Private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia confronted Bajan with the original Articles of Partnership of Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., a certified public accounting firm registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission in 2003. The document showed Bajan among its partners and bore a signature she eventually acknowledged was hers.

But Bajan repeatedly said she could not remember signing the document or the circumstances surrounding her departure from the firm. She also failed to recall signing an amended Articles of Partnership in 2015 that removed her name.

Article continues after this 

“I’m really sorry, Your Honor. I cannot really remember all these documents,” Bajan told the court after long pauses.

Presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero repeatedly pressed her to answer directly, reminding her to look at the documents instead of the defense lawyers when responding.

“Did you file the amended Articles of General Partnership in 2015 removing your name from the accounting firm?” Escudero asked.

When Bajan again said she could not remember, Escudero warned that the court could issue orders compelling her to answer.

The presiding officer also questioned how an accountant, whose profession requires meticulous attention to documents, could not recall when she left a firm or whether she had signed papers bearing her name.

Divinagracia asked that the record reflect her observation that Bajan appeared unwilling or hesitant to answer.

Potential conflict

The testimony also raised questions about a potential conflict of interest. Bajan acknowledged that she had been a partner at Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano & Co., which later became Elises & Ciudadano. She said the firm was her first employer and that she withdrew from the partnership in 2015, before her appointment as Davao City accountant in 2016, when Duterte was mayor.

The prosecution presented General Information Sheets identifying Elises & Ciudadano as the external auditor, from 2019, of several companies linked to Duterte and Carpio, including GenCorp Industries Inc., Metro City Chow, Town Timesquare Bee Corp., City Hall King Chow, Chinese Gen Bee, Carpio Lawyer, Davao New Royal Taipan and Great Jolly Times Food Corp.

Defense counsel Lindon Bacquel argued that Bajan was no longer connected with the firm when it audited the companies. Bajan likewise said she had no knowledge of the firm’s auditing work after her departure.

Disbelief

Senator-judge Risa Hontiveros expressed disbelief over Bajan’s inability to remember signing an important document involving a private company with which she had been associated for more than a decade.

Senator-judge Lito Lapid later quipped that Bajan might even have forgotten her birthday, drawing laughter at the end of the tense exchange. He said he felt sorry for her and suspected she might have been used, urging her to tell the truth because the senator-judges only wanted to establish what had happened.

Tulfo, meanwhile, questioned Bajan’s apparent evasiveness.

“Yesterday, one witness was laughing. Today, this witness is very evasive and pretending not to know. Why can’t we cite these people in contempt so that the impeachment court will be respected?” he said.

Escudero’s warning on contempt and perjury came after Senator-judge Vicente “Tito” Sotto III asked what sanctions could be imposed on witnesses who lie under oath.

“They may be subject to contempt by the court,” Escudero said, adding that witnesses could also face perjury cases before the proper prosecutor’s office or courts because their statements were made under oath.

Senator-judge Panfilo “Ping” Lacson reminded the court that its authority to punish contempt was expressly provided under the rules governing impeachment proceedings. He said the previous day’s hearing had not been good for the court because a witness had smirked and laughed, almost making a mockery of the proceedings.

Property record discrepancies

The court’s scrutiny also extended to Enumerables, the defense’s second witness, who was questioned over a 751-square-meter property declared in Duterte’s SALN.

The property’s Transfer Certificate of Title identified its location as Barangay Matanos, which Enumerables said does not exist in Samal, while the city’s tax records placed it in Barangay San Isidro.

Enumerables said the property could be identified through matching market and assessed values but admitted he could not be certain that it was the same property declared in Duterte’s SALN.

The acquisition cost also differed: the deed of sale listed P3.45 million, while the joint SALN of Duterte and Carpio declared P4.04 million.

Enumerables confirmed the amount in the deed but could not independently establish that the two documents referred to the same property.

Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo faulted the assessor for failing to alert the Register of Deeds about the conflicting records, warning that such discrepancies could expose unsuspecting property buyers to questionable land titles. Lacson also urged him to correct the confusing records.

In an earlier press briefing, prosecution spokesperson Robert Ace Barbers earlier described the testimony of the defense’s first witness, Davao City assessor Jaime Adalin, as “incredible,” saying the witness had been evasive in explaining why a property owned by Carpio was supposedly the same lot declared in Duterte’s SALN.

Defense spokesperson Michael Poa declined to respond to Barbers’ criticism, invoking the sub judice rule.

Trial timeline

Escudero said he hoped the trial would conclude before Christmas or New Year, although he stressed that the court would not restrict the defense’s witnesses merely because their testimonies were repetitive. Only irrelevant evidence, he said, would justify limiting their presentation.

Meanwhile, Duterte spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. said resignation had never crossed the Vice President’s mind because she was elected by the people. He described the impeachment proceedings as politicking and said Duterte was prepared to let the trial run its course. —With reports from Keith Clores and Isabelle Pechay

World.title: Romualdez suspended for 90 days
World.content:
Former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Third Division on Tuesday ordered the 90-day preventive suspension of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Ferdinand Martin Romualdez, who is charged with plunder over allegations that he received P7.44 billion in kickbacks from government infrastructure projects funded under the national budgets from 2022 to 2025.

In a resolution, the antigraft court directed Romualdez “to cease and desist from the functions of his office or any other office,” Clerk of Court Dennis Pulma told reporters.

“[The] court also has ordered the Clerk of Court to furnish a copy of the resolution to the Speaker of the House through the Office of the Secretary General and also to request from the said office or offices to inform the court of any action taken within a period of five days from receipt of the resolution,” he said.

Article continues after this 

READ: Sandiganbayan airs concerns after inspecting BJMP facility

The Office of the Ombudsman, which filed the plunder case against Romualdez, had accused him of using his influence as the Speaker at the time to manipulate the national budget to his advantage. Romualdez, however, denied the allegation, saying he did not have “functional control” over the whole budget approval process.

Earlier on Tuesday, Navotas Rep. Toby Tiangco told the Sandiganbayan Third Division that House lawmakers had to pay a 20 percent “tariff” or “commission” to get more funding for their projects in the chamber’s version of the 2025 national budget and 2025 General Appropriations Act.

READ: Over P27-B projects allegedly inserted for Romualdez – witness

Tiangco, however, clarified that it was only his “understanding” that Romualdez had known and authorized the collection of commissions.

Article continues after this 

Testifying as a witness at the bail hearing of Romualdez, who is currently detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas, Quezon City, Tiangco confirmed to defense attorney Thea Daep during cross-examination that he heard about the alleged practice during House deliberations on last year’s budget.

According to Tiangco, when he would approach then Speaker Romualdez to request additional funding or amendments in the budget, the latter would refer him to Ako Bicol Rep. Elizaldy “Zaldy” Co, the House appropriations committee chair at the time.

Article continues after this 

“But with regard to this P200 million request that you mentioned, you did not go directly to accused Romualdez, who is your cousin by affiliation … neither did you go directly to Zaldy Co, correct?” Daep asked Tiangco, citing his judicial affidavit.

‘Family discount’

“The reason you did this … is because you had been hearing at that time about the 20-percent commission for additional funding,” she said, with Tiangco confirming the information.

He also affirmed other details in his affidavit, including the time Pampanga Rep. Aurelio “Dong” Gonzales told him that instead of 20 percent, the commission from his requested funding would be reduced to 10 percent, calling it a “family discount.”

Tiangco also noted that on Nov. 24, 2024, he met with Romualdez and President Marcos at Bahay Pangulo, where the President “raised concerns about funding that had been removed from the budget,” including allocations for foreign-assisted flagship projects and maintenance projects of the Department of Public Works and Highways.

Tiangco recalled that Marcos told Romualdez: “You are taking the funds for big projects.”

“Romualdez then responded that whatever the President wanted would be restored in the bicameral conference process,” the Navotas lawmaker said.

Later on, Tiangco said Romualdez called him to his office on Dec. 2, 2024, for a private discussion about the 20-percent commission.

“According to you, you were disappointed because when you told him about this, you were disappointed because his response was, ‘You should have just gone straight to me,’” Daep said.

World.title: AFP probes alleged data breach involving Air Force
World.content:
File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Armed Forces of the Philippines said on Tuesday it was investigating a reported data breach involving the Philippine Air Force (PAF) following online claims that sensitive personnel and administrative records had been compromised.

AFP spokesperson Col. Francel Margareth Padilla said that military cybersecurity units were verifying the information but stressed that “at this point, these are mere speculations.”

She told reporters in a briefing at Camp Aguinaldo, Quezon City, that the AFP monitors thousands of attempted cyberattacks daily and maintains safeguards to protect its systems.

Article continues after this 

“There is no impenetrable system. What is important is that we have the proper security in place,” Padilla said.

READ: AFP urges responsible behavior after editor tagged in hacking its site

Deep Web Konek, a Philippine-based cybersecurity advocacy and threat intelligence group, earlier posted on its Facebook page that a hacker had obtained files from the PAF’s Human Resource Management Information System.

It said the supposedly compromised records included confidential command orders, logistics and promotion documents, information on military camps and bases, and personnel names and identification numbers.

Downloadable

The supposed hacker reportedly claimed that the files were available for download on a dark web forum.

Article continues after this 

Asked whether the alleged leak of military personnel records could compromise operations, Padilla said the potential impact would depend on the nature and extent of the information involved.

She did not say when the investigation would be completed, saying the AFP would release updates once its technical personnel submitted their findings.

Article continues after this 

PAF spokesperson Col. Alvin Jay Capinguian, meanwhile, said the Air Force’s 950th Cyber Wing was coordinating with the AFP Cyber Command to verify the reports.

“The Air Force did its due diligence. We checked and elevated everything to the AFP Cyber Command,” he added. /cb

World.title: DSWD reminder: Cash ‘ayuda’ not for gadgets
World.content:
In this May 2026 photo, DSWD officers are distributing aid to people entitled to receive a cash subsidy from the government. —Inquirer photo/Grig C. Montegrande

MANILA, Philippines — Critics of the government’s various “ayuda” schemes may not find this amusing.

The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) on Tuesday reminded beneficiaries of its cash assistance program that the aid being handed out was meant for basic necessities.

The DSWD issued the statement as it took note of social media posts showing that people enrolled in its Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport (Uplift) program bought gadgets instead.

Article continues after this 

“We are saddened by viral posts or videos such as those, especially as there are those in crisis needing assistance,” said the DSWD spokesperson, Assistant Secretary Irene Dumlao.

READ: P397-M ‘duplicate’ payments found in DSWD ‘ayuda’ scheme

“There are vulnerable individuals out there who rely on our social welfare programs as their last source of help. Casting doubt or making fun of our programs is a direct hit to those individuals seeking cash assistance,” she added.

Nonessentials

According to the agency, the posts “sparked some comments from netizens who deplored the fact that some beneficiaries are just using the money for nonessential and fancy items.”

“We know that those posts may just be for content on social media, showing how after getting financial aid they go to the mall or gadgets store. But we appeal to the beneficiaries to also give respect to the program and to what you represent,” said Dumlao.

Article continues after this 

READ: Another ‘ayuda’: P12,000 each for 7.5M families, says Marcos

“If it will cause misunderstanding, let’s be responsible not to turn the program into content,” she added.

Article continues after this 

The Uplift was established by the Marcos administration through Executive Order No. 110, which the President signed on March 24 this year in response to economic disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict.

Under the program, households already covered by the DSWD’s Pantawid Pamilyang Pilipino Program and the Walang Gutom Program will receive a one-time cash aid of P2,000.

Meanwhile, poor and near-poor households identified through the Philippine Statistics Authority’s community-based monitoring system, as well as low-income Social Security System members, will receive P2,000 monthly for six months.

‘Insensitive’

“Our Uplift cash assistance is only enough to support and help with daily expenses. It will not be enough to buy luxury items. Even still, misleading posts affect the public, that’s why for the qualified beneficiaries, please make use of the cash aid for your basic needs,” said Dumlao in Tuesday’s statement.

“Let us meaningfully use the help we receive from the programs of the agency, and let’s not make fun of it because we become insensitive to those who truly need financial assistance,” she added.

Inquirer files

World.title: Balicasag tour guide fees questioned
World.content:
CALL FOR REVIEW Balicasag Island in Panglao, Bohol, as seen in this file photo, is at the center of a proposed inquiry into environmental and entrance fees charged to Department of Tourism-accredited tour guides accompanying visitors. —Leo Udtohan

TAGBILARAN CITY, BOHOL, Philippines — A Bohol provincial board member has sought an inquiry into the collection of environmental or entrance fees from Department of Tourism (DOT)-accredited tour guides accompanying visitors to Balicasag Island in Panglao town, citing the need for clear and consistent policies across the province’s tourism destinations.

Lawyer Jiselle Rae Aumentado Villamor, chair of the provincial board’s committee on tourism, raised the issue in a privilege speech on Tuesday, asking the provincial government to determine the legal basis for the fees, the collecting authority, and whether tour guides are covered by the charges.

Villamor said the concern was brought to the provincial government’s attention through a Facebook message reporting that accredited tour guides were being asked to pay environmental fees.

Article continues after this 

READ: Bohol tourist arrivals drop 22% in first half of year

Legitimate interest

She also cited an open letter from tourism stakeholders addressed to the Panglao municipal government seeking exemption from entrance fees while guides accompany tourists in the performance of their duties.

Villamor said it was important to establish whether the charges were environmental user fees imposed under national environmental and protected-area laws or entrance fees authorized by a local government ordinance or an agreement with a tourism destination operator.

READ: Bohol governor hopeful of tourism industry rebound

“These are not necessarily the same and may have different legal bases, purposes, and collecting authorities,” she said.

Article continues after this 

Villamor stressed that the provincial government had a legitimate interest in the matter because Bohol has several protected landscapes, seascapes, marine sanctuaries and other environmentally significant destinations.

“If the matter involves a national policy, then we must understand its broader implications for the other protected seascapes and landscapes in Bohol,” she said.

Article continues after this 

Villamor clarified that her initiative was not intended to undermine the authority of the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Panglao municipal government or other concerned agencies.

She also cautioned against assuming that accreditation automatically exempts tour guides from legally imposed fees.

“While accreditation does not automatically entitle anyone to an exemption from a lawfully imposed fee, their circumstances deserve consideration, particularly when they enter these destinations in the performance of their professional responsibilities,” Villamor said.

She proposed referring the matter to the committee on tourism for an inquiry in aid of legislation, in coordination with other appropriate committees.

Villamor recommended inviting representatives from the DENR, protected-area management authorities, DOT, Panglao municipal government, accredited tour guides, boat operators and other tourism stakeholders.

World.title: Myanmar Embassies Push Tax, Remittance Rules as Migrant Backlash Grows Across Asia
World.content:
Embassies operated by Myanmar’s cash-strapped military regime have intensified efforts to extract foreign currency from overseas workers, even as migrant opposition grows across Asia.

For the past two weeks, Myanmar missions have repeatedly ordered that all passport applications must be accompanied by official evidence of remittance and tax payments.

The regime enforced a mandatory 25 percent remittance requirement alongside 2 percent income tax on migrant workers in 2023 — measures widely seen as a bid to bolster foreign currency reserves amid severe shortages.

In the latest notices, Myanmar missions in Singapore, Hong Kong and Macau declared Monday that migrants applying for a Passport for Job (PJ) or PJ extension must include proof of tax payment and remittance of a quarter of their earnings over the past three months through official regime channels.

“The Myanmar embassy is issuing the order but nobody wants to use official remittance channels,” a 30-year-old Myanmar national working at a florist in Singapore told The Irrawaddy.

“Applicants may comply with the rule for three months, but otherwise, they will continue to use alternative channels that are convenient, pay more, and don’t siphon money to the military.”

He added that waiting times for passport extension appointments have also expanded dramatically under the regime’s new digital identification system (UID), prompting worker fears of being stranded in a legal limbo.

“A friend of mine has been waiting three months for an appointment; previously it took just two weeks to extend a passport.”

The precise number of Myanmar migrants in Singapore is unknown, but Myanmar labor department data from 2024 suggested a sharp increase since 2021, prompting predictions they could reach 200,000 in a few years.

Other major destinations for Myanmar migrant workers are South Korea and Japan, which recruit through formal MOU frameworks and offer comparatively higher wages.

Regime embassies in Seoul and Tokyo were among the first to double down, issuing notices that workers must comply with remittance and tax rules in exchange for passport extensions.

“It’s a new requirement. Even If workers have not used official channels before, they must do so before applying for an extension,” a South Korea-based Myanmar national who assists migrant workers told The Irrawaddy.

“Workers have no option if they need their passports extended. So, they have to comply for at least three months,” she said.

She echoed the complaints of long appointment waiting times, higher application costs, and workers’ reluctance to use official channels that offer lower exchange rates while funneling money to the military regime.

Meanwhile, the regime’s embassy in Thailand — home to the largest Myanmar migrant community of roughly four million — is reportedly demanding remittance and tax evidence before it issues or extends PJs. Agents say the embassy requires proof of payments, adding that appointment waiting times are unpredictable.

“The process is really complicated now. We have been told to submit remittance proof, even though they haven’t publicly announced it,” a Bangkok-based agent told The Irrawaddy.

The regime’s Certificate of Identity (CI) process to identify undocumented workers in Thailand was rejected by over 2 million migrants in a recent poll. Only 15,000 out of nearly 750,000 ID-less migrants have shown up at Thai CI centers amid a widespread boycott triggered by the tax and remittance rules.

Thailand’s Labor Ministry has voiced opposition to the rules, which it views as a violation of worker rights. However, regime Labor Minister Maung Myint pressed the issue on Sunday, insisting that CI applicants must abide by the remittance and tax mandates.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Routs Resistance HQ on Bago–Mon Border
World.content:
Myanmar’s military regime says it has seized 11 resistance bases along the border of Bago Region and Mon State, including the shadow National Unity Government (NUG)’s Special Region Military Command.

Regime media said the military launched a major “counter-terrorism operation” from Theinzayat along the mountainous route through Mon State’s Kyaikhto and Bago’s Shwegyin townships on Nov. 3.

From Nov. 4 to 7, it seized four temporary posts of the ethnic Karen National Liberation Army (KNLA) in Kyaikhto.

On Nov. 8, the regime seized another five resistance bases, including the Special Region Military Command northeast of Theinzayat, which it said was the nerve center of regional operations of the heartland People’s Defense Forces (PDF) loyal to the shadow government.

Here the resistance manufactured “homemade mortars, firearms, ammunition and explosives for their operations,” the report said.

The regime previously bombed the command on Sept. 24, killing six people including prominent Air Force defector Nay Win Aung.

A PDF fighter in the southern region confirmed the loss of the regional HQ.

“Yes, it’s true, the situation is worse than in the news,” he told The Irrawaddy.

Other resistance sources said intense fighting continues, ranging from ground battles to airstrikes using drones and fighter jets.

Neither the KNLA nor the NUG responded to inquiries from The Irrawaddy.

The regime said it seized 97 small arms, 12,285 ammunitions, 362 drops bombs, 139 mines as well as drones and two vehicles but attached no figures to the resistance’s “heavy casualties.”

Prominent military defector Zin Yaw said the regime raid seems to have taken the resistance by surprise, quoting sources as saying it involved roughly 1,000 troops.

“We have to wait and see how far they can advance into resistance territories since resistance forces are on high alert now and the clashes will become more intense,” he added.

World.title: Blue Tsunami Claims a Congressional Champion of Myanmar’s Cause
World.content:
It is now widely known that Republicans suffered a crushing defeat in last week’s U.S. midterm elections. Some voters simply disliked the Republican candidates running in their districts, while others, who might ordinarily have voted Republican, chose to vote against them simply because they belonged to Trump’s party. Their thinking was essentially this: “I want to teach Trump a lesson. As long as it’s not your guy, I’ll vote for anyone else.”

Take Senator Susan Collins of Maine, for example. Known as a moderate Republican, she defied her own party by voting alongside Democrats during Trump’s second impeachment trial to convict him for his role in the January 6 insurrection, earning his lasting enmity in the process. Yet she, too, lost her seat in this election.

Another casualty of the election was my own congressional representative, Congressman Bill Huizenga, who represents Michigan’s Fourth Congressional District. His defeat represents a painful loss for those of us who support Myanmar’s pro-democracy movement. We have lost someone who has done a great deal to advance our cause.

Huizenga is a seasoned congressman who has served eight terms since 2011. As a senior member of Congress, he held influential positions on several important committees. He served as vice chair of the House Financial Services Committee, chair of the House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on South and Central Asia, and vice chair of the Congressional Burma Caucus.

Through his involvement with the Burma Caucus, in particular, he supported Myanmar’s cause both publicly and behind the scenes. Some of these efforts are ones I am sharing publicly for the first time.

One such instance involved Ashin Nat Zaw, a Myanmar-born monk from Buffalo, New York, who was detained by the junta during a visit to Myanmar. The U.S. government, through the State Department and its embassy in Myanmar, sought his release, as he had returned to Myanmar as a U.S. citizen. Huizenga played a role in that effort.

I know this firsthand because a community liaison from Buffalo contacted me and asked for help connecting her with Huizenga’s office. I facilitated that connection. These were the kinds of things he did quietly, behind the scenes, without seeking publicity.

On the public front, he worked to advance the BRAVE Burma Act and helped push for its passage by the House. After Trump issued his order terminating Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Myanmar nationals, not a single Republican member of Congress seemed willing to speak up. Huizenga, however, joined Democratic Congressman Ami Bera of California, Gregory Meeks of New York and others in introducing legislation seeking to restore TPS for Myanmar nationals. However, the protections were ultimately terminated in August despite a temporary court-ordered reprieve.

Just last month, he also spearheaded a letter, signed by five other bipartisan members of the Burma Caucus, urging the United States to continue supporting Ambassador Kyaw Moe Tun as Myanmar’s permanent representative to the United Nations.

But none of these efforts happened in a vacuum. We must recognize that members of Congress are elected to represent the people of their own districts—their American constituents—and to address their concerns. They have no obligation to do anything for Myanmar. It is the responsibility of the Myanmar community in each congressional district to educate, persuade and encourage its representatives to take an interest in our cause.

And this does not happen overnight. It takes time, patience and the cultivation of relationships. There are various ways to establish that initial connection. Someone who already knows the congressman might introduce us. We might repeatedly write letters, submit statements and request meetings until we finally get an opportunity to speak with him. We might also reach out through religious channels, among other approaches.

One thing is certain: unlike some wealthier communities, we Burmese have never had the financial resources to buy our way into political influence.

Before the 2021 military coup in Myanmar, Huizenga knew little about the country. Although there was a Burmese community in his district, it was nowhere near as large as those in Indianapolis or Fort Wayne. To put things into perspective, approximately 350,000 votes were cast in this congressional district in the 2026 election, while the entire Burmese community’s voting strength amounted to only about 4,000 votes.

We had to work extremely hard to break through and get him to pay attention to Myanmar’s affairs. The fact that our city already had a Burma Center, established some 15 years ago, gave us an advantage. Through five years of cultivating relationships, explaining our cause, and educating his office, we developed close ties with him and his staff. Even the recent letter supporting Kyaw Moe Tun was the result of our activists suggesting to his office that such a letter would be worthwhile and guiding them toward issuing it.

This is how grassroots advocacy works.

Losing someone with whom we had built such a close and trusting relationship is an enormous loss for us. The newly elected Democratic congressman who replaces him will likely know little or nothing about Myanmar. We will have to start all over again, building relationships and educating him about our cause from scratch. Furthermore, as a freshman congressman, he will have little influence in the House and is unlikely to secure a position on any of its important committees.

We did everything we could to help Huizenga win reelection. But, as mentioned earlier, our community’s approximately 4,000 votes were a mere drop in the ocean compared with the 350,000 votes cast in the district. He, too, was swept away by the blue tsunami.

I hate to say it, but even within our own Burmese community, there were people who did not want to vote for him because they viewed him as something of a MAGA Republican—a Trump supporter.

In my view, however, even if he had been reelected, his presence alone would not have significantly altered the balance of power between Democrats and Republicans in Congress. But among the 435 members of the House of Representatives, only four or five genuinely understand and support Myanmar’s cause. Losing even one of them is a significant setback, and finding a replacement is no easy task.

That is why, when it came time to vote, I encouraged members of our community to consider splitting their tickets. They could vote for Democrats in other races if they wished, but I urged them to vote for Huizenga, the Republican, in our congressional race. Unfortunately, our efforts still fell short.

In addition to Huizenga, Representative Young Kim (R-California), another member of the Burma Caucus, lost her reelection bid. Longtime supporter of Myanmar Senator Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) will retire from his Senate position and political career in January 2027. Myanmar desperately needs newer members of Congress to champion its cause.

I would like to take this opportunity to express my deepest gratitude and respect to Congressman Huizenga for his unwavering support of Myanmar’s cause. In appreciation of his efforts, I am sharing some of his behind-the-scenes contributions that many people may not have known about. I would also like to extend my special thanks to his entire staff, who worked closely with our community and with whom we developed a close and trusting relationship.

Thank you, Congressman Huizenga, for standing with the people of Myanmar.

Than N. Oo is a co-founder of advocacy group Free Myanmar and writes frequently about Myanmar’s political developments.

World.title: Bangladesh Confirms Talks With AA Over Rohingya Repatriation
World.content:
Bangladesh has confirmed it is holding discussions with the ethnic Arakan Army (AA) in tandem with talks with Myanmar’s regime as it seeks a solution to the long-running Rohingya refugee crisis.

Speaking at a policy dialogue in Dhaka on Sunday, Shama Obaed Islam, Bangladesh’s state minister for foreign affairs, said the government had formed a committee to develop a national strategy on the Rohingya issue and was engaging both Naypyitaw and the AA, according to Bangladeshi outlets.

The minister said relying solely on conventional diplomatic channels to secure the return of Rohingya refugees was unrealistic.

Her remarks were a rare public acknowledgment that Bangladesh is in contact with the AA, which now controls 14 of 17 townships in Rakhine State and virtually the entire Bangladesh-Myanmar border following a series of battlefield victories over Myanmar military forces since late 2023.

At the same event, former Bangladesh interim government adviser and retired Brigadier General M Sakhawat Hossain argued that Dhaka should maintain good relations with the AA and engage with it either directly or through intermediaries. He said Bangladesh needed to view the Rohingya issue strategically, noting that the group had become a dominant force in Rakhine, which shares a border with Bangladesh.

“We have to play a strategic game. Sooner or later, Rakhine will become either a confederated state or something similar. We must maintain good relations and negotiate with the Arakan Army, either directly or through third parties,” he was quoted as saying.

The AA’s territorial gains have forced Bangladesh to adapt to new realities across the frontier. According to the Center for Arakan Studies, Bangladeshi authorities have gradually adopted a pragmatic approach toward trade with AA-controlled areas, acknowledging the group’s control of border infrastructure even without formally recognizing it.

Cross-border trade through the Teknaf-Kanyinchaung route resumed earlier this year after prolonged disruption caused by fighting in Rakhine. Traders say Bangladesh, alongside India, has become an increasingly important source of food, medicine and other essential supplies for communities in AA-held territory, as the regime has imposed blockades on roads and waterways linking the state with rest of the country.

The Rohingya refugee crisis remains among Bangladesh’s most pressing concerns. The country hosts more than one million Rohingya refugees, most of whom fled a military crackdown in northern Rakhine in 2017. Repatriation efforts led by Bangladesh and Myanmar have repeatedly failed to produce results.

Analysts argue that any future repatriation plan will require cooperation from the AA, which controls much of the territory to which refugees would eventually return.

Despite renewed diplomatic efforts, major obstacles remain. The Myanmar regime’s Foreign Ministry said in August that it had verified nearly 309,000 Rohingya in Bangladesh as former residents of Rakhine State, but said repatriation would proceed only when security conditions improve. It also insisted that only about 540,000 Rohingya had fled to Bangladesh.

During the recent UN General Assembly, Bangladesh called on the international community to help repatriate 1.2 million Rohingya. The UN has meanwhile warned that ongoing fighting and military airstrikes in Rakhine mean conditions are not yet conducive to the safe and voluntary return of refugees.

World.title: Oxford Museum Makes ‘Historic’ Return of Naga Human Remains
World.content:
OXFORD, United Kingdom—An Oxford University museum on Monday returned the remains of 39 people taken during Britain’s colonial rule in India to members of its Naga community.

Almost 30 people from the community based in northeastern Nagaland, a mountainous state bordering Myanmar, traveled to Britain for the ceremony, which the museum’s director, Laura Van Broekhoven, called a “historic moment.”

The handover at the Pitt Rivers Museum came as part of a broader trend among Western museums reassessing how they acquired exhibits from other cultures, particularly human remains, and in some cases returning them.

The Pitt Rivers, an ethnographic museum founded in the 19th century, has already handed back human remains to indigenous communities in Australia, New Zealand and the United States.

The Oxford museum has more than 6,000 objects representing Naga culture, the largest collection in the world, and is giving back “ancestral human remains,” mainly skulls, to the Naga people.

Van Broekhoven hailed it as “a historic moment that will be part of stories told to next generations” in a speech as both sides signed a formal agreement on the handover.

The remains were already “on their way to Heathrow” airport, the museum director said, after overcoming “so much red tape everywhere.”

The museum only removed all human remains from display in 2020, much later than most museums, and still has around 2,700 remains in storage, she told AFP.

These “were collected in times that had different ethics, different thinking, which was not unproblematic when we look at it with the eyes of today,” she said.

‘Respectful rest’

Housed in a Victorian Gothic building, the museum is a dark atmospheric space with glass cases crammed with objects, many with handwritten labels.

Naga tribal leaders united for the handover and planned to bury the remains together under a joint memorial in a park.

“We shall put them to respectful rest,” one of the tribal leaders, Thejao Vihienuo, told AFP.

The 73-year-old, draped in a traditional shawl, also visited with other Nagas last year as part of the lengthy process.

“It’s been six years of working alongside each other on a very delicate matter,” the museum director said.

The Naga remains were brought to Oxford between 1910 and 1940. Most were collected by two colonial administrators who were anthropologists.

The museum says on its website that items collected during this era were “frequently confiscated during punitive military expeditions, rather than freely given.”

While in Oxford, the delegation met descendants of one of the anthropologists.

“The manner in which these human remains were taken away from our land leaves much for us to speculate,” said Vihienuo.

“I suspect that nobody would have given the skull of his father or his grandfather as a gift to another person.”

The Naga people once practiced headhunting, severing heads of enemies as trophies, but also kept heads of their own chiefs “at the center of the villages” and one of the remains is a chief’s head, said anthropologist Dolly Kikon, a member of Nagaland’s Lotha-Naga community.

World.title: Myanmar Foreign Debt Falls to $10.8b but Experts Warn of Collapse
World.content:
Despite World Bank data showing Myanmar’s foreign debt fell to US$ 10.8 billion in 2025, experts warn loan repayments by the internationally isolated regime are fuelling economic collapse.

Myanmar’s external debt dropped from $13.5 billion in 2021 to $10.8 billion in 2025, according to the latest figures released by the World Bank on November 5. The report said public and public-guaranteed loans account for 95 percent ($10.3 billion) of the total debt which comes under three categories: multilateral, bilateral, and private creditors.

The World Bank and International Monetary Fund are Myanmar’s primary multilateral lenders, owed $3.8 billion, with Japan and China its largest bilateral creditors (owed over $1.5 billion).

As Myanmar’s top international donor, Japan funds special economic zones and large-scale infrastructure including railways and power grids. Japan remains Myanmar’s biggest creditor despite cancelling over 300 billion yen ($3 billion) in debt to facilitate financial reintegration in 2013 and then suspending new loans after the 2021 coup.

Meanwhile, Chinese loans have financed key infrastructure, energy, pipelines, and Belt and Road projects across Myanmar. Regular regime payments halved Chinese debt from $3 billion to around 1.5 billion between 2021 and 2025.

However, analysts warn that the heavy burden of foreign currency repayments amid an international aid freeze and deepening economic crisis are fuelling kyat depreciation and severe shortages.

“Having to make loan repayments during an economic crisis and foreign currency shortage has driven the country into trouble,” said a local economist, who requested anonymity for safety reasons.

“Repayments may reduce the debt, but there is no money left for imports — and no international aid to cover the outflows.”

He added that as a developing nation, Myanmar is dependent on international funding such as concessional loans and development grants to fund large-scale infrastructure.

Post-coup economic mismanagement compounded by foreign sanctions and an exodus of foreign investors have plunged Myanmar into severe economic crisis. At the same time, escalating armed conflict around key economic projects has stalled their development.

Against this backdrop, the regime’s Ministry of Finance and Revenue recently stated that the soaring 2025–26 budget deficit was driven by a drop in funding from its closest allies, China, India, and Russia, as key projects hit security snags. Speaking to lawmakers, deputy minister Kyaw Htin acknowledged that the expected foreign funding failed to materialize.

With access to international loans limited, the rubber-stamp parliament in October approved short-term export credit from Belarus, sparking widespread criticism that the high-interest loan repayments will only deepen hardships for the Myanmar public.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Plans April Vote in 55 Constituencies Despite Continued Clashes
World.content:
Myanmar’s regime plans to hold elections in 55 constituencies across 37 townships on April 4, 2027, including 12 townships where it has regained at least partial control from resistance forces in recent years. Voting was not held in those 12 townships during the regime’s general election in December 2025 and January 2026, which was widely dismissed as a sham.

In an announcement Thursday, the regime said it would hold voting in 34 Lower House constituencies, using the first-past-the-post (FPTP) system; five Upper House constituencies; and 16 regional/state parliament constituencies across the country.

The townships include Tonzang and Falam in northern Chin State and Tigyaing, Banmauk and Indaw in Sagaing Region, all recaptured by the regime this year, as well as Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region, which it recaptured in 2025.

Also included on the regime’s list of townships scheduled to vote in April are Sagaing’s Kawlin, which the Myanmar military recaptured in 2024, and the Sagaing resistance strongholds of Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo and Taze.

A military analyst pointed out that the regime only controls the towns in Pale, Yinmarbin, Shwebo, Taze, Tigyaing, Banmauk and especially Indaw.

“The regime wants to show it is able to control the whole country, and that its administration is operating,” said Zin Yaw, a military defector who has monitored Myanmar’s conflicts since defecting after the coup.

The absence from the list of southern Chin State towns that the regime has been trying to retake since May 2026, as well as Arakan Army-controlled towns in Rakhine State, amounts to an admission by the regime that it hasn’t been able to restore its authority in these areas, he said.

The regime announced Lower House elections in Myeik, Tanintharyi Region; Nyaunglebin, Pauk Khaung and Padaung in Bago Region; Chauk and Minbu in Magwe Region; Pyin Oo Lwin, Meiktila, Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; Kyaikmayaw in Mon State; Mayangone, Shwepyithar, Hlegu, Tamwe, Cocokyun and Hlaing Tharyar in Yangon Region; Kyaukme, Monghpyak, and Mong Pan in Shan State; Maubin in Ayeyarwady Region; and Zabuthiri, Dekkhinathiri and Ottarathiri in Naypyitaw.

The Upper House constituencies on the list are in Kachin State, Chin State, Magwe Region, Bago Region and Mandalay Region.

The list also includes state/regional parliament constituencies in Tonzang and Falam in Chin State; Tigyaing, Banmauk, Indaw, Kawlin, Pale, Yinmarbin, Taze and Shwebo in Sagaing Region; Zigon and Thegon in Bago Region; Natogyi, Singu and Mogoke in Mandalay Region; and Yegyi in Ayeyarwady Region.

The Myanmar military recently suffered heavy losses to resistance ambushes in Indaw Township. Clashes continue there and in upper Sagaing.

Despite the ongoing armed conflicts in many areas, political parties cooperating with the regime’s electoral process said they are making preparations for the vote.

Saw Than Myint, joint secretary of the Shan and Ethnic Democratic Party (SNDP), which secured 37 seats in the regime-backed general election, said the party plans to compete in the upcoming by-election but is still discussing details.

People’s Pioneer Party (PPP) chair Saw Han Aye said the party hopes to field candidates in at least one-third of the 55 constituencies, as required under the Political Parties Registration Law for parties competing at the national level.

He acknowledged that security concerns remain in some areas, adding that participation would ultimately depend on individual candidates’ willingness.

The PPP was founded by Thet Thet Khine, a former regime minister who was barred in October 2025 from running in the general election on grounds of violating rules on personal debts.

The Irrawaddy contacted People’s Party chair Ko Ko Gyi, a former 88 Generation student protest leader, about the party’s plans but received no response.

Coup leader Min Aung Hlaing’s regime organized the nationwide election in three phases in December 2025 and January 2026, with voting in 263 out of 330 townships. Civilian leaders, including Aung San Suu Kyi, remained imprisoned, while major opposition parties had been dissolved.

With only nine parties participating at the national level, the election was dominated by the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) and allied parties, allowing the USDP to secure a majority of the seats.

Since installing himself as president in April, Min Aung Hlaing has launched a diplomatic campaign in an effort to gain legitimacy for his regime, visiting China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia and India, while his military forces continue targeting civilians in attacks and atrocities. The absence of elections in the 55 constituencies has underlined his regime’s lack of legitimacy, observers say.

World.title: Over 2m Myanmar Migrants in Thailand Reject Regime’s Identity Document
World.content:
Over 2 million Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand have participated in a poll calling on the parallel National Unity Government (NUG) to issue identity documents amid a mass boycott of the regime’s new Certificate of Identity (CI) process.

The poll also aims to demonstrate to the Thai government that they recognize the NUG as their legitimate government, not the military regime.

Thailand hosts an estimated 4 million Myanmar workers, both documented and undocumented. Migrant worker groups estimate that at least 600,000 are required to apply for CIs in this round. However, most are staying away from the regime’s newly opened Thai CI centers in protest against new tax and remittance rules that critics condemn as extortion. To apply, workers must prove they have remitted 25 percent of their wages through official regime channels and paid 2 percent annual income tax. The vast majority are refusing, fearing payment would help fund the regime’s war on civilians while lending it political legitimacy.

Meanwhile, Thai opposition lawmakers and labor rights groups have urged the government to review or scrap the centers, branding them a threat to national security and sovereignty.

The workers themselves made their overwhelming opposition clear in a weeklong online poll launched Sunday by the Myanmar Migrant Workers’ Representative Coordinating Committee in Thailand (MMWRCCT). Many appealed to Thai authorities to grant them work and residency permits without the CI document.

The poll result reflected resounding support among migrant workers for an alternative identification process managed by the NUG, Khin Soe of the MMWRCCT told The Irrawaddy.

“The regime CI process is a trap to extract foreign currency and information for military conscription,” he said. “The workers know this, so they don’t want to apply.”

He said the poll result would be sent to the NUG’s Labour Department to push for worker ID issuance, while a separate workers’ online petition would be delivered to the Thai government.

“The Thai government may argue it has to cooperate with the regime on the CI process to ensure national security, but we are appealing to them on humanitarian grounds. If they need an alternative authority to issue identity documents, this poll shows that millions of workers want the NUG to do it. As guests living under Thai law, we are not making demands, we are simply presenting these results as a respectful request,” Khine Soe said.

Launched on October 18, the campaign and petition contain four requests, including the right to stay and work legally without a CI, and has drawn support from Thai labour rights groups and politicians.

Among them is MP Anuson Tamajai, a prominent economist who urged the government to review or cancel the CI centers, arguing their unchecked operations compromise national security and sovereignty.

Highlighting migrant workers’ indispensable role in Thailand’s economy, he also called for an investigation into whether demanding remittance and tax payments in exchange for ID certificates violates Thai law.

The Thailand Migration Reform group recently warned that allowing Naypyitaw to control migrant registration “undermines Thai sovereignty and fuels corruption.” It urged Thai authorities to revert to the Pink Card system for migrant workers.

On Friday, Thai Labor Minister Julapun Amornvivat told media after a meeting of the Foreign Workers Management Policy Committee that CIs are required by migrants’ countries of origin for identity verification, but the process operates entirely within Thai territory.

He said his ministry will send a formal letter to its regime counterpart expressing opposition to the mandatory remittance policy, arguing it undermines migrant worker rights and fails to align with international standards.

Dismissing the backlash, the cash-strapped regime has doubled down on its push to skim foreign currency from low-paid overseas workers. Newly appointed Labor Minister Maung Myint has threatened workers with legal action and a ban on returning home if they don’t make tax and remittance payments.

However, the boycott shows no sign of weakening, with only a trickle of applicants reported at the five CI centres across Thailand since they opened on October 14.

World.title: Kazakhstan Expects Electricity Surplus Despite Data Center Valley Project, Officials Say
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan expects to move from an electricity deficit to a surplus in 2028, with excess generating capacity projected to reach 2.8 gigawatts by 2029 and approximately 5 gigawatts by 2035, even after the launch of energy-intensive projects such as Data Center Valley, KEGOC Chairman of the Management Board Nabi Aitzhanov said at a Nov. 10 press briefing.

“Even after the launch of the Data Center Valley project, the country will maintain an electricity surplus,” he said.

To meet growing demand and strengthen energy independence, Kazakhstan plans to commission more than 26 gigawatts of new generating capacity by 2035. Nuclear energy and clean coal generation are among the priorities.

The country’s energy infrastructure modernization and expansion were also discussed at a government meeting chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov. The agenda included upgrading existing power plants and electricity and heating networks, developing new generation facilities and addressing staffing shortages in the energy and housing and utilities sectors.

Government seeks to address energy sector staffing shortages

Energy Minister Yerlan Akkenzhenov reported that consumers are supplied with electricity and heat and that the country’s energy infrastructure is prepared for the heating season. According to the minister, average funding for repair work increased by 27%. As a result, equipment wear at power plants declined to 52%, electricity networks to 65.7% and heating networks to 48%. The number of technological disruptions decreased by an average of 6% compared with the previous year.

Bektenov stressed the need to continue building new power plants and modernizing existing facilities, transmission lines, clean coal generation and renewable energy sources. He also highlighted the importance of training qualified energy specialists, ensuring continuity between generations of professionals and building a sustainable workforce, particularly in view of the development of nuclear energy.

The Ministries of Science and Higher Education, Education and Energy, together with regional administrations, have been instructed to prepare an action plan to address the shortage of specialists in the energy sector and housing and utilities services.

Digital fire prevention system undergoing pilot testing

Kazakhstan has built 19 fire stations this year, including seven multifunctional facilities designed to accommodate both firefighting and medical services. The country is also purchasing more than 160 fire engines, around 1,500 pieces of equipment and over 2,000 sets of protective clothing. Kazakhstan is also introducing a digital system to improve fire prevention in residential areas. The Tumar 112 mobile application is currently undergoing pilot testing in the Abai Region, Emergency Situations Minister Murat Mukhanov reported.

The application will enable electronic records of residential inspections, document fire risks through photographs and geolocation, and create a unified database.

“Over time, the accumulated information will make it possible to identify the most vulnerable houses, track the elimination of identified violations and provide emergency services with up-to-date information to support prompt decision-making when reports of fires are received,” Mukhanov said.

Following the pilot, the system is expected to be introduced in other regions.

Ekibastuz power plant expansion on schedule

Construction of the third and fourth power units at Ekibastuz GRES-2 is proceeding according to schedule, Ansar Aidarov, chairman of the management board of Samruk Energo, reported.

The third unit is scheduled to launch in 2028, while the fourth is expected to enter operation in October 2030. According to him, around 450 workers are currently involved in construction. Boiler equipment deliveries are underway, while turbine equipment is expected to begin arriving early next year for installation in 2027.

Aidarov said no delays had been recorded in the construction schedule.

World.title: Kazakhstan Calls for Dialogue and Mutual Trust at Collective Security Forum in Moscow
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s Foreign Minister Mukhtar Tileuberdi called for stronger international dialogue, mutual trust and respect for international law while addressing the International Forum on Collective Security in Moscow, Russia.

Tileuberdi delivered remarks at the plenary session, highlighting declining trust among states as a challenge to the international order and the authority of international law.

He emphasized that a stable international order cannot rely solely on the balance of power but must be grounded in international law, mutual trust and the ability of countries to maintain dialogue even amid serious disagreements.

The minister expressed confidence in further strengthening international cooperation, stressing that the future of Eurasia should not be shaped by confrontation or dividing lines.

Instead, he said, it should be built on mutual respect, trust and the willingness of states to address common challenges together.

The forum’s program also included an exhibition showcasing products and technologies in collective security.

World.title: Kazakhstan Ranks Among Top 50 Countries for Opportunities in Best Countries 2026
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan ranked 44th among 100 countries in the Opportunities category of the Best Countries 2026 ranking, placing it among the top 50 countries for conditions related to business, employment, education, social protection and access to financial resources.

The country received an average score of 53.9 points in the category, with particularly high assessments for social protection, personal income taxation and educational attainment. Kazakhstan ranked 53rd overall with a score of 53.8 points.

The ranking was compiled by U.S. News & World Report in cooperation with the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania. This year’s edition assessed 100 countries across eight categories using 100 indicators.

Unlike previous editions, which relied on public perception surveys, the 2026 ranking is based on statistical data collected from international organizations and other sources.

Social protection and education among Kazakhstan’s strongest areas

The Opportunities category evaluates conditions for entrepreneurship, employment, education, social protection, taxation and access to financial resources.

Kazakhstan received 94.1 points out of 100 for social protection, 80.2 points for personal income taxation and 71.8 points for educational attainment. The country profile also lists an average of 12.5 years of schooling.

The scores reflect the ranking’s assessment methodology and should not be interpreted as direct measures of population coverage. For example, the 94.1-point score for social protection does not mean that 94.1% of the population is covered by government programs.

Kazakhstan ranks 50th in healthcare and 54th in infrastructure

Kazakhstan placed 50th in the healthcare category, with a score of 64.2 points. The assessment considered access to medical care, life expectancy, the availability of doctors, vaccination and healthcare infrastructure.

The country profile lists 3.8 doctors per 1,000 people and a life expectancy of 74.4 years.

In infrastructure, Kazakhstan ranked 54th with 64 points. The category covers access to electricity, transport networks, internet connectivity, water supply, sanitation and energy system resilience.

According to the ranking, 97.9% of the population has access to basic sanitation services. Average broadband internet speed was listed at 88.1 megabits per second.

Kazakhstan placed 53rd in the overall ranking, with 53.8 points. Uzbekistan ranked 76th with 46.8 points, placing 23 positions below Kazakhstan.

The overall assessment covers a broad range of factors, including economic development, healthcare, governance, infrastructure and societal well-being.

Best Countries 2026 introduces new methodology

Published annually since 2016, the Best Countries ranking underwent a significant methodological revision in 2026.

The new framework uses 100 indicators drawn from more than 30 organizations and data sources, including the World Bank, United Nations agencies and the International Labour Organization.

The indicators are grouped into eight categories designed to assess different aspects of national well-being. The importance assigned to each category was determined through a survey of 42 international experts from academia, think tanks and international organizations.

According to the methodology, the experts distributed 100 points across the eight categories based on their importance to a country’s prosperity, operational health and societal well-being.

The revised approach means that Kazakhstan’s 2026 results cannot be directly compared with its positions in previous editions, which were based on perceptions of countries rather than statistical indicators.

World.title: INMerge Innovation Summit to Bring Global Speakers to Baku This November
World.content:
ASTANA – The INMerge Innovation Summit, one of the region’s largest innovation platforms, will bring together internationally recognised figures from technology, business, sports and academia in Baku on Nov. 30-Dec. 1.

Organized by Azerbaijan’s PASHA Holding, the summit will take place at the Baku Congress Center and focus on innovation, technology leadership, startups and business cooperation across the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Middle East and Europe.

The two-day event will feature keynote speeches, panel discussions and networking opportunities, bringing together representatives of international companies, investors, startups and public institutions.

Among the confirmed speakers are Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak, former Google X Chief Business Officer Mo Gawdat, Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph, former professional tennis player Maria Sharapova, Amazon Chief Technology Officer Werner Vogels, former OpenAI executive Zack Kass and Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull.

The program will also feature Greg Hoffman, former chief marketing officer at Nike, and Joel Mokyr, a professor at Northwestern University and the 2025 Nobel Prize laureate in Economic Sciences.

Established by PASHA Holding in 2021, INMerge is an annual innovation and technology summit designed to connect corporations, investors, startups and government representatives from different regions. The platform aims to encourage regional cooperation and contribute to Baku’s development as an innovation hub.

The summit has also received positive feedback from prominent international figures who attended previous editions. Wozniak described his participation in the Baku event as memorable.

“It was my honor and privilege to speak at the INMerge Innovation Summit in Baku. I really enjoyed the opportunity to visit Azerbaijan, see all of the amazing developments occurring there and to participate in a world-class Summit. It was an experience I will never forget,” Wozniak said, according to the summit’s press service.

Chris Barton, founder of Shazam, also highlighted the event’s atmosphere and exchange of ideas.

“INMerge Innovation Summit was a highlight for me because of the incredible energy, passion, and exchange of ideas from so many innovators in one place,” he said.

At the 2025 edition, the summit attracted more than 5,000 participants, over 180 speakers, 122 startups and 80 investors.

World.title: COP31: Transforming Kazakhstan’s Emissions Trading System Through Digitalization
World.content:
From Nov. 9 to 20, Antalya, Türkiye, is hosting the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31). Its main themes are climate finance, adaptation, the energy transition, reducing the energy intensity of buildings and reporting on commitments made.

Since the first days of its independence, Kazakhstan has been an active and responsible participant in global processes on sustainable development and climate change: it signed and ratified the Kyoto Protocol in 2009 and subsequently joined the Paris Agreement in 2016.

This was preceded by extensive expert and analytical work by the Ministry of Environmental Protection, renamed the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources in 2021, with support from the World Bank, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Development Program (UNDP), national experts and the National Chamber of Entrepreneurs of Kazakhstan.

Today, Kazakhstan positions itself as a leader in advancing the green energy transition not only in Central Asia but also across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). Kazakhstan was the first country in the region to adopt a Strategy for Achieving Carbon Neutrality by 2060. This year, by Sept. 1 order of the Prime Minister, a Plan of Organizational Measures for implementing the Strategy was approved.

The plan will help integrate decarbonization principles into all areas of the national economy, including sectoral planning systems and the monitoring, reporting and accounting of greenhouse gas emissions on an innovative, digital basis.

The initiative of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to harness the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) is especially relevant to resetting the country’s national emissions trading system. Speaking at the BRICS+ summit on Sept. 13, he again underlined the role of AI in global development and noted that “Kazakhstan regards AI as a strategic priority and is ready to use its advanced computing infrastructure, as well as national and UN digital centers, to expand effective cooperation” for the country’s sustainable development.

COP31 experts note a revival of global carbon trading, particularly in the submission of projects to the voluntary carbon market, which undergo a multi-stage review by the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM). As regards the regulated greenhouse gas market – existing national emissions trading systems and their participation in global carbon trading – discussions continue on avoiding double counting and on building the necessary carbon infrastructure.

Among Asian countries, Kazakhstan was one of the first to launch an emissions trading system (KazETS). It covers 220 installations in the six basic sectors of the economy and is now undergoing a transformation through the development and introduction of auctioning and of production benchmarks drawing on EU and OECD experience. At the same time, full participation of Kazakh enterprises in global carbon trading and access to the carbon markets of other countries require, first and foremost: a gradual phase-out of free allowances; a higher price per tonne of greenhouse gases; the transfer of the existing MRV (monitoring, reporting and verification) system to a digital platform.

For Kazakh exporters, the absence of a modern, internationally recognised infrastructure for monitoring, reporting and verifying CO₂ emissions, and of verifiers accredited in line with international requirements, is currently a serious challenge. At the same time, the experience of leading carbon market players and platforms such as Sylvera, BeZero Carbon, Isometric and Calyx Global shows that AI makes it possible to assess the integrity and risks of carbon projects, to evaluate the carbon footprint and the contribution of enterprises and sectors to the Sustainable Development Goals, and to build digital solutions, including under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

At COP31, the National Pavilion of Kazakhstan will also present a number of digital solutions for resetting the national ETS and creating a regional digital climate hub with the support of the UNFCCC. We hope that this initiative, developed by experts of Astana Hub together with Green Academy, the University of Central Asia and the Kunayev Institute of Mining, with the support of the Swedish company Planboo and SagtaAI, will be supported by the delegations of the Central Asian countries and included in the outcome document of COP31.

The author is Professor Dr. Bakhyt Yessekina, a member of the Green Council under the President of Kazakhstan. Yessekina is the head of the Green Academy Scientific Research and Education Center.
