World.title: Police divers to search rivers as hunt for missing boy enters fifth day
World.content:
Police have widened the search for a 17-year-old boy who disappeared in dense bush in Victoria's east on Friday.

William was camping with his step-brother near Walhalla East, in Gippsland, when he disappeared on Friday, November 6.

Police divers will today search nearby rivers as the search enters its fifth day.

He was last seen about 4pm near Stoney Creek Road, near the town of Cowwarr, after walking a short distance from their drop-off location to collect additional camping equipment.

He failed to return, prompting his step-brother to search the area, but there was no sign of him.

Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said search crews had already covered a large area of bushland and would extend the search perimeter today.

William disappeared near the W2 Track in Wahalla East. (ABC Gippsland: Jarrod Whittaker)

"We've had a look at the mapping of where we've searched. It's amazing how much ground that we've covered," he said.

"So today, we're going to look a bit further out."

Police divers are searching rivers as part of Wednesday's operation, alongside a helicopter, off-road motorbikes and specialist Search and Rescue personnel.

About 40 to 50 people are searching on foot, with police maintaining the same resources deployed on Tuesday.

Acting Inspector Benbow said there were no plans to scale back the operation.

" There's nothing that we're not doing to try to find William, and we're still very hopeful that today might be the day. "

The search is focused about 6 kilometres north-west of Cowwarr Weir, closer to the township of Cowwarr than Walhalla, off Stoney Creek Road.

Mr Benbow said William was last seen near a makeshift campsite beside the river, where there were stairs leading down to the water.

William was wearing only shorts and work boots, having removed his shirt in the warm weather.

His mobile phone, food and water were left behind, while a fishing tackle box, pillows and a fold-out tabletop are unaccounted for.

Police have used a helicopter as part of their search for missing teen William. (ABC News: Jack Colantuono)

Mr Benbow said police were looking into whether he had continued walking, taken shelter or been injured.

"There are a lot of tracks up there. There's a river, but you never know, everyone's different," he said.

World.title: Live: Greens blast Labor over preferences ahead of Victorian election battle
World.content:
Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell has accused Labor of doing a "dodgy backroom deal" by depriving the minor party of preferences in the hard-fought seat of Prahran.

As the ABC revealed yesterday, Labor will run an open ticket in the inner-city seat, which includes the suburbs South Yarra and Windsor. This means Labor will not direct supporters where to put their remaining votes on the ballot.

Prahran always goes down to preferences, so Labor's how-to-vote cards here have significant flow-on effects for Opposition Leader Jess Wilson's chances of forming majority government.

Labor has previously given its preferences to the Greens here, which helped the minor party claim the seat. But the Greens lost Prahran last year when Labor sat out a by-election, denying them the necessary preferences.

Greens candidate Angelica di Camillo is attempting to unseat local Liberal member Rachel Westaway.

Victorian Greens leader Ellen Sandell said Labor's decision to run an open ticket was "frankly unforgivable".

"After months of scaremongering about a Liberal-One Nation government, Labor is now using its preferences to help elect one," Sandell said. "This could be one of the most consequential elections in the state's history. The result may come down to a single seat, and a divisive party like One Nation could hold the balance of power. It is frankly unforgivable that Labor would do a dodgy backroom deal to help elect a Liberal-One Nation government — and it's something that Victorian voters will not easily forget."

World.title: Culturally safe medical hub stops men 'walking out the door'
World.content:
There can be many barriers to someone seeking medical help, including location, language and cultural sensitivities.

This is particularly so for Indigenous men living in northern Western Australia.

Australian Institute of Health and Welfare data shows men are less likely to see a GP than women, and one-in-five men do not visit a doctor at all.

In Kununurra, a remote town 3,000km north of Perth, a dedicated Men's Hub opened earlier this year to break down the barriers that stop Indigenous men from accessing timely care.

The hub, which offers walk-in GP appointments and social, emotional and addiction support, is operated by Ord Valley Aboriginal Health Service (OVAHS).

Caleb Edelsten and Shaun Cox say OVAHS' Men's Hub has seen a growing number of new and returning patients. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

OVAHS chief operating officer Caleb Edelsten said the centre was opened after the organisation noticed "reduced engagement by male patients".

"Men more broadly engage less with health services," he said.

" But they're more likely to have a higher mortality rate related to preventable diseases. "

Mr Edelsten said since the centre opened, about 180 men had used it and many returned for follow-ups.

Chronic conditions, chronic avoidance

The Institute's data also shows Indigenous men are 2.3 times more likely to experience disease and have significantly higher rates of chronic and acute conditions, such as kidney diseases, diabetes and mental and substance use disorders.

Kununurra's Dr Milo Murphy urged men to present to the GP earlier.

Dr Milo Murphy says Aboriginal men are less likely to engage with health services, but more likely to have chronic diseases. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"There's going to be less complications down the road," he said.

Dr Murphy said he had seen new patients over the past month for a check-up or "men's business," a term used to refer to STI checks.

"These are people who haven't been to OVHAS or to a health service before," he said.

"So it's the first time they've actually sought help because I would assume they feel comfortable going to a service which only caters for men."

Dr Murphy says late diagnosis and missed appointments can produce poorer health outcomes. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Culturally sensitive care

Men's hub manager Shaun Cox, who is also an Aboriginal Health Practitioner, said it was important to create a safe environment.

"The first thing they see is blokes in the reception, which makes it easier for them to come in and more relaxed, " he said.

Shaun Cox says Aboriginal men face significant barriers in accessing healthcare services. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

Mr Cox said cultural laws, which prevented Aboriginal men from speaking with and being near some female family members, made it difficult for men to attend the clinic for appointments.

"Blokes come in and the mother-in-law is sitting there, and they just walk straight back out," he said.

"We are all Aboriginal men."

As a field officer, Indigenous man Michael Merrison, known as Tucker, helps local men get to appointments.

Michael Merrison or "Tucker" says he loves his job as a field officer, helping to get local men to the clinic. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

"We go and go; there was one patient… 15 times we had to go there," he said, explaining how it can take a few attempts to reach patients.

But Mr Merrison said trust could make a big difference in improving health outcomes.

"As soon as you pull up, they say, 'OVAHS is here, Oh, Tucker is here'. So you build up a relationship," he said.

Reaching more men

Gija man Peter Brandy is one of the patients at the Men's Hub.

OVAHS Men's Hub patient Peter Brandy says he is hopeful Aboriginal men can have better health and wellbeing outcomes with better support. (ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio)

He remembers growing up on a cattle station where you could "have a bad cold and struggle with it for six weeks".

Mr Brandy said things had improved for Aboriginal men and the Men's Hub was part of that change.

"Having a yarn is one of the best medicines," he said.

Meanwhile Mr Edelsten said OVAHS would like to offer more GP appointments in the future if funding allowed.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer returns to witness box for cross-examination over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

The former NSW police officer returns to the witness box today to face further cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon on Tuesday. Rocco Fazzari

The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

He has given the following evidence in cross-examination:

Lamarre-Condon denied stalking Baird in 2023 after their first break-up in April that year. The men had met in Sydney in October 2022, the court has heard, and their relationship was non-exclusive, but the accused said they started going on “romantic dates” in December that year.

He rejected a suggestion by the prosecution on Tuesday that he was obsessed with Baird “right from the start”. “Smitten, yes. Obsessed, no,” the accused said.

The court has heard the men resumed contact briefly around August or September 2023, after their first break-up, before Baird ended the relationship permanently in November 2023. Lamarre-Condon admitted he invaded Baird’s privacy and went through his phone on two occasions in March and April 2023.

He denied that he had broken into Baird’s home on August 17, 2023, after the TV presenter responded to a text message he sent but did not engage with his suggestion of a catch-up. He said that Baird “did invite me to stay the night” later that day, and he used a key left out for him.

The court has heard Baird woke to a man he did not recognise standing over his bed and chased him out of the home. He reported the alleged break-in and theft of his phone and wallet to the police. Lamarre-Condon has said he was trying to look through Baird’s phone and put a bobby pin in the lock so that if Baird woke up he wouldn’t think it was him.

The court has heard that police found CCTV footage on Lamarre-Condon’s iCloud account of Baird on a date with another man at the Royal Hotel in Paddington on May 19, 2023. He denied he was stalking Baird and misusing his authority as a police officer to access CCTV of him.

The accused said last week that he came across the footage while helping police colleagues with official duties, following a potential assault nearby. Baird had invited him to “swing by” the hotel in uniform while he was working, he said.

He rejected Hatfield’s suggestion that it appealed to him that Baird was a TV presenter. “Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner,” he said. “We actually never really talked much about his work. I wasn’t really interested in that, to be honest.”

He also denied that he had misrepresented the nature of his relationship with Baird in a video he made of them on a farm stay holiday in March 2023.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Republicans shield Hegseth from impeachment after Trump, Vance circle wagons
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Republicans shield Hegseth from impeachment after Trump, Vance circle wagons Michael Koziol Updated November 11, 2026 — 11:26am ,first published November 11, 2026 — 4:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: Republicans saved Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth from an impeachment vote in the US Congress, using their numbers in the House of Representatives to refer the matter to a committee, effectively killing it off. The vote on Tuesday evening (US time) was 211 to 204 in favour of a referral to the House Judiciary Committee. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican congressman who started the proceedings, was the only Republican to support an immediate vote on impeachment. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth labelled the impeachment proceedings a “farce” and an act of sabotage. AP Photo/Nathan Howard But 11 Democrats, including former speaker Nancy Pelosi, missed the vote. If they had attended and voted with their colleagues, Hegseth would have faced the full impeachment resolution. It means Hegseth will avoid impeachment for now – at least until the Democrats gain control of both chambers of Congress early next year, following their dramatic victories at last week’s midterm elections.



President Donald Trump celebrated what he called “the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot”. The Democrats “continue to weaponise and abuse the United States of America”, he added, even though the resolution was brought by a Republican. Earlier, at a feisty morning news conference, Hegseth slammed the proceedings against him as a politically motivated stunt by a disgruntled politician, as he drew comparisons between himself and Donald Trump. Loading Hegseth insisted all his actions in office had been legal, including the war in Iran and extrajudicial killing of suspected drug traffickers in international waters, while framing the impeachment resolution as an attack on American troops the day before Veterans Day. “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle,” he said. “A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.”



Massie, who is from Kentucky, will exit Congress at the end of this year after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger. He has opposed the president on multiple issues, including initiating the Epstein Files Transparency Act. His eight articles of impeachment, filed on Monday, accuse Hegseth of unlawfully keeping US troops engaged in the Iran war in contravention of a congressional resolution, ignoring laws that aim to reduce civilian casualties, abducting Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, overseeing the extrajudicial killing of suspected drug traffickers, suppressing free speech and initiating an illegal war in Yemen. Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, who brought the impeachment resolution against Pete Hegseth. AP Photo/Allison Robbert “The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorise the activity,” Massie said on X during Hegseth’s news conference. “Operation Epic Fury has been under way for 256 days. Congress has not authorised it. Hegseth is breaking the law. Not even debatable.” Before last week’s midterm elections, there was speculation that Hegseth – a former Fox News anchor with no government experience before being appointed defence secretary – would be ousted from cabinet as part of a post-election reshuffle.



But as the administration prepares for two years of fights with Democrats in Congress, Trump strongly backed his defence secretary, and Republicans - some of whom have reservations about Hegseth - toed in line when it came to vote. Hegseth compared himself directly with Trump, who was impeached in the House twice during his first term. This impeachment attempt was a “show trial against the president and the secretary of war”, Hegseth said. Pete Hegseth vigorously defended his actions and their legality at a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday. AP Photo/Nathan Howard “We’ve seen this show before. They impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call ... If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.” Hegseth queried why his predecessor Lloyd Austin, a Democrat under Joe Biden, was not impeached over the botched US withdrawal from Afghanistan, or for allowing a Chinese spy balloon to fly over the country for a week.



And he said the impeachment attempt sent a signal to America’s adversaries that the US would punish its own soldiers and civilian military leaders for executing lawful orders. “It tells them that a single rogue legislator loaded with personal animus for the president can attempt to veto national security decisions made by the duly elected commander-in-chief,” Hegseth told reporters. “This is not patriotism, this is sabotage.” US Vice President JD Vance, an opponent of the war in Iran, said the impeachment proceeding was baseless. Bloomberg Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance joined Trump in coming to Hegseth’s aid, despite his criticism of the Iran war, for which he blamed the Republicans’ midterm election losses. Vance said it was obvious the defence secretary had not committed impeachable offences. “Like so much of Congress, impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking,” he said on X.

World.title: Macquarie admits ‘bonus’ savings rate failure, agrees to pay $14 million
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeRegulation Macquarie admits ‘bonus’ savings rate failure, agrees to pay $14 million Millie Muroi November 11, 2026 — 11:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Macquarie Bank has admitted to failing to prevent confusion to new savings account customers over a “welcome rate” offer, agreeing to pay a $14 million penalty and acknowledging it did not respond in a timely manner to complaints. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission said on Wednesday the bank, which faced the NSW Supreme Court, had admitted to contravening the Corporations Act and failed to take necessary steps to ensure statements about its “welcome rate” were clear and not likely to cause confusion to new customers. Macquarie said while its actions were not deliberate, it should have better explained how the welcome rate applied. Peter Braig Between December 1, 2021 and September 9, 2022, Macquarie had described its welcome rate on the Macquarie Savings Account as a “welcome variable rate” and a “bonus” which the commission alleged could lead customers to believe it was paid on top of the standard variable rate. Instead, the welcome rate generally operated as a fixed rate that applied instead of – rather than in addition to – the standard rate during the four-month promotional period.



As interest rates increased during 2022, the initial margin between the welcome rate and the standard variable rate could narrow or disappear. If the standard rate rose above the welcome rate, the customer’s rate increased only to match the standard rate. Related Article Updated

Home loans CBA’s late mortgage payments tick up as interest rate rises bite The commission and Macquarie jointly proposed the bank pay a $14 million penalty to the court, in addition to the $8.8 million in remediation initiated by Macquarie which has already been paid to nearly 40,000 customers. Macquarie also admitted its advertising framework was not sufficiently rigorous to identify the risk that customers could misunderstand the offer. The commission said the bank lacked clear internal guidance about how the product operated and customer complaints did not prompt a “sufficiently timely correction.” ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said customers should not have to scrutinise every transaction to check their bank has paid the correct interest or charged them correctly.



“This wasn’t just unclear wording,” he said. “Macquarie’s systems and controls were not rigorous enough to identify the risk that customers would misunderstand how the welcome rate worked. At a time when Australians are contending with cost-of-living pressures, consumers deserve clear information about savings rates and the financial benefits they are promised.” The proposed resolution will need approval from the court which determine whether the proposed orders are appropriate and whether any other orders should be made. ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said customers should not have to scrutinise every transaction to check their bank has paid the correct interest or charged them correctly. Oscar Colman In a media release, Macquarie said it would not contest the court proceeding and acknowledged it had contravened its obligation to provide financial services efficiently, honestly and fairly. “The matter arose because, when standard variable rates increased and exceeded the welcome rate, customers were instead paid the higher standard variable rate though some expected a bonus margin over that rate,” it said. “Macquarie acknowledges that some of the wording on its website was not sufficiently clear and may have caused confusion.”



Related Article Superannuation The ‘immediate warning sign’ to protect your super Macquarie head of banking and financial services Ben Perham said while the commission has acknowledged the bank’s actions were not deliberate, the bank apologised for any confusion caused. “We should have better explained on our website how the welcome rate would be applied,” he said. Perham said the $8.8 million in compensation it had already chosen to pay would put customers in the position that they would have been if the welcome rate was a fixed bonus interest margin. “Additionally, we have conducted a thorough review of all product descriptions we use across our website in relation to our transaction and savings account products and have prioritised the uplift of our governance, systems, controls, and procedures associated with the creation, approval and publishing of any future customer-facing collateral,” he said.



The bank said the matter was identified and fully accounted for in Macquarie’s financial year ended March 31, 2026. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: CBA’s late mortgage payments tick up as interest rate rises bite
World.content:
Updated BusinessBanking & financeHome loans CBA’s late mortgage payments tick up as interest rate rises bite Nick Bonyhady Updated November 11, 2026 — 11:09am ,first published November 11, 2026 — 7:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. More Australians are struggling with their mortgage repayments as interest rates rise and inflation stays high, the nation’s largest bank has reported in an earnings release that also came with almost $3 billion in profit. In a trading update issued on Wednesday, the Commonwealth Bank said it recorded a seven-basis-point increase in home loans with payments more than 90 days overdue, taking the rate of overdue loans in its books to 0.80 per cent. Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn says his bank is committed to helping customers with the cost of living. Dominic Lorrimer The update covers the quarter that ended on September 30 and showed the bank made $2.8 billion in profit, with operating income up 3 per cent but expenses up by the same amount. That profit figure was flat on preceding quarters but up 8 per cent on the same period in the last financial year. The market greeted the news positively, sending CBA shares up about 0.8 per cent to $170 at 10.15am on Wednesday while the overall ASX200 index was down.



CBA attributed the higher home loan arrears to cost-of-living pressures from higher interest rates and inflation. It made a $105 million provision to guard against any issues in its loan book, though actual losses for the bank from failed loans – which are a lagging indicator – remain below pre-pandemic levels. In total, the bank’s provisions for bad loans were flat at $6.5 billion as other types of loans performed well, which CBA said gave it “strong” coverage for any issues. Earlier this week, ANZ reported a similar increase in the number of customers struggling to repay home loans, taking the percentage of loans in its book that were more than 90 days overdue to 0.95 per cent. The Reserve Bank of Australia increased the cash rate to an 18-year-high on November 3 in its fifth hike this year. Those increases, which are designed to curb inflation, have added hundreds of dollars a month in interest payments to an average Australian mortgage.



“It is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer,” RBA governor Michele Bullock said at the time. Related Article Exclusive

First home buyers The type of home buyer falling behind on their loan Chief executive Matt Comyn said in a statement that CBA was committed to helping its customers through the higher cost of living and defended the strength of the Australian economy. “Higher inflation and interest rates continue to place uneven pressure on household incomes and business activity,” he said. “While economic growth is slowing, the Australian economy remains resilient, supported by low unemployment and a strong public infrastructure and private investment pipeline.” Data from property analysis company Cotality shows house prices in Australia’s capital cities have fallen 8.1 per cent in the last seven months, just short of the largest fall in 40 years.



CBA recorded a 13.6 per cent increase in the volume of business loans for the quarter and 6.6 per cent for home loans. Applications for new home loans though remained 16 per cent behind the same quarter last financial year. Analysts at investment bank Citi said the result was slightly worse than they had expected because of weaker trading income, triggered by rising rates, and more bad debts. “Overall, only a modest miss for a quarterly, but it may disappoint given the sharp run in the shares,” wrote analysts Thomas Strong and Nilesh Bhaiya in a note to clients seen by this masthead. Kalyn Ponga hopes his enthralling international rivalry with Australian counterpart Reece Walsh will be outdone in the Rugby League World Cup final. When the New Zealand fullback and Walsh faced off at the start of the tournament, they left fans praising the duel as one of the best one-on-one battles experienced in Test football. Both scored breathtaking individual tries, with Walsh also producing a brilliant covering tackle to prevent his opposite No.1 from crossing in the corner. Kalyn Ponga was electric against Tonga upon his comeback from a broken arm. Getty Images Ponga was ultimately sidelined with a broken arm until the weekend’s semi-final triumph of Tonga – having 11 screws and a plate put into the bone – as he revealed he sought inspiration from Jahrome Hughes, who made a similarly hasty recovery.



“I was still a bit nervous coming into the game, naturally, coming back from an injury like that,” Ponga said, when asked how the arm had held up. “But, honestly, from the get-go, once you get into the game and start being focused you forget about it. “As soon as the game [against the Kangaroos] was over, someone told me Hughsey came back in three weeks. It was a bit of a challenge in my mind. I was always determined to come back, and if he could do it, I could do it, and he gave me a lot of confidence throughout the weeks that I could get back.” Now, Ponga and Walsh will line up in the final at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday as the most eagerly watched players on the field.



Reminded of his and Walsh’s rivalry, the Newcastle Knights star offered a small smile – the pair maintain a close friendship from their time in Queensland Maroons State of Origin camps. “I respect Reece a lot. He’s a good friend, obviously a teammate in the past,” Ponga said. “I think we all love seeing Reece do well, and we all love those sorts of battles – it’s always love off the field but hopefully we can both make [Sunday] entertaining. “No doubt he’s got the same mindset as me: just do our role for the team and, obviously, make the most of our opportunities and put ourselves in the game. “Every game is different, you don’t know what’s going to unfold.



“There are always going to be moments of individual brilliance at this level. There are so many quality players and, hopefully, we can have a few more than them.” So brilliant were Ponga’s two showings this World Cup – claiming man-of-the-match honours on Saturday with three try assists, three linebreak assists and 198 running metres – he has been uttered as a prospect for the Golden Boot award. But Walsh might be the biggest threat for that prize – culminating in scoring a hat-trick against Samoa to vindicate coach Kevin Walters’ decision to entrust him with the fullback jumper at the expense of James Tedesco. While highlight-reel moments from Walsh and Jack Bostock led Australia to a 26-24 win against the Kiwis when they last fought, what was perhaps more gratifying about the former’s semi-final heroics was he did not need to overplay his hand.



Despite crossing the white line three times, his ability to support five-eighth Cameron Munster’s vision – who came up with three try assists – reaped such rewards. Kangaroos hooker Harry Grant stopped short of labelling the Walsh-Ponga clash as the match-up that would decide the trophy, claiming “as much as Reece and Kalyn set the show alight in game one, that’s in the past”. He warned against Australia expecting their enigmatic fullback to produce magic on his own. “It’s all about preparing well and making sure we’re not looking for those big moments, but really narrowing in on the small parts of our game we want to go after.



“We know we’ve got the strike in the team, and they can have their own opportunities when they do come,” Grant said. Related Article NRL 2026 Titans legend’s warning as Harry Grant poaching rumours swirl “[Walsh and Ponga] are in sweet spots in their game, and we’ve seen that over the course of the campaign. But we can only try and maximise the opportunities we give Reece, and nullify the opportunities that Kalyn has. “Both are incredible players, both are unique players to our game, and I think we should celebrate that at all costs.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Capability X takes AI brains to the industrial jungle
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Capability X takes AI brains to the industrial jungle Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 11, 2026 — 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Perth AI developer Capability X, a technology outfit built on the smell of an oily rag, is preparing for its ASX debut tomorrow under the ticker CX8 with $12 million in its back pocket and an artificial intelligence (AI) platform designed to make industrial workplaces safer, smarter and ultimately more automated. And if founder and chief executive Chris Eastwell gets his way - using workplace safety as a springboard for boosting industrial productivity and potentially one day even automating operations - the company could become to industrial data what Tesla has become to automotive intelligence. Capability X’s CX remote is a portable, ruggedised remote operations system that enables the control and monitoring of remotely operated vehicles (ROV’s), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV’s) and robotic systems technology. At the heart of Capability X’s technology is CX Edge, a ruggedised computing platform that combines light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors, stereoscopic cameras, communications systems and proprietary AI software, all in a briefcase-sized unit. LiDAR uses laser pulses to measure distances, while stereoscopic cameras provide depth perception. Together, they build a three-dimensional “digital twin” of the surrounding workplace, giving the AI a ringside seat as people, vehicles and machinery go about their business.



‘Our vision at Capability X is to keep people out of harm’s way while helping businesses operate more safely.’ Capability X managing director and chief executive officer Chris Eastwell Capability X says its AI technology can recognise objects, movement and potential dangers, using information collected from industrial sites to continually improve its software. Much like Tesla learns from real-world driving conditions, the company aims to use its growing network of industrial devices to provide valuable operational intelligence by learning from the movement of workers and machinery rather than roads and traffic. Picture a bustling port terminal, with towering cranes swinging massive containers through the air, trucks weaving between stacks of cargo and workers navigating the organised chaos. Capability X’s CX Protect safety system uses the CX Edge platform and AI software to monitor those movements, identify dangerous proximity events and alert operators to emerging risks before an incident occurs. That intelligence could also reveal bottlenecks and unnecessary movements, potentially lifting customers’ productivity and bottom lines.



Through “edge computing”, the company’s CX Edge devices analyse information on site rather than sending it to distant data centres, enabling faster responses with less reliance on external networks. Eastwell compares the integrated platform to a smartphone and its coordination of remote assets to Uber. Capability X managing director and chief executive officer Chris Eastwell said: “Our vision at Capability X is to keep people out of harm’s way while helping business to operate more safely, efficiently and productively- on a global scale.” Established in November 2022, Eastwell largely bootstrapped Capability X for two years, even as the fledgling business began securing its first commercial contracts. Eastwell has brought two decades of industry experience to the venture, having previously run Greatship Subsea Solutions in Australia and overseen marine asset integrity for Fugro across Australia and New Zealand. The company’s early consultancy and technology-design work involved WA Police in 2023 and subsea specialist Shelf Subsea, later acquired by DeepOcean.



A commercial breakthrough came in 2023 when ASX-listed Bhagwan Marine engaged Capability X to provide technology for remotely operating offshore equipment. The relationship has since blossomed into a multi-year arrangement spanning CX Remote, CX Connect and CX Protect, delivering an integrated suite of communications and safety systems, according to the company’s prospectus. The agreement runs through December 2028. Despite the early success, management says Capability X has undertaken virtually no formal marketing, focusing instead on engineering and industrial relationships. And there’s plenty of engineering muscle behind the ambition. Six software engineers report to chief technology officer Adrian Kirk-Burnnand, who has more than 23 years’ experience in sectors including mining and fintech.



In-house teams cover computer vision, AI, communications, robotics, mechatronics and hardware manufacturing and assembly, backed by remote operations, network management and security monitoring centres. Leading the commercial charge is chief commercial officer Lex Simons, a geophysicist with 14 years at Woodside Energy under his belt, while former federal minister Ian Campbell chairs the company. Capability X’s home base, located at the Perth International Telecommunications Centre. The operation runs from Telstra’s International Telecommunications Centre at Cullacabardee, north of Perth, cheek by jowl with world-class command and communications infrastructure. For its business model, Capability X has taken a leaf out of the software-as-a-service (SaaS) playbook, leasing its hardware and software to customers under multi-year subscription-style arrangements rather than selling equipment outright. The approach turns each installation into a steady stream of recurring revenue, with the potential to build a growing income stream as more customers come on board.



Beyond its flagship safety technology, the company offers CX Remote, a remote-control platform that allows command centres to monitor and operate underwater vehicles, drones and robots from afar, keeping personnel well clear of potentially dangerous environments. Meanwhile, its CX Connect solution provides secure communications and situational awareness between remote equipment, operators and command centres. Rounding out the suite is CX1, which combines the company’s technologies with engineering, system design and ongoing operational support to deliver customised solutions for complex industrial environments. Capability X has also secured a two-year agreement with Perth-based offshore operator GO Offshore to supply CX Protect monitoring systems under a hardware-and-software lease arrangement. The agreement, signed in November 2025, includes three one-year renewal options. However, the company’s contract with logistics heavyweight Qube Ports provides perhaps its strongest commercial endorsement yet. Capability X’s CX Protect Operating System visualisation- producing a live digital twin (marine support vessel rendered), to identify potential danger events and non-compliances and alert deck crew and supervisors.



In December 2025, Qube signed a three-year deal to deploy Capability X’s CX Protect technology across its port operations, targeting risks associated with cargo-handling movements, while boosting operational efficiency. Mining offers another market where machinery and workers share challenging environments, while defence offers further opportunities in robotics, unmanned systems and remote command. The company has memoranda of understanding with an Australian and an international defence contractor and showcased CX Edge alongside Defence West at the 2026 Land Forces exposition. To support its growth, the company has already secured a $40,000 handout from the WA State government for the 2024 rollout of CX Edge. The prospectus also highlights an application for a hefty $4.2 million federal Industry Growth Program grant that, if approved, would further add to the company’s burgeoning war chest. Capability’s credentials were further recognised at the Robotics & AI Award at Perth’s international Robopalooza festival in October 2025. Adding to the accolades, CX Protect and CX Remote were finalists in separate 2026 innovation awards; membership in Perth-based AROSE offers further robotics collaboration.



With the technology gaining commercial traction on home soil, Capability X is now casting its net beyond Australia’s shores. The company’s prospectus identifies contracts to supply its technology to Brunei’s oil and gas sector and is pursuing further deployments in other neighbouring countries. China is also on the radar, with opportunities identified in oil and gas and ports. A memorandum of understanding with a Timor-Leste partner could open another door, with potential applications spanning government infrastructure, remote operations and the oil and gas sector. American market research and management consultants Frost & Sullivan estimate a theoretical global total addressable market exceeding $280 billion annually across defence, oil and gas, mining and ports. However, that figure represents the broader market opportunity rather than revenue currently being generated or business immediately available to the company. Perth corporate advisory outfit Westar Capital has played a key role in steering Capability X towards the ASX boards, backing its funding journey through two seed capital raisings worth $2 million each at 10 cents and 16 cents a share, before supporting its $12 million initial public offering. The company has now wrapped up its float at 20 cents a share and will debut on the ASX on November 12 under the ticker CX8, subject to the exchange’s admission and quotation requirements. Armed with a fresh war chest, Capability X plans to ramp up manufacturing, accelerate product development and push further into domestic and international markets.



For Capability X, however, the bigger prize lies beyond preventing workplace accidents. Its technology could ultimately help customers squeeze more productivity from their industrial operations, reduce costs and shift increasingly complex tasks into the hands of remote operators and intelligent machines. If Capability X can get its growing network of intelligent devices to deliver on those lofty goals, workplace safety may prove to have been merely the steel-capped boot that kicked the door down to a global opportunity. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Former NSW Police officer returns to witness box for cross-examination over alleged murders of Jesse Baird, Luke Davies
World.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

The former NSW police officer returns to the witness box today to face further cross-examination by Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC.

A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon on Tuesday. Rocco Fazzari

The 31-year-old has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant. His case is that he acted in self-defence, the 15-person jury has been told.

He has given the following evidence in cross-examination:

Lamarre-Condon denied stalking Baird in 2023 after their first break-up in April that year. The men had met in Sydney in October 2022, the court has heard, and their relationship was non-exclusive, but the accused said they started going on “romantic dates” in December that year.

He rejected a suggestion by the prosecution on Tuesday that he was obsessed with Baird “right from the start”. “Smitten, yes. Obsessed, no,” the accused said.

The court has heard the men resumed contact briefly around August or September 2023, after their first break-up, before Baird ended the relationship permanently in November 2023. Lamarre-Condon admitted he invaded Baird’s privacy and went through his phone on two occasions in March and April 2023.

He denied that he had broken into Baird’s home on August 17, 2023, after the TV presenter responded to a text message he sent but did not engage with his suggestion of a catch-up. He said that Baird “did invite me to stay the night” later that day, and he used a key left out for him.

The court has heard Baird woke to a man he did not recognise standing over his bed and chased him out of the home. He reported the alleged break-in and theft of his phone and wallet to the police. Lamarre-Condon has said he was trying to look through Baird’s phone and put a bobby pin in the lock so that if Baird woke up he wouldn’t think it was him.

The court has heard that police found CCTV footage on Lamarre-Condon’s iCloud account of Baird on a date with another man at the Royal Hotel in Paddington on May 19, 2023. He denied he was stalking Baird and misusing his authority as a police officer to access CCTV of him.

The accused said last week that he came across the footage while helping police colleagues with official duties, following a potential assault nearby. Baird had invited him to “swing by” the hotel in uniform while he was working, he said.

He rejected Hatfield’s suggestion that it appealed to him that Baird was a TV presenter. “Jesse Baird could have been a garbage cleaner,” he said. “We actually never really talked much about his work. I wasn’t really interested in that, to be honest.”

He also denied that he had misrepresented the nature of his relationship with Baird in a video he made of them on a farm stay holiday in March 2023.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491, and Lifeline on 13 11 14.

World.title: Republicans shield Hegseth from impeachment after Trump, Vance circle wagons
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaUS politics Republicans shield Hegseth from impeachment after Trump, Vance circle wagons Michael Koziol Updated November 11, 2026 — 11:26am ,first published November 11, 2026 — 4:39am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Washington: Republicans saved Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth from an impeachment vote in the US Congress, using their numbers in the House of Representatives to refer the matter to a committee, effectively killing it off. The vote on Tuesday evening (US time) was 211 to 204 in favour of a referral to the House Judiciary Committee. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican congressman who started the proceedings, was the only Republican to support an immediate vote on impeachment. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth labelled the impeachment proceedings a “farce” and an act of sabotage. AP Photo/Nathan Howard But 11 Democrats, including former speaker Nancy Pelosi, missed the vote. If they had attended and voted with their colleagues, Hegseth would have faced the full impeachment resolution. It means Hegseth will avoid impeachment for now – at least until the Democrats gain control of both chambers of Congress early next year, following their dramatic victories at last week’s midterm elections.



President Donald Trump celebrated what he called “the EXONERATION of a Great American Patriot”. The Democrats “continue to weaponise and abuse the United States of America”, he added, even though the resolution was brought by a Republican. Earlier, at a feisty morning news conference, Hegseth slammed the proceedings against him as a politically motivated stunt by a disgruntled politician, as he drew comparisons between himself and Donald Trump. Loading Hegseth insisted all his actions in office had been legal, including the war in Iran and extrajudicial killing of suspected drug traffickers in international waters, while framing the impeachment resolution as an attack on American troops the day before Veterans Day. “What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it’s not accountability. It’s a political spectacle,” he said. “A personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment. It’s a farce, and it’s a stunt, and everybody knows it.”



Massie, who is from Kentucky, will exit Congress at the end of this year after losing his primary to a Trump-backed challenger. He has opposed the president on multiple issues, including initiating the Epstein Files Transparency Act. His eight articles of impeachment, filed on Monday, accuse Hegseth of unlawfully keeping US troops engaged in the Iran war in contravention of a congressional resolution, ignoring laws that aim to reduce civilian casualties, abducting Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, overseeing the extrajudicial killing of suspected drug traffickers, suppressing free speech and initiating an illegal war in Yemen. Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, who brought the impeachment resolution against Pete Hegseth. AP Photo/Allison Robbert “The law requires our military to withdraw from hostilities within 60 days if Congress does not authorise the activity,” Massie said on X during Hegseth’s news conference. “Operation Epic Fury has been under way for 256 days. Congress has not authorised it. Hegseth is breaking the law. Not even debatable.” Before last week’s midterm elections, there was speculation that Hegseth – a former Fox News anchor with no government experience before being appointed defence secretary – would be ousted from cabinet as part of a post-election reshuffle.



But as the administration prepares for two years of fights with Democrats in Congress, Trump strongly backed his defence secretary, and Republicans - some of whom have reservations about Hegseth - toed in line when it came to vote. Hegseth compared himself directly with Trump, who was impeached in the House twice during his first term. This impeachment attempt was a “show trial against the president and the secretary of war”, Hegseth said. Pete Hegseth vigorously defended his actions and their legality at a press conference at the Pentagon on Tuesday. AP Photo/Nathan Howard “We’ve seen this show before. They impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call ... If standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I’ll take that company every day of the week.” Hegseth queried why his predecessor Lloyd Austin, a Democrat under Joe Biden, was not impeached over the botched US withdrawal from Afghanistan, or for allowing a Chinese spy balloon to fly over the country for a week.



And he said the impeachment attempt sent a signal to America’s adversaries that the US would punish its own soldiers and civilian military leaders for executing lawful orders. “It tells them that a single rogue legislator loaded with personal animus for the president can attempt to veto national security decisions made by the duly elected commander-in-chief,” Hegseth told reporters. “This is not patriotism, this is sabotage.” US Vice President JD Vance, an opponent of the war in Iran, said the impeachment proceeding was baseless. Bloomberg Meanwhile, Vice President JD Vance joined Trump in coming to Hegseth’s aid, despite his criticism of the Iran war, for which he blamed the Republicans’ midterm election losses. Vance said it was obvious the defence secretary had not committed impeachable offences. “Like so much of Congress, impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking,” he said on X.

World.title: Macquarie admits ‘bonus’ savings rate failure, agrees to pay $14 million
World.content:
BusinessBanking & financeRegulation Macquarie admits ‘bonus’ savings rate failure, agrees to pay $14 million Millie Muroi November 11, 2026 — 11:14am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Macquarie Bank has admitted to failing to prevent confusion to new savings account customers over a “welcome rate” offer, agreeing to pay a $14 million penalty and acknowledging it did not respond in a timely manner to complaints. The Australian Securities and Investments Commission said on Wednesday the bank, which faced the NSW Supreme Court, had admitted to contravening the Corporations Act and failed to take necessary steps to ensure statements about its “welcome rate” were clear and not likely to cause confusion to new customers. Macquarie said while its actions were not deliberate, it should have better explained how the welcome rate applied. Peter Braig Between December 1, 2021 and September 9, 2022, Macquarie had described its welcome rate on the Macquarie Savings Account as a “welcome variable rate” and a “bonus” which the commission alleged could lead customers to believe it was paid on top of the standard variable rate. Instead, the welcome rate generally operated as a fixed rate that applied instead of – rather than in addition to – the standard rate during the four-month promotional period.



As interest rates increased during 2022, the initial margin between the welcome rate and the standard variable rate could narrow or disappear. If the standard rate rose above the welcome rate, the customer’s rate increased only to match the standard rate. Related Article Updated

Home loans CBA’s late mortgage payments tick up as interest rate rises bite The commission and Macquarie jointly proposed the bank pay a $14 million penalty to the court, in addition to the $8.8 million in remediation initiated by Macquarie which has already been paid to nearly 40,000 customers. Macquarie also admitted its advertising framework was not sufficiently rigorous to identify the risk that customers could misunderstand the offer. The commission said the bank lacked clear internal guidance about how the product operated and customer complaints did not prompt a “sufficiently timely correction.” ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said customers should not have to scrutinise every transaction to check their bank has paid the correct interest or charged them correctly.



“This wasn’t just unclear wording,” he said. “Macquarie’s systems and controls were not rigorous enough to identify the risk that customers would misunderstand how the welcome rate worked. At a time when Australians are contending with cost-of-living pressures, consumers deserve clear information about savings rates and the financial benefits they are promised.” The proposed resolution will need approval from the court which determine whether the proposed orders are appropriate and whether any other orders should be made. ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said customers should not have to scrutinise every transaction to check their bank has paid the correct interest or charged them correctly. Oscar Colman In a media release, Macquarie said it would not contest the court proceeding and acknowledged it had contravened its obligation to provide financial services efficiently, honestly and fairly. “The matter arose because, when standard variable rates increased and exceeded the welcome rate, customers were instead paid the higher standard variable rate though some expected a bonus margin over that rate,” it said. “Macquarie acknowledges that some of the wording on its website was not sufficiently clear and may have caused confusion.”



Related Article Superannuation The ‘immediate warning sign’ to protect your super Macquarie head of banking and financial services Ben Perham said while the commission has acknowledged the bank’s actions were not deliberate, the bank apologised for any confusion caused. “We should have better explained on our website how the welcome rate would be applied,” he said. Perham said the $8.8 million in compensation it had already chosen to pay would put customers in the position that they would have been if the welcome rate was a fixed bonus interest margin. “Additionally, we have conducted a thorough review of all product descriptions we use across our website in relation to our transaction and savings account products and have prioritised the uplift of our governance, systems, controls, and procedures associated with the creation, approval and publishing of any future customer-facing collateral,” he said.



The bank said the matter was identified and fully accounted for in Macquarie’s financial year ended March 31, 2026. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. Sign up to get it every weekday morning.

World.title: CBA’s late mortgage payments tick up as interest rate rises bite
World.content:
Updated BusinessBanking & financeHome loans CBA’s late mortgage payments tick up as interest rate rises bite Nick Bonyhady Updated November 11, 2026 — 11:09am ,first published November 11, 2026 — 7:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. More Australians are struggling with their mortgage repayments as interest rates rise and inflation stays high, the nation’s largest bank has reported in an earnings release that also came with almost $3 billion in profit. In a trading update issued on Wednesday, the Commonwealth Bank said it recorded a seven-basis-point increase in home loans with payments more than 90 days overdue, taking the rate of overdue loans in its books to 0.80 per cent. Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn says his bank is committed to helping customers with the cost of living. Dominic Lorrimer The update covers the quarter that ended on September 30 and showed the bank made $2.8 billion in profit, with operating income up 3 per cent but expenses up by the same amount. That profit figure was flat on preceding quarters but up 8 per cent on the same period in the last financial year. The market greeted the news positively, sending CBA shares up about 0.8 per cent to $170 at 10.15am on Wednesday while the overall ASX200 index was down.



CBA attributed the higher home loan arrears to cost-of-living pressures from higher interest rates and inflation. It made a $105 million provision to guard against any issues in its loan book, though actual losses for the bank from failed loans – which are a lagging indicator – remain below pre-pandemic levels. In total, the bank’s provisions for bad loans were flat at $6.5 billion as other types of loans performed well, which CBA said gave it “strong” coverage for any issues. Earlier this week, ANZ reported a similar increase in the number of customers struggling to repay home loans, taking the percentage of loans in its book that were more than 90 days overdue to 0.95 per cent. The Reserve Bank of Australia increased the cash rate to an 18-year-high on November 3 in its fifth hike this year. Those increases, which are designed to curb inflation, have added hundreds of dollars a month in interest payments to an average Australian mortgage.



“It is going to make people feel like it’s a recession because they feel poorer,” RBA governor Michele Bullock said at the time. Related Article Exclusive

First home buyers The type of home buyer falling behind on their loan Chief executive Matt Comyn said in a statement that CBA was committed to helping its customers through the higher cost of living and defended the strength of the Australian economy. “Higher inflation and interest rates continue to place uneven pressure on household incomes and business activity,” he said. “While economic growth is slowing, the Australian economy remains resilient, supported by low unemployment and a strong public infrastructure and private investment pipeline.” Data from property analysis company Cotality shows house prices in Australia’s capital cities have fallen 8.1 per cent in the last seven months, just short of the largest fall in 40 years.



CBA recorded a 13.6 per cent increase in the volume of business loans for the quarter and 6.6 per cent for home loans. Applications for new home loans though remained 16 per cent behind the same quarter last financial year. Analysts at investment bank Citi said the result was slightly worse than they had expected because of weaker trading income, triggered by rising rates, and more bad debts. “Overall, only a modest miss for a quarterly, but it may disappoint given the sharp run in the shares,” wrote analysts Thomas Strong and Nilesh Bhaiya in a note to clients seen by this masthead. “I was still a bit nervous coming into the game, naturally, coming back from an injury like that,” Ponga said, when asked how the arm had held up. “But, honestly, from the get-go, once you get into the game and start being focused you forget about it. “As soon as the game [against the Kangaroos] was over, someone told me Hughsey came back in three weeks. It was a bit of a challenge in my mind. I was always determined to come back, and if he could do it, I could do it, and he gave me a lot of confidence throughout the weeks that I could get back.” Now, Ponga and Walsh will line up in the final at Suncorp Stadium on Sunday as the most eagerly watched players on the field.



Reminded of his and Walsh’s rivalry, the Newcastle Knights star offered a small smile – the pair maintain a close friendship from their time in Queensland Maroons State of Origin camps. “I respect Reece a lot. He’s a good friend, obviously a teammate in the past,” Ponga said. “I think we all love seeing Reece do well, and we all love those sorts of battles – it’s always love off the field but hopefully we can both make [Sunday] entertaining. “No doubt he’s got the same mindset as me: just do our role for the team and, obviously, make the most of our opportunities and put ourselves in the game. “Every game is different, you don’t know what’s going to unfold.



“There are always going to be moments of individual brilliance at this level. There are so many quality players and, hopefully, we can have a few more than them.” So brilliant were Ponga’s two showings this World Cup – claiming man-of-the-match honours on Saturday with three try assists, three linebreak assists and 198 running metres – he has been uttered as a prospect for the Golden Boot award. But Walsh might be the biggest threat for that prize – culminating in scoring a hat-trick against Samoa to vindicate coach Kevin Walters’ decision to entrust him with the fullback jumper at the expense of James Tedesco. While highlight-reel moments from Walsh and Jack Bostock led Australia to a 26-24 win against the Kiwis when they last fought, what was perhaps more gratifying about the former’s semi-final heroics was he did not need to overplay his hand.



Despite crossing the white line three times, his ability to support five-eighth Cameron Munster’s vision – who came up with three try assists – reaped such rewards. Kangaroos hooker Harry Grant stopped short of labelling the Walsh-Ponga clash as the match-up that would decide the trophy, claiming “as much as Reece and Kalyn set the show alight in game one, that’s in the past”. He warned against Australia expecting their enigmatic fullback to produce magic on his own. “It’s all about preparing well and making sure we’re not looking for those big moments, but really narrowing in on the small parts of our game we want to go after.



“We know we’ve got the strike in the team, and they can have their own opportunities when they do come,” Grant said. Related Article NRL 2026 Titans legend’s warning as Harry Grant poaching rumours swirl “[Walsh and Ponga] are in sweet spots in their game, and we’ve seen that over the course of the campaign. But we can only try and maximise the opportunities we give Reece, and nullify the opportunities that Kalyn has. “Both are incredible players, both are unique players to our game, and I think we should celebrate that at all costs.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Capability X takes AI brains to the industrial jungle
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Capability X takes AI brains to the industrial jungle Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward November 11, 2026 — 11:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Perth AI developer Capability X, a technology outfit built on the smell of an oily rag, is preparing for its ASX debut tomorrow under the ticker CX8 with $12 million in its back pocket and an artificial intelligence (AI) platform designed to make industrial workplaces safer, smarter and ultimately more automated. And if founder and chief executive Chris Eastwell gets his way - using workplace safety as a springboard for boosting industrial productivity and potentially one day even automating operations - the company could become to industrial data what Tesla has become to automotive intelligence. Capability X’s CX remote is a portable, ruggedised remote operations system that enables the control and monitoring of remotely operated vehicles (ROV’s), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV’s) and robotic systems technology. At the heart of Capability X’s technology is CX Edge, a ruggedised computing platform that combines light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors, stereoscopic cameras, communications systems and proprietary AI software, all in a briefcase-sized unit. LiDAR uses laser pulses to measure distances, while stereoscopic cameras provide depth perception. Together, they build a three-dimensional “digital twin” of the surrounding workplace, giving the AI a ringside seat as people, vehicles and machinery go about their business.



‘Our vision at Capability X is to keep people out of harm’s way while helping businesses operate more safely.’ Capability X managing director and chief executive officer Chris Eastwell Capability X says its AI technology can recognise objects, movement and potential dangers, using information collected from industrial sites to continually improve its software. Much like Tesla learns from real-world driving conditions, the company aims to use its growing network of industrial devices to provide valuable operational intelligence by learning from the movement of workers and machinery rather than roads and traffic. Picture a bustling port terminal, with towering cranes swinging massive containers through the air, trucks weaving between stacks of cargo and workers navigating the organised chaos. Capability X’s CX Protect safety system uses the CX Edge platform and AI software to monitor those movements, identify dangerous proximity events and alert operators to emerging risks before an incident occurs. That intelligence could also reveal bottlenecks and unnecessary movements, potentially lifting customers’ productivity and bottom lines.



Through “edge computing”, the company’s CX Edge devices analyse information on site rather than sending it to distant data centres, enabling faster responses with less reliance on external networks. Eastwell compares the integrated platform to a smartphone and its coordination of remote assets to Uber. Capability X managing director and chief executive officer Chris Eastwell said: “Our vision at Capability X is to keep people out of harm’s way while helping business to operate more safely, efficiently and productively- on a global scale.” Established in November 2022, Eastwell largely bootstrapped Capability X for two years, even as the fledgling business began securing its first commercial contracts. Eastwell has brought two decades of industry experience to the venture, having previously run Greatship Subsea Solutions in Australia and overseen marine asset integrity for Fugro across Australia and New Zealand. The company’s early consultancy and technology-design work involved WA Police in 2023 and subsea specialist Shelf Subsea, later acquired by DeepOcean.



A commercial breakthrough came in 2023 when ASX-listed Bhagwan Marine engaged Capability X to provide technology for remotely operating offshore equipment. The relationship has since blossomed into a multi-year arrangement spanning CX Remote, CX Connect and CX Protect, delivering an integrated suite of communications and safety systems, according to the company’s prospectus. The agreement runs through December 2028. Despite the early success, management says Capability X has undertaken virtually no formal marketing, focusing instead on engineering and industrial relationships. And there’s plenty of engineering muscle behind the ambition. Six software engineers report to chief technology officer Adrian Kirk-Burnnand, who has more than 23 years’ experience in sectors including mining and fintech.



In-house teams cover computer vision, AI, communications, robotics, mechatronics and hardware manufacturing and assembly, backed by remote operations, network management and security monitoring centres. Leading the commercial charge is chief commercial officer Lex Simons, a geophysicist with 14 years at Woodside Energy under his belt, while former federal minister Ian Campbell chairs the company. Capability X’s home base, located at the Perth International Telecommunications Centre. The operation runs from Telstra’s International Telecommunications Centre at Cullacabardee, north of Perth, cheek by jowl with world-class command and communications infrastructure. For its business model, Capability X has taken a leaf out of the software-as-a-service (SaaS) playbook, leasing its hardware and software to customers under multi-year subscription-style arrangements rather than selling equipment outright. The approach turns each installation into a steady stream of recurring revenue, with the potential to build a growing income stream as more customers come on board.



Beyond its flagship safety technology, the company offers CX Remote, a remote-control platform that allows command centres to monitor and operate underwater vehicles, drones and robots from afar, keeping personnel well clear of potentially dangerous environments. Meanwhile, its CX Connect solution provides secure communications and situational awareness between remote equipment, operators and command centres. Rounding out the suite is CX1, which combines the company’s technologies with engineering, system design and ongoing operational support to deliver customised solutions for complex industrial environments. Capability X has also secured a two-year agreement with Perth-based offshore operator GO Offshore to supply CX Protect monitoring systems under a hardware-and-software lease arrangement. The agreement, signed in November 2025, includes three one-year renewal options. However, the company’s contract with logistics heavyweight Qube Ports provides perhaps its strongest commercial endorsement yet. Capability X’s CX Protect Operating System visualisation- producing a live digital twin (marine support vessel rendered), to identify potential danger events and non-compliances and alert deck crew and supervisors.



In December 2025, Qube signed a three-year deal to deploy Capability X’s CX Protect technology across its port operations, targeting risks associated with cargo-handling movements, while boosting operational efficiency. Mining offers another market where machinery and workers share challenging environments, while defence offers further opportunities in robotics, unmanned systems and remote command. The company has memoranda of understanding with an Australian and an international defence contractor and showcased CX Edge alongside Defence West at the 2026 Land Forces exposition. To support its growth, the company has already secured a $40,000 handout from the WA State government for the 2024 rollout of CX Edge. The prospectus also highlights an application for a hefty $4.2 million federal Industry Growth Program grant that, if approved, would further add to the company’s burgeoning war chest. Capability’s credentials were further recognised at the Robotics & AI Award at Perth’s international Robopalooza festival in October 2025. Adding to the accolades, CX Protect and CX Remote were finalists in separate 2026 innovation awards; membership in Perth-based AROSE offers further robotics collaboration.



With the technology gaining commercial traction on home soil, Capability X is now casting its net beyond Australia’s shores. The company’s prospectus identifies contracts to supply its technology to Brunei’s oil and gas sector and is pursuing further deployments in other neighbouring countries. China is also on the radar, with opportunities identified in oil and gas and ports. A memorandum of understanding with a Timor-Leste partner could open another door, with potential applications spanning government infrastructure, remote operations and the oil and gas sector. American market research and management consultants Frost & Sullivan estimate a theoretical global total addressable market exceeding $280 billion annually across defence, oil and gas, mining and ports. However, that figure represents the broader market opportunity rather than revenue currently being generated or business immediately available to the company. Perth corporate advisory outfit Westar Capital has played a key role in steering Capability X towards the ASX boards, backing its funding journey through two seed capital raisings worth $2 million each at 10 cents and 16 cents a share, before supporting its $12 million initial public offering. The company has now wrapped up its float at 20 cents a share and will debut on the ASX on November 12 under the ticker CX8, subject to the exchange’s admission and quotation requirements. Armed with a fresh war chest, Capability X plans to ramp up manufacturing, accelerate product development and push further into domestic and international markets.



For Capability X, however, the bigger prize lies beyond preventing workplace accidents. Its technology could ultimately help customers squeeze more productivity from their industrial operations, reduce costs and shift increasingly complex tasks into the hands of remote operators and intelligent machines. If Capability X can get its growing network of intelligent devices to deliver on those lofty goals, workplace safety may prove to have been merely the steel-capped boot that kicked the door down to a global opportunity. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au
