World.title: Moa Point restart delayed by a week
World.content:
Wellington's troubled waste water treatment plant at Moa Point will not restart for another week as further checks on the ventilation system are needed.

Water entity Tiaki Wai said it aimed to reopen the plant on 17 November.

In February, the waste water treatment plant suffered a catastrophic failure during a storm.

RNZ viewed the inside of the plant last week for the first time since then.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407938538112

Tiaki Wai said it found more testing of the plant's ventilation system was needed during final readiness checks.

"The ventilation system remains the key area requiring additional commissioning and testing before the plant can restart. We need to be fully satisfied that the system is operating as intended before restarting the plant."

It recognised the frustration the delay could cause but it remained on track to restart the plant by the end of November.

World.title: Woman admits trying to kill her mother with poisoned tea, setting house on fire
World.content:
A woman has pleaded guilty to attempting to poison her mother with a cup of tea and burn her house down.

The woman appeared in the Auckland High Court on Wednesday morning, accused of lacing a cup of tea with insecticide.

She was also charged with arson after setting fire to her mother's property on the same day in June.

The woman was initially charged with attempted murder. However, she later pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of attempting to poison and admitted the arson.

Her mother and other family members were present in court and backed her application for restorative justice.

World.title: Kaitāia mill could close in months with 157 jobs at risk
World.content:
Efforts to save almost 160 jobs at Kaitāia's remaining timber mill appear to have failed.

The Far North town's Triboard Mill, which is owned by Japanese forestry company Juken New Zealand, has been on the market since March.

However, the company said on Wednesday it had been unable to find a buyer willing to take on the current workers.

The news comes just a week after new labour force data showed Northland's unemployment rate was the highest in the country at 8.3 percent.

The two Kāitaia mills were next to each other on the northern outskirts of town.

The Northland Mill produced veneer while the Triboard Mill makes a manufactured wood product used in the construction industry.

According to Workers First Union, the Kāitaia mills are the seventh and eighth wood-processing plants to close around the country in the past two years.

Other mills to have closed include the paper production line at Kinleith Mill in Tokoroa (with the loss of 230 jobs), Eves Valley Sawmill in Tasman (140 jobs), and Karioi Pulpmill and Tangiwai Sawmill in Ruapehu (200 jobs).

Juken NZ executive director Yasufumi Tsuchiya said negotiations to sell the land, buildings and machinery were continuing with a potential buyer, who could restart the mill in future with a new workforce.

If the sale fell through the mill would be closed down and efforts to sell the land and assets would continue.

Either way, the company would stop operating the mill by March next year at the latest.

Tsuchiya said consultation with workers about those two options had started.

Juken's other Kaitāia operation, the Northland Mill, closed in August with the loss of about 60 jobs.

The Triboard Mill had 140 employees but another 17 jobs had been transferred from the closed Northland Mill.

Between then the two mills were the town's biggest employer after Te Whatu Ora/Health New Zealand.

Juken's Northland Mill was shut down in August. Peter de Graaf

Tsuchiya said the company had made "considerable efforts" to find a buyer willing to keep the mill open with its current staff.

Juken's decision to exit Kāitaia reflected weaker demand in key markets, rising costs - including power - and not enough work to sustain current operations.

The company had another Triboard mill in Wairarapa.

If the sale was successful, the timing of any restart and any future employment opportunities would be matters for the prospective buyer.

"No decisions have been made, and we will carefully consider the feedback we receive from employees during consultation before the Board determines the way forward," Tsuchiya said.

The company looked forward to working constructively with local and central government, and other stakeholders, throughout the process, he said.

Consultation with employees run until 25 November.

The closure of the town's last mill is expected to have significant downstream effects, with many other companies - including trucking and construction firms - relying on Juken NZ contracts and products.

'Calamitous for Kāitaia'

Former Northland Age editor and long-time Kāitaia resident Peter Jackson said the closure would be "a calamity".

He had reported on the challenges facing the mill for decades but was still taken by surprise by this morning's announcement.

"A lot of people, a lot of little businesses around Kāitaia really depend on the wages that mill produces. Without them, it's going to be tough for a lot of people. And the people who were working there of course, it's going to be bloody hard for them. It'll be calamitous for Kāitaia, it really will."

Jackson said the mill had always seemed tenuous, and at the mercy of the market for Triboard going up and down, but had always survived in the past.

It would be hard to replace that number of jobs, he said.

World.title: Incoming National, Labour MPs on why they chose politics and next steps
World.content:
Audio player for " Weekly Political Panel: Blair Cameron and Chris Flatt " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2530195%2Fincoming-national-labour-mps-on-why-they-chose-politics-and-next-steps

Weekly Political Panel: Blair Cameron and Chris Flatt Morning Report Download MP3 13m

Two fresh MPs from Labour and National have congratulated each other on being in Parliament, as they describe what they want their contributions to look like.

National's incoming Nelson MP Blair Cameron says he's "absolutely someone" to talk with friends across the aisle as he joined incoming Labour list MP Chris Flatt on Morning Report's political panel for the first time.

Flatt said it was a "bittersweet time", as the party welcomes new members and farewells those who didn't make it back to Parliament.

Cameron, who ousted Labour's Rachel Boyack in Nelson, said he had a "huge amount of respect" for her, given her contribution over time and her kind and gracious approach to conceding in person.

Host John Campbell described it as "such a tonally different panel," following the kind and respectful introductions and a somewhat fractious campaign with a lot of negative attacks, "long may it last."

Cameron described himself as having grown up in the small rural farming community of Methven, raised by his mum who was working and studying full time to be a teacher, and dad who worked at a working men's club.

He went on to work at Princeton University and the International Monetary Fund. He returned to New Zealand in 2020 and settled in Nelson.

Labour's Chris Flatt (left) and National's Blair Cameron on Morning Report. RNZ

Cameron got involved in politics because he started to get "a little bit frustrated" with some things going on in government.

He missed out in the last election by 26 votes, and is "stoked" to get in this time.

Labour's Flatt lives in Cambridge, with parents who came to New Zealand in the 60s. He was raised in Papatoetoe before living in Finland on exchange.

"Incredibly important in my political formation, seeing a a country, a social democratic country, which does not have a problem with the tax system that redistributes into health and education in Finland."

He then studied politics and law, and worked in Australia within the union movement before coming "back to Aotearoa."

He was the National Secretary of the Dairy Workers Union, but pay equity changes and the "absolute attacks on work rights by the coalition government" propelled him to get into politics directly.

Asked what he hoped to achieve with his time in parliament, Cameron said he wanted to be the best MP for Nelson.

He described a meeting he was at where no young people said they wanted to remain in Nelson after finishing school.

"It's known as a very good place to retire, but I think we need to really grow economic opportunities in our region so that young people see that they can build a future there," said Cameron.

He said he didn't mind if kids travelled and studied overseas but, "I want them always to have the option to be building their future in Nelson and in Tasman."

Cameron described Nelson as having "amazing national parks."

"We have amazing outdoor activities. I think we have the best climate in the world."

Flatt similarly described wanting to be working hard in his electorate, despite being a list MP. He said the Waikato had amazing agriculture, and some of the best energy in the world, "it's a geothermal hub of the world."

"Yet when I was on the campaign trail in places such as Putāruru or Tokoroa, even Taupō, just a couple of blocks away from very rich tourist areas, there is a loss of hope.

"There's a loss of jobs. There's a loss of desire to stay in Aotearoa. And I hear consistently of people saying our kids have gone and we want them back. We want our whānau here."

Flatt also pointed to his union and primary industry background in terms of wanting to have a discussion about workers' rights and a productive economy, pointing to the Uber law in particular.

Campbell finished by wishing them well, and wishing they may have a friendship "across the aisles."

"We've both got big smiles on our faces as you said that," Cameron responded, "so I think so."

Flatt added there were a lot of similarities in a number of MPs they found over the induction process.

"Different views on how to achieve that, but I think there's a very common goal between a number of MPs that are incoming and look forward to working with all of the new crew, including Blair - congratulations again, Blair, on on your win."

World.title: Weather: Severe thunderstorm alert in South Island, more downpours for Bay of Plenty
World.content:
Thunderstorms could hit parts of the lower South Island on Wednesday afternoon, MetService warns.

A severe thunderstorm watch was issued for southern Southland and inland parts of Clutha and Dunedin from 2pm to 7pm.

There was a moderate risk of severe thunderstorms with localised downpours of 25-40mm an hour, the forecaster said.

The ranges of Westland District around and north of Mt Cook were under a heavy rain watch until 9pm.

Further north, Christchurch is forecast to have dry, sunny weather with temperatures in the mid-20s.

Video player removed for printing https://youtu.be/NLQeCGs-dH4?si=1flGUjne3VuDej4V

In the North Island, Eastern Bay of Plenty and the northern Gisborne/Tairawhiti ranges could get get a further 75mm of rain, after Tuesday's downpours in the region.

"We've still got this band of rainfall across the eastern side, and as we head through the afternoon we'll find the return of more showers, some heavy and thundery," meteorologist John Law said.

World.title: Family struggling with aftermath of Myers Park playground attack, father says
World.content:
The father of a five-year-old girl attacked at a central Auckland playground says the whole family is struggling with the psychological aftermath.

A 20-year-old man charged with the attempted murder of the girl at Myers Park playground won't be tried until 2028.

The girl was critically injured on Sunday 25 October at 4.45pm.

She had since recovered at Auckland's Starship Hospital and been released.

The accused man made his second appearance at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday morning, but did not enter a plea.

His interim name suppression was extended and his trial was set for 8 February 2028.

The girl's father has set up a Givealittle page seeking financial support for his daughter and family.

He said his daughter had numerous lacerations to her head, along with injuries to two fingers.

The money would be used for long-term family recovery - which could include day-to-day support, therapy, and potential cosmetic surgery.

Speaking to Stuff in late October, the girl's father said she had post-traumatic stress disorder in her own way.

"Because she is young and children at that age undergo it in a different way compared to adults, so most of the time she behaves normally but from time to time she asks questions about what has happened and similar things," he told Stuff.

The alleged attacker was taken to hospital in serious condition following the incident as a result of self-inflicted injuries.

World.title: Explainer: Can my employer force me to take annual leave over Christmas?
World.content:
Explainer - Christmas is just over the horizon. Can your employer force you to take leave over the holiday period?

Many companies shut down entirely for the Christmas break from late December to early January as families head off to campgrounds, baches and beaches around Aotearoa.

But what if you don't want to take leave, or don't have enough time saved up?

"Employees can raise their concerns, but they cannot simply opt out of a lawful annual closedown because they would rather take leave at another time," said Aishleen Sluiters, partner at the employment law firm Edwards Sluiters.

Here are the options employees have.

Do I have to take leave over Christmas?

If your employer has notified you they are having an annual closedown, they can require you to take your leave at a particular time each year.

If you've got annual leave backed up, you'll have to use it.

"The law allows an employer to require employees to take annual leave during that closedown, even if the employee disagrees," Sluiters said.

Under the Holidays Act 2003, an employer is only allowed to have one annual closedown in any 12-month period - it doesn't have to be over Christmas.

It can also be a partial closedown of just part of a workplace, or for different parts of a workplace at different times, perhaps over seasonal work demands.

You can also have a closedown where the workplace stays open, but the employer temporarily stops work for some employees, leaving a skeleton crew to staff it.

Business are allowed to have annual closures. RNZ Marika Khabazi

What does my boss have to tell me about closedowns?

Your employer must give at least 14 days' notice that a closedown period is going to be enforced.

Employees can challenge being forced to take leave if the workplace hasn't given that notice, ignored a more generous employment agreement, or is trying to use the annual closedown rules for a closure that doesn't qualify under them.

"A good first step is to check the employment agreement and raise the problem with the employer. An employment lawyer can help explain the options," Sluiters said.

"If the employer has breached minimum entitlements, enforcement options may be available through a Labour Inspector or the Employment Relations Authority. The right approach depends on the specific breach."

However, starting in 2028, there are going to be some changes, due to the Employment Leave Bill passed this year. It comes into effect 6 August 2028, repeals and replaces the Holidays Act 2003 and will bring in many changes in the future to how leave is calculated.

Employers will then have to give 21 days' notice of an annual closedown instead of 14. That notice must also now be given in writing and include information about the dates of the annual closedown, any requirements for employees to take paid or unpaid leave, and any other leave arrangements that are available.

But until mid-2028, the current rules remain in place.

Employees and employers can also agree to other kinds of closedowns outside the annual closedown rules, Employment New Zealand says.

What if I don't have enough annual leave?

If you don't have enough leave, you'll need to talk to your employer about options. That could include taking leave in advance or taking some as unpaid leave.

"There is no automatic hardship exemption in the closedown rules," Sluiters said.

"Financial difficulty does not, by itself, give an employee the right to keep working or require the employer to provide extra paid leave."

You could also make an agreement with your employer to use up other kinds of leave during an annual closedown, such as alternative holidays.

Do public holidays count as part of my leave balance?

No.

This year, the public holidays over summer are Christmas Day on Friday 25 December, Boxing Day which is going to be observed on Monday 28 December, New Year's Day on Friday 1 January and Day After New Year's Day which will be observed on Monday 4 January.

If you're a new employee, you might not be entitled to annual leave. RNZ / Diego Opatowski

What if I'm a new employee and don't have any holiday time yet?

Currently, you have to work 12 months of continuous employment before your four weeks of annual leave begins. Individual employment agreements could offer different terms.

"An employee can raise the issue early and ask whether the employer will agree to leave in advance," Sluiters said.

"That means taking paid annual leave before the employee has become entitled to it. The employer can agree but does not have to."

If the employee isn't entitled to annual holidays at all yet, they must be paid 8 percent of their gross earnings so far as of the annual closedown date, according to Employment New Zealand, and also move the anniversary date for their annual holidays entitlement to either the date the annual closedown starts, or another nearby date that their employer picks.

It's all rather complicated, but is explained in full detail on Employment NZ's website here.

That's also another thing that will change in 2028 with the new law - an employee's leave entitlement will then begin immediately from the start of employment, instead of waiting a year to kick in.

Look, I'm going to Bali and I want to use my leave time at another time of the year instead. Can I?

That's really up to your individual employer, but it's not a mandatory right for workers.

"Employees can ask to preserve their annual leave for a later trip, but the employer is not required to agree," Sluiters said. A lawful closedown means employers can require you to use your available annual leave.

"There may still be options to discuss. For example, an employee could ask whether work will be available during the closedown. This is something to negotiate, not a right to keep working."

An employee could also ask to take leave in advance for the later trip or use an existing alternate holiday day to fill the gap, she said.

"The best practical step for an employee is to discuss both the closedown and their later trip before making non-refundable bookings."

Many workers will still be asked to show up over Christmas. Ke-Xin Li / RNZ

I don't want to work over Christmas at all but I'm being asked to. Can I fight it?

"Employees do not automatically get the whole Christmas break off," Sluiters said.

"For ordinary working days, the employee and employer generally need to agree on annual leave dates. An employer must not unreasonably refuse an annual leave request."

Your employer can only require you to work on a public holiday if it falls on a day you would have otherwise worked, or if working on the holiday is part of your employment agreement, according to Employment New Zealand.

If you're being told to work on a public holiday outside your agreed hours, it has to be covered under an availability clause in your agreement.

And of course, if you work on a public holiday, you must be paid time and a half and given a day in lieu if it would be an otherwise working day for you (unless you're employed only to work on public holidays).

It's best to look at your own circumstances now if you haven't, as holiday rosters are quickly being settled as end-of-year preparations kick in.

World.title: No risk to community after police presence in Matamata
World.content:
There is no risk to the community after police had visible presence in Matamata on Wednesday morning.

Police said they made the enquiries into a report of concern.

"Following a number of enquiries, we've been unable to verify any criminal offending and do not believe there is any ongoing risk to the community."

Stuff had reported St John were in the area.

World.title: 'Discrimination' claim as AFLW player delisted weeks out from giving birth
World.content:
The AFLW pregnancy policy has been called into question as Gold Coast Suns player Georgia Clayden was delisted this week, just weeks before she is due to give birth.

Clayden spent this season on the inactive list with "injury (pregnancy)". The club announced on Tuesday that Clayden and fellow player Sienna McMullen were informed they would not be offered contracts for the 2027 season.

Former AFLW All-Australian-turned-commentator Kate McCarthy said more needed to be done to protect and support AFLW players and female athletes who choose to become mothers during their playing careers.

"A player should be able to make the incredible life decision to start a family without fearing it could come at the expense of their football career," McCarthy wrote on Instagram

Loading Instagram content

"There needs to be greater security and a genuine opportunity for players to return to the game after giving birth."

North Melbourne premiership player Eilish Sheerin responded publicly to McCarthy's post: "So well said. In other industries this would be viewed as discrimination."

Last December, former Carlton captain Kerryn Peterson was told by Carlton that she would not be offered a contract for 2026, just months after she gave birth to her first child.

Peterson was placed on the inactive list for this season after welcoming her newborn son, Max, in August, and had planned to return to the Blues the following season.

Essendon welcomed Bess Keaney back onto its list after she had a baby last season. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Alternatively, Essendon's Bess Keaney rejoined her club's primary list this season after having a baby last year. She was placed on the club's inactive list with "injury" (pregnancy).

Rules within the Collective Bargaining Agreement allow for players returning from pregnancy to come off the inactive list at any point.

Replacement players signed in the meantime are then able to see out the entirety of their one-season contract, with the team in question allowed to have a squad of 31 for the remainder of that season.

In order for a player to return from the inactive list after pregnancy, they must be assessed as medically fit by the club doctor or an AFL medical officer.

McCarthy said it was not simply on clubs to offer this, as they needed greater support in this area too and called for policy change.

"With such limited spots in the AFLW, clubs are already forced to make incredibly difficult list management decisions. The current systems put both players and clubs in an unfair position," McCarthy said.

"Clubs should have the ability to retain a player returning from maternity leave without that player occupying one of their limited list spots. This would give the athlete the time and security to work towards returning to the level required, while allowing clubs the flexibility to manage their lists if that player isn't ready to return.

"Becoming a mother should not mean putting your football career at risk. And clubs shouldn't be forced into a position where supporting a player's return comes at the expense of another list spot. We should be creating a system that supports both. Right now, we're not."

World.title: Legends urge Australia to 'move on' from Sandpapergate amid opposing claims
World.content:
Adam Gilchrist has warned Australian cricket must move on from the Sandpapergate saga, with the drama overshadowing the start of the men's summer.

The renewed fallout from the 2018 ball-tampering scandal continues to dominate headlines just two days out from the first ODI against England, with all focus on Usman Khawaja's book, Sabr.

Cricket Australia has ruled out reopening the investigation into Cape Town 2018, with CEO Todd Greenberg warning a consensus between players will likely never be reached.

Khawaja denies starting 'witch-hunt' over Sandpapergate claims Usman Khawaja rejects claims he has reopened some of Australian crickets biggest wounds just to sell copies of his new book as he admits concerns it may have damaged friendships.

In the past week, Khawaja has claimed that the whole team knew of plans to use sandpaper on the ball, and that it was also implemented in the Test prior at St George's Park, Gqeberha.

David Warner has backed those claims, labelling CA's initial investigation as "rushed and botched" after it found only he, Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith knew of the plan.

Mitchell Starc then denied any knowledge of the sandpaper plot when he became the first player from the match to front the media on Tuesday, citing a statement he and his fellow bowlers made in 2021.

Gilchrist said he was unsure what it could do to the Test team, ahead of a nine-month stint in which Australia hosts New Zealand then tours India and England.

But he was insistent the time had come to draw a line under the drama.

Adam Gilchrist (pictured) played 96 Tests and won three one day World Cups for Australia between 1999 and 2008. (Getty Images: PA Images/EMPICS Sport)

Asked what impact the flare-up could have, Gilchrist said: "I don't know, we will have to wait and see.

"I would suspect there are some frustrated guys because there are some differing stories floating around.

"But it's up to them to work out. It's probably best to work it out privately rather than in the public space.

"That's up to them. There are some people who have been deeply affected in a tough way, so they will want to move on from it."

Asked if it could hurt the Test team ahead of a home series against New Zealand in less than a month, Gilchrist insisted it was time to move on.

David Warner (left) has labelled Khawaja's recollection of the events as "100 per cent accurate". (Getty Image: Alex Davidson, ICC)

"If we keep getting daily Instagram updates, it will keep bubbling away," the former vice-captain said at Kayo Cricket's summer launch event.

"Guys have had their say. We've just got to deal with it and move on."

Gilchrist's comments came as former teammate Mark Waugh backed CA's stance of not reopening the investigation.

"We're going in circles with someone saying this and someone saying the opposite. Are we ever going to get to the middle ground?" Waugh said.

"I don't think we will. Because opinions are different. With someone saying this and someone saying that, you can only believe what they're saying.

Cricket Australia boss Todd Greenberg (right) has suggested the investigation into the incident will not be reopened. (Getty Images: Philip Brown)

"Unless there's other evidence, I don't know where you go with it, so I think you've just got to move on."

Australian Cricketers' Association chief executive Paul Marsh also suggested on Tuesday it was understandable that each player's version of events could be different.

"Eight years on, it is understandable that those involved may have different recollections and perspectives of what took place," he said in a statement.

"Players and staff at the heart of the issue are entitled to share their experiences, just as others are entitled to put such a challenging period in their life behind them.

"There are no winners in this issue, and nothing can undo what happened.

"But we must recognise that there are humans in the centre of this and we are calling for the ongoing vitriol directed at those involved to come to an end."

AAP

World.title: Sinner targeting Australian Open return after earlier 'impossible goal'
World.content:
Two-time Australian Open winner Jannik Sinner says he is targeting the Melbourne major for his big-time comeback as he embarks on the road to regaining his world number one status.

Sinner has lost his primacy in the global rankings after 95 weeks at the summit to Alexander Zverev, having not played since winning Wimbledon in July due to a right knee injury.

"The aim is to go to Australia. The aim is also maybe to do a couple of tournaments first," Sinner told a press conference in Milan on Tuesday.

Alcaraz downs Shelton in final to claim maiden Paris Masters title Carlos Alcaraz wins the elusive Paris Masters for the first time in his career, claiming his fifth title win of the calendar year.

"Right now, I have to respect the protocols because if we rush things we could have more serious problems. I have a ‌lot of faith ‌in the process, ⁠and I'm working toward that objective.

"Initially, we had an impossible goal for my ​return in mind, so we took a different path. I'm a tennis player, not a doctor, so my only option is to trust them.

"I miss playing tennis. Right now, however, it is crucial that I take care of my body, because I want to keep playing for another 10 to 15 years."

Sinner indicated he would probably return to the court in the Six Kings Slam exhibition in Saudi Arabia in late December. The Riyadh event was postponed because of the conflict in the Middle East.

"That [is the target] but we all know the situation what's there at the moment, which is not the best, so this is not our decision as players, this is a more general decision," Sinner said.

Sinner has not played since winning his second-career Wimbledon title in July. (Getty Images/Frey)

"But I think if we want to prepare for Australia [and] I'm not playing since Wimbledon, some matches before might be very helpful."

Wimbledon was the 25-year-old Italian's fifth grand slam title in less than three years, the first being his 2024 Australian Open victory.

His rise to the top was masterminded by Australian coach Darren Cahill, ⁠who stepped down last week after four ‌years at Sinner's side.

Sweden's ​Magnus Norman has joined Sinner's coaching set-up and Cahill backed the pick.

"There's a tweet I wrote ​back in 2013 about how Norman has the ability to improve every player he coaches," he said.

"I wasn't involved in the selection process, but I believe it's an excellent ​choice."

Australia's Darren Cahill (left) is no longer a part of Sinner's coaching set-up. (Getty Images: Andy Cheung)

Sinner said Cahill was like a "second dad" and that ​the ​two would remain close friends, adding that former ​world number two Norman shared many similarities with the South Australian.

"[Norman] ‌worked with [Stan] Wawrinka for many years and has been through a lot," Sinner said.

"He accepts the way we are already working, which is important to me so that I don't have to change everything all over again.

"I need to add 1 per cent each year to improve as a player."

"You have to ask yourself a lot of questions to get inside the mind ​of the ‌player you're coaching — that's how you earn his trust," Cahill added.

"We've built and shaped an incredible team, but 99 per cent ​of what's been achieved is down to him.

"He's the one who goes out onto the court. Everyone else contributes the final 1 per cent, and that's what makes the difference."

AAP

World.title: Khawaja denies starting 'witch-hunt' over Sandpapergate claims
World.content:
Usman Khawaja has defended his version of events about the Australian Test team's 2018 ball-tampering saga in South Africa, after former teammate Mitchell Starc maintained the bowling group had no idea about Sandpapergate.

During a wideranging interview on 7.30, Khawaja stuck to his guns on the issue once again splitting Australian cricket eight years after the infamous Test match in Cape Town when batsman Cameron Bancroft was caught using sandpaper on the ball.

Khawaja also denied he intended to start a "witch-hunt" or use the saga to sell copies of his newly released book, while conceding he was unsure if his claims would damage friendships he made throughout his career, especially with current Australian captain Pat Cummins.

"I'm not here to inflame the situation anymore," Khawaja said.

"I'm not here to go on a witch-hunt.

"All I've ever wanted is for us to take accountability as a team, and I don't think that's a lot to say.

"I'm not asking a lot from people and I say, 'We were a part of it. That was us.' Let's just take accountability.

"I was here to tell my truth, what I saw, what I felt, and to stick with those three guys that were made out to be the only people who have taken it [accountability]."

The three players Khawaja referred to were his childhood friend David Warner, then-Australian Test captain Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft.

Cameron Bancroft and Steve Smith speak with umpires during the Test match. (Getty Images: Ashley Vlotman)

Smith and Warner, who was the vice-captain, were banned from cricket for 12 months and Bancroft received a nine-month ban.

Warner has since backed Khawaja's version of events "100 per cent", but on Tuesday afternoon Starc told Fox Cricket's season launch that he did not know a substance was taken onto the field to tamper with the ball.

In 2021, Starc joined fellow bowlers Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon in releasing a statement disputing any suggestion they had prior knowledge of ball-tampering plans.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers, but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

Cummins has not spoken publicly since the release of Khawaja's book titled Sabr: Finding my way in cricket and life.

Khawaja echoed comments made by former coach Darren Lehmann that ball tampering had been around a long time.

"If you read my book … the whole team was the architect," he said.

"Whether one person ball tampers or another.

"And when I say we were all the architects, I mean, we all need to take accountability as a team.

"I've been very clear not naming names."

He also denied his book was forcing anyone else to admit fault.

"I'm not forcing anyone to do anything," he said.

"Pat Cummins is a good friend of mine. Mitchell Starc, other players in the team, Shaun Marsh, Mitch Marsh; they're all very good friends of mine."

Khawaja 'not sure' friendship will survive this

Khawaja spoke to 7.30 about the special bond between him and Cummins, who he said had a "special place" in his heart.

Usman Khawaja and Pat Cummins were longtime teammates. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"I always used to go off the field when they used to spray alcohol, and then Pat Cummins called me back. [That was] the first time in my life I felt really part of the Australian cricket team.

"That's why I've always had so much love for Patty.

" Even when I talk about it now, it's a very emotional time, a very emotional feeling for me. "

Asked if his book might damage that friendship, Khawaja said he didn't know.

"I'm not sure," Khawaja admitted.

"I've been friends with Pat a long time.

"I've given my reasons at the end of the day … I've always stood for my values and what I think is right … but I can't speak for Pat."

Not about selling books, Khawaja says

While Khawaja was also critical of Cricket Australia's investigation of the incident, describing it as being "rushed", he was asked about the timing of the revelations made in his book.

"A lot of people have put up a narrative that I'm somehow gaining from this, but at no stage was sandpaper ever discussed in 2023 when I signed my book deal," Khawaja said.

"My manager didn't even know about it until six months ago. Neither did anyone really at Penguin.

"All they said to me was, 'Write your story.' Whether I wrote about sandpaper or not would not have made one bit of difference.

"When I gave it to them six months ago, they were shocked because I don't really talk about this to anyone.

"I could have taken it out and they couldn't say a word, but I chose to put it in there."

Khawaja, the first Muslim to play cricket for Australia, wrote in the book about his role as a trailblazer for South Asian Australian cricketers.

At times during his career, the issue of racism was raised. Khawaja himself, in his book, says he felt that after Smith was banned, he was not made captain because of the colour of his skin.

Tim Paine became Test captain after Steve Smith was stood down. (AAP: Scott Barbour)

Rather than say being overlooked was racism, Khawaja said it was simply how he felt at the time.

"There's no concrete evidence of that in terms of what I heard," Khawaja said.

"Whenever I talk about racism or anything along those lines, it's how I feel at the time, but yes that's how I felt.

"I caveat that at the same time with a year later, when Tim Paine was captain, I look back on it and I think, actually … Tim Paine was a great captain.

"At the time, I felt a bit aggrieved, but when I look back on it, I actually don't think it was the wrong decision."
